Principal and Architect

Writing as an architect, technical strategy, governance, large migrations, org design, influence, growing engineers, and enterprise multi-tenant SaaS.

Part 51 — Writing as an Architect: RFCs, Design Docs and Decision Records

Somewhere around staff level, the shape of your day changes. You spend less time typing code and more time typing prose. This is not a demotion from engineering into administration. It is the moment your output stops being measured in pull requests and starts being measured in decisions other people make because of what you wrote.

Part 44 told you that writing becomes the primary tool at staff level, and gave you the four documents worth mastering. Part 49.6 showed you the skeleton of an Architecture Decision Record. This Part is the full craft: how to write documents that teams actually read, argue with, agree to, and then act on — months after you wrote them and often without you in the room.

The reader this Part assumes is a strong senior engineer who can already design a system. You know how to choose between PostgreSQL and DynamoDB, how to shape an event schema, how to run a migration. What you may not yet do reliably is get thirty other engineers, two product managers and a finance partner to agree to your design before you write a line of code. That agreement is manufactured on paper. This Part teaches the manufacturing.

51.1 Why writing is the architect's primary tool

Concept

Writing is how an architect scales past the reach of their own hands and their own voice. A conversation persuades the people in the room, once, and then decays. A document persuades everyone who reads it, including people who join the company a year later, and it does not change its story between the first reader and the hundredth.

An architect's job is to make good decisions happen across many teams without having authority over those teams. The only tool that does that cheaply, repeatedly and at scale is the written word. Code is also writing, but code only talks to the computer and to the people reading that exact file. A design doc talks to the whole organisation about why the code is shaped the way it is.

Why does it exist?

Imagine you are the only person who understands why the payment service retries with a two-second backoff and gives up after five attempts. That knowledge lives in your head. Three things now happen, all bad. First, every engineer who touches that code has to interrupt you to understand it, so you become a bottleneck. Second, when you are on holiday, nobody can safely change it, so the system freezes around your absence. Third, when you leave, the knowledge leaves with you, and six months later someone changes the backoff to fix an unrelated bug and causes an outage.

Writing exists to break all three. The decision, the reasoning and the alternatives you rejected go on paper. Now the knowledge is one-to-many, it survives your absence, and it survives you. A senior engineer who does not write is a single point of failure wearing a hoodie.

There is a second, subtler reason. Writing forces clarity that talking does not. You can hand-wave through a meeting. You cannot hand-wave through a paragraph. When you try to write "we will make the system more scalable" and then have to say what that means with a number, you discover that you do not actually know. The blank page is the cheapest design review you will ever get, and it happens before anyone else wastes time on your idea.

Mental model

Imagine the difference between teaching one apprentice at your workbench and writing a book. The apprentice learns fast because you adapt to them in real time, but you can only have one apprentice, they forget half of it, and when they leave the shop the lesson is gone. The book is slower and more painful to produce, you cannot see the reader's face, so you have to anticipate every misunderstanding in advance — but it teaches ten thousand people, it says the same thing every time, and it outlives you by a century.

A conversation is the apprentice. A document is the book. An architect who refuses to write is choosing to have one apprentice at a time for the rest of their career.

How it works

Writing does its work through four distinct mechanisms, and it helps to know which one you are relying on in any given document.

  1. One-to-many broadcast. You write once; N people read it. Your leverage is multiplied by N. A one-page strategy memo read by 80 engineers is 80 person-readings for one writing effort.
  2. Persistence. The document does not evaporate when the meeting ends. Six months later, when someone asks "why did we choose RabbitMQ over Kafka", the answer is a link, not a reconstruction from memory that may be wrong.
  3. Asynchrony. Readers consume it on their own schedule, in their own timezone, at their own reading speed. A reviewer in another country does not need to be awake at the same time as you. This is how a company with offices in three continents aligns at all.
  4. Forced precision. The act of writing surfaces the gaps in your own thinking before anyone else sees them. This is the mechanism that improves your decision, not just its distribution.
Conversation:  you --speak--> few people --forget--> nothing persists
Document:      you --write--> many people --store--> persists --> new joiners
                        \--forces you to be precise before anyone reads it

Practical example

Your e-commerce company has a recurring problem: order notifications (order placed, order shipped, out for delivery) are sent by direct synchronous HTTP calls from the order service to an in-house notification service. When the notification service is slow, placing an order becomes slow. When it is down, orders fail. You have decided the right fix is an event-driven pipeline with an outbox table and a Kafka topic.

You could call a meeting and explain this. Eight people would nod. Two of them would misremember the retry semantics. The mobile team, who were not invited, would be surprised a month later when notification ordering changed. And when a new engineer joins the notifications team next quarter, they would have no idea why any of it is shaped the way it is.

Instead you write an RFC. The RFC is read by the order team, the notifications team, the mobile team, the platform team who own the Kafka cluster, and your director. Each reads it when convenient. Each comments inline. By the time you hold a thirty-minute decision meeting, every serious objection has already been raised and answered in the margins, and the meeting is a formality that ratifies a decision the document already made. That is the leverage. The full worked RFC is in section 51.9.

Artifact example

Here is the difference writing makes, shown as two versions of the same decision. First, the decision as it lives in someone's head and gets spoken in a hallway:

"Yeah, we should probably move notifications to events. The sync calls
are a problem. I'll look into Kafka."

Nobody can act on that. Nobody can disagree with it precisely. It commits to nothing and teaches nobody. Now the same decision, written:

## Decision: order notifications move to an event-driven pipeline

**Status:** Proposed (RFC-114), decision meeting 2026-03-12
**Problem:** The order service makes a synchronous HTTP call to the
notification service on every order event. p99 of POST /orders is
820 ms, of which 340 ms is the notification call. When the
notification service degrades, order placement degrades with it.
In the last 90 days this caused 2 partial order outages (INC-3391,
INC-3407).
**Proposal:** Write notification intents to an outbox table inside
the order-placement transaction, relay them to a Kafka topic
`order.events.v1`, and have the notification service consume
asynchronously. Target: remove the notification call from the order
hot path entirely; POST /orders p99 budget 480 ms.
**Alternatives considered:** (1) keep sync with a circuit breaker,
(2) fire-and-forget async HTTP, (3) RabbitMQ instead of Kafka. See §4.
**Rollback:** feature flag `notifications.transport`; flip back to
sync in under 5 minutes. Outbox rows are retained either way.

The second version can be reviewed, disagreed with on specific points, approved, and read by a new joiner in two years. It names the incidents. It names the numbers. It names the rollback. That is what writing buys you.

Real-world scenario

A payments platform grows from 15 to 90 engineers in two years. In the early days nothing is written down; the four founding engineers hold the whole architecture in their heads and in Slack. This works beautifully at 15 people and catastrophically at 90. New engineers cannot find out why the double-entry ledger forbids updates, so they write an update and corrupt a balance. Two teams independently build two different idempotency-key schemes because neither knew the other existed. An auditor asks for the data-retention policy and three people give three different answers.

The turning point is not a new tool. It is a principal engineer who starts writing: a decision record for the ledger invariant, an RFC for a single idempotency standard, a one-page data-retention policy. Within two quarters, the number of "why is it like this" interruptions to the founding engineers drops by more than half, and the two idempotency schemes converge on one. Nothing about the code got better first. The writing came first, and the code followed.

Failure scenario

A talented architect joins a 200-engineer company and designs, in her head and in whiteboard sessions, a genuinely excellent plan to consolidate three overlapping inventory systems. She explains it brilliantly in meetings. Everyone agrees in the room. Nothing happens.

Six months later nothing has changed, and she is baffled, because everyone agreed. The failure is that she never wrote it down. Each team remembered a slightly different version of the plan. There was no single artifact to point at when priorities were set, so inventory consolidation lost every prioritisation argument to things that were written as crisp proposals. The best idea in the building died because it existed only as spoken words, and spoken words cannot compete with a written one-pager for a quarter's funding.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The document nobody reads. Forty pages, no summary, no clear ask. It is written but it is not read, so it has the cost of writing and the leverage of a conversation. Length is a bug, not a virtue.
  • The decision already made. A document written to create the appearance of consultation, where the author has no intention of changing anything. Reviewers smell this instantly and stop engaging, which poisons the well for your honest documents later.
  • Writing instead of deciding. Some people hide in documents to avoid the discomfort of deciding. A design doc that has been "in review" for three months is a decision being avoided, not analysed.
  • Stale documents treated as current. A design doc that described the system two years ago, never updated, now actively misleads. An out-of-date document is worse than no document because people trust it.
  • Writing for the wrong audience. A strategy memo for executives written in the language of Kafka partitions. The audience cannot act on it, so it has no effect.
  • The solution looking for a problem. A document that starts from "we should use technology X" and reverse-engineers a justification. The giveaway is a thin problem section and a lavish solution section.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

The principal engineer treats writing as the highest-leverage activity available to them, and schedules it like the important work it is rather than squeezing it into the gaps. They ask, before writing anything: who is the audience, what do I want them to do differently after reading, and what is the shortest document that achieves that. They write the ask and the summary first, at the top, because they assume most readers stop after the first screen.

They also know that writing is thinking. They do not write to communicate a decision they have already made; they write to make the decision, and they let the act of writing change their mind. A principal who finishes a design doc believing exactly what they believed when they started it did not use the document, they just transcribed a prejudice.

And they are ruthless about length, because they respect their readers' time as a scarce, expensive resource. A one-page memo that 80 people read and act on beats a twenty-page document that three people skim. If a document must be long, it leads with a summary that stands alone, and everything after the summary is for the small number of people who need the detail.

Common mistakes

  • Treating writing as documentation you do after the fact. By then the decision is made, the context is lost, and the document is an archaeology project nobody wants to do.
  • Optimising for brevity over clarity, or clarity over brevity. You want both. The skill is saying the necessary thing in the fewest words, not saying fewer things.
  • Writing to impress rather than to inform. Big words and long sentences signal insecurity, not seniority. The most senior writing is the plainest.
  • Never writing at all, and relying on being in every meeting. This caps your influence at the number of meetings you can attend, and makes you a bottleneck.
  • Burying the ask. If a reader cannot tell in the first paragraph what you want them to do, they will not do it.

Interview questions

  1. Why is writing considered a core skill for staff-plus engineers, when the job is technical? Expected answer: because influence at that level is cross-team and without authority, and the only tool that scales across teams, persists, and works asynchronously is writing. It also forces clarity in the author's own thinking. Why it matters: it tests whether the candidate understands that the job changes shape, not just grows. Follow-up: name a decision you made better because you had to write it down.

  2. A great idea of yours never got adopted despite everyone agreeing in the meeting. What probably went wrong, and what would you do differently? Expected answer: it was never written as a single durable artifact, so it could not compete for prioritisation and each team remembered a different version. Next time, write a one-pager with a clear ask, pre-wire the key people, and make it the thing people point at. Follow-up: who specifically would you pre-wire and why.

  3. When is writing a document the wrong move? Expected answer: when the decision is cheap and reversible (just decide and move), when a conversation genuinely suffices, or when a document would be used to fake consultation. Why it matters: tests judgement about proportionality, not dogma.

Practical exercise

Take a decision you made in the last month that currently lives only in your head or in Slack — a retry policy, a schema choice, a library you picked. Write it up in the short decision format shown in the Artifact example above: status, problem with at least one real number, proposal, alternatives, rollback. Keep it under 250 words.

Acceptance criteria: a reader who was not involved can state what was decided, why, what was rejected, and how to undo it, without asking you a single question. If they need to ask you anything, the document failed; fix it until it does not.

51.2 Document types and when to use each

Concept

There is not one architect's document; there is a small family of them, and each has a job. Using the wrong one is like using a screwdriver as a chisel — it sort of works, and it ruins both the tool and the work. A one-pager is for getting a quick yes on a direction. An RFC is for getting many teams to agree on a change. A design doc is for working out how to build something. An ADR records a single decision so the future knows why. Knowing which to reach for is half the skill.

Why does it exist?

Different situations need different amounts of ceremony. Imagine you decide, with one teammate, to rename a confusing internal variable. Writing a six-section RFC for that is absurd; it would take longer than the change and nobody would read it. Now imagine you want to move 25 services onto a new error format. Deciding that in a Slack thread is equally absurd; it will be forgotten, contested, and half-adopted.

The family of document types exists so the ceremony matches the stakes. Light decisions get light documents. Heavy, cross-team, expensive-to-reverse decisions get heavy documents. Picking the right weight is what stops you from either drowning small decisions in process or letting big ones slip through on a verbal nod.

Mental model

Imagine a set of forms at a bank. A deposit slip is one line. A loan application is several pages. A mortgage is a folder. You do not fill in a mortgage folder to deposit twenty dollars, and you do not get a mortgage on a deposit slip. The size of the form matches the size and risk of the transaction. The architect's documents are the same: match the form to the size of the decision.

How it works

Each document type has a distinct shape, audience, and lifecycle. Here is the family, ordered roughly from lightest to heaviest.

flowchart TB
    A["How big and how reversible is the decision"] -->|"tiny, reversible, one team"| ONE["One-pager or Slack"]
    A -->|"a single choice worth remembering"| ADR["ADR"]
    A -->|"a system to build, one team owns"| DD["Design doc"]
    A -->|"a change many teams must agree to"| RFC["RFC"]
    A -->|"direction for a year or more"| STRAT["Strategy memo"]
    A -->|"something broke, we must learn"| PIR["Post-incident review"]
  • One-pager. One page, one idea, one ask. Used to test a direction cheaply before investing in a full design. Audience: your lead and one or two peers. Lifecycle: short; it either becomes a design doc or it dies.
  • ADR (Architecture Decision Record). One decision, its context, the options, the choice and the consequences. Covered in Part 49.6. Used to record why a single choice was made so the future does not have to guess. Audience: anyone who later touches the thing. Lifecycle: immutable once accepted; superseded by a new ADR, never edited.
  • Design doc. How you will build a specific system or feature. Context, requirements with numbers, the proposed design, alternatives, risks, rollout. Audience: the team that will build and operate it, plus reviewers. Lifecycle: alive during design, then a reference.
  • RFC (Request for Comments). A proposal for a change that needs agreement from people outside your team. Structurally similar to a design doc but with an explicit review-and-decision process bolted on. Audience: all affected teams. Lifecycle: draft, review, decide, accepted or rejected.
  • Tech spec. The detailed, implementation-level description once a design is agreed: exact endpoints, schemas, error codes. Audience: implementers. Lifecycle: alive until built, then it should match the code or be deleted.
  • Post-incident review (PIR). What broke, the timeline, the root cause, the actions. Covered operationally in Part 37. Audience: the org, blamelessly. Lifecycle: permanent record; actions tracked to completion.
  • Strategy memo. Where we are going technically over a year or more, and why. Audience: leadership and the whole org. Lifecycle: long; revisited each planning cycle. Covered fully in Part 52.

Practical example

Your team runs the inventory service. Over three months you face four situations, and each wants a different document.

  1. You are wondering whether to add a read replica for inventory reads. You are not sure it is worth it. You write a one-pager: here is the read load, here is the replica cost, here is the latency we would save, should we do a spike. Your lead reads it in five minutes and says yes.
  2. The spike confirms it, and you need to design how reads route to the replica and how you handle replication lag on the "is this in stock" check. You write a design doc. Your team reviews it.
  3. Along the way you decide to use PostgreSQL streaming replication rather than logical replication. That single choice is worth remembering, so you write an ADR.
  4. The replica causes a brief incident when stale reads oversell a popular item. You write a PIR and add an action to read stock-critical checks from the primary.

Four documents, four jobs, matched to four sizes of decision.

Artifact example

A filled-in one-pager, the lightest and most under-used document in the family. This is the whole thing — one page is the point.

# One-pager: add a read replica for inventory reads

**Author:** you | **Date:** 2026-02-03 | **Ask:** approve a 1-week spike

## Problem
Inventory read traffic is 4,200 req/s at peak, all hitting the primary.
The primary is at 70% CPU at peak, mostly from reads. Write traffic is
only 180 req/s. We are one Black-Friday away from the primary saturating,
and we cannot scale reads without scaling writes we do not need.

## Proposed direction
Add one PostgreSQL streaming read replica. Route all catalog-style reads
(product detail, listing, search facets) to it. Keep the stock-decrement
write path and the "can I buy this right now" check on the primary.

## Why now
Peak season is 3 months out. A replica is roughly $320/month on our
instance class. The alternative — vertically scaling the primary — is
~$1,100/month and still couples reads to writes.

## Risks / open questions
- Replication lag on "in stock" reads could oversell. Spike must measure
  real lag under load and decide which reads are lag-sensitive.
- Connection pool split between primary and replica. Needs a plan.

## Ask
One engineer, one week, to run a load test against a replica and come back
with measured lag and a recommended read-routing split. Not a commitment
to ship — a commitment to measure.

Notice what makes it work: a numbered problem, a concrete direction, a cost comparison, named risks, and an ask that is small and specific ("one engineer, one week, to measure" — not "approve the whole project"). A reader can say yes to that in thirty seconds.

Real-world scenario

A food-delivery company has no document conventions. Every decision, large or small, happens in Slack or in meetings. The result is predictable: small decisions consume meeting time out of proportion to their stakes, and large decisions get made without the right people, then re-litigated endlessly because there is no record of why.

A principal engineer introduces exactly three document types, and no more: a lightweight ADR for recorded decisions, a design doc template for anything one team builds, and an RFC process for anything cross-team. He deliberately refuses to add more types, because a zoo of document types is its own kind of process bloat. Within a quarter, the "why did we do it this way" questions have somewhere to point, cross-team changes stop surprising people, and meeting time drops because the reversible stuff gets decided in a one-pager instead of a meeting.

Failure scenario

A team adopts an RFC process and applies it to everything, including a one-line config change and a variable rename. Each RFC requires three reviewers and a decision meeting. Velocity collapses. Engineers start routing around the process — making changes without RFCs and backfilling fake ones — which is worse than having no process, because now the documents lie.

The root cause is a category error: they used the heaviest document for the lightest decisions. The fix is not to abandon RFCs; it is to reserve them for decisions that are cross-team or expensive to reverse, and to let everything else happen in a one-pager, an ADR, or just a pull request.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • One document type for everything. Either everything is an RFC (process bloat) or nothing is written (chaos). Both are failures of matching weight to stakes.
  • Design doc that is really a tech spec. It drowns the reader in endpoint signatures before they understand the problem. Separate the "why and what" (design doc) from the "exact how" (tech spec).
  • ADR that gets edited. Someone updates an accepted ADR to reflect a new decision. Now the record of what you believed in 2024 is gone. ADRs are immutable; you supersede them.
  • Strategy memo written like a design doc. Too much implementation detail, not enough direction and business framing. Leadership cannot act on it.
  • No PIR for a near-miss. Teams write PIRs for outages but not for the time something almost broke. The near-misses are the cheapest lessons you will ever get; skipping them wastes them.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They keep the number of document types small on purpose. Three or four well-understood types beat a dozen precisely specified ones, because people can actually remember when to use three. They match ceremony to stakes instinctively, reaching for the one-pager far more often than juniors expect, because most decisions are smaller and more reversible than they feel in the moment.

They also understand that the document type sets reader expectations. When someone opens an RFC, they know they are being asked to comment and that a decision will follow. When they open an ADR, they know it is a record, not a debate. These shared expectations are most of the value of having named types at all — the type tells the reader how to engage before they read a word of content.

Common mistakes

  • Inventing a new document type for every situation. Nobody can remember them, so nobody uses them correctly.
  • Using an RFC when a one-pager would do. You spend a week of review on a decision that was reversible in an afternoon.
  • Using a Slack thread when an RFC was needed. The cross-team decision is made by whoever was awake, and re-litigated forever because there is no record.
  • Editing ADRs in place. You destroy the historical record that is the entire point of an ADR.
  • Skipping the PIR because "it wasn't that bad". The cheap lessons get thrown away.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through the documents you would use over the life of a medium-sized feature, and why each. Expected answer: one-pager to test the direction, design doc to work out how, ADR for any single durable decision, tech spec for implementers if needed, PIR if something breaks. Why it matters: tests whether they match ceremony to stakes rather than applying one tool to everything.

  2. Your company's RFC process has become a bottleneck. What do you do? Expected answer: narrow its scope to cross-team or hard-to-reverse decisions, push everything else to lighter documents, and fix the review latency (pre-wiring, time-boxed review windows). Do not abolish it; right-size it. Follow-up: how would you decide what still requires an RFC.

  3. What is the difference between a design doc and an ADR, and why keep both? Expected answer: a design doc works out how to build something and is alive during design; an ADR records a single decision and its reasoning and is immutable. You keep both because the design doc rots as the system evolves, but the ADR preserves why a specific choice was made even after the design has moved on.

Practical exercise

List the last ten engineering decisions your team made. For each, write down which document type (if any) was used, and which type should have been used given its size and reversibility. Count the mismatches.

Acceptance criteria: you can identify at least two decisions that got more ceremony than they needed and at least one that got less than it needed. Propose, in two sentences, the smallest set of document types your team should standardise on.

51.3 The anatomy of a strong design doc

Concept

A design doc has a skeleton, and the skeleton is not decoration. Each section exists to answer a question a serious reviewer will ask, in the order they ask it. Context, then goals and non-goals, then requirements with numbers, then the proposed design, then the alternatives you rejected, then the tradeoffs, risks, rollout, rollback, observability, cost, and open questions. Skip a section and you leave a question unanswered, which means a reviewer has to ask it, which means a round trip, which means delay. The skeleton is how you answer the questions before they are asked.

Why does it exist?

Imagine reviewing a design with no structure — just three pages of prose. You have to hunt for the goals. You cannot tell what is explicitly out of scope, so you raise concerns about things the author never intended to build. You cannot find the rollback plan, so you do not know if this is safe to ship. You and the author go back and forth for days extracting information that a template would have surfaced in one pass.

The skeleton exists to make review fast and complete. Every reviewer knows where to find the rollback plan because it is always in the same place. Every author is reminded to think about observability because there is a heading demanding it. The structure is a checklist disguised as a document format, and the checklist is drawn from the senior mantra: can it time out, can it fail, can it become slow, can it duplicate, can it return a wrong response, can it partially succeed.

Mental model

Imagine the pre-flight checklist a pilot runs before takeoff. It is not there because pilots are forgetful idiots; it is there because even experts miss things under pressure, and the cost of missing one is catastrophic. The checklist is boring and it saves lives precisely because it is boring and complete. A design doc template is the pre-flight checklist for shipping a system: it makes you check the landing gear (rollback) and the fuel (cost) every single time, so you never discover at 30,000 feet that you forgot.

How it works

Walk the sections in order. Each has a specific job.

1. Context         -> why are we even talking about this
2. Goals           -> what does success look like, measurably
3. Non-goals       -> what are we deliberately NOT doing
4. Requirements    -> the numbers: load, latency, consistency, scale
5. Proposed design -> the actual plan, with diagrams
6. Alternatives    -> what else we considered and why we rejected it
7. Tradeoffs       -> what we are giving up with the chosen design
8. Risks           -> what could go wrong and our mitigation
9. Rollout         -> how we ship it safely, in stages
10. Rollback       -> how we undo it if it goes wrong
11. Observability  -> how we will know it is working in production
12. Cost           -> money and operational cost
13. Open questions -> what we have not resolved yet
  • Context. The situation and why it needs changing, with evidence. Incidents, growth numbers, cost curves. A reviewer should finish this section agreeing there is a problem worth solving, before you have proposed anything.
  • Goals. What success looks like, measurably. "Reduce POST /orders p99 from 820 ms to under 480 ms" is a goal. "Make orders faster" is a wish.
  • Non-goals. What you are deliberately not doing. This is the most skipped and most valuable section; it stops reviewers from raising objections about scope you never intended, and it protects you from scope creep later.
  • Requirements. The constraints the design must meet, in numbers. Peak load, acceptable latency, consistency needs, data volume, compliance boundaries.
  • Proposed design. The plan. Diagrams first (context, then components, then the critical sequence), then prose. This is the heart, but it is only credible because the sections before it established the problem and the constraints.
  • Alternatives considered. The other designs you genuinely weighed, each with why you rejected it. Covered in depth in 51.4 because people do this badly.
  • Tradeoffs. What the chosen design costs you. Honest designs name their downsides. "This removes the hot-path call but adds eventual consistency; a notification may arrive up to 2 seconds after the order."
  • Risks. What could go wrong, each with a mitigation or a reason it is acceptable.
  • Rollout. The staged plan: feature flag, percentage ramp, which environments first.
  • Rollback. How you undo it, how fast, and what state is left behind.
  • Observability. The metrics, logs, traces and alerts that will tell you it is healthy. If you cannot say how you will know it works, you are not ready to build it.
  • Cost. Infrastructure money and operational cost (new on-call surface, new failure modes).
  • Open questions. What you have not resolved. Naming these honestly makes the doc more credible, not less.

Practical example

For the notification pipeline from 51.1, the requirements section — the numbers — looks like this:

## Requirements

- **Throughput:** 1,200 order events/sec at peak (Black Friday 2025
  measured peak was 1,050; 15% headroom).
- **Latency:** removing the notification call must bring POST /orders
  p99 from 820 ms to under 480 ms. End-to-end notification delivery
  p95 under 10 seconds is acceptable (it was synchronous before, so
  this is a relaxation customers will not notice).
- **Delivery:** at-least-once. A duplicate notification is acceptable
  if rare; a lost "order shipped" notification is not.
- **Ordering:** per order, events must be delivered in order (placed
  before shipped before delivered). Across orders, no ordering needed.
- **Durability:** no notification intent may be lost if the order
  transaction committed. This is why we need the outbox.
- **Consistency:** the outbox write must be in the same transaction as
  the order write, so an order cannot commit without its notification
  intent.

Every line is a constraint the design must satisfy, and every line has a number or a hard rule. The ordering requirement, for instance, immediately tells the reader we need a partition key of order ID on the Kafka topic. The requirements section does design work before the design section starts.

Artifact example

The non-goals section, filled in for the same project. This is the section juniors skip and principals treasure.

## Non-goals

- **We are NOT changing the content or templates of notifications.**
  Same emails, same push copy. This is a transport change only.
- **We are NOT building a general-purpose event bus for the whole
  company.** This topic is for order events consumed by notifications.
  A company-wide event platform is a separate, larger decision (see
  the platform team's roadmap).
- **We are NOT guaranteeing exactly-once delivery.** At-least-once
  plus idempotent consumers is our target. Chasing exactly-once would
  double the complexity for a problem (rare duplicate emails) we can
  tolerate.
- **We are NOT migrating SMS notifications in this phase.** SMS has a
  different provider and rate limits; it stays synchronous for now and
  moves in a later phase.

Look at what this buys you. A reviewer who was about to write "but what about SMS?" sees it is explicitly deferred and moves on. A reviewer who was about to argue for exactly-once semantics sees you considered and rejected it, with a reason. The non-goals section pre-empts entire branches of review discussion. Without it, you would spend the review defending scope you never wanted.

Real-world scenario

A ride-booking company adopts a design doc template with exactly these sections and makes one section mandatory that teams used to skip: observability. The rule is simple — no design review is scheduled until the observability section is filled in with the specific metrics and alerts.

The effect is quiet but large. Teams start designing their monitoring before they build, which means the dashboards and alerts ship with the feature instead of being bolted on after the first incident. Mean time to detection for new features drops because the detection was designed in. One template section, made mandatory, changed when monitoring got designed from "after the outage" to "before the launch".

Failure scenario

An engineer writes a beautiful design doc with a detailed proposed design and no rollback section. The design is approved, built, and shipped. In production it causes a subtle data-consistency bug under load. The on-call engineer tries to roll it back and discovers there is no clean rollback — the new code wrote data in a new format that the old code cannot read, and nobody thought about the reverse migration.

The incident lasts four hours longer than it needed to, because the rollback was designed live, under pressure, at 2 a.m. Had the rollback section been filled in during review, a reviewer would have caught that the data format change was not backward-compatible, and the design would have included a reverse path from the start. The missing section was not paperwork; it was the difference between a five-minute rollback and a four-hour incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Goals that are not measurable. "Improve performance" cannot be checked, so you never know if the project succeeded. Every goal needs a number.
  • No non-goals. Reviewers raise scope you never intended; scope creeps during build. Always write non-goals.
  • Proposed design before context. The reader does not yet believe there is a problem, so the design feels like a solution looking for one.
  • Rollback that is not actually possible. A data format change with no reverse path. The rollback section must be tested in thinking, not just written.
  • Observability as an afterthought. "We'll add dashboards later" means you ship blind and design your monitoring during the first incident.
  • Open questions hidden to look decisive. Pretending you have resolved everything erodes trust when the gaps surface later. Name them.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat the template as a thinking tool, not a form to fill. When they get to the rollback section and cannot write a clean one, they take that as a signal that the design is wrong, not that the section is annoying — a design you cannot undo is a design you should fear. When they get to the cost section and the number is uncomfortable, they let that reshape the design.

They put diagrams at the top of the proposed design, because a reader absorbs a system faster from a picture than from paragraphs, and they put the summary and the ask at the very top of the whole document, above context, because they assume busy readers stop early. They write non-goals carefully, because they have learned that most painful review cycles come from arguing about scope nobody agreed on, and non-goals end that argument before it starts.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping non-goals. The single most common and most costly omission.
  • Vague goals. "Make it faster" instead of "p99 under 480 ms".
  • Rollback written but never pressure-tested. It reads fine and does not actually work.
  • Design section with no diagram. Reviewers reconstruct the system in their heads, each slightly differently, and review the wrong thing.
  • Treating the template as bureaucracy. Filling sections to tick boxes rather than to think. The template is a checklist for your own reasoning.

Interview questions

  1. What sections must a design doc have, and which one is most often skipped to everyone's regret? Expected answer: context, goals, non-goals, requirements, design, alternatives, tradeoffs, risks, rollout, rollback, observability, cost, open questions — and non-goals is the most skipped and most valuable, because it bounds scope and pre-empts review arguments. Follow-up: give an example of a non-goal that saved a review.

  2. A design doc has a great proposed design but no rollback plan. Why is that dangerous, and what would you do as a reviewer? Expected answer: without a rollback plan you may ship something you cannot safely undo, turning a quick revert into a long incident; as a reviewer, block approval until the rollback is concrete and, specifically, until backward compatibility of any data changes is addressed. Why it matters: tests whether they think about operability, not just the happy path.

  3. Why insist that every goal in a design doc has a number? Expected answer: because without a number you cannot tell whether the project succeeded, you cannot size the design against the requirement, and "better" is unfalsifiable. Numbers turn opinions into engineering. Follow-up: turn "improve reliability" into a measurable goal.

Practical exercise

Take the most recent design doc your team wrote (or one you can find). Check it against the thirteen-section skeleton. For each missing or weak section, write one sentence saying what question a reviewer could not answer because of the gap.

Acceptance criteria: you produce a list of the doc's structural gaps, and for at least the rollback, non-goals and observability sections you can state the concrete risk each gap created. Rewrite the goals section so every goal has a number.

51.4 Writing alternatives honestly, and running the RFC process

Concept

Two skills live together here because they are the heart of getting a design agreed. The first is writing the alternatives you rejected honestly, so reviewers trust that you actually considered them rather than building a lineup of strawmen to make your favourite look good. The second is running the RFC process — the machinery of drafting, pre-wiring reviewers, collecting async comments, resolving them, and reaching a decision — so that the honest document actually produces a decision instead of an endless thread.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a design doc with an "alternatives considered" section that lists two options: your proposal, described in loving detail, and "do nothing", described as obviously terrible. A smart reviewer reads that and thinks: this person already decided, and the alternatives are theatre. Trust evaporates. They stop believing your tradeoffs too, because if you misrepresented the alternatives, what else did you shade.

Honest alternatives exist to earn trust and to actually find the best design. Sometimes writing an alternative fairly makes you realise it is better than your proposal, which is the system working. The RFC process exists because a good document on its own does not create alignment; alignment is manufactured by getting the right people to engage with the document before the decision, so the decision is theirs too, not something imposed on them.

Mental model

Imagine a courtroom where the prosecution writes the defence's argument. If they write it as a weak, obviously-wrong case, the jury sees through it and distrusts the whole trial. The strawman is a weak defence argument written by the prosecution. To be believed, you must state the opposing case as strongly as its real advocates would — steelman it, not strawman it. A reviewer who reads their own objection, stated fairly, and then sees a genuine answer to it, is won over. A reviewer who reads a caricature of their objection digs in.

How it works

First, honest alternatives. For each real alternative, write three things: what it is, its genuine advantages, and the specific reason you rejected it for this context. The reason must be contextual, not universal — "Kafka is bad" is not a reason; "Kafka adds a cluster we would have to operate for a throughput we will not reach for two years" is.

Second, the RFC process. It has a lifecycle:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft
    Draft --> PreWired: share with key reviewers 1-1
    PreWired --> InReview: open for async comments
    InReview --> InReview: resolve comments
    InReview --> DecisionMeeting: major objections resolved
    DecisionMeeting --> Accepted
    DecisionMeeting --> Rejected
    DecisionMeeting --> Draft: needs rework
    Accepted --> Superseded: a later RFC replaces it
    Rejected --> [*]
    Superseded --> [*]

The steps:

  1. Draft. You write the document. It is not shared widely yet.
  2. Pre-wire. Before opening it to everyone, you talk one-on-one to the two or three people most likely to object or most affected. Part 44.4 called this pre-socialising. Either they change your mind (saving you a public failure) or you incorporate their concern and they become supporters. Proposals that first appear in a big meeting mostly die there.
  3. Open for review. The document goes to all affected teams with a clear comment deadline. Asynchronous, so people in every timezone can engage.
  4. Resolve comments. You respond to every comment: accept and change the doc, or explain why not. A comment left unresolved is a reviewer left unconvinced.
  5. Decision meeting. A short, scheduled meeting (often thirty minutes) where the decision is ratified. If pre-wiring worked, this is a formality. Its real job is to force a decision date so the RFC does not drift forever.
  6. Status lifecycle. The RFC is marked Accepted, Rejected, or needs rework. Accepted RFCs can later be Superseded by a new one — never edited to say something different.

Practical example

For the notification RFC, the alternatives section, written honestly:

## Alternatives considered

### A. Keep synchronous, add a circuit breaker
Keep the direct HTTP call but wrap it in a circuit breaker so order
placement is not blocked when notifications degrade.
- **Advantages:** smallest change, no new infrastructure, no eventual
  consistency, easy to reason about.
- **Why rejected:** when the breaker is open, notifications are simply
  dropped, not deferred. We would lose "order shipped" emails during
  exactly the incidents when customers are most anxious. Durability
  requirement (no lost notification if the order committed) is not met.

### B. Fire-and-forget async HTTP (no outbox)
Order service calls notifications asynchronously, not awaiting the result.
- **Advantages:** removes the call from the hot path with almost no new
  infrastructure.
- **Why rejected:** if the order commits and the process crashes before
  the async call fires, the notification is lost. No durability. This is
  the classic dual-write problem (see Part 19.4); the outbox exists
  specifically to solve it.

### C. RabbitMQ instead of Kafka
Use RabbitMQ, which the team already operates, instead of Kafka.
- **Advantages:** we already run it, lower operational cost, simpler,
  per-message acknowledgement fits at-least-once naturally.
- **Why NOT clearly rejected:** this is genuinely close. See §Tradeoffs.
  We lean Kafka because the platform team is standardising on it for
  event streaming and two other consumers are likely within a year. If
  that standardisation slips, RabbitMQ is the better choice for this
  alone. We will confirm with the platform team before the decision
  meeting.

Notice option C. It is not dismissed; it is admitted to be close, and the real deciding factor (an organisational bet on Kafka, not a technical superiority) is stated plainly. That honesty is what makes reviewers trust options A and B were also fairly judged.

Artifact example

A comment-resolution log — the record that shows reviewers were heard. This is what turns "I left a comment and it was ignored" into "I left a comment and here is what happened".

## Review comments and resolutions (RFC-114)

| # | Reviewer | Comment | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Priya (platform) | Confirm Kafka standardisation is real before we commit a consumer to it. | Confirmed in 1-1; platform roadmap Q3 has 2 more producers. Added to §4C. ACCEPTED. |
| 2 | Sam (notifications) | Per-order ordering — how do we guarantee it? | Partition the topic by order_id so all events for one order go to one partition. Added to design §5. ACCEPTED. |
| 3 | Lena (mobile) | Will push notification latency get worse? | p95 end-to-end moves from ~1s to <10s. We judge this acceptable; mobile confirmed. NOTED, no change. |
| 4 | Raj (order) | Outbox table will grow forever. Cleanup? | Added a relay-then-delete step and a daily sweep of rows older than 7 days. Added to §5. ACCEPTED. |
| 5 | Sam (notifications) | Should we do exactly-once? | Out of scope; non-goal. At-least-once + idempotent consumer. Pointed to non-goals §3. DECLINED, with reason. |

Every comment has a visible outcome. Two changed the design (comments 2 and 4 are genuinely better for the change). One was declined with a reason and a pointer. This table is the single most powerful trust-builder in the RFC process: reviewers see that engaging actually changes things, so they keep engaging on your future RFCs.

Real-world scenario

A staff engineer at an e-commerce company has a 90% hit rate on getting RFCs accepted, far above her peers. People assume she writes better documents. She does write well, but the real reason is pre-wiring. Before any RFC goes wide, she has a fifteen-minute call with each of the three or four people who could kill it: the owner of the affected system, the skeptic who always has good objections, and whoever controls the resource she needs.

By the time the RFC opens for review, those people have already shaped it and feel ownership of it. The public review surfaces only minor comments, because the major objections were handled in private where nobody had to lose face. Her decision meetings are ten minutes long. Her peers who skip pre-wiring have two-hour debates in the open and a 50% acceptance rate. Same documents, different process, double the success.

Failure scenario

An engineer writes a technically excellent RFC and opens it cold to twenty people with no pre-wiring. The owner of the system being changed first hears about the proposal when it lands in their inbox, framed as nearly decided. They feel ambushed. In the public thread, defending their territory, they raise every possible objection, some real and some face-saving. Other reviewers pile on. The thread reaches sixty comments. The decision meeting becomes a two-hour argument. The RFC is sent back for rework, loses momentum, and quietly dies three weeks later.

The document was fine. The process killed it. One fifteen-minute call with the system owner before going wide would have turned an ambush into a collaboration, and the sixty-comment thread into a five-comment one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Strawman alternatives. Rejected options described weakly. Reviewers lose trust in the whole document.
  • No pre-wiring. Key people first see the proposal in public and feel ambushed, so they fight it in the open.
  • Comments left unresolved. A reviewer whose comment got no response is a reviewer who will not support the RFC and will remember next time.
  • No decision deadline. The RFC drifts in "review" forever. Someone must own forcing a decision date.
  • Editing an accepted RFC to change the decision. You destroy the record. Supersede instead.
  • Decision meeting doing the review. If major objections are still live at the meeting, pre-wiring and async review failed, and the meeting becomes a design session that runs over and resolves nothing.
  • The author who argues every comment. Defending every point, even minor ones, signals you want to win rather than find the best answer. Concede the small stuff fast.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They spend more effort on the alternatives section than on their own proposal, because they know that is where trust is won or lost, and because writing an alternative fairly is the best way to discover their own proposal is wrong before shipping it. They pre-wire as a reflex, not as a special effort — they would never dream of opening a consequential RFC cold, because they have watched too many good proposals die in public ambushes.

They treat every comment as a debt to be settled, visibly, because an unresolved comment is an unconvinced reviewer and reviewers have long memories. And they force a decision date, because they have seen RFCs rot in review for months while the problem they addressed got worse. A decision — even a "no" — is better than a document in limbo, because a "no" frees everyone to do something else.

Common mistakes

  • Strawmanning alternatives to make the proposal look inevitable. The giveaway is that no alternative has any real advantages listed.
  • Skipping pre-wiring to save time. It costs far more time later in a hostile public thread.
  • Treating the decision meeting as the review. By then it is too late to raise major objections gracefully.
  • Never closing the RFC. It drifts; the problem festers; momentum dies.
  • Winning every argument. You can win the review and lose the willingness of people to work with you again.

Interview questions

  1. How do you write the "alternatives considered" section so reviewers trust it? Expected answer: steelman each alternative — state its real advantages, then give a contextual, specific reason for rejecting it; and be willing to admit when an alternative is close. Strawmen destroy trust in the whole document. Why it matters: tests intellectual honesty, which is the currency of architecture influence.

  2. Walk me through how you take an RFC from draft to decision. Expected answer: draft, pre-wire the key reviewers one-on-one, open for async review with a comment deadline, resolve every comment visibly, hold a short decision meeting that ratifies rather than debates, mark status. Follow-up: who exactly do you pre-wire and what do you say to them.

  3. An RFC has been in review for six weeks with no decision. What is wrong and how do you fix it? Expected answer: no owner is forcing a decision date, or major objections were never pre-wired so the public thread stalled. Fix: pre-wire the remaining blockers privately, set a hard decision date, and make the call — even a "no" is better than limbo. Why it matters: tests whether they drive closure rather than admire the problem.

Practical exercise

Take a decision you are currently facing. Write the alternatives section: at least two real alternatives besides your preferred option, each with genuine advantages and a contextual reason for rejection. Then write down who you would pre-wire before opening it for review, and the one sentence you would say to each to bring them on board.

Acceptance criteria: at least one alternative has advantages strong enough that a reasonable person could pick it, and your rejection reason is specific to your context (mentions your numbers, your team, or your constraints) rather than a universal claim. You can name the two or three people whose buy-in determines whether this gets approved.

51.5 Running design reviews, and diagrams that earn their place

Concept

Two more skills that make documents work. The first is running a design review well — both as the author presenting your work and as a reviewer critiquing someone else's. A design review is not a meeting where people admire a diagram; it is a structured attempt to break a design on paper, cheaply, before production breaks it expensively. The second is drawing diagrams that genuinely help: the C4 model for showing systems at the right zoom level, sequence diagrams for flows over time, and data-flow diagrams for how information moves. A good diagram replaces three paragraphs; a bad one adds confusion.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a design review with no structure. The author talks for forty minutes. Reviewers interrupt with whatever occurs to them. The loud people dominate, the quiet expert says nothing, and the meeting ends with a vague "looks good" that commits no one. The design ships with its flaws intact, and you find them in production.

Structured review exists to find flaws while they are still cheap to fix — in a document, flaws cost an edit; in production, they cost an incident. Good diagrams exist because systems are spatial and temporal, and prose is neither. Trying to describe a request flowing through six components in a paragraph forces the reader to build the picture in their own head, and every reader builds a slightly different one, so they review different systems.

Mental model

For reviews, imagine a structural engineer reviewing a bridge design. They do not say "nice bridge". They systematically ask: what is the maximum load, what happens in high wind, what if this joint fails, how do you inspect it, how do you repair it. They are trying to find the failure before it is built. A design review is the same adversarial, systematic probing, done kindly.

For diagrams, imagine trying to give someone directions to your house using only words, versus handing them a map. The map is not decoration; it is a fundamentally better medium for spatial information. The C4 model is a set of maps at different zoom levels — country, city, street, building — so the reader can zoom to the level they need without getting lost.

How it works

The design review. As author: send the document at least two days before the meeting with an explicit ask to read it first; the meeting is for discussion, not for reading aloud. Open by stating the decision you need and the specific areas where you want scrutiny. Then shut up and let people probe. As reviewer: come having read it, and probe systematically against the dimensions that matter.

A reviewer's checklist, by dimension:

Reliability:  Can it time out? Fail? Partially succeed? What's the blast radius?
              What happens when a dependency is down?
Data:         Is there a dual-write? Can data be lost or duplicated? Is the
              migration reversible? Any unbounded growth?
Security:     Authn/authz on every path? Any injection surface? Secrets handled?
              Is tenant/user data isolated?
Cost:         What does this cost at peak? Does cost scale with load in a
              surprising way? Any unbounded query or fan-out?
Operability:  How do we know it's healthy? How do we roll back? Who gets paged?
Scaling:      What breaks first at 10x? Is there a hot key, hot partition,
              single-writer bottleneck?

The C4 model. Four levels of diagram, from most zoomed-out to most zoomed-in. You rarely need all four; pick the levels your reader needs.

flowchart TB
    L1["Level 1: System Context - our system, its users, external systems"]
    L2["Level 2: Container - the deployable pieces: app, DB, queue, cache"]
    L3["Level 3: Component - the modules inside one container"]
    L4["Level 4: Code - classes - rarely drawn, the code is the truth"]
    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4
  • Level 1, System Context: your system as one box, surrounded by the users and external systems it talks to. For non-technical and cross-team readers.
  • Level 2, Container: the deployable units — the NestJS app, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, the workers — and how they connect. The most useful level for most design docs.
  • Level 3, Component: the modules or services inside one container. For the team building it.
  • Level 4, Code: class-level detail. Almost never worth drawing; the code is the source of truth and the diagram rots instantly.

Sequence diagrams show a flow over time — who calls whom, in what order. Best for request paths and protocols. Data-flow diagrams show how data moves and transforms through a system, ignoring timing. Use each for its job: sequence for "what happens when a user clicks buy", data-flow for "how an order event reaches the warehouse".

Practical example

The Level 2 container diagram for the notification pipeline, which does more to align reviewers than three pages of prose:

flowchart LR
    client["Mobile / Web client"] -->|"POST /orders"| order["Order Service (NestJS)"]
    order -->|"write order + outbox row - one tx"| pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    relay["Outbox Relay (worker)"] -->|"poll unsent rows"| pg
    relay -->|"publish order.events.v1"| kafka[["Kafka topic"]]
    kafka -->|"consume"| notif["Notification Service (NestJS)"]
    notif -->|"send"| email["Email provider"]
    notif -->|"send"| push["Push provider"]

A reviewer sees in one glance: the write and the outbox row are in one transaction (durability), a separate relay publishes to Kafka (so the order path does not wait on Kafka), and notifications are fully off the hot path. Three of the design's most important properties are visible without a word of prose. That is a diagram earning its place.

Artifact example

A filled-in reviewer's checklist from an actual review of the notification RFC — this is what a good reviewer hands back, rather than "LGTM".

## Review of RFC-114 (reviewer: staff eng, platform)

**Reliability**
- [x] Order path no longer depends on notification service — good.
- [!] What happens if the Outbox Relay crashes? Rows pile up, notifications
      delayed. Need an alert on oldest-unsent-row age. NOT in observability
      section. BLOCKING until added.
- [x] At-least-once + idempotent consumer handles duplicates. Fine.

**Data**
- [x] Outbox write in same tx as order — dual-write avoided. Correct.
- [!] Outbox cleanup: §5 says delete after relay. If relay deletes before
      Kafka ack, a crash loses the row. Confirm: ack from Kafka THEN delete,
      or mark-sent then sweep. Clarify. BLOCKING.
- [x] Topic partitioned by order_id — per-order ordering holds. Good.

**Security**
- [x] Topic is internal, no PII beyond order_id and status. Acceptable.

**Cost**
- [x] One topic, modest volume (~1,200/s). Negligible over existing cluster.

**Operability**
- [!] Rollback flag is good. Add: what if we flip back to sync — do
      un-relayed outbox rows get double-sent? Need a reconciliation note.

**Verdict:** Approve with 3 blocking items (oldest-unsent alert,
relay-delete ordering, rollback double-send). Strong design otherwise.

This is a review that does work. It approves the direction, names three specific, fixable blockers with reasons, and is organised so the author can act on each one. It is adversarial in the kind way — it is trying to break the design on paper so production cannot.

Real-world scenario

A company institutes a rule: every design review must have at least one reviewer from outside the authoring team, and that reviewer must come with a filled-in checklist, not vibes. At first engineers grumble that it slows reviews. Within two quarters, the data tells a different story: designs reviewed under the new rule have measurably fewer production incidents in their first 90 days, because the outside reviewer catches the assumptions the authoring team shares and therefore cannot see. The classic catch is the authoring team all assuming a dependency is always available, and the outsider asking the obvious question nobody inside thought to ask: "what happens when it is down?"

Failure scenario

A design review is scheduled, but nobody reads the document beforehand. The author spends thirty minutes reading it aloud. The remaining fifteen minutes produce a few shallow comments. The design is approved. Nobody noticed that the proposed design did a dual write — writing to the database and publishing to a queue as two separate operations — because reviewing a dual write requires actually thinking about the failure mode, and you cannot think while someone reads slides at you.

In production, the dual write does exactly what dual writes do: the process crashes between the two writes, the data and the event diverge, and a slow drip of inconsistency corrupts downstream systems for weeks before anyone notices. The review existed. It just did not review anything, because the document was read in the meeting instead of before it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The read-aloud review. The meeting is spent reading the document, leaving no time to probe it. Send it in advance; refuse to proceed if people have not read it.
  • The rubber stamp. "Looks good" with no probing. The review happened on paper but not in substance.
  • The pile-on. Reviewers compete to find flaws to look smart, and the author gets demoralised rather than helped. Reviews are collaborative, not competitive.
  • Only insiders review. The authoring team's shared blind spots go uncaught. Always include an outside reviewer.
  • Diagram at the wrong zoom. A Level 4 class diagram in a doc for executives, or a one-box Level 1 diagram for the team who has to build it. Match the level to the reader.
  • Diagrams that lie. A diagram drawn at design time and never updated, now showing a system that no longer exists. A wrong diagram is worse than none.
  • Everything in one giant diagram. Twenty-five boxes and fifty arrows. Nobody can read it. Split into several small diagrams at different levels.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

As an author, they want the review to find flaws, genuinely, because a flaw found in review costs an edit and a flaw found in production costs an incident and their credibility. So they open the review by pointing at the parts they are least sure of, inviting attack, rather than defending. As a reviewer, they probe systematically against reliability, data, security, cost and operability, because they know their intuition will miss a dimension if they do not have a checklist.

On diagrams, they draw at the level the reader needs and no deeper, and they put the container diagram near the top of almost every design doc because it aligns everyone on the shape of the system before any argument about details. They keep diagrams small — several little ones beat one enormous one — and they are honest that Level 4 code diagrams are almost always a waste, because the code is the truth and the diagram is stale the moment it is drawn.

Common mistakes

  • Reviewing without reading first. The meeting becomes a reading, and nothing gets probed.
  • "LGTM" culture. Approvals without scrutiny, which is the same as no review.
  • No outside reviewer. Shared blind spots survive.
  • One giant diagram at the wrong zoom level. Either too detailed for the audience or too vague for the builders.
  • Letting diagrams rot. Keeping a diagram in a living doc that no longer matches reality.
  • Treating the review as adversarial combat. Winning the review instead of improving the design.

Interview questions

  1. How do you run a design review as the author so that it actually finds problems? Expected answer: send the doc in advance and require reading before the meeting; open by naming where you are least confident and inviting attack; let reviewers probe rather than defending; include at least one outside reviewer. Why it matters: tests whether they see review as a cheap way to find flaws or as a ritual to survive.

  2. Explain the C4 model and when you would use each level. Expected answer: context (system as one box, for cross-team/non-technical readers), container (deployable units, the most useful level for design docs), component (modules inside one container, for the builders), code (class level, rarely worth drawing). Match the level to the reader. Follow-up: which level would you put in a doc for executives, and which for the implementing team.

  3. A design with a dual write passed review. How did the review fail, and how would you prevent it? Expected answer: reviewers did not probe the data dimension — specifically "can the two writes diverge on a crash" — likely because they had not read the doc beforehand or lacked a checklist. Prevent it with pre-reading, a data-reliability checklist item (dual-write detection), and an outside reviewer. Why it matters: connects review discipline to a concrete, common production failure.

Practical exercise

Take a system you own and draw its C4 Level 2 container diagram in Mermaid: every deployable unit and datastore, and the connections between them, with the key property of each connection labelled (which calls are synchronous, which are in-transaction, which are async). Then write the reviewer's checklist you would want someone to apply to it, filling in the reliability and data rows with the two questions you are least confident you can answer well.

Acceptance criteria: the diagram has fewer than 15 nodes, every connection is labelled, and the checklist surfaces at least one real weakness in your own system that you had not consciously articulated before drawing it.

51.6 Worked example: a full RFC for event-driven order notifications

We have referred to this RFC throughout the Part. Here it is in full, as a single artifact you can read end to end and use as a template. It is written at the length a real RFC of this size would be — long enough to decide on, short enough to read in one sitting. Read it as a reader would, then read the annotations after it.

Artifact example

# RFC-114: Move order notifications to an event-driven pipeline

**Status:** Proposed
**Author:** [you]
**Reviewers:** order team, notifications team, mobile, platform, director
**Created:** 2026-02-20
**Decision meeting:** 2026-03-12
**Supersedes:** none

## Summary and ask

Today the order service calls the notification service synchronously on
every order event. This couples order placement to notification health:
when notifications degrade, orders degrade. We propose writing
notification intents to an outbox table in the order transaction, relaying
them to a Kafka topic, and consuming them asynchronously.

**Ask:** approve this design and the allocation of 2 engineers for ~5 weeks.

## 1. Context

POST /orders currently does, synchronously:
1. Validate and persist the order (PostgreSQL).
2. Call POST notification-service/send (HTTP) for the "order placed"
   notification, awaiting the response.

Measured, last 30 days:
- POST /orders p50 = 190 ms, p99 = 820 ms.
- Of the p99, ~340 ms is the notification call.
- 2 partial order outages caused by notification degradation:
  INC-3391 (notification DB slow, 22 min, ~4,100 orders delayed),
  INC-3407 (notification deploy, 11 min, ~1,900 orders failed outright).

The coupling is the problem. Notifications are not order-critical, but
today they can fail an order.

## 2. Goals

- Remove the notification call from the order hot path. Target POST
  /orders p99 < 480 ms.
- No order should ever fail because notifications are degraded.
- No notification intent lost if the order transaction committed.

## 3. Non-goals

- NOT changing notification content or templates.
- NOT building a company-wide event bus.
- NOT guaranteeing exactly-once (at-least-once + idempotent consumer).
- NOT migrating SMS in this phase (different provider; stays sync).

## 4. Requirements

- Throughput: 1,200 order events/sec peak (measured peak 1,050 + 15%).
- End-to-end notification delivery p95 < 10 s (relaxed from sync; fine).
- Delivery: at-least-once. Lost "order shipped" unacceptable; rare
  duplicate acceptable.
- Ordering: per order (placed -> shipped -> delivered). None across orders.
- Durability: intent must survive if the order committed.

## 5. Proposed design

In the order-placement transaction, write the order AND a row to an
`outbox` table. A separate Outbox Relay worker polls unsent rows,
publishes them to Kafka topic `order.events.v1` (partitioned by
order_id), and only after Kafka acknowledges, marks the row sent. A daily
sweep deletes sent rows older than 7 days. The notification service
consumes the topic and sends notifications, deduplicating on
(order_id, event_type) so a redelivery does not double-send.

[container diagram — see §51.5]

outbox table:
  id BIGSERIAL PK, aggregate_id UUID, event_type TEXT,
  payload JSONB, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, sent_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL
  INDEX on (sent_at) WHERE sent_at IS NULL   -- find unsent fast

## 6. Alternatives considered

A. Sync + circuit breaker — drops notifications when open; no durability.
B. Fire-and-forget async HTTP — dual-write, loses intent on crash.
C. RabbitMQ instead of Kafka — genuinely close; chosen Kafka because
   platform is standardising on it and 2 more consumers are likely in a
   year. If that slips, RabbitMQ wins. Confirmed with platform (see log).
(Full write-up in §51.4.)

## 7. Tradeoffs

- We gain decoupling and durability; we accept eventual consistency
  (notification up to ~10 s after order, vs synchronous today).
- We add an outbox relay and a Kafka consumer to our operational surface.
- Duplicate notifications become possible (idempotent consumer makes
  them rare and harmless).

## 8. Risks and mitigations

- Relay crash -> notifications delayed. Mitigation: alert on oldest
  unsent-row age > 60 s.
- Relay deletes before Kafka ack -> lost intent. Mitigation: ack THEN
  mark sent; sweep deletes only sent rows.
- Consumer lag under peak. Mitigation: alert on consumer lag; topic
  partitioned so we can scale consumers.

## 9. Rollout

1. Ship outbox write behind flag `notifications.transport=outbox`, but
   KEEP the sync call too (dual-run). Compare.
2. Shadow: relay publishes, notification service consumes and logs but
   does NOT send (sync still sends). Verify events match.
3. Ramp: flip consumers to send, sync call to no-op, at 1% -> 10% ->
   50% -> 100% over a week.

## 10. Rollback

Flip `notifications.transport` back to `sync`. Under 5 min. Outbox rows
are retained; un-relayed rows are swept, not re-sent, so no double-send
on rollback (see comment #5 resolution).

## 11. Observability

- Metric: POST /orders p99 (goal < 480 ms).
- Metric: oldest unsent outbox row age (alert > 60 s).
- Metric: Kafka consumer lag on order.events.v1 (alert > 30 s).
- Metric: notification send success rate per event_type.
- Log: every relay publish and consumer dedupe-skip, with order_id.

## 12. Cost

Negligible marginal Kafka cost (existing cluster, ~1,200 msg/s). One new
worker (shares existing node pool). Net: lower infra pressure on the
order service primary, which was absorbing notification-call connection
load.

## 13. Open questions

- Do we backfill the outbox for in-flight orders at cutover, or accept a
  brief window where old orders use sync? Leaning: accept the window.
- Retention of 7 days for sent outbox rows — enough for replay/debug?
  Confirm with notifications team.

Why this RFC works

Read it again with the craft in mind and notice the moves.

The summary and ask are first, and they stand alone. A director who reads only the summary knows what is being proposed, why, and what it costs (2 engineers, 5 weeks). Everything else is for people who need more.

The context proves there is a problem before proposing anything. It names two real incidents with durations and order counts. A reviewer finishes section 1 already agreeing something must change, which means the rest of the document is answering "which fix" rather than "is there a problem".

The goals are numbers (p99 < 480 ms), so success is checkable. The non-goals pre-empt four entire branches of review argument — SMS, exactly-once, company event bus, template changes — before anyone raises them.

The requirements do design work: the ordering requirement forces partitioning by order_id, which then appears in the design. The reader can trace each design choice back to a requirement.

The alternatives are honest, and option C openly admits the deciding factor is an organisational bet, not technical superiority. That honesty makes the whole document trustworthy.

The rollout is staged with a shadow phase, so the new path is proven to match the old before it takes over. The rollback is specific, fast, and — crucially — addresses the double-send edge case a reviewer raised, showing the review changed the design. The observability section names the exact metrics and alert thresholds, so the system ships with its monitoring rather than bolting it on after the first incident.

And the open questions are honest. The author does not pretend to have resolved the backfill question; naming it makes the document more credible, and it gives the decision meeting something concrete to settle.

Real-world scenario

This RFC, in a real company, would go through the process from 51.4. The author pre-wires the platform lead (to confirm the Kafka bet), the notifications lead (to confirm the consumer design and retention), and the order lead (to confirm the outbox cleanup). By the time it opens for review, those three are supporters. The public review surfaces the three blocking items from the 51.5 checklist — oldest-unsent alert, relay-delete ordering, rollback double-send — all of which the author fixes, visibly, in the comment-resolution log. The decision meeting is twenty minutes and ends in acceptance. Total elapsed time: about three weeks from draft to accepted, most of it waiting for async review, almost none of it in meetings.

Practical exercise

Take a change you want to make that affects at least one team other than your own. Write it up as an RFC using the exact thirteen-numbered-section structure above. Enforce three rules on yourself: the summary and ask must stand alone and fit on one screen; every goal must have a number; and the alternatives section must contain at least one option you can imagine a reasonable colleague preferring.

Acceptance criteria: a reviewer from another team can read only your summary and know what you want and what it costs; every design choice in section 5 can be traced to a requirement in section 4; and your rollback in section 10 is specific enough that an on-call engineer could execute it at 2 a.m. without asking you anything.

51.7 ADR chains, keeping docs alive, and the anti-patterns

Concept

Three final threads that separate people who write documents from people whose documents still matter years later. The first is the ADR chain: how a sequence of decision records tells the story of a choice made, lived with, and eventually replaced — because decisions have a life, and the record should show it. The second is keeping docs alive: fighting doc rot by linking documents to the code and tickets they describe, and superseding decisions rather than letting them quietly become lies. The third is the catalogue of doc anti-patterns — the predictable ways documents fail — so you can recognise and avoid them.

Why does it exist?

Imagine joining a team and finding an ADR that says "we chose Elasticsearch for search". You build on that assumption. Then you discover, by accident, that the team actually moved to a different engine a year ago, and the ADR was never updated. The record did not just fail to help you; it actively misled you into wrong decisions. One stale document can cost more than ten missing ones, because a missing document makes you ask and a stale one makes you confidently wrong.

ADR chains and superseding exist because decisions are not permanent, and a record that pretends they are will eventually lie. Linking docs to code and tickets exists because a document disconnected from the thing it describes drifts away from reality the moment the code changes. And naming the anti-patterns exists because they are so common that you will produce them by default unless you can see them coming.

Mental model

Imagine a legal system where a new law can repeal an old one, but the old law stays in the books marked "repealed by Act of 2026", with a pointer to what replaced it. You can always see what the law was, when it changed, and why. You never have to guess whether a law is current, because its status is explicit. An ADR chain is exactly this: each decision stays on the record, and when a later decision replaces it, the old one is marked "Superseded by ADR-N" rather than deleted. The history is the point.

How it works

ADR chains. An ADR is immutable once accepted. When the decision changes, you write a new ADR that references and supersedes the old one. Over years, this produces a chain that tells a story.

flowchart LR
    A["ADR-012: Choose Elasticsearch for product search (2024)"]
    B["ADR-031: Add Postgres full-text as cheaper fallback (2025)"]
    C["ADR-047: Replace Elasticsearch with OpenSearch, retire the cluster (2026)"]
    A -->|"superseded by"| C
    A -->|"amended by"| B
    B -->|"superseded by"| C
