Each ADR in the chain records what was true at the time, so a new engineer reading ADR-047 can follow the links back and understand not just what search engine they run today, but the whole arc: why Elasticsearch was chosen, what problem drove the Postgres fallback, and what finally forced the move to OpenSearch. The chain is institutional memory.

Keeping docs alive. Three practices fight rot:

  1. Link docs to code and tickets. The design doc links to the pull requests that implemented it; the code links back to the design doc and the ADR (a comment or a // see ADR-047 reference); the RFC links to the Jira epic. When any one changes, the links lead you to the others.
  2. Supersede, do not edit. Accepted ADRs and RFCs are immutable. A changed decision is a new document that supersedes the old, with the old marked superseded. Living documents (like a current-architecture overview) are explicitly marked as living and dated.
  3. Date everything and mark status. Every document has a visible status (Draft, Accepted, Superseded, Living) and a last-reviewed date. A reader can tell at a glance whether to trust it.

The anti-patterns. The predictable failure shapes:

Solution looking for a problem -> thin problem section, lavish solution
The 40-page doc nobody reads   -> no summary, no clear ask, buried decision
The decision already made       -> fake consultation; reviewers sense it, disengage
The strawman alternatives       -> rejected options described weakly (see 51.4)
Doc rot                         -> stale doc trusted as current
The template filled with blanks -> sections present but empty or "TODO"

Practical example

A new engineer joins the search team and needs to understand why the system is shaped the way it is. Instead of interrupting three people, they open the current-architecture doc, which is marked "Living, last reviewed 2026-09". It links to ADR-047 as the current search decision. ADR-047 opens with "Supersedes ADR-012 and ADR-031" and a paragraph on the arc. Fifteen minutes of reading replaces half a day of interruptions and produces a more accurate understanding than any single person could have given, because no single person remembered the whole two-year story. That is what a maintained ADR chain buys.

Artifact example

The worked ADR chain for choosing and then replacing a search engine over two years — the second worked example the outline asks for. Shown as three linked records, abbreviated to their decision-bearing parts.

# ADR-012: Use Elasticsearch for product search
Status: Superseded by ADR-047 (2026-05)
Date: 2024-03
Context: PostgreSQL LIKE queries on 2M products are slow (>900 ms) and
  cannot do relevance ranking or faceting. Product wants typo tolerance
  and facets.
Decision: Adopt a managed Elasticsearch cluster. Index products via an
  outbox-driven sync from PostgreSQL.
Consequences: New cluster to operate. Relevance and facets solved.
  Eventual consistency between PG and the index (acceptable, ~seconds).

---

# ADR-031: Add PostgreSQL full-text search as a fallback tier
Status: Superseded by ADR-047 (2026-05)
Date: 2025-02
Context: Elasticsearch cluster is our single most expensive service
  ($3,400/mo) and causes 60% of search-feature incidents. Many queries
  are simple prefix lookups that do not need ES.
Decision: Route simple autocomplete/prefix queries to PostgreSQL
  full-text (tsvector + GIN). Keep ES for relevance/faceted search.
Consequences: ES load drops ~40%. Two search paths to maintain. This is
  a bridge, not a destination.

---

# ADR-047: Replace Elasticsearch with OpenSearch; retire the ES cluster
Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-05
Supersedes: ADR-012, ADR-031
Context: Our Elasticsearch version reached end of support; the licence
  terms changed; cost rose to $4,100/mo. OpenSearch is API-compatible
  for our usage, cheaper on our cloud, and the platform team already
  runs one for logs.
Decision: Migrate the product index to the shared OpenSearch cluster
  using a parallel-run (Part 54): dual-index, compare results on 100%
  of queries for 2 weeks, cut reads over behind a flag, retire ES.
  Keep the PostgreSQL full-text tier from ADR-031 unchanged.
Consequences: ~$2,000/mo saved. One fewer cluster we operate alone.
  Migration risk managed by parallel run. ADR-031's PG tier survives.

Read as a chain, these three records tell the full two-year story: a search engine chosen for good reasons, a pragmatic cost-cutting bridge added when it got expensive, and a clean replacement when the version and licence forced the issue — with the useful part of the bridge (the Postgres tier) deliberately kept. A single engineer rarely holds all of this; the chain does.

Real-world scenario

A company runs an architecture wiki with hundreds of pages. Over three years, most of it rots — pages describe systems that no longer exist, decisions that were reversed, services that were deleted. New engineers learn to distrust the wiki entirely, which means the good pages are wasted too. A principal engineer fixes this not by rewriting everything but by introducing two rules: every page must carry a status and a last-reviewed date, and any decision page must be either immutable-and-superseded or explicitly marked living. Pages past a review date without a refresh get an automatic "possibly stale" banner. Within a quarter, engineers trust the wiki again, because they can now tell at a glance which pages to believe. The content barely changed; the trustworthiness signals changed, and trust is what makes documentation worth having.

Failure scenario

A team keeps all its decisions in a single "Architecture" wiki page that everyone edits in place. Over two years it is edited hundreds of times. A dispute arises: did we or did we not decide to drop support for the legacy API in 2025? Nobody can tell, because the page only ever shows its current state, and the current state has been overwritten dozens of times. There is no record of what was decided when, or why. The team spends a week reconstructing the history from Slack and memory, reaches no firm answer, and makes a worse decision than they would have if the original reasoning had survived. Editing decisions in place destroyed exactly the thing decision records exist to preserve: the history.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Editing an ADR in place. The history is destroyed; you can no longer tell what you believed or why. Supersede instead.
  • Doc rot trusted as current. A stale document actively misleads. Status and dates let readers calibrate trust.
  • Links that break. A design doc links to a ticket that was deleted; the chain of context snaps. Link to durable identifiers, and link bidirectionally.
  • The "living" document that nobody reviews. Marked living but last touched eighteen months ago. Living means someone owns reviewing it on a cadence; without that, it is just rot with a nicer label.
  • Superseding without linking. A new ADR replaces an old one but does not reference it, so a reader of the old one never learns it was replaced. Always mark the old one superseded, with a pointer.
  • Anti-patterns combined. The 40-page doc that is also a solution looking for a problem with strawman alternatives — common, and fatal to any chance of the idea landing.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat the historical record as an asset the organisation owns, not as clutter. They never edit an accepted decision; they supersede it, because they know a future engineer's correct decision depends on understanding the arc, not just the current state. They design documentation so that trust is legible — status, dates, ownership — because a body of docs is only worth maintaining if people believe it, and belief depends on being able to tell the fresh from the stale at a glance.

They are allergic to the anti-patterns because they have been burned by all of them. They can smell a solution-looking-for-a-problem from the shape of the document — thin problem, lavish solution — and they will send it back regardless of how good the solution is, because a solution to a problem you have not established is a liability. And they keep documents short and linked, because a document disconnected from the code and tickets it describes is a document that will drift into fiction.

Common mistakes

  • Editing decisions in place. Destroys the history that is the whole point.
  • No status or date on documents. Readers cannot tell the current from the obsolete, so they distrust all of it.
  • "Living" documents with no owner or review cadence. Rot wearing a respectable label.
  • Superseding silently. The old document never points to its replacement, so readers of it are misled.
  • Not recognising the anti-patterns in your own drafts. Everyone writes a solution-looking-for-a-problem occasionally; the skill is catching it before others do.

Interview questions

  1. Why are ADRs immutable, and what do you do when a decision changes? Expected answer: immutability preserves the historical record of what you believed and why at a point in time; when a decision changes you write a new ADR that supersedes the old, mark the old one superseded with a pointer, and the chain tells the story. Why it matters: tests whether they value institutional memory over tidiness.

  2. How do you fight doc rot across a large architecture wiki? Expected answer: make trust legible with status and last-reviewed dates, distinguish immutable/superseded decisions from explicitly-owned living docs, link docs to code and tickets bidirectionally, and flag stale pages automatically. You cannot keep everything fresh, but you can make freshness visible. Follow-up: why is a stale doc worse than a missing one.

  3. Name three document anti-patterns and how you would catch each. Expected answer: solution looking for a problem (thin problem section — send back for a real problem statement), the 40-pager nobody reads (no summary/ask — demand a standalone summary), strawman alternatives (rejected options with no real advantages — demand a steelman). Why it matters: tests whether they can review documents, not just write them.

Practical exercise

Find a decision your team made and reversed at some point. Write the two ADRs that should exist: the original decision (with its real context and consequences at the time) and the superseding decision (referencing the first, with the reason the original stopped being right). Then audit three documents your team relies on and add a status and last-reviewed date to each, marking any that are actually stale.

Acceptance criteria: the two ADRs together let a new engineer understand the full arc of the decision without talking to anyone, the superseding ADR explicitly points back to the original, and your three audited documents now each carry a status that tells a reader whether to trust them.

51.9 The post-incident review as a document, and writing at scale

Concept

Two topics that extend the Part's craft. The post-incident review (PIR) is a document type with its own discipline: a blameless account of what broke, a precise timeline, the real root cause, and tracked actions — written so the organisation learns rather than assigns blame. And writing at scale is what changes when an organisation has hundreds of documents and dozens of authors: the need for discoverability, templates that enforce quality, a culture that reads and comments, and metrics for whether the documentation is actually healthy. Both are where the individual craft of writing meets the organisational reality of many documents and many readers.

Why does it exist?

Imagine an incident handled well operationally but never written up, or written up as a blame exercise ("the on-call engineer made a mistake"). In the first case, the lesson evaporates and the same incident recurs next quarter. In the second, people learn to hide their involvement in incidents, so the information needed to prevent recurrence dries up. The blameless PIR exists to capture the lesson and to do so in a way that keeps people sharing, so the organisation actually learns from its failures (Part 37 covers the operational side; here we focus on the document).

Writing at scale exists as a distinct concern because the problems change with volume. One author writing ten documents can keep them findable and current by memory. Fifty authors writing hundreds of documents cannot — without deliberate discoverability, templates, a reading culture, and health metrics, the documentation becomes an unnavigable, rotting pile that nobody trusts, wasting all the individual writing effort. Writing at scale is about the systems that keep a large body of documents valuable.

Mental model

For the PIR, imagine an aviation accident investigation. It is meticulous (a precise timeline), it seeks the systemic root cause (not "the pilot erred" but "why did the system let a tired pilot make that error"), and it is explicitly blameless, because the goal is preventing the next crash, not punishing this one — and punishment would make people hide information, making flying less safe. A PIR is the aviation investigation of a software incident: blameless, precise, systemic, aimed at prevention.

For writing at scale, imagine a library. One person's bookshelf needs no system — they know where everything is. A library with a million books needs a catalogue (discoverability), acquisition standards (templates/quality), librarians who weed outdated books (fighting rot), and usage statistics (health metrics). Writing at scale is running a library, not a bookshelf: the systems that keep a large collection findable, current, and trusted.

How it works

The post-incident review as a document:

A good PIR contains:
- Summary: what happened, impact (users affected, duration, $), in 2-3 lines.
- Timeline: precise, timestamped sequence (detection -> diagnosis -> mitigation
  -> resolution). The timeline often reveals the real improvement areas (e.g.
  detection took 40 min -> the lesson is faster detection).
- Root cause: the SYSTEMIC cause, blamelessly. Not "X forgot" but "the system
  allowed X to happen because there was no guardrail." Five-whys to get there.
- What went well: what limited the damage (so you keep doing it).
- Action items: specific, owned, dated, tracked to completion. A PIR whose
  actions are never done is theatre.
- Blameless throughout: no names-as-causes; systemic framing only.

The blameless framing is the load-bearing discipline: the moment a PIR assigns personal blame, people stop contributing honestly to future ones, and the organisation stops learning. The goal is a better system, not a culprit.

Writing at scale:

  • Discoverability. A large body of documents is worthless if nobody can find the relevant one. Needs search, consistent naming, linking, and an index or catalogue. The best document is useless if the reader cannot find it.
  • Templates that enforce quality. At scale, you cannot rely on every author knowing the craft; templates (Part 51.8) bake in the structure so every design doc, RFC, and PIR has the sections it needs, raising the floor across all authors.
  • A reading and commenting culture. Documents only work if people read and engage with them; this is cultural (Part 57.6) — norms that reviewing a doc is real work, that comments get resolved, that the author gets feedback.
  • Health metrics. Signals that the documentation is actually working: are docs being read (view counts), are they current (last-reviewed dates, Part 51.7), are decisions findable, are PIR actions completed. Metrics turn "we have docs" into "our docs are healthy or not".

Artifact example

A post-incident review, filled in blamelessly — the artifact that turns an incident into an organisational lesson.

# PIR: order placement outage, 2026-10-14

## Summary
Order placement failed for ~22 minutes (14:02-14:24 UTC), ~4,100 orders
delayed, ~$180k in delayed revenue (recovered). Cause: the notification
service saturated and, because order placement called it synchronously, order
placement saturated too. (This incident motivated RFC-114, §51.6.)

## Timeline (precise, timestamped)
- 14:02 notification DB hit connection limit; notification calls slowed.
- 14:02 order placement p99 spiked (it awaits the notification call).
- 14:09 first alert fired (order error rate). DETECTION TOOK 7 MIN — a lesson.
- 14:14 on-call identified the coupling to notifications.
- 14:18 mitigated: feature-flagged the notification call to fire-and-forget.
- 14:24 order placement recovered.

## Root cause (systemic, blameless)
Order placement was SYNCHRONOUSLY coupled to the notification service, so the
notification service's saturation propagated to order placement. The system
ALLOWED a non-critical dependency to fail a critical path. This is an
architectural coupling, not a person's error.

## What went well
- The feature flag let us mitigate in 4 minutes once diagnosed. Keep using flags.

## Action items (owned, dated, tracked)
1. Decouple notifications from order placement via outbox+events (RFC-114).
   Owner: [you]. Due: Q1. [THIS IS THE REAL FIX — removes the coupling.]
2. Add an alert on notification-DB connection saturation (detection was 7 min).
   Owner: notifications team. Due: 2 weeks.
3. Add a circuit breaker as interim protection until #1 ships.
   Owner: order team. Due: 1 week.

## Blameless note
No individual caused this. The architecture coupled a critical path to a
non-critical dependency. We fix the architecture.

The PIR's power is that it is precise (a timestamped timeline that itself reveals a lesson — 7-minute detection), systemic and blameless (the root cause is an architectural coupling, explicitly "not a person's error"), and action-oriented (specific, owned, dated actions tracked to completion, with the real fix identified). It turns an incident into a durable organisational lesson and a concrete improvement plan, and it does so in a way that keeps people contributing honestly to future PIRs — which is what makes an organisation learn from failure rather than repeat it.

Real-world scenario

An organisation treats PIRs as blameless learning documents and tracks their actions to completion. Over time, this produces a visible effect: classes of incidents stop recurring, because each PIR's actions actually address the systemic cause and get done. The PIR for the notification-coupling outage, for instance, drives the RFC-114 decoupling (§51.6), after which that entire class of incident (a non-critical dependency failing a critical path via synchronous coupling) becomes impossible. Because the PIRs are blameless, people contribute honestly — the on-call engineer who mitigated describes exactly what happened without fear, so the timeline is accurate and the lesson is real. And because the documents are discoverable, a new engineer facing a similar situation can find the PIR and learn from it. The PIRs, as documents, are the mechanism by which the organisation's hard-won incident lessons become permanent, findable, and acted-upon — which is the whole point of writing them down rather than just resolving the incident and moving on.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat the PIR as a learning document whose blamelessness is non-negotiable, because they know that the moment blame enters, honest contribution stops and the organisation stops learning from its failures. They insist the root cause be systemic (what the system allowed, not who erred) and the actions be specific, owned, dated, and tracked to completion, because a PIR whose actions are never done is theatre that produces the same incident again. They read the timeline for the lessons it reveals (slow detection, slow mitigation) beyond the immediate cause.

On writing at scale, they understand that the problems change with volume: a large body of documents needs discoverability (or the best document is unfindable and useless), templates (to raise quality across many authors), a reading culture (or documents are written and never engaged with), and health metrics (to know whether the documentation is actually working). They treat the organisation's documentation as a system to be maintained — a library, not a bookshelf — because they know that without those systems, the collective writing effort rots into an untrusted, unnavigable pile. The principal's view is that writing is high-leverage only if the documents are findable, current, read, and (for PIRs) acted upon — so they invest in the systems that keep a large body of documents genuinely valuable.

Common mistakes

  • PIRs that assign blame, which stops honest contribution and kills organisational learning.
  • PIRs with a shallow root cause ("X forgot") instead of the systemic cause the five-whys reveals.
  • PIR actions that are never tracked to completion, so the same incident recurs.
  • Writing many documents with no discoverability, so they cannot be found and the effort is wasted.
  • No reading culture, so documents are written but never engaged with or acted on.

Interview questions

  1. What makes a post-incident review effective, and why is blamelessness essential? Expected answer: a precise timestamped timeline, a systemic root cause (what the system allowed, not who erred), what went well, and specific owned dated actions tracked to completion; blamelessness is essential because the moment a PIR assigns personal blame, people hide their involvement in future incidents, the information needed to prevent recurrence dries up, and the organisation stops learning. Why it matters: tests whether they understand the PIR's purpose is learning, not blame.

  2. What changes about writing when an organisation has hundreds of documents and many authors? Expected answer: the problems shift from individual craft to systems: discoverability (search, naming, indexing — an unfindable document is useless), templates (to raise quality across many authors), a reading-and-commenting culture (so documents are engaged with), and health metrics (reads, currency, action completion) to know if the documentation is working. It becomes running a library, not a bookshelf. Why it matters: tests whether they can think about documentation at organisational scale.

  3. A PIR identified "the on-call engineer made a mistake" as the root cause. What's wrong with that? Expected answer: it is a blameful, shallow root cause — it stops at a person instead of asking why the system allowed the error (no guardrail, bad tooling, a coupling); it discourages honest future contribution; and it produces no systemic fix, so the incident recurs. The real root cause is what the system allowed, found via the five-whys, and the fix addresses the system. Why it matters: tests understanding of systemic, blameless root-cause analysis.

Practical exercise

Take a recent incident (or near-miss) and write its PIR: a summary with impact, a precise timestamped timeline, a systemic and blameless root cause (use the five-whys to get past the surface), what went well, and specific owned dated actions. Then assess your organisation's documentation at scale: can people find the relevant documents, are there templates, is there a reading culture, and are PIR actions tracked to completion.

Acceptance criteria: your PIR's root cause is systemic and blameless (what the system allowed, not who erred), its timeline is precise enough to reveal secondary lessons (like detection time), and its actions are specific, owned, dated, and framed as tracked to completion; and your scale assessment identifies at least one gap in discoverability, templates, reading culture, or action tracking that is reducing the value of your organisation's documents.

51.10 A quick-reference for the architect's writing

This closing section is a compact reference you can return to — a distillation of the Part into the few decisions and checks that matter most when you sit down to write.

The document-choice decision

Tiny, reversible, one team        -> a one-pager or a Slack message
A single decision worth remembering -> an ADR (immutable; supersede, don't edit)
A system one team will build        -> a design doc (13 sections; never skip
                                       non-goals, rollback, observability)
A change many teams must agree to   -> an RFC (pre-wire -> async review ->
                                       decision meeting; resolve every comment)
Direction for a year or more        -> a strategy memo (Part 52)
Something broke                     -> a blameless PIR (systemic cause, tracked
                                       actions)

The pre-write checklist

Before writing any document, answer these four questions, because they determine everything that follows:

1. WHO is the audience? (Engineers? Executives? Many teams? A future joiner?)
2. WHAT do I want them to DO differently after reading? (The ask.)
3. What is the SHORTEST document that achieves that? (Respect their time.)
4. What is my own position, and am I willing to let writing CHANGE it?
   (Writing is thinking, not transcription of a prejudice.)

The pre-publish checklist

Before sharing a design doc or RFC, verify:

[ ] The summary and the ask are FIRST and stand alone (busy readers stop early).
[ ] Every goal has a NUMBER (so success is checkable).
[ ] Non-goals are written (so scope arguments are pre-empted).
[ ] The alternatives are STEELMANNED, with contextual rejection reasons (trust).
[ ] The rollback is specific and actually possible (an on-call can run it at 2am).
[ ] Observability is named (specific metrics + alert thresholds).
[ ] A container diagram (C4 L2) shows the system's shape (align before detail).
[ ] The key reviewers have been PRE-WIRED (no public ambush).
[ ] It's the shortest version that does the job.

The reviewer's probe list

When reviewing someone else's design, probe systematically rather than by vibe:

Reliability: can it timeout, fail, partially succeed? Blast radius? Dependency down?
Data:        dual-write? Can data be lost/duplicated? Reversible migration? Unbounded growth?
Security:    authn/authz on every path? Injection? Secrets? Tenant/user isolation?
Cost:        cost at peak? Surprising scaling? Unbounded query/fan-out?
Operability: how do we know it's healthy? How do we roll back? Who's paged?
Scaling:     what breaks first at 10x? Hot key, hot partition, single-writer?

The enduring principles

Six things to remember when the specifics fade:

  • Writing is the architect's highest-leverage tool: one-to-many, persistent, async, and it forces your own clarity.
  • Match the document's weight to the decision's size and reversibility.
  • The most-skipped sections — non-goals, rollback, observability — are the ones that save you from incidents and scope wars.
  • Steelman what you reject; strawmen destroy trust in the whole document.
  • The RFC process, not the document alone, creates alignment: pre-wire, resolve every comment, force a decision date.
  • Keep decisions immutable and superseded, not edited; the chain is institutional memory no one person holds.

Return to this reference whenever you sit down to write as an architect; the deeper reasoning behind each line is in the sections above.

Senior Checklist — Part 51

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can pick the right document type for the size and reversibility of a decision
  • I write a design doc with all thirteen sections, and I never skip non-goals, rollback or observability
  • Every goal I write has a number, so success is checkable
  • I steelman the alternatives I reject, with contextual reasons, not strawmen
  • I pre-wire the key reviewers one-on-one before opening an RFC for review
  • I resolve every review comment visibly, so reviewers know they were heard
  • I force a decision date rather than letting an RFC drift forever
  • I draw C4 diagrams at the level the reader needs, and keep them small and honest
  • I supersede decisions rather than editing them in place, and my ADRs form a readable chain
  • I can recognise the doc anti-patterns in my own drafts before anyone else does

Part 51 — Key Takeaways

  • Writing is the architect's primary tool because it is one-to-many, persistent, asynchronous, and it forces clarity in your own thinking before anyone else wastes time on your idea.
  • Match the document to the decision: a one-pager for small reversible choices, an ADR for a single durable decision, a design doc to work out how, an RFC for cross-team agreement, a strategy memo for direction.
  • A strong design doc has a skeleton for a reason; each section answers a reviewer's question in advance, and the most-skipped sections — non-goals, rollback, observability — are the ones that save you from incidents and scope wars.
  • Every goal needs a number, or you will never know whether the project succeeded.
  • Write alternatives honestly; steelman the options you reject, because strawmen destroy trust in the entire document.
  • The RFC process, not the document alone, creates alignment: pre-wire the key reviewers privately, collect comments async, resolve every one visibly, and force a decision date.
  • Run design reviews as a cheap attempt to break the design on paper; require reading beforehand, include an outside reviewer, and probe reliability, data, security, cost and operability systematically.
  • Diagrams earn their place when they replace prose; use the C4 levels for the right zoom, keep diagrams small, and never let them rot into fiction.
  • Decisions have a life: keep ADRs immutable, supersede rather than edit, and let the chain preserve the institutional memory no single person holds.
  • Fight doc rot by making trust legible — status, dates, ownership — because one stale document trusted as current costs more than ten missing ones.
  • The best architecture writing is the plainest: lead with the ask, respect the reader's time, and keep it the shortest length that does the job.

51.8 Reusable templates and building the writing habit

Concept

Everything in this Part becomes real only if you can produce it on a normal Tuesday without heroics. Two things make that possible. The first is a small set of reusable templates — skeletons you copy and fill, so you are never staring at a blank page and never forgetting a section under deadline pressure. The second is a writing habit — the practice, cadence and small techniques that turn writing from a dreaded occasional event into a routine part of how you work. A principal engineer who writes well does not have more talent; they have templates and a habit.

Why does it exist?

Imagine every design doc started from nothing. Each author would invent their own structure, forget a different section each time, and spend the first hour deciding what sections to have instead of thinking about the actual problem. Reviewers would face a different shape every time and never know where to find the rollback plan. Templates exist to remove that waste: the structure is a solved problem, so all your energy goes into the content.

The habit exists because writing under pressure, cold, occasionally, produces bad writing. The engineer who writes a document only when forced, twice a year, is always rusty, always slow, and always resents it. The engineer who writes something small every week — a decision note, a short update, an ADR — stays fluent, so when the big RFC is needed, it is just a longer version of a thing they do all the time.

Mental model

Imagine a chef's mise en place: before service, everything is chopped, measured and arranged, so that during the rush the chef is assembling, not scrambling. Templates are your mise en place for writing — the structure is prepped in advance, so when the moment comes you are filling in content, not inventing a format under pressure. And the habit is practice: a chef who cooks every day is fast and calm during the rush; one who cooks twice a year is slow and panicked. Writing is the same muscle.

How it works

Templates. Keep a small, shared library: a one-pager, a design doc, an ADR, an RFC, a PIR. Each is a copyable skeleton with the sections and one line of guidance per section. Store them where people start documents, so copying the template is easier than not. The templates in this section are complete enough to use directly.

The habit works through a few concrete practices:

1. Write the doc BEFORE the work, not after. The doc is the design, not a record of it.
2. Write a little every week: a decision note, an ADR, an update. Stay fluent.
3. Draft ugly, then edit. Separate getting it down from getting it right.
4. Summary and ask FIRST, always. Write it last, put it first.
5. Time-box the first draft. Ninety minutes, then stop and share for feedback.
6. Read it aloud once. Your ear catches what your eye skips.

The order of writing matters more than people expect. You draft the body first, discover what you actually think, then write the summary and ask last — because you cannot summarise an argument you have not yet made. But you place the summary first, because the reader needs it first. Writing order and reading order are opposites, and confusing them is why so many summaries are vague.

Practical example

An engineer adopts the "write the doc before the work" rule for a schema-change project. Forced to write the rollback section before writing any migration, she realises her planned change — dropping a column — is not reversible once data is gone. That single realisation, surfaced by the template section before she wrote a line of SQL, reshapes the whole plan into an expand-contract migration (Part 31) that is reversible. The template did not document her design; it fixed it, before the cost of the mistake could be incurred.

Artifact example

The ADR template, filled in, short enough to write in fifteen minutes and complete enough to be worth keeping. This is the everyday document that keeps you fluent.

# ADR-052: Use idempotency keys on all payment-mutating endpoints

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-04-18
**Deciders:** payments team, [you]
**Supersedes:** none

## Context
Clients retry failed payment requests (timeouts, flaky mobile networks).
Without idempotency, a retry can charge a customer twice. We had 11 such
double-charge incidents in the last quarter, each a manual refund and a
support ticket. We need retries to be safe.

## Decision
Every payment-mutating endpoint (charge, refund, capture) requires an
`Idempotency-Key` header. We store (key, request-hash, response) in a
`idempotency_keys` table with a 24h TTL. A repeat key returns the stored
response without re-executing. A repeat key with a DIFFERENT request body
returns 409 Conflict.

## Consequences
- Retries become safe; double-charges from client retries eliminated.
- Clients MUST generate and send a key; we document this and reject
  mutating requests without one (400) after a 1-month grace period.
- One new table, modest write volume. TTL sweep keeps it bounded.
- This is now a standard; new mutating endpoints inherit it by default.

This ADR is complete, specific (names the incident count, the header, the 409 behaviour, the TTL), and immutable. In two years, an engineer wondering why every payment endpoint demands an idempotency key has the full answer in one screen. It took fifteen minutes to write and will save hours of confusion. Writing several of these a quarter is how you stay fluent for the RFC that matters.

Real-world scenario

A team introduces a shared template library and a norm: no design work starts without a design doc, and the design doc is the first deliverable, reviewed before code. Skeptics predict it will slow everything down. The opposite happens. Because the templates make starting cheap and the habit makes writing fast, docs stop being a bottleneck. And because flaws surface in the rollback and non-goals sections during design rather than in production, the team's incident rate on new features drops noticeably over two quarters. The writing did not slow delivery; it moved the discovery of problems earlier, where they are cheap, which sped up the parts that used to be slow — the firefighting.

Failure scenario

An engineer who never built a writing habit is suddenly asked to produce a company-critical RFC for a database migration, with executives waiting. Cold and rusty, he stares at the blank page for a day, then produces a sprawling, structureless draft with no summary, no non-goals, and a rollback section that says "we'll figure it out". The review is a disaster: reviewers cannot find the decision, argue about scope he never meant to include, and lose confidence in the migration itself. The migration slips a quarter, not because the plan was bad but because the engineer could not communicate it under pressure. Had he written a small document every week for the past year, the big one would have been routine.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Template worship. Filling every section because it exists, even when a section genuinely does not apply, producing padded documents. Templates are a prompt, not a mandate; skip what truly does not apply, but say why.
  • Writing the doc after the work. It becomes documentation, not design, and loses the chance to fix the design cheaply.
  • Perfectionism on the first draft. Editing while drafting kills momentum. Draft ugly, then edit.
  • Summary written first and left vague. You cannot summarise an argument you have not made. Write the summary last, place it first.
  • No habit, only heroics. Writing only when forced keeps you perpetually rusty, so every document is slow and painful.
  • Templates that are too heavy. A thirteen-section template applied to a two-day task. Keep a light one-pager template for small things.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They invest in templates as a leverage multiplier for the whole org, not just themselves — a good shared template makes every engineer's documents better and more consistent, which is a larger return than improving their own writing alone. They treat writing as a routine muscle, not a special event, and they write small things constantly, so the large things are never a cold start.

They are disciplined about writing the document before the work, because they have learned that the design doc is where the design actually happens — the typing is just transcription once the thinking is done well. And they draft fast and ugly, then edit, because they know the fear of the blank page is really the fear of writing something imperfect, and the cure is to write something imperfect on purpose and fix it.

Common mistakes

  • Reinventing structure every time instead of keeping copyable templates.
  • Writing documentation after the fact instead of writing the design as a document first.
  • Trying to write a polished first draft, which produces paralysis.
  • Only writing when forced, which keeps you permanently rusty.
  • Making every template heavy, so people avoid them for small tasks.

Interview questions

  1. Why write the design doc before doing the work rather than after? Expected answer: because the document is where the design actually gets worked out; sections like rollback and non-goals surface flaws while they are cheap to fix, and writing afterward reduces the doc to lossy documentation that misses the chance to improve the design. Why it matters: tests whether they see writing as thinking or as paperwork.

  2. You freeze up in front of a blank page before a big document. What techniques get you unstuck? Expected answer: start from a template so the structure is solved; draft ugly and edit later; time-box the first draft; write the summary last and place it first; keep a weekly writing habit so you are never cold. Follow-up: why write the summary last.

  3. What goes in your team's template library, and why keep it small? Expected answer: one-pager, design doc, ADR, RFC, PIR — a small set because people can only remember when to use a few, and a small set with clear purposes beats a precise taxonomy nobody follows. Why it matters: tests judgement about process weight.

Practical exercise

Create (or adapt) a template library of five documents for your team: one-pager, design doc, ADR, RFC, PIR. Each should be a copyable skeleton with one line of guidance per section. Then commit to the habit for four weeks: write one small document each week — an ADR for a decision you make, a one-pager for an idea, or a short PIR for a near-miss.

Acceptance criteria: the templates live where people start documents (so copying is easier than not), the one-pager and ADR templates each fit on one screen, and after four weeks you have four real documents written and can honestly say the fourth was faster and easier to write than the first.

Part 52 — Technical Strategy, Vision and Roadmaps

Part 44 said that writing a technical strategy is one of the things that distinguishes staff from senior, and gave a one-paragraph definition. Part 49.5 gave you a build-versus-buy decision table. This Part is the full discipline of technical strategy: what it actually is (and what people wrongly call strategy), how to write one that survives contact with reality, how to connect a two-to-three-year vision to the business, how to sequence a multi-quarter roadmap, how to manage technical debt as a portfolio rather than a guilty backlog, and how to decide whether to adopt a new technology at all.

The word "strategy" is the most abused word in engineering. Most things called strategy are either a list of goals ("be more reliable"), a wish ("move to microservices"), or a roadmap with the reasoning removed. Real strategy is rarer and more useful than any of those, and this Part is about producing the real thing.

The reader this Part assumes is a senior or staff engineer who can design systems and is now being asked, explicitly or by the gap they can feel, to set direction for more than their own team — to answer "where are we going and why" for a group of teams or a whole engineering org.

52.1 Strategy versus vision versus roadmap versus plan

Concept

Four words get used interchangeably and mean four different things, and conflating them is the root of most bad "strategy" documents. A strategy is a way of overcoming a specific challenge: a diagnosis of the situation, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions. A vision is a description of a desirable future state, years out, that gives everyone a shared direction. A roadmap is a time-ordered sequence of what you will do to move toward the vision, respecting dependencies and capacity. A plan is the detailed, near-term breakdown of the next slice of the roadmap into tasks, owners and dates.

They nest: the vision sets the destination, the strategy explains how you will get there despite the obstacles, the roadmap sequences the moves, and the plan executes the next move.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a team that has a roadmap but no strategy. The roadmap says: Q1 split the monolith's payment module, Q2 adopt Kafka, Q3 move to Kubernetes. It looks organised. But ask "why these, in this order, and what are we trying to achieve" and nobody can answer, because the roadmap is a list of activities with the reasoning deleted. When priorities shift — and they always do — the team has no basis for deciding what to drop, because they never knew why anything was on the list. They cut the wrong thing, or they cling to all of it and burn out.

The distinction exists so that each artifact can do its job. A vision without a strategy is a daydream. A strategy without a roadmap never gets executed. A roadmap without a strategy is a to-do list that collapses under the first reprioritisation. A plan without a roadmap is busywork. You need all four, and you need to know which one you are writing.

Mental model

Imagine planning a journey across a continent.

Vision:   "Reach the west coast" — the destination, inspiring, durable.
Strategy: "The mountains block the direct route, and winter is coming.
           So we go south around the range before the passes close, trading
           distance for safety." — the way past the specific obstacle.
Roadmap:  "Week 1 reach the river crossing; week 2 the southern pass;
           week 3 the plains." — the sequence, respecting terrain.
Plan:     "Tomorrow: pack, buy supplies, leave by 6am, make 40 miles."
          — the next concrete steps.

The vision never changes. The strategy changes if the obstacle changes (the pass is already closed — now what). The roadmap changes often as you learn the terrain. The plan changes daily. People who call a roadmap a strategy have a journey with a to-do list but no reasoning about the mountains, and they are the ones who walk straight into a closed pass.

How it works

The four artifacts differ along clear dimensions. This table is the one to internalise.

Dimension Vision Strategy Roadmap Plan
Question it answers Where are we going? How do we get there despite the obstacle? In what order do we move? What do we do next?
Horizon 2 to 5 years 1 to 3 years 2 to 6 quarters This quarter / sprint
Changes Rarely When the obstacle or landscape changes Every quarter as you learn Constantly
Contains A desirable future state Diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions Sequenced initiatives with dependencies Tasks, owners, dates
Fails when It is just a slogan It is a list of goals with no diagnosis It has no reasoning behind the order It is disconnected from the roadmap
Audience Everyone Leadership and senior engineers Teams and their leads The executing team

The flow between them:

flowchart LR
    V["Vision - where we're going - 2-5 yrs"] --> S["Strategy - how, past the obstacle - 1-3 yrs"]
    S --> R["Roadmap - sequence - 2-6 quarters"]
    R --> P["Plan - next steps - this quarter"]
    P -->|"what we learn executing"| R
    R -->|"what we learn about the obstacle"| S

Note the feedback arrows. Execution teaches you about the terrain, which updates the roadmap; the roadmap sometimes teaches you the obstacle is different than you thought, which updates the strategy. The vision rarely moves. A team that never updates its roadmap from execution learnings is marching to a map it knows is wrong.

Practical example

An e-commerce company is slowing down. Features that took two weeks now take six. Here is each artifact for that situation, done right.

  • Vision: "Any team can ship a customer-facing change end to end in under a day, independently, without waiting on another team." Durable, inspiring, measurable, years out.
  • Strategy: "The slowdown is caused by a single shared monolith and a single shared database that every team deploys and migrates together, so every change is serialised behind every other change [diagnosis]. We will reduce coupling by giving teams ownership of bounded contexts with their own data and deploy pipelines, extracting services only where a team is genuinely blocked, and we will refuse to extract services that are not blocked because that trades one kind of coupling for a worse one [guiding policy + what we refuse]. Concretely: establish a modular monolith with enforced boundaries first, extract the two most-blocked contexts, and build the platform that makes independent deploys cheap [coherent actions]."
  • Roadmap: "Q1 enforce module boundaries + CI per module. Q2 extract payments (most-blocked) with its own DB. Q3 build the service template + deploy platform. Q4 extract fulfilment."
  • Plan: "This sprint: add the lint rule blocking cross-module imports, split the test suite per module, document the first module's public interface."

Notice the strategy is the only artifact with a diagnosis and a refusal. That is what makes it a strategy and not a roadmap.

Artifact example

The same situation, shown as the one-paragraph "strategy kernel" — the test of whether you have a strategy at all. If you cannot fill all three slots with specifics, you have a wish, not a strategy.

## Strategy kernel: engineering velocity

DIAGNOSIS (the crux of the problem, honestly):
One monolith + one shared database means every team's deploys and schema
migrations are serialised. Lead time for a change has risen from ~10 to
~30 days as the team grew from 12 to 45. The problem is COUPLING, not
effort or skill.

GUIDING POLICY (the approach, including what we will NOT do):
Reduce coupling by giving teams ownership of bounded contexts with their
own data and independent deploys. Extract services ONLY where a team is
measurably blocked. We will NOT do a big-bang microservices rewrite, and
we will NOT extract a service just because a boundary exists — unblocking
is the only justification.

COHERENT ACTIONS (moves that reinforce each other):
1. Modular monolith with enforced boundaries (enables later extraction).
2. Extract the two most-blocked contexts, each with its own DB.
3. Build a service template + deploy platform (makes #2 cheap and repeatable).
These compound: #1 makes #2 safe, #3 makes #2 and all future extractions cheap.

This kernel is three paragraphs and it is worth more than a forty-slide deck, because it names the real problem, commits to an approach, says what it refuses to do, and shows that the actions reinforce each other rather than being a random list. If someone asks "should we extract the reporting service", you can answer from the kernel: is reporting blocked? No? Then no.

Real-world scenario

A VP asks a principal engineer for "a technical strategy" and gets handed, by three different teams, three documents: a list of goals ("improve reliability, reduce costs, increase velocity"), a roadmap ("Q1 Kafka, Q2 K8s"), and a vision slogan ("world-class engineering"). None of them is a strategy. The principal engineer's job is to produce the missing middle: the diagnosis of why the company is where it is, the guiding policy for getting out, and the coherent actions. When he does, the three existing documents suddenly have a spine — the goals become the vision's measures, the roadmap's order now has a reason, and the slogan has substance. The strategy did not replace the other artifacts; it connected them.

Failure scenario

A company publishes a "technical strategy" that is really a list of aspirations: be more scalable, be more reliable, adopt modern technology, reduce technical debt. Everyone nods; it sounds right. But because there is no diagnosis and no guiding policy, it provides no basis for any actual decision. When two teams want the same engineers, the strategy cannot adjudicate, because "be more scalable" and "be more reliable" both sound strategic and point in different directions. When a tempting new technology appears, the strategy cannot say no, because "adopt modern technology" says yes to everything. The document exists, it was expensive to produce, and it changes nothing — because a list of good things is not a strategy. Strategy is choice, and a document that chooses nothing is not one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Roadmap called strategy. A sequence of activities with the reasoning removed. Collapses under the first reprioritisation because nobody knows why anything is on it.
  • Goals called strategy. "Be more reliable, be faster." Sounds strategic, adjudicates nothing, says no to nothing.
  • Vision with no strategy. An inspiring destination and no account of the obstacle in the way. A daydream.
  • Strategy with no diagnosis. Jumps straight to actions without naming the real problem, so the actions often address a symptom, not the cause.
  • Strategy that refuses nothing. If it does not say what you will not do, it is not making choices, so it is not a strategy.
  • Never updating from execution. Treating the roadmap as fixed and ignoring what building teaches you about the terrain.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They know which of the four they are writing and never confuse them, because each has a different job and conflating them produces documents that do none of the jobs. They treat the diagnosis as the hard, valuable part — most people skip straight to actions, and most bad strategy is an action list addressing a misdiagnosed problem. They insist that a real strategy says what it refuses to do, because a strategy that says yes to everything has made no choices and will not survive the first resource conflict.

They also keep the vision stable and the roadmap fluid, and they are suspicious of anyone whose roadmap never changes — it means execution is teaching them nothing, or they are not listening. And they write the strategy kernel first, in three paragraphs, before any deck, because if it cannot be said in three paragraphs the thinking is not done.

Common mistakes

  • Calling a roadmap a strategy, so the plan collapses the moment priorities shift.
  • Writing a list of goals and believing it is strategy, because it adjudicates nothing.
  • Skipping the diagnosis and jumping to actions that treat symptoms.
  • Refusing to refuse anything, which means no real choices were made.
  • Freezing the roadmap and ignoring what execution reveals about the terrain.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a strategy and a roadmap, and why does it matter? Expected answer: a strategy is a diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions for overcoming a specific obstacle; a roadmap is a time-ordered sequence of initiatives. It matters because a roadmap without a strategy has no reasoning behind the order, so it collapses under reprioritisation and cannot tell you what to cut. Why it matters: this is the central confusion in the whole topic.

  2. I give you a "strategy" that says: be more scalable, reliable, and modern. What is wrong with it? Expected answer: it is a list of goals, not a strategy — no diagnosis of the real problem, no guiding policy, and crucially it refuses nothing, so it cannot adjudicate a resource conflict or say no to a tempting technology. Follow-up: turn it into a real strategy for a specific situation.

  3. Why must a strategy say what you will not do? Expected answer: because strategy is choice; finite resources mean choosing some things is refusing others, and a document that commits to everything has made no choices and provides no basis for decisions. Why it matters: tests whether they understand the essence of strategy versus aspiration.

Practical exercise

Pick a real challenge your engineering org faces (velocity, reliability, cost, a platform gap). Write its strategy kernel: three paragraphs — diagnosis (the honest crux of the problem, with a number), guiding policy (the approach plus at least one explicit "we will NOT"), and coherent actions (three moves that reinforce each other). Then separately write the one-sentence vision it serves.

Acceptance criteria: the diagnosis names a cause, not a symptom, and includes a number; the guiding policy contains at least one concrete refusal; the three actions can be shown to reinforce one another (each makes the next cheaper or safer); and a colleague reading the kernel can use it to say no to a plausible-but-off-strategy proposal you give them.

52.2 Writing a strategy: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions

Concept

A good strategy has exactly three parts, and they must appear in order: a diagnosis that names the real problem honestly, a guiding policy that chooses an overall approach to that problem (including what you will not do), and a set of coherent actions that carry out the policy and reinforce one another. This structure comes from Richard Rumelt's work on strategy and it is the single most useful frame an engineering leader can hold. Most documents called strategy are missing the diagnosis entirely and are therefore a list of actions solving an unstated, often wrong, problem.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a doctor who skips the diagnosis and jumps straight to treatment: "take these pills, do this exercise, change your diet". The treatments might be individually fine, but without a diagnosis they are a guess, and if the real problem is something else entirely, the treatments waste time while the patient gets worse. Strategy without diagnosis is exactly this: a set of actions that might be fine but are untethered from the actual problem, so they often treat a symptom while the disease progresses.

The three-part structure exists to force the diagnosis to come first, and to make the actions provably follow from it. It also exists to make strategy falsifiable: if you state the diagnosis, someone can check whether it is right, and if the actions do not follow from the policy, someone can point that out. A list of goals cannot be wrong; a diagnosis can, which is what makes it useful.

Mental model

Imagine a detective. The bad detective arrests the first plausible suspect (jumps to an action). The good detective first works out what actually happened (diagnosis), then decides on an approach to catch the culprit given the constraints (guiding policy — "we cannot prove intent, so we build the timeline from the physical evidence"), then takes specific steps that each advance that approach and support the others (coherent actions — interview the witness whose testimony anchors the timeline, then get the records that corroborate it). The structure is: understand, decide an approach, act coherently. Skip the understanding and you arrest the wrong person confidently.

How it works

Each part has a job and a quality test.

1. Diagnosis. Name the crux of the problem — the one or two things that, if addressed, unlock the rest. Good diagnosis is simplifying: it cuts through the overwhelming detail of the situation to the thing that matters. It must be honest, including the parts that embarrass you. Quality test: does it identify a cause, not a symptom, and is it specific enough to be wrong?

2. Guiding policy. The overall approach to the diagnosed problem. It is a method, not a goal. It channels effort in one direction and, crucially, rules out others. Quality test: does it say what you will not do, and would a smart colleague be able to propose a different policy for the same diagnosis (if not, it is not really a choice)?

3. Coherent actions. The concrete, coordinated moves that carry out the policy. "Coherent" is the operative word: the actions must reinforce each other, not pull in different directions or merely coexist. Quality test: does each action make another cheaper, safer, or more likely to succeed — or are they just a list?

flowchart TB
    D["Diagnosis: the real problem - a cause, not a symptom"] --> G["Guiding policy: the approach + what we refuse"]
    G --> A1["Action 1"]
    G --> A2["Action 2"]
    G --> A3["Action 3"]
    A1 -.->|"reinforces"| A2
    A2 -.->|"reinforces"| A3
    A1 -.->|"reinforces"| A3

The dotted reinforcement arrows are what separate coherent actions from a to-do list. If you remove them and the actions still stand alone, you have a list, not a strategy.

Practical example — good versus bad

A ride-booking company has a reliability problem. Here is the same situation strategised badly and well.

Bad strategy (goals disguised):

Our strategy is to achieve 99.95% availability, reduce incident count by 50%, improve our on-call experience, and adopt chaos engineering.

This is four goals. No diagnosis (why is reliability bad?), no policy (what is the approach?), no coherence (chaos engineering and on-call experience are unrelated moves). It cannot adjudicate anything and it says no to nothing.

Good strategy:

Diagnosis: 70% of our customer-facing incidents in the last year originated in two places: the shared payments database (a single point of failure three services depend on) and uncontrolled retry storms (services retry aggressively with no backoff or circuit breaking, so one slow dependency cascades into a full outage). Reliability is not a culture problem or an effort problem; it is these two specific architectural weaknesses.

Guiding policy: We will eliminate the two structural causes before investing in anything else reliability-related. We will NOT spend this year on chaos engineering, extra on-call tooling, or a general "reliability culture" push — those address symptoms or come later. We concentrate force on the two causes.

Coherent actions: (1) Give payments its own database and remove the other two services' direct access, replacing it with an API — this removes the single point of failure. (2) Ship a shared resilience library (timeouts, backoff, circuit breaker) and make it the default in the service template — this ends retry storms. (3) Add the two alerts that would have caught both failure classes early (payments-DB saturation, retry-rate spike). Action 2's library is what makes action 1's new payments API safe to call; action 3 catches regressions of both. They reinforce.

The good version diagnoses a cause, refuses three tempting-but-wrong investments, and its three actions reinforce each other. That is a strategy.

Artifact example

A one-page technical vision document (2-3 year horizon) connected explicitly to business goals — the artifact that sits above the strategy and gives it a destination.

# Technical Vision 2026-2028: Independent, reliable delivery

## The future we are building toward (3 years)
Any product team can design, ship, and operate a customer-facing change
end to end — in under a day, during business hours, without coordinating
a release with another team, and without fearing a cascading outage.

## Why this matters to the business
- Faster time-to-market: today a feature takes ~30 days of lead time;
  the business wants to test 3x as many ideas per quarter. That is only
  possible if teams ship independently.
- Reliability as a growth lever: each hour of payment downtime costs an
  estimated $45k in lost orders and churn. Structural reliability
  protects revenue, not just uptime SLAs.
- Scaling the org: we plan to grow from 45 to ~100 engineers. Coupled
  systems do not scale with headcount; independent teams do.

## The three pillars (what must be true)
1. OWNERSHIP: every bounded context has one team, its own data, and its
   own deploy pipeline.
2. SAFETY: every service ships with timeouts, backoff, circuit breaking
   and the standard alerts, by default, from the template.
3. SELF-SERVICE: creating, deploying and observing a service is a
   paved-road operation, not a ticket to the platform team.

## How we will know we are getting there (the measures)
- Lead time for change: 30 days -> under 1 day (DORA).
- Deploy frequency: weekly -> on-demand, multiple per day.
- Change failure rate: hold under 15% while frequency rises.
- Cross-team blocking dependencies per feature: ~3 -> near 0.

## What this vision is NOT
Not a mandate for microservices everywhere. Not a rewrite. Not a reason
to adopt every modern tool. The simplest architecture that delivers
independent, reliable delivery wins.

The vision is inspiring but grounded: it names the future state, ties each benefit to a business number ($45k/hour, 3x ideas, 45-to-100 engineers), states the pillars that must be true, gives DORA-style measures so progress is checkable, and — like a good strategy — says what it is not. A vision that cannot be measured is a slogan; this one can.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer writes the vision above and the reliability strategy from the practical example. A quarter later, an enthusiastic team proposes adopting a fashionable service mesh "for reliability". The principal does not argue about the mesh on its merits. He points at the diagnosis: our incidents come from a shared database and retry storms, not from a lack of mesh features. A mesh would add operational surface without touching either cause. The proposal is declined in five minutes, with the strategy as the reason, and the team redirects its energy to the resilience library, which does address the diagnosed cause. That is strategy doing its job: making a hard decision easy and fast because the reasoning was done in advance.

Failure scenario

An org adopts a strategy with a strong guiding policy ("concentrate on the two structural causes") but incoherent actions, chosen by committee so every team got their pet project in: give payments its own database (good, on-policy), and adopt a new programming language (unrelated), and rewrite the mobile API (unrelated), and ship the resilience library (on-policy). The two on-policy actions get half the resources because the two off-policy ones consumed the rest. A year later reliability is marginally better, the language migration is half-done and now a liability, and the strategy is declared a failure. The diagnosis was right and the policy was right; the actions were an incoherent compromise that diluted the force the policy demanded. Coherence is not optional; it is where strategies are usually killed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No diagnosis. Jumps to actions; often treats a symptom while the real cause worsens.
  • Diagnosis that is a symptom. "We have too many incidents" is a symptom; "a shared database is a single point of failure for three services" is a cause.
  • Guiding policy that is a goal. "Be more reliable" is a goal; "eliminate the two structural causes before anything else" is a policy.
  • Incoherent actions. A committee-compromise list where off-policy items dilute the on-policy ones. The most common way good strategies die.
  • No refusal. The policy does not rule anything out, so force is never concentrated.
  • Diagnosis nobody will say aloud. The real cause is politically awkward (a VP's pet project, a sacred-cow service), so the strategy quietly addresses something safer and achieves nothing.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They spend most of their strategy effort on the diagnosis, because it is the hardest and most valuable part and because a wrong diagnosis makes everything downstream wrong. They are willing to name the awkward cause — the sacred-cow service, the decision a senior leader made — because a strategy that flinches from the real problem is theatre. They treat the guiding policy's refusals as the heart of the choice, and they guard the coherence of the actions fiercely against committee dilution, because they have watched good strategies die not from a bad diagnosis but from an action list that tried to please everyone.

They also connect the strategy upward to a measurable vision and a business number, because a strategy that engineers love but that leadership cannot connect to revenue, cost or risk will lose its funding to one that can. The vision is how the strategy earns its budget.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping the diagnosis and producing an action list that treats symptoms.
  • Writing a symptom as the diagnosis, so the actions miss the cause.
  • A guiding policy that is secretly a goal, choosing no approach.
  • Letting the action list become a committee compromise, destroying coherence.
  • Avoiding the politically awkward real cause, so the strategy quietly addresses something safe and useless.

Interview questions

  1. What are the three parts of a strategy, and which is hardest and most valuable? Expected answer: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions; the diagnosis is hardest and most valuable because a wrong one makes everything downstream wrong, and most "strategies" skip it. Follow-up: give an example of a cause versus a symptom in a diagnosis.

  2. Your strategy has a good diagnosis and policy, but after a year it failed. What is the most likely reason? Expected answer: incoherent actions — a committee compromise where off-policy initiatives diluted the on-policy ones, so force was never concentrated as the policy demanded. Why it matters: tests whether they know where strategies actually die, which is usually in the actions, not the thinking.

  3. Why must a technical vision be measurable, and how do you tie it to the business? Expected answer: an unmeasurable vision is a slogan with no way to know if you are progressing; you tie it to business by connecting each pillar to a number leadership cares about — revenue protected, time-to-market, cost, ability to scale the org. Follow-up: turn "world-class reliability" into a measurable, business-connected vision.

Practical exercise

Take the strategy kernel you wrote in 52.1 and stress-test its three parts. For the diagnosis, ask a trusted colleague whether it names a cause or a symptom, and whether there is a more honest (possibly more awkward) diagnosis you avoided. For the actions, draw the reinforcement arrows: can you show each action making another cheaper or safer? Remove any action that stands alone and does not reinforce the others. Then write the one-page vision it serves, with at least three business-connected measures.

Acceptance criteria: your diagnosis survives the cause-versus-symptom test; your guiding policy contains at least one refusal a reasonable person might have chosen differently; every surviving action demonstrably reinforces at least one other; and your vision has at least three measures each tied to a business number (revenue, cost, time-to-market, or org scale).

52.3 Building a multi-quarter roadmap: sequencing, dependencies and capacity

Concept

A roadmap turns a strategy into a sequence of initiatives over time. The craft is not drawing the Gantt chart; it is the sequencing — deciding what comes before what, so that dependencies are respected, risk is front-loaded, early wins build momentum, and the plan fits the capacity you actually have rather than the capacity you wish you had. A roadmap that ignores dependencies builds the roof before the walls. A roadmap that ignores capacity promises twelve quarters of work in four and fails publicly.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a strategy with five coherent actions and no roadmap. The teams start all five at once, because they are all important. Each is now understaffed, each takes three times as long, and three of them turn out to depend on the fourth, which nobody sequenced first, so they stall halfway and have to be redone. A year later, five things are 60% done, which in software means zero things are done, because a half-built platform has all the cost and none of the benefit.

The roadmap exists to impose an order that respects reality: you cannot build the service-extraction on top of boundaries you have not enforced yet; you cannot ship three platform features with a team that can ship one. Sequencing is how a strategy becomes achievable instead of merely correct.

Mental model

Imagine building a house. You cannot choose the order of construction freely: the foundation must precede the walls, the walls precede the roof, the plumbing rough-in must happen before the walls are closed up. Some things can happen in parallel (electrical and plumbing), some strictly cannot (roof after walls). And you have a fixed crew — five builders, not fifty — so even work that could be parallel is limited by how many hands you have. A roadmap is the construction schedule: it respects what must come first, parallelises what can, and never schedules more simultaneous work than the crew can do. Build the roof first and it collapses; that is a dependency violation. Schedule ten tasks for five builders and everything slips; that is a capacity violation.

How it works

Four forces shape the sequence.

  1. Dependencies. Some initiatives are prerequisites for others. Map them as a directed graph; the roadmap must be a valid ordering of that graph (nothing scheduled before its prerequisites).
  2. Risk. Front-load the riskiest, most uncertain work. If something might be impossible or might blow up the plan, you want to learn that in quarter one, when you can still adjust, not in quarter four, when the whole roadmap depends on it.
  3. Momentum. Schedule an early, visible win. Teams and stakeholders lose faith in long programs that show nothing for six months. An early win buys you the patience to do the slow structural work.
  4. Capacity. The total work scheduled in any quarter must fit the teams you have, with realistic allowance for on-call, interrupts, and the fact that people take holidays and leave. Over-scheduling is the most common roadmap failure.
flowchart LR
    B["Enforce module boundaries (Q1)"] --> E1["Extract payments (Q2)"]
    T["Service template + platform (Q2-Q3)"] --> E1
    T --> E2["Extract fulfilment (Q4)"]
    E1 --> E2
    B --> E2

This dependency graph for the velocity strategy shows why boundaries (B) and the platform/template (T) must precede extractions (E1, E2): you cannot cleanly extract a service whose boundaries are not enforced, and extracting without the template means hand-rolling pipelines each time. A valid roadmap respects every arrow.

A capacity view sits alongside it:

Quarter Team Platform (6 eng) Team Payments (5 eng) Team Fulfilment (5 eng)
Q1 Boundary lint + CI split Support boundary work in payments module Support boundary work
Q2 Service template v1 Extract payments (own DB) Business-as-usual + readiness
Q3 Deploy platform (self-service) Harden payments service Prep fulfilment extraction
Q4 Platform support + next paved road BAU Extract fulfilment

Each cell is one team's quarter, and no team has two major initiatives at once. That is a capacity-honest roadmap.

Practical example

A food-delivery company's platform team wants to deliver three things from its strategy: a service template, a self-service deploy platform, and a centralised secrets manager. All three are valuable. A naive roadmap starts all three in Q1. The capacity-honest, dependency-aware roadmap sequences them: the secrets manager first (Q1), because both the template and the deploy platform need to consume secrets, so it is a prerequisite; the service template second (Q2), as the most visible early win that every team immediately benefits from; the deploy platform third (Q3), the largest and riskiest piece, scheduled once the team has shipped two successes and built confidence and once its prerequisites exist. Same three initiatives, but sequenced so each is fully staffed, dependencies are respected, and momentum is built before the hard part.

Artifact example

A multi-quarter roadmap one-pager — the artifact you actually circulate. It leads with the strategy it serves, shows the sequence with its reasoning, and is explicit about capacity and what is deliberately deferred.

# Platform Roadmap 2026 (serves the Engineering Velocity strategy)

## What this roadmap delivers
Independent, safe, self-service delivery for product teams. See strategy
kernel: the crux is coupling; these initiatives remove it.

## Sequence and reasoning
| Q | Initiative | Why now (dependency / risk / momentum) |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Secrets manager | Prerequisite: template & deploy platform both need it. Low risk, do it first. |
| Q1 | Boundary enforcement (lint + CI) | Prerequisite for any clean extraction. Cheap, high leverage. |
| Q2 | Service template v1 | Early visible win — every team benefits immediately. Depends on secrets. |
| Q2 | Extract payments | Most-blocked context. Depends on boundaries. Front-loads extraction risk. |
| Q3 | Self-service deploy platform | Largest, riskiest. Scheduled after 2 wins build confidence + prereqs exist. |
| Q4 | Extract fulfilment | Depends on template + platform being real. Cheap by now. |

## Capacity assumptions (honest)
- Platform team = 6 engineers, but plan for ~4.5 effective (on-call,
  interrupts, 1 known departure in Q2). Roadmap is sized to 4.5, not 6.
- Product teams contribute ~1 eng each during their own extraction quarter.

## Explicitly deferred (NOT this year)
- Multi-region deploys (no business driver yet; revisit 2027).
- Service mesh (our incidents are not mesh-shaped; see reliability strategy).
- Internal developer portal UI (the CLI paved road is enough for now).

## How we'll know it's working
- Lead time for change trending 30d -> <5d by Q4 (on the way to <1d).
- Two services extracted and independently deployable by year end.
- Platform team interrupt load (tickets) falling as self-service lands.

Notice the three features that make it credible: the "why now" column gives a reason for every position in the sequence (so it survives reprioritisation), the capacity section plans for 4.5 effective engineers not the nominal 6 (so it is achievable), and the "explicitly deferred" section says no to three tempting things (so scope is controlled). A roadmap without those three is a wish list with dates.

Real-world scenario

A new engineering director inherits a roadmap that promises fourteen initiatives in the year with a team that can realistically deliver five. Everyone knew it was undeliverable, but nobody wanted to be the one to cut it, so it was approved and is now failing on every front. The principal engineer helps the director fix it with one move: size the roadmap to 4.5 effective engineers per team (accounting for on-call, interrupts and a known departure), which forces the fourteen initiatives down to five, and make the nine deferred items explicit in a "not this year" section with reasons. The painful part is not the sequencing; it is saying no to nine things stakeholders wanted. But the honest roadmap, delivered, beats the dishonest one, failed — and the explicit "not this year" list actually reduces thrash, because stakeholders stop re-asking for things they can see were deliberately deferred.

Failure scenario

A team builds a roadmap that ignores a dependency. It schedules "extract the payments service" in Q1 and "enforce module boundaries" in Q3, because boundaries felt like cleanup and extraction felt urgent. In Q1 they try to extract payments and discover the module has tendrils into six other modules that import its internals directly — exactly what boundary enforcement would have surfaced and prevented. The extraction balloons from one quarter to three, drags in five other teams to untangle the imports, and misses its deadline badly. The work was all necessary; the order was wrong. Boundaries were a prerequisite for extraction, and scheduling the prerequisite after the thing that needed it turned a clean one-quarter job into a three-quarter mess. Dependency order is not a nicety; it is the difference between a smooth roadmap and a cascading slip.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Over-scheduling. Sizing the roadmap to nominal headcount instead of effective capacity (minus on-call, interrupts, departures, holidays). The most common failure; everything slips.
  • Dependency violation. Scheduling something before its prerequisite, so it balloons when the missing foundation surfaces.
  • Risk at the end. The riskiest, most uncertain initiative scheduled last, so you discover it is infeasible after everything downstream has committed to it.
  • No early win. Six months of invisible structural work; stakeholders lose faith and pull funding before the payoff.
  • No explicit deferrals. Everything that was not chosen stays implicitly "maybe", so stakeholders keep re-asking and the team keeps re-litigating.
  • Roadmap never revisited. Treated as a contract rather than a living plan; it drifts from reality as the quarter teaches you things.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They sequence by dependency and risk first, momentum second, and they are ruthless about capacity, because they have learned that the gap between nominal and effective headcount is where roadmaps quietly die.
