They front-load risk deliberately — they want the thing that could sink the plan to be attempted early, while there is still room to adjust, not discovered in Q4. They insist on at least one early, visible win, because they know that a long program with nothing to show loses its funding before it can deliver, however correct it is.

They also make deferrals explicit, because an unstated "no" gets re-asked endlessly, and a stated "no, and here is why, revisit in 2027" actually sticks and reduces thrash. And they treat the roadmap as a living document that the quarter's learnings revise, not a contract — a roadmap that never changes means execution is teaching nobody anything.

Common mistakes

  • Sizing to nominal headcount, so the roadmap is undeliverable from day one.
  • Violating dependency order because the dependent work felt more urgent than its prerequisite.
  • Scheduling the riskiest work last, so infeasibility is discovered too late to adjust.
  • No early win, so the program loses faith and funding before the payoff.
  • Leaving deferrals implicit, so stakeholders re-ask and the team re-litigates endlessly.

Interview questions

  1. How do you sequence a multi-quarter roadmap? Expected answer: respect dependencies (nothing before its prerequisite), front-load risk (learn the plan-killers early), schedule an early visible win for momentum, and size everything to effective (not nominal) capacity. Follow-up: why front-load risk rather than tackle the easy things first.

  2. A roadmap promised fourteen initiatives and delivered four. Diagnose it. Expected answer: almost certainly over-scheduled against nominal rather than effective capacity; probably also lacked explicit deferrals so scope was never controlled. Fix by sizing to effective capacity and making the cut list explicit with reasons. Why it matters: tests capacity realism, the most common roadmap failure.

  3. Why make deferred items explicit instead of just leaving them off the roadmap? Expected answer: an unstated "no" gets re-asked and re-litigated, consuming energy; an explicit "not this year, here's why, revisit then" sticks, reduces thrash, and shows stakeholders their request was considered, not forgotten. Why it matters: tests understanding of roadmaps as communication tools, not just plans.

Practical exercise

Take the coherent actions from your strategy (52.1/52.2) and build a four-quarter roadmap. Draw the dependency graph first (as a Mermaid diagram), then place initiatives in quarters respecting it, front-loading risk and scheduling one early win. Build a capacity table that uses effective headcount (subtract a realistic amount for on-call, interrupts and known departures). Finally, write the "explicitly deferred" section with at least three items and a reason for each.

Acceptance criteria: the sequence violates no dependency arrow; the riskiest initiative is in Q1 or Q2; there is a visible win by Q2; the total work per quarter fits effective (not nominal) capacity; and the deferred list says no to at least three tempting things with reasons.

52.4 Managing technical debt as a portfolio

Concept

Technical debt is usually treated as a guilty backlog — an undifferentiated pile of "stuff we should clean up someday" that always loses to features. Managing it as a portfolio means treating it the way a finance team treats debt and investments: classify it by type, quantify its ongoing cost in real units (incidents, lead-time, toil hours), decide which debt is worth paying down and which to carry deliberately, and fund the paydown through explicit mechanisms rather than hope. Part 48 catalogued the anti-patterns that create debt; this section is about managing the debt you have.

Why does it exist?

Imagine your personal finances as one undifferentiated pile labelled "money stuff". You could not decide whether to pay off the credit card (28% interest) or the mortgage (4%), because you never separated them or measured their cost. You would make random payments and stay poor. Technical debt treated as one pile behaves the same way: you cannot decide what to fix because you never classified it or measured what it costs you, so paydown is random and ineffective, and debt work always loses to features because it has no number to defend itself with.

The portfolio approach exists to give debt a cost you can measure and compare, so that paying it down becomes a rational investment decision ("this debt costs us 40 engineer-hours a month; fixing it costs 120 hours; it pays back in three months") rather than a guilt-driven, losing argument against features.

Mental model

Imagine a portfolio of loans. Some are high-interest (they cost you a lot every month you carry them). Some are low-interest (cheap to carry, no rush). Some you took on deliberately and plan to pay off at a specific time (a bridge loan). Some are predatory and compounding (they get worse fast). A good portfolio manager does not pay them all off equally; they attack the high-interest compounding debt first, carry the cheap debt happily, and plan the deliberate debt's payoff. Technical debt is identical: the skill is knowing the interest rate of each piece and attacking in the right order, not feeling guilty about all of it at once.

How it works

Three steps: classify, quantify, fund.

Classify. Not all debt is the same. A useful taxonomy:

Type What it is Example Treatment
Deliberate + prudent Chosen shortcut with a plan to fix "Ship with a manual process now, automate in Q2" Track; pay off as planned
Deliberate + reckless Shortcut with no plan "No tests, no time" Stop creating it; schedule paydown
Accidental + prudent Learned a better way after the fact "Now we know the right boundary" Refactor opportunistically
Accidental + reckless Didn't know what you were doing Tangled module from a rushed junior Prioritise by cost
Bit rot / decay Debt from the world changing EOL dependency, deprecated API Treat as maintenance, schedule before EOL

Quantify. Give each significant piece of debt a cost in real units, measured, not guessed:

  • Incident cost: how many incidents (and hours of outage, and dollars) did this debt cause last quarter?
  • Lead-time cost: how much longer does a typical change take because of this debt? (e.g. "touching the order module requires understanding 4,000 lines of tangled code, adding ~2 days per change").
  • Toil hours: how many hours of manual work per week does this debt impose? (e.g. "the manual reconciliation this missing automation requires: 6 hours/week").

Fund. Debt paydown needs a funding mechanism, because it loses to features by default:

1. The 20% rule:     a fixed fraction of every team's capacity goes to debt,
                     always, no negotiation. Simple, sustainable, invisible gains.
2. Debt sprints:     periodic sprints dedicated to paydown. Visible but easy to
                     cancel when features are hot.
3. Attach to features: pay down the debt in the area a feature touches, funded
                     by the feature. "Boy scout rule" at project scale.
4. Fund the top N:   quantify, rank by cost, and explicitly fund paying down the
                     highest-cost items as named projects with ROI.

Most mature orgs use a blend: a baseline 20% for small continuous paydown, plus explicitly-funded projects for the few high-cost items that need a concentrated effort.

Practical example

An order team's "order module" is their worst debt. Managed as a portfolio: they classify it as accidental+reckless (grew tangled over three years of rushed changes). They quantify it: it caused 4 of last quarter's 9 incidents (~6 hours outage, ~$30k), and every change to it takes ~2 extra days (measured across the last 20 changes), and it generates ~6 hours/week of manual order-correction toil. That is a concrete, defensible cost: roughly 2 engineer-days per change plus 6 hours/week plus a share of incident cost. They estimate the refactor at 6 engineer-weeks. The ROI argument writes itself: 6 weeks of investment against ~25 engineer-days/quarter of ongoing cost means payback in under a quarter. Funded as a named project, not as guilty backlog, it gets done — because it has a number.

Artifact example

A technical-debt register with the portfolio framing — the artifact that turns "we have a lot of debt" into fundable decisions.

# Technical Debt Register — Order Platform (reviewed quarterly)

| Item | Type | Measured cost / quarter | Fix estimate | Interest | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tangled order module | Accidental/reckless | 4 incidents (~$30k), +2d per change (~25 eng-days), 6h/wk toil | 6 eng-weeks | HIGH | FUND NOW (project ORD-refactor, Q2) |
| No idempotency on refunds | Deliberate/reckless | 11 double-refund incidents, ~22h support | 1 eng-week | HIGH | FUND NOW (ADR-052) |
| Sequelize + TypeORM both used | Accidental/prudent | Confusion, ~0.5d onboarding/eng, no incidents | 4 eng-weeks | LOW | CARRY — cheap to hold, revisit 2027 |
| Manual tier-config deploy | Deliberate/prudent | 2h/wk toil, planned to automate | 1 eng-week | MEDIUM | PAY in 20% capacity, Q2-Q3 |
| EOL Node 18 | Bit rot | None yet; EOL in 8 months | 2 eng-weeks | MEDIUM (rising) | SCHEDULE before EOL (Q3) |

## Funding
- Baseline: 20% of order-team capacity to the MEDIUM items continuously.
- Named projects: the two HIGH items funded explicitly, with ROI above.
- Carry list: the LOW item is deliberately NOT funded; carrying it is cheaper
  than fixing it. We revisit if its cost rises.

What makes this work: every item has a measured cost (not "it feels bad"), an "interest" rating that drives order, and an explicit decision including the deliberate choice to carry the cheap debt. The carry decision is as important as the fund decision — paying down low-interest debt is wasting money you could spend on high-interest debt. A register that funds everything equally is as wrong as one that funds nothing.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer inherits an org where "tech debt" is a constant losing argument: every retro, engineers plead for debt time, and every planning cycle, features win. She changes the argument's shape, not its volume. She builds the register above, with measured costs, and reframes each high-cost item as an ROI proposition to the product and finance partners: "the order module costs us roughly 25 engineer-days a quarter in slowed changes and a share of our incident bill; six weeks fixes it; it pays back in under a quarter". Suddenly the debt work wins, not because she argued harder but because it stopped being a feelings-based plea and became an investment with a return. The quantification did what three years of pleading could not.

Failure scenario

A team runs quarterly "debt sprints" — a full sprint every quarter dedicated to paydown. It sounds disciplined. But debt sprints are the easiest thing to cancel: every quarter a feature is hot, the debt sprint is "just this once" deferred, and after a year it has run twice out of four times. Worse, because all debt work is concentrated into these sprints, no paydown happens the rest of the time, so debt accumulates for ten weeks and gets a partial cleanup for two. The team feels like they are managing debt because the sprints exist on the calendar; the debt grows anyway. The mechanism was too cancellable and too lumpy. A continuous 20% baseline — invisible, non-negotiable, always running — would have paid down more debt with less drama, precisely because it is never a discrete thing anyone can cancel.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Treating all debt as one pile. No classification, no measurement, so paydown is random and always loses to features.
  • Paying down cheap debt. Fixing low-interest items feels productive but wastes capacity that high-interest debt needs.
  • Debt sprints that get cancelled. Too easy to defer when features are hot; paydown becomes lumpy and incomplete.
  • Unmeasured debt. "It feels bad" cannot win against a feature with a revenue number. Without a measured cost, debt loses every argument.
  • Never carrying debt deliberately. Trying to fix everything; some debt is genuinely cheaper to carry than to fix, and refusing to carry it wastes effort.
  • Deliberate/reckless debt created silently. Shortcuts taken with no record, so they are never scheduled for paydown and compound invisibly.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They refuse to argue about debt in the language of guilt and instead force it into the language of cost and return, because they know an unmeasured plea loses to a measured feature every time. They classify debt so that they can attack the high-interest, compounding items first and happily carry the cheap items — they treat "we will deliberately not fix this, it is cheaper to hold" as a legitimate, even wise, decision rather than a failure.

They favour a continuous baseline (the 20% rule) over lumpy debt sprints, because the baseline is non-negotiable and therefore survives hot-feature quarters, while sprints are the first thing cut. And they make the deliberate debt the org takes on visible — recorded in the register with a payoff plan — so that today's prudent shortcut does not quietly become tomorrow's reckless compounding liability that nobody remembers choosing.

Common mistakes

  • No classification or measurement, so debt is one guilty pile that always loses.
  • Spending paydown capacity on low-interest debt because it is easy and feels productive.
  • Relying on debt sprints that get cancelled whenever features are hot.
  • Arguing for debt work with feelings instead of numbers, guaranteeing it loses to features.
  • Never deliberately carrying cheap debt, wasting effort fixing things that did not need fixing.

Interview questions

  1. How do you decide which technical debt to pay down? Expected answer: classify it, quantify each item's ongoing cost in real units (incidents/dollars, lead-time, toil hours), rank by "interest rate", and fund the highest-cost compounding items first while deliberately carrying cheap debt. Follow-up: give an example of debt you would deliberately NOT fix.

  2. Debt work always loses to features at your company. How do you change that? Expected answer: stop arguing in the language of guilt and start measuring debt's cost, then frame paydown as ROI — "this debt costs X engineer-days/quarter, the fix costs Y, payback in Z". A number can compete with a feature's number; a feeling cannot. Why it matters: this is the core skill — making debt fundable.

  3. Why prefer a continuous 20% baseline over quarterly debt sprints? Expected answer: the baseline is non-negotiable and continuous, so it survives hot-feature quarters and pays down debt steadily; debt sprints are lumpy and the easiest thing to cancel when features are urgent, so they often do not happen and debt accumulates between them. Follow-up: when might an explicitly-funded project beat both.

Practical exercise

Build a technical-debt register for a system you work on. List the five worst pieces of debt. For each: classify it (type), measure its cost per quarter in at least one real unit (incidents/dollars, extra lead-time days, or toil hours — measure, do not guess), estimate the fix, rate its "interest", and make an explicit decision (fund now / pay in baseline / carry / schedule before EOL). Make sure at least one item is a deliberate "carry" decision.

Acceptance criteria: every item has a measured (not guessed) cost in a real unit; the items are ranked by interest rate, not by how annoying they feel; at least one high-interest item has a defensible ROI argument (cost per quarter versus fix estimate); and you have deliberately chosen to carry at least one low-interest item rather than fix it.

52.5 Evaluating and adopting new technology

Concept

New technology arrives constantly, and someone on your team always wants to adopt the latest thing. Evaluating technology well means having a repeatable process: explicit evaluation criteria, a proof of concept designed to answer a real question, a total-cost-of-ownership calculation that includes the costs people forget, an honest look at the exit cost (how hard is it to leave), and a staged adoption model so you can commit incrementally rather than all at once. Part 49.5 gave you build-versus-buy; this section is about how to assess a specific new technology before it becomes load-bearing.

Why does it exist?

Imagine adopting a new database because a benchmark showed it was fast, with no evaluation of operability, hiring, ecosystem, or exit cost. Two years later it is load-bearing, the one engineer who understood it has left, it has no managed offering on your cloud, the ecosystem of tools you rely on does not support it, and migrating off it would take a year. The benchmark was true and irrelevant; the costs that actually mattered were never evaluated. This happens constantly, because adopting technology is exciting and evaluating it is tedious.

The evaluation process exists to make the boring-but-decisive factors — operability, TCO, exit cost, team skill — as visible as the exciting one (it is fast!), so the decision accounts for the full lifetime cost of living with the technology, not just the demo.

Mental model

Imagine adopting a pet versus buying a toy. A toy you evaluate on whether it is fun right now. A pet you must evaluate on fifteen years of feeding, vet bills, walks, what happens when you travel, and the pain of rehoming if it does not work out. Load-bearing technology is a pet, not a toy: the purchase price (does it work in the demo) is the smallest cost. The real evaluation is the lifetime of care — operating it, hiring for it, upgrading it — and the exit cost if you need to rehome it. People who evaluate technology like a toy end up with a pet they cannot afford and cannot give away.

How it works

Evaluation criteria. A scorecard, weighted by what matters for your context:

- Fit: does it solve our actual, measured problem? (not a problem we imagine)
- Operability: can we run it in production? Managed option? Observability?
- Maturity: how long has it existed? Who runs it at our scale? Breaking changes?
- Ecosystem: do our tools, ORMs, cloud, hiring pool support it?
- Team skill: can our team operate it, or is it one person's knowledge?
- Exit cost: how hard is it to leave if we must? (reversibility, Part 49)
- TCO: total cost of ownership over 3 years, not the sticker price.
- Community/vendor health: active? funded? or dying?

Proof of concept, designed to answer a question. A POC is not "let's play with it". It is an experiment designed to answer the one or two questions that would kill the adoption. If the risk is "can it handle our write volume", the POC loads it to 2x your peak write volume and measures. If the risk is "is it operable", the POC includes running it through a simulated failure and a version upgrade. A POC that does not try to kill the technology is a toy demo.

Total cost of ownership (TCO). The costs people forget:

Cost category Often forgotten? Example
Licence / usage fees No $X/month
Infrastructure Sometimes Nodes, storage, network
Operational effort YES On-call, upgrades, patching: ~0.5 engineer
Training / ramp YES Every engineer spends days learning it
Integration YES Making it work with your existing stack
Migration in Sometimes Getting your data/code onto it
Exit cost ALWAYS What it costs to leave, years later
Opportunity cost YES What the team is NOT building while adopting this

Adoption stages (the tech-radar model: assess, trial, adopt, hold). You do not go from "never used it" to "load-bearing" in one step:

flowchart LR
    AS["ASSESS - read, watch, one engineer explores"] --> TR["TRIAL - use on a low-risk, real project"]
    TR --> AD["ADOPT - default choice for this problem"]
    AD --> HO["HOLD - stop new use, plan exit"]
    AS -.->|"fails evaluation"| X["Reject"]
    TR -.->|"disappoints in practice"| X
  • Assess: worth knowing about; one person explores it, no commitment.
  • Trial: use it on a real but low-stakes project to learn its true costs, with a clear exit if it disappoints.
  • Adopt: it has earned the default position for this class of problem.
  • Hold: stop starting new things on it; it is on the way out.

Practical example

A team wants to adopt a new message broker because it benchmarks faster than their current RabbitMQ. Run through the process: the fit question is "is message throughput actually our problem?" — measured answer: no, RabbitMQ is at 8% of its capacity; speed is not a problem they have. That alone should stop the adoption, and does. The exciting factor (faster) was answering a question nobody asked. Had fit passed, the next killers would have been operability (no managed option on their cloud, so +0.5 engineer of ops) and exit cost (a year to migrate off). The process converts "it's faster!" into "it solves a problem we don't have, at a cost we'd pay for years" — a clear no, reached in a week instead of a two-year regret.

Artifact example

A technology evaluation scorecard, filled in for the message-broker question — the artifact that makes the decision legible and defensible.

# Technology Evaluation: Adopt [NewBroker] to replace RabbitMQ?

**Question driving this:** a benchmark showed NewBroker is 3x faster.
**Real question we must answer:** is broker throughput our problem? And
if we adopt, what is the 3-year cost?

| Criterion | Weight | Score (1-5) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fit (solves a real, measured problem) | 5 | 1 | RabbitMQ at 8% capacity. Speed is NOT our problem. |
| Operability | 4 | 2 | No managed option on our cloud. We'd self-host. |
| Maturity | 3 | 3 | ~4 years old, few at our scale. |
| Ecosystem | 3 | 2 | No first-class NestJS transport; we'd write glue. |
| Team skill | 4 | 1 | Zero in-house. One engineer interested. |
| Exit cost | 5 | 2 | ~1 year to migrate off once load-bearing. |
| 3-yr TCO vs status quo | 5 | 2 | +0.5 eng ops + training + migration. Higher, not lower. |

**POC that would change our mind:** none needed — fit already fails.
If fit passed, POC would load-test at 2x peak AND run a version upgrade
and a node-failure drill to test operability (the real risks).

**Decision: REJECT (ASSESS only).** The deciding factor is fit: it solves
a problem we do not have. We keep RabbitMQ. Revisit only if measured
broker load exceeds 50% of RabbitMQ capacity.

The scorecard's power is that it weights fit and exit cost highest, scores the exciting factor (speed) as irrelevant because fit fails, and records a falsifiable condition for revisiting (50% capacity). It turns a seductive benchmark into a defensible, boring, correct "no".

Real-world scenario

An engineering org adopts a "tech radar" and reviews it quarterly. Each technology sits in assess, trial, adopt, or hold. The discipline it enforces is subtle but powerful: nothing is allowed to jump from assess straight to load-bearing. A team excited about a new framework must first trial it on a low-stakes project with a defined exit. Twice in the first year, technologies that looked great in assessment disappointed in trial — the operability was worse than advertised — and were dropped at the trial stage, having cost one low-risk project instead of becoming a load-bearing regret. The radar did not slow the org down; it moved the failures to the cheap stage, which is the entire point of staged adoption.

Failure scenario

A staff engineer, genuinely excited, champions adopting a cutting-edge datastore after an impressive conference talk and a weekend POC that loaded a few thousand rows and felt fast. It skips trial and goes straight into a new, important service. For six months it is fine. Then the service grows, and the datastore's weaknesses — poor operability, a tiny ecosystem, one in-house expert — all surface at once, during an incident. The expert has since left. There is no managed option. Migrating off, now that it is load-bearing, is a nine-month project that consumes a team that should have been building features. The weekend POC answered "is it fun" (yes) and never asked "can we operate this for three years and leave it if we must" (no). Every cost that mattered was skipped because the exciting one was so compelling.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • POC that only tests the happy path. It confirms the technology is fun, not that it is operable, scalable or leavable. Design the POC to try to kill the technology.
  • Evaluating on the sticker price, ignoring TCO. The operational, training, integration and exit costs dwarf the licence fee and are the ones forgotten.
  • Skipping the trial stage. Jumping from assess to load-bearing, so failures surface in production instead of in a cheap low-stakes project.
  • No exit-cost analysis. Adopting something you can never leave, which turns every future weakness into a trap.
  • Fit never checked. Adopting a solution to a problem you do not actually have (the "it's faster" trap when speed is not your constraint).
  • Resume-driven development. Adopting technology because it is interesting or good for careers, not because it solves a measured problem.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They weight fit and exit cost above everything, because a technology that does not solve a real problem is pure cost, and a technology you cannot leave turns every future weakness into a trap. They design POCs to attack the technology at its riskiest point — load, failure, upgrade, operability — rather than to enjoy it, because a POC that does not try to kill the candidate tells you nothing about living with it. They compute TCO including the costs everyone forgets (operational effort, training, exit) and they are skeptical of any evaluation dominated by a single exciting number.

Above all, they bias toward the boring, proven choice and put the burden of proof on the exception, exactly as Part 49 does — because the cost of a wrong adoption is paid for years, and the cost of sticking with the boring thing is usually just mild disappointment. They know that most "we need to adopt X" is resume-driven or hype-driven, and they are comfortable being the person who asks "what measured problem does this solve" and lets the silence answer.

Common mistakes

  • A POC that only proves it is fun, never testing operability, scale, or exit.
  • Evaluating on sticker price, ignoring the operational, training and exit costs that dominate TCO.
  • Skipping trial and making a new technology load-bearing before learning its real costs.
  • Never checking fit, adopting a solution to a problem you do not have.
  • Resume-driven adoption, choosing technology for interest rather than measured need.

Interview questions

  1. How do you evaluate whether to adopt a new technology? Expected answer: score it against weighted criteria (fit, operability, maturity, ecosystem, team skill, exit cost, TCO, vendor health), run a POC designed to attack its biggest risk, compute 3-year TCO including forgotten costs, and adopt in stages (assess, trial, adopt). Weight fit and exit cost highest. Follow-up: what costs do people most often forget in TCO.

  2. A benchmark shows a new tool is 3x faster. Walk me through your thinking. Expected answer: first ask whether speed is a measured problem for us; if the current tool is at 8% capacity, the benchmark is true and irrelevant. Then weigh operability, exit cost and TCO, which usually dominate. Do not adopt a solution to a problem you do not have. Why it matters: tests resistance to the single-number trap.

  3. Why adopt technology in stages instead of committing once you've decided? Expected answer: staged adoption (assess, trial, adopt) moves failures to the cheap stage — a trial on a low-stakes project reveals operability problems that a demo hides, before the technology becomes load-bearing and expensive to leave. Follow-up: what makes a good trial project.

Practical exercise

Pick a technology someone on your team has proposed adopting (or one you are tempted by). Build the evaluation scorecard: weight the criteria for your context, score each honestly, and especially fill in the fit, exit-cost and 3-year TCO rows with real reasoning. Then design the POC: write down the single question that, if answered "no", would kill the adoption, and how the POC would answer it.

Acceptance criteria: fit and exit cost are weighted among the highest; the TCO includes at least three commonly-forgotten costs (operational effort, training, exit); your POC is designed to attack the biggest risk rather than to enjoy the technology; and you reach a defensible decision with a falsifiable condition for revisiting it.

52.6 Build vs buy at scale, the tech radar, and saying no

Concept

Three connected skills that round out strategy. Build vs buy at company scale extends the Part 49.5 decision table into the territory that only matters at scale: vendor risk, lock-in, contract terms, and what happens when a vendor is acquired or raises prices. The tech radar is the living artifact that records where every technology sits (adopt, trial, assess, hold) and keeps those decisions honest and visible. And saying no to technology is the discipline — often the single most valuable thing a principal does — of choosing the boring option and refusing the exciting one when the exciting one does not earn its cost.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a company that buys a critical SaaS tool on a great price, makes it load-bearing, and signs a one-year contract with auto-renewal. Two years in, the vendor is acquired, the price triples at renewal, the new owner deprecates the feature the company depends on, and there is no realistic alternative because the data is locked in a proprietary format. The build-vs-buy decision looked right at the time because it only considered today's price and today's features, not vendor risk, lock-in, and contract terms — the things that only bite at scale and over time.

The tech radar exists because technology decisions made once and never revisited silently rot: a tool adopted three years ago may now be the wrong choice, but without a radar nobody re-examines it. And saying no exists because the default pressure in engineering is always toward more technology, and someone senior has to be willing to be the one who says the boring choice wins, or the stack accretes complexity until it collapses under its own weight.

Mental model

For build vs buy at scale, imagine renting versus buying a house, but the landlord can change the rent at any renewal, can decide to sell the house out from under you, and has the only key to the furniture you put inside. Renting (buying SaaS) is cheaper and faster to start and someone else fixes the roof — but you are exposed to the landlord's decisions, and if they lock your furniture in, you cannot leave. Building is the mortgage: more upfront, slower, but nobody can change the terms on you or lock you out. At scale, the landlord's power (vendor risk and lock-in) matters as much as the rent (the price).

For saying no, imagine a chef with a pantry. A great chef is defined as much by the ingredients they refuse to add as by the ones they use. A dish with every ingredient in the pantry is inedible. Saying no to technology is curating the pantry so the dish stays coherent.

How it works

Build vs buy at scale adds dimensions beyond the Part 49.5 table:

Dimension Buy (SaaS/vendor) Build Open source
Time to value Fast Slow Medium
Ongoing cost Predictable until renewal Engineer time forever Engineer time (you operate it)
Vendor risk HIGH: acquisition, price hikes, deprecation, shutdown None Project can die; community can fork
Lock-in Often severe (proprietary formats, APIs) None Low to medium
Contract terms Negotiable at scale: SLAs, price caps, data egress, exit clauses N/A Licence terms (watch for relicensing)
Control Low Total High
Differentiation Use for non-differentiating needs Build only your actual edge Either

The governing rule: buy or adopt open source for what does not differentiate you; build only what is your actual competitive edge. You do not build your own email provider; you do build the pricing engine that is your business. And at scale, negotiate the contract terms that de-risk the buy decision: price caps on renewal, data-export rights (reducing lock-in), SLAs with teeth, and exit clauses.

The tech radar is a quadrant chart (or just a table) placing each technology in a ring:

ADOPT   -> proven here; default choice for its problem
TRIAL   -> worth pursuing on a real low-risk project; not yet default
ASSESS  -> worth exploring; one person, no commitment
HOLD    -> stop new use; existing use being wound down or frozen

Keeping it honest means: everything is dated and owned, "hold" is used (a radar with no holds is a radar nobody is willing to retire anything on), and it is reviewed on a cadence so adopt-ring entries that have gone stale get demoted.

Saying no is a repeatable move: ask "what measured problem does this solve", "what does it cost over three years including exit", and "what is the boring alternative and why is it not enough". If the exciting technology cannot beat the boring one on a real problem, the answer is no, and you say it clearly, with the reasoning, so it does not get re-asked.

Practical example

A ride-booking company needs a feature-flag system. Build vs buy at scale: feature flags do not differentiate them (every company has them; customers do not choose them for their flag system), so the default is buy or open source, not build. Buying a SaaS flag product is fast but introduces vendor risk (every request checks flags; a vendor outage is their outage) and lock-in. They negotiate: an SLA with credits, a self-hosted relay so a vendor outage degrades gracefully, and data-export rights. An open-source flag system avoids vendor risk but costs operational effort. They choose the SaaS with the negotiated terms, because the operational cost of self-hosting exceeds the managed vendor risk once the risk is contracted down. The key move is that they did not build (it is not their edge) and did not buy naively (they negotiated the terms that de-risk the buy at scale).

Artifact example

A tech radar snapshot plus a "saying no" decision record — two artifacts that keep the stack honest.

# Tech Radar — Backend (reviewed 2026-Q2, owner: principal eng)

## Data stores
- ADOPT: PostgreSQL 17 (default for all transactional data)
- ADOPT: Redis (caching, rate limits, sorted sets)
- TRIAL: pgvector (RAG search POC, 1 team, exit defined)
- ASSESS: ClickHouse (for analytics; assessing vs warehouse)
- HOLD: MongoDB (2 legacy services; no new use; migrating to PG)

## Messaging
- ADOPT: RabbitMQ + Postgres outbox (current default)
- ASSESS: Kafka (would adopt IF multi-consumer streaming need materialises)

## Explicitly rejected this quarter (the "no" log)
- NewBroker: solves throughput we don't have (RabbitMQ at 8%). REJECTED.
- Service mesh: our incidents aren't mesh-shaped. REJECTED (see reliability strategy).
- GraphQL for internal services: one client, no diversity problem. REJECTED (Part 49.3).

---

# Decision: we will NOT adopt Kafka yet (saying no)
**Proposal:** adopt Kafka as our event backbone.
**Measured problem it would solve:** multi-consumer event streaming. We
have ONE consumer today (notifications); RabbitMQ + outbox serves it.
**3-yr cost of adopting now:** a cluster to operate (+~0.5 eng), training,
migration of the outbox relay. Exit cost: medium.
**Boring alternative:** keep RabbitMQ + outbox. It meets today's need.
**Decision:** HOLD on Kafka at ASSESS. Adopt IF/WHEN a second and third
consumer materialise (platform roadmap suggests ~1 year). Falsifiable
trigger: 3+ independent consumers of order events planned. Until then, no.

The radar makes every position visible and dated, uses HOLD honestly (MongoDB is being retired), and keeps a "no" log so rejected technologies do not keep coming back. The Kafka decision is a model "no": it names the measured problem, admits the boring alternative suffices, and sets a falsifiable trigger for revisiting — so it is a disciplined "not yet", not a dogmatic "never".

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer is known in her org as the person who says no to technology, and she wears it as a compliment. Her value is not that she blocks things; it is that her "no" is always reasoned, falsifiable, and recorded, so it sticks and reduces thrash. When a team proposes the fashionable thing, they know she will ask "what measured problem, what three-year cost, why is the boring option not enough", so they either come prepared with real answers (and she says yes) or they realise themselves that the answer is no. Over three years, her discipline keeps the stack small enough that the org can actually operate it — a stack of six well-understood technologies instead of twenty half-understood ones. The things she said no to were individually plausible; saying no to all of them was what kept the system comprehensible.

Failure scenario

A company buys a critical analytics SaaS on an attractive two-year deal with no exit clause, no price cap, and data stored in the vendor's proprietary format with export available only through a slow, rate-limited API. It becomes load-bearing: dashboards, alerts and a customer-facing feature all depend on it. At renewal, the vendor — now acquired — quadruples the price and makes the new price conditional on a three-year commitment. The company has no leverage: migrating off would take six months because of the proprietary format and the painful export, and losing the tool would break a customer feature. They pay the 4x. The build-vs-buy decision was made on price and features alone; vendor risk, lock-in and contract terms were never evaluated, and at scale those are exactly the dimensions that determine whether a buy decision is a bargain or a trap.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Building what does not differentiate you. Writing your own email provider or auth system, burning engineering on a solved problem that is not your edge.
  • Buying naively at scale. No price cap, no exit clause, no data-export rights, proprietary lock-in — turning a cheap buy into an inescapable trap.
  • A radar with no "hold" ring. Nobody is willing to retire anything, so the stack only grows.
  • A radar nobody reviews. Adopt-ring entries go stale; the radar describes the past, not the present.
  • Saying no dogmatically. "Never Kafka" instead of "not until 3+ consumers"; a reasoned, falsifiable no is durable, a dogmatic one is brittle and gets overridden.
  • No "no" log. Rejected technologies keep coming back every quarter because the reasoning was never recorded.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They apply the differentiation rule rigorously: build only the thing that is the company's actual edge, buy or adopt open source for everything else, because engineering capacity spent re-solving solved problems is capacity stolen from the thing only you can build. At scale they treat the contract as part of the architecture — price caps, exit clauses and data-export rights are reliability features, because they determine whether you can leave a vendor who turns hostile.

They treat saying no as a core, high-value activity rather than an obstruction, and they make every no reasoned, falsifiable and recorded, because a no with a trigger ("adopt when X is true") is a disciplined decision that sticks, while a dogmatic no is brittle and a silent no gets re-asked forever. And they keep the radar honest by using the hold ring and reviewing on a cadence, because a stack that only grows eventually exceeds the org's ability to operate it.

Common mistakes

  • Building non-differentiating technology instead of buying or adopting open source.
  • Buying without negotiating the terms that de-risk it (caps, exit, export) at scale.
  • Treating the radar as a one-time artifact instead of a reviewed, dated, owned living document.
  • Saying no dogmatically instead of with a falsifiable trigger, so the no gets overridden.
  • Not recording the no, so rejected ideas return every planning cycle.

Interview questions

  1. How does build vs buy change at company scale compared to for a small team? Expected answer: at scale, vendor risk (acquisition, price hikes, deprecation), lock-in (proprietary formats), and contract terms (caps, exit clauses, data export) dominate, alongside the rule to build only what differentiates you. A cheap buy with no exit clause can become an inescapable trap. Follow-up: what contract terms would you insist on for a load-bearing SaaS.

  2. What makes a good "no" to a proposed technology? Expected answer: it names the measured problem the technology would solve, shows the boring alternative suffices, states the three-year cost including exit, and — crucially — sets a falsifiable trigger for revisiting, so it is a disciplined "not yet" rather than a dogmatic "never", and it is recorded so it does not get re-asked. Why it matters: saying no well is a principal's highest-leverage habit.

  3. Why keep a tech radar, and what makes one honest? Expected answer: it records where every technology sits (adopt/trial/assess/hold) so decisions stay visible and get revisited; it is honest when it uses the hold ring (willing to retire things), dates and owns entries, keeps a "no" log, and is reviewed on a cadence so stale adopt entries get demoted. Follow-up: what does an empty hold ring tell you.

Practical exercise

Build a one-page tech radar for your team's backend stack: place every significant technology in adopt, trial, assess or hold, with a date and owner, and make sure the hold ring is not empty. Then write one "saying no" decision record for a technology you are choosing not to adopt: name the measured problem it would solve, the boring alternative, the three-year cost, and a falsifiable trigger for revisiting.

Acceptance criteria: your radar uses all four rings (including at least one honest hold), every entry is dated; and your "no" record is falsifiable — it states a specific condition under which the answer would become yes, rather than rejecting the technology forever.

52.7 Worked example: strategy for scaling from 12 to 80 engineers

This section brings the whole Part together in one worked case: an e-commerce company growing from a single monolith with 12 engineers to 80 engineers over two years. It is the kind of situation where a principal engineer is asked for "a technical strategy", and it exercises every tool in this Part — the strategy kernel, the vision, the roadmap, debt as a portfolio, and the discipline to say no.

The situation

GreenCart sells groceries online. Today: 12 engineers, one NestJS monolith on one PostgreSQL database, deploying together a few times a week. It works. The company just raised money and will hire to 80 engineers over two years to expand into new cities and new product lines. The CTO asks the principal engineer: "what is our technical strategy for this growth?"

The naive answer is "microservices and Kubernetes", and it is wrong, because it is an action list with no diagnosis. Here is the real strategy.

The strategy kernel

DIAGNOSIS:
A monolith with 12 engineers works because 12 people can coordinate one
deploy and one database. At 80 engineers, that same architecture means 80
people serialised behind one deploy pipeline and one schema. Lead time,
today ~1 week, would balloon toward a month, and the blast radius of each
deploy would become terrifying. The crux is NOT that the monolith is bad;
it is that SHARED, COORDINATED deploys and data do not scale with headcount.
We also lack the platform (templates, pipelines, observability standards)
that lets teams operate independently — today the 12 share tribal knowledge.

GUIDING POLICY:
Scale by reducing coordination, not by adopting fashionable architecture.
Give teams ownership of bounded contexts with their own data and deploys,
extracting services ONLY where coordination is the measured bottleneck.
Build the platform that makes independent operation cheap BEFORE extracting
widely. We will NOT do a big-bang rewrite, will NOT adopt microservices as
a goal, and will NOT add Kubernetes/Kafka/mesh unless a measured need
appears. The boring, staged path wins.

COHERENT ACTIONS:
1. Convert the monolith to an enforced modular monolith (clear module
   boundaries, own-your-tables rule, lint-enforced). Enables everything else.
2. Build the paved road: service template, CI/CD pipeline, observability
   and on-call standards. Makes independent operation cheap and repeatable.
3. Extract the 2-3 most coordination-bound contexts (payments, catalog,
   fulfilment) onto their own data and deploys, using the paved road.
These reinforce: #1 makes #3 safe, #2 makes #3 cheap and makes new teams
productive on day one.

The vision it serves

# Vision 2026-2028: 15 teams shipping independently
In two years, GreenCart runs as ~15 stream-aligned teams, each owning a
bounded context end to end — its own data, deploys, and on-call — able to
ship multiple times a day without coordinating with another team, on a
paved road that makes a new service a day-one operation, not a quarter-long
setup.

## Business connection
- Expansion speed: new cities/product lines need teams that can move
  independently; coupled systems cap us at the speed of the slowest team.
- Hiring ROI: we will spend ~$20M on 68 new engineers over 2 years. Coupled
  architecture wastes that spend on coordination overhead; independent teams
  convert headcount into output.
- Reliability: blast radius per deploy shrinks from "the whole site" to "one
  context", protecting revenue as traffic grows.

## Measures
- Lead time: ~7 days -> under 1 day.
- Teams able to deploy independently: 1 -> 15.
- New-service setup time: ~1 quarter -> under 1 day (paved road).
- Change failure rate held under 15% while deploy frequency rises 10x.

The roadmap (abbreviated)

Year 1
  Q1: Module boundaries enforced + CI split (action 1). Low risk, prereq.
  Q2: Paved road v1 — service template + pipeline (action 2). Early win.
  Q3: Extract payments (most coordination-bound). Front-loads extraction risk.
  Q4: Observability + on-call standards baked into the paved road.
Year 2
  Q1: Extract catalog. Cheap now — paved road exists.
  Q2: Extract fulfilment. New teams onboard onto the paved road directly.
  Q3-Q4: Remaining contexts split as teams grow into them; platform hardening.

Capacity: sized to effective headcount, ramping as hires land (12 -> ~40
by end of Y1 -> ~80 by end of Y2). Platform team formed first, in Q1.

Explicitly deferred: Kubernetes (revisit when deploy volume justifies the
ops cost; today ECS-style is enough), Kafka (one consumer today; ASSESS),
multi-region (no business driver yet), service mesh (no mesh-shaped
problems). All on the radar, none adopted without a measured trigger.

The debt portfolio angle

As GreenCart extracts services, it accumulates and pays debt deliberately. The "shared database" phase of extraction — where the new service still reads the old tables during transition — is deliberate, prudent debt, tracked with a payoff date (full data ownership by the end of each extraction quarter). The team resists the temptation to pay down cheap debt (the dual-ORM situation) and funds the high-interest debt (the tangled order module) as a named project before extracting fulfilment, because extracting a tangled module is far more expensive than extracting a clean one. The register from 52.4 governs this.

Why this strategy is right

Trace it against the Part. It starts with a diagnosis (shared coordinated deploys and data do not scale with headcount), not an action list. Its guiding policy refuses three fashionable things (big-bang rewrite, microservices-as-goal, premature K8s/Kafka/mesh) and concentrates force on reducing coordination. Its actions are coherent — boundaries enable extraction, the paved road makes extraction cheap and new teams productive. The roadmap respects dependencies (boundaries and paved road before wide extraction), front-loads risk (payments extraction in Y1 Q3, not Y2), schedules an early win (paved road v1), and is sized to effective capacity that ramps with hiring. New technology is held at assess with falsifiable triggers. And debt is managed as a portfolio, paying the high-interest items before they make extraction expensive.

The naive "microservices and Kubernetes" answer would have produced a distributed monolith (services split along the org chart before boundaries were understood — exactly the Part 55 failure), a premature platform the 12-person team could not operate, and a year lost to a rewrite. The boring, staged, diagnosis-driven strategy converts 68 new hires into independent output. That difference — between an exciting answer and a correct one — is the entire value of knowing how to do technical strategy.

Practical exercise

Take your own organisation's next big change (significant growth, a new market, a platform shift, a reliability push). Produce the full set of artifacts for it, each consistent with the others: a strategy kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy with refusals, coherent actions), a one-page measurable vision tied to business numbers, a dependency-respecting and capacity-honest roadmap with explicit deferrals, and a note on how you would manage the debt the change creates as a portfolio.

Acceptance criteria: the diagnosis names a cause, not a symptom; the policy refuses at least two tempting things; the actions reinforce one another; the roadmap violates no dependency and is sized to effective capacity; at least two technologies are explicitly deferred with falsifiable triggers; and the whole set is coherent — a reader can see how the vision, strategy, roadmap and debt plan all serve the same diagnosis.

52.8 Communicating, measuring, and sustaining a strategy

Concept

A strategy that is written but not communicated, measured, or sustained is a document, not a direction. Three disciplines turn a strategy kernel into a living force in the organisation: communicating it so people actually internalise it (repetition until bored, embedding it in decisions), measuring it so you know whether it is working and can adjust (leading indicators, checkpoints, falsifiable signals), and sustaining it across the quarters and the inevitable pressures that erode it (defending it against thrash, revisiting it deliberately rather than abandoning it reactively). This is the difference between a strategy that changes what the organisation does and one that sits in a wiki nobody follows.

Why does it exist?

Imagine writing an excellent strategy kernel, presenting it once in an all-hands, and then returning to daily work. Three months later, nobody remembers it, teams are making decisions that contradict it, and there is no way to tell whether it is working. The strategy existed but had no effect, because a strategy communicated once is forgotten, a strategy never measured cannot be known to work or adjusted, and a strategy never defended erodes under the constant pressure of competing priorities. The disciplines exist because the hard part of strategy is not writing it — it is making it actually direct the organisation's behaviour over time, which requires relentless communication, measurement, and defence.

Mental model

Imagine a ship's captain who sets a heading but then never repeats it to the crew, never checks the compass, and never corrects when currents push the ship off course. The ship drifts wherever the currents take it, regardless of the heading the captain once announced. Communicating the strategy is repeating the heading until every crew member knows it; measuring it is checking the compass and the ship's actual position; sustaining it is correcting for the currents (competing priorities, pressures) that constantly push the ship off the heading. A strategy without these is a heading announced once and then abandoned to the currents — the ship goes wherever the pressures push it, not where the strategy intended.

How it works

Communicating the strategy:

- Repeat it until you're bored of saying it (and then keep going). People need
  to hear a direction many times before it sticks and shapes their decisions.
- Embed it in decisions: when you decide something, reference the strategy
  ("per our strategy to reduce coupling, we're extracting payments"). This
  teaches people to use it as a decision tool (the test of good direction, Part 44).
- Make it usable: the kernel (diagnosis, policy, actions) is short enough that
  people can hold it and apply it to say no to off-strategy proposals (52.1).
- Translate for audiences: engineers get the technical version, leadership gets
  the business version (Part 56.2).

Measuring the strategy:

- Leading indicators: metrics that show EARLY whether the strategy is working,
  before the lagging outcome arrives (e.g. for a velocity strategy: lead-time
  trending down, teams deploying independently rising — before the final goal).
- Checkpoints: scheduled points to assess progress against the roadmap (52.3)
  and the strategy's expected effects.
- Falsifiable signals: define in advance what would show the strategy is WRONG
  (per Part 49 — "if lead time hasn't improved in 2 quarters, the diagnosis was
  wrong"), so you can adjust rather than persist in a failing direction.

Sustaining the strategy:

- Defend it against thrash: competing priorities constantly pull resources off
  the strategy; the principal protects the strategic work (Part 56.5).
- Revisit deliberately, not reactively: update the strategy when the diagnosis
  changes or the measurement shows it's wrong — not every time a shiny new thing
  appears. Deliberate revision; not abandonment under pressure.
- Keep the vision stable while the roadmap flexes (52.1): the destination holds;
  the path adjusts as you learn.
flowchart LR
    S["Strategy kernel"] --> C["Communicate: repeat, embed in decisions"]
    C --> M["Measure: leading indicators, checkpoints, falsifiable signals"]
    M --> R{"Working?"}
    R -->|"yes"| SUS["Sustain: defend against thrash"]
    R -->|"no (signal fired)"| ADJ["Adjust deliberately (diagnosis was wrong)"]
    SUS --> M
    ADJ --> S

Artifact example

A strategy scorecard — the artifact that makes a strategy measured and sustained rather than forgotten.

# Strategy scorecard: Engineering Velocity (reviewed monthly)

## The kernel (repeated at the top every time — repetition is the point)
Diagnosis: coupling (one monolith + one DB) serialises all deploys.
Policy: reduce coupling via bounded-context ownership; extract only where blocked;
  NOT a big-bang rewrite.
Actions: (1) enforce boundaries, (2) extract 2 most-blocked contexts, (3) build
  the paved road.

## Leading indicators (early signals it's working)
- Lead time for change: 30d -> 18d (trending down — ON TRACK).
- Teams able to deploy independently: 1 -> 3 (rising — ON TRACK).
- Cross-team blocking dependencies/feature: 3 -> 1.8 (falling — ON TRACK).

## Checkpoints (vs roadmap, 52.3)
- [x] Boundaries enforced (Q1) [x] Paved road v1 (Q2) [>] Payments extracted (Q3)

## Falsifiable signal (defined in advance — would show the strategy is WRONG)
"If lead time hasn't improved by Q3, the diagnosis (coupling) was wrong and we
reassess." Status: improving, so the diagnosis holds.

## Sustaining
- Thrash watch: a VP proposed pausing the extraction for a feature push. Held
  the line — the extraction IS what enables faster features (reframed, Part 56).
- Next revisit: Q3 checkpoint. Not revising before then absent a fired signal.

The scorecard's power is that it repeats the kernel every time (repetition is how a strategy sticks), tracks leading indicators (early signals, not just the final outcome), checks progress against the roadmap, states the falsifiable signal defined in advance (so a failing strategy is adjusted rather than persisted in), and records the sustaining work (defending against thrash, deliberate revisit timing). It turns the strategy from a one-time document into a monitored, defended, living direction — which is the difference between a strategy that works and one that is forgotten.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer writes a strong strategy and then does the unglamorous work of making it live. She references it in every relevant decision ("per our strategy..."), repeats it so often she worries she is boring people (and then keeps going, because she notices it is finally shaping their decisions). She tracks leading indicators monthly, so when lead time starts trending down she can show the strategy is working, and she has defined in advance the signal that would show it is wrong. When competing priorities threaten to pull resources off the strategic work, she defends it — reframing the strategic work as what enables the competing priority rather than opposing it. Two years later, the strategy has actually changed what the organisation built, because she communicated, measured, and sustained it relentlessly. A peer who wrote an equally good strategy and presented it once finds it forgotten within a quarter, contradicted by daily decisions, with no way to tell if it worked. The difference was not the quality of the strategy but the discipline of making it live — which is the part most people skip and the part that actually produces the effect.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They know that writing the strategy is the easy part and making it direct the organisation's behaviour is the hard part, so they invest relentlessly in communicating it (repeating it past the point of their own boredom, embedding it in decisions so people learn to use it as a tool), measuring it (leading indicators for early signal, falsifiable signals defined in advance so a wrong strategy is adjusted not persisted in), and sustaining it (defending the strategic work against the constant pull of competing priorities, revisiting deliberately rather than abandoning reactively).

They treat the falsifiable signal as the mark of an engineering strategy rather than a belief (Part 49): by defining in advance what would show the strategy is wrong, they can adjust with evidence rather than either persisting stubbornly in a failing direction or abandoning a working one at the first pressure. They keep the vision stable while letting the roadmap flex, correcting for the currents without changing the destination. The principal understands that a strategy's effect is produced entirely by the discipline of making it live — communicated, measured, defended — and that the many good strategies that change nothing fail not in the thinking but in this sustaining work.

Common mistakes

  • Communicating the strategy once and assuming it stuck, so it is forgotten within a quarter.
  • Not embedding it in decisions, so people never learn to use it as a tool.
  • Measuring only the lagging outcome, with no leading indicators to show early whether it is working.
  • No falsifiable signal, so a failing strategy is persisted in (belief, not engineering) or a working one abandoned under pressure.
  • Not defending the strategy against thrash, so competing priorities erode the strategic work.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make a strategy actually direct the organisation's behaviour, not just sit in a wiki? Expected answer: communicate it relentlessly (repeat past your own boredom, embed it in decisions so people use it as a tool), measure it (leading indicators for early signal, checkpoints, falsifiable signals defined in advance), and sustain it (defend the strategic work against thrash, revisit deliberately not reactively). The hard part of strategy is making it live, not writing it. Why it matters: most good strategies change nothing because this work is skipped.

  2. Why define a falsifiable signal for a strategy in advance? Expected answer: so you can adjust with evidence rather than either stubbornly persisting in a failing direction or abandoning a working one at the first pressure; defining in advance what would show the strategy is wrong (e.g. "if lead time hasn't improved in 2 quarters, the diagnosis was wrong") turns the strategy from a belief into engineering (Part 49). Why it matters: tests whether they treat strategy as falsifiable.

  3. A VP wants to pause your strategic work (service extraction) for a feature push. How do you respond? Expected answer: defend the strategic work by reframing, not opposing — the extraction is what enables faster feature delivery (per the strategy's diagnosis that coupling slows features), so pausing it slows the very thing the VP wants; make the tradeoff explicit (Part 56.5) and hold the line unless the measurement shows the strategy is wrong. Sustaining a strategy means defending it against thrash. Why it matters: tests whether they can sustain a strategy under pressure.

Practical exercise

Take the strategy kernel you built earlier in this Part and make it measurable and sustainable. Define its leading indicators (early signals it is working, not just the final outcome), its checkpoints (against the roadmap), and its falsifiable signal (what, defined in advance, would show the strategy is wrong). Then write how you will communicate it (where you will repeat it, how you will embed it in decisions) and how you will sustain it (what thrash you anticipate and how you will defend against it).

Acceptance criteria: your strategy has leading indicators that show early whether it is working (not only the lagging outcome); it has a falsifiable signal defined in advance, so a failing strategy would be adjusted with evidence; you have a concrete plan to communicate it repeatedly and embed it in decisions; and you anticipate the thrash that will threaten it and how you will defend the strategic work — demonstrating that you can make a strategy live rather than letting it be forgotten.

52.9 Strategy anti-patterns and the strategy review

Concept

Two final tools. The strategy anti-patterns are the recurring ways technical strategy goes wrong, gathered into one catalogue so you can recognise and avoid them. And the strategy review is the regular forum where a strategy is examined — is the diagnosis still right, are the actions working, has the landscape changed — so that strategy is a living, periodically-revisited thing rather than a document written once and left to rot. Together they are how a principal keeps strategy honest and current over time.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a strategy written once, never reviewed, while the world changes around it. The diagnosis that was right eighteen months ago may be stale (the problem has shifted), the actions may be complete or failing, and the landscape (team size, technology, business direction) may have moved — but because nobody reviews it, the organisation keeps following a strategy that no longer fits. The strategy review exists to prevent this: to periodically ask whether the strategy is still right and adjust it deliberately, keeping it a living direction rather than a stale document.

The anti-patterns catalogue exists because technical strategy fails in predictable, recognisable ways — the roadmap-called-strategy, the goal-list, the diagnosis-free action list, the strategy that refuses nothing — and naming them lets a principal catch these failures in their own strategy and others' before they do damage. Both exist to keep strategy honest: the review keeps it current, and the anti-patterns catalogue keeps it from being the common non-strategies that masquerade as strategy.

Mental model

Imagine a ship's navigation that is set once at departure and never revisited, even as storms, currents, and new information arrive. The ship follows the original heading into dangers the captain could have avoided by re-checking the chart. The strategy review is re-checking the chart periodically — is the destination still right, has the landscape changed, is the current heading still the best way there — and adjusting. The anti-patterns are the common navigation mistakes (following a heading with no destination, a destination with no route, a route that ignores the storms) that a good navigator recognises and avoids. Strategy, like navigation, must be both initially sound (avoiding the anti-patterns) and periodically re-checked (the review).

How it works

The strategy anti-patterns (gathered from across the Part):

- The roadmap-called-strategy: a sequence of activities with the reasoning
  removed; collapses under reprioritisation (52.1).
- The goal-list: "be scalable, reliable, modern" — adjudicates nothing, refuses
  nothing (52.1/52.2).
- The diagnosis-free action list: jumps to actions without naming the real
  problem, so it treats symptoms (52.2).
- The symptom-as-diagnosis: "too many incidents" (symptom) instead of the cause
  (52.2).
- The refuse-nothing strategy: says yes to everything, so no real choices (52.2).
- The incoherent actions: a committee-compromise list where off-policy items
  dilute the on-policy ones — where good strategies usually die (52.2).
- The undeliverable roadmap: sized to nominal not effective capacity (52.3).
- The unquantified-debt plea: arguing for debt work with feelings not numbers (52.4).
- The single-number tech adoption: adopting on one exciting metric, ignoring fit
  and exit cost (52.5).
- The write-once strategy: never reviewed, so it goes stale (this section).

The strategy review:

- Cadence: review the strategy regularly (e.g. quarterly), at a checkpoint.
- Questions to ask:
  * Is the DIAGNOSIS still right? Has the problem shifted?
  * Are the ACTIONS working? (The leading indicators, 52.8.) Did any fire a
    falsifiable signal that the strategy is wrong?
  * Has the LANDSCAPE changed? (Team size, technology, business direction, a new
    constraint or opportunity?)
  * Should we ADJUST — the actions, the roadmap, or (rarely) the diagnosis?
- Deliberate adjustment, not reactive thrash: adjust when the review shows cause,
  not every time a shiny new thing appears (52.1 — vision stable, roadmap flexes).
- Keep it honest: the review is a place to admit an action isn't working and
  change it, not to defend the original strategy regardless.
flowchart LR
    S["Strategy"] --> AV["Avoid the anti-patterns (sound strategy)"]
    AV --> REV["Strategy review (quarterly)"]
    REV --> Q{"Diagnosis still right? Actions working? Landscape changed?"}
    Q -->|"still fits"| CONT["Continue (don't thrash)"]
    Q -->|"shifted / not working / changed"| ADJ["Adjust deliberately"]
    ADJ --> S
    CONT --> REV

Artifact example

A strategy review record — the artifact that keeps a strategy living and honest.

# Strategy review: Engineering Velocity (Q3 review)

## Is the diagnosis still right?
Original: coupling (one monolith + one DB) serialises deploys. STILL RIGHT — the
coupling remains the binding constraint; no change.

## Are the actions working? (leading indicators, 52.8)
- Boundaries enforced: DONE, holding. Lead time 30d -> 15d (working).
- Paved road v1: DONE, adopted. (Working.)
- Payments extraction: IN PROGRESS, on track.
- Falsifiable signal check: "if lead time hadn't improved by Q3" — it HAS
  (30d->15d), so the diagnosis holds. No signal fired.

## Has the landscape changed?
- Team grew faster than planned (12 -> 50, ahead of schedule). ADJUSTMENT: pull
  the next extraction (catalog) forward a quarter — more capacity available.
- New: a compliance requirement for EU data residency emerged. NOT in the current
  strategy. DECISION: add a residency work-stream (small) to the roadmap; it
  doesn't change the diagnosis but adds a constraint.

## Adjustments (deliberate, not thrash)
- Pull catalog extraction forward (more capacity).
- Add EU residency work-stream (new constraint).
- NOT changing: the diagnosis, the guiding policy, the vision. The strategy is
  working; we adjust the roadmap, not the direction.

## Anti-pattern self-check
- Still a real strategy (diagnosis + policy + coherent actions)? YES.
- Still refusing things (no big-bang rewrite, no premature K8s)? YES, held the
  line on a K8s proposal this quarter.

The review record's power is that it periodically re-examines the strategy honestly — is the diagnosis still right (yes), are the actions working (yes, per leading indicators and the falsifiable-signal check), has the landscape changed (yes — faster growth and a new residency requirement) — and adjusts deliberately (pull an extraction forward, add a residency work-stream) without thrashing the core direction. The anti-pattern self-check keeps the strategy from decaying into a non-strategy. This turns strategy from a write-once document into a living, periodically-revisited direction that stays current and honest.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They keep the anti-patterns catalogue in mind as a checklist against their own and others' strategies, because they know technical strategy fails in predictable, recognisable ways — and catching the roadmap-called-strategy, the goal-list, the diagnosis-free action list, the refuse-nothing strategy, or the incoherent actions early prevents the organisation from following a non-strategy that will collapse. They treat strategy as a living thing that must be periodically reviewed, because they know a write-once strategy goes stale as the diagnosis shifts, actions complete or fail, and the landscape changes.

They run the strategy review honestly — genuinely asking whether the diagnosis still holds, whether the actions are working (via leading indicators and falsifiable signals, 52.8), and whether the landscape has changed — and they adjust deliberately rather than defending the original strategy regardless or thrashing it at every new idea. They keep the vision stable while letting the roadmap flex, adjusting the path when the review shows cause while holding the direction steady. The principal understands that good strategy requires both initial soundness (avoiding the anti-patterns) and ongoing honesty (the review that keeps it current), and that the many strategies that fail do so either by being a non-strategy from the start or by going stale from never being revisited.

Common mistakes

  • Not recognising the anti-patterns in your own strategy (roadmap-as-strategy, goal-list, diagnosis-free, refuses-nothing).
  • Writing a strategy once and never reviewing it, so it goes stale as the landscape changes.
  • Defending the original strategy in reviews regardless of whether it's working, instead of honestly adjusting.
  • Thrashing the strategy at every new idea, instead of adjusting deliberately when the review shows cause.
  • Changing the vision when only the roadmap needs to flex, destabilising the direction.

Interview questions

  1. What are the common ways technical strategy fails, and how do you recognise them? Expected answer: the roadmap-called-strategy (activities with reasoning removed), the goal-list (adjudicates nothing), the diagnosis-free action list (treats symptoms), the symptom-as-diagnosis, the refuse-nothing strategy (no real choices), the incoherent-actions committee compromise (where strategies usually die), the undeliverable roadmap (nominal not effective capacity), and the write-once strategy (never reviewed, goes stale). Recognise them by checking for a real diagnosis, a policy that refuses things, and coherent actions. Why it matters: catching these early prevents following a non-strategy.

  2. How and why do you review a strategy over time? Expected answer: review it on a cadence (e.g. quarterly), asking whether the diagnosis is still right, whether the actions are working (leading indicators, falsifiable signals), and whether the landscape has changed (team, technology, business, new constraints) — then adjust deliberately (the roadmap/actions, rarely the diagnosis) when the review shows cause, keeping the vision stable. Because a write-once strategy goes stale as the world changes around it. Why it matters: tests whether they treat strategy as living, not a one-time document.

  3. In a strategy review, the diagnosis still holds but the landscape changed (faster growth, a new compliance requirement). What do you do? Expected answer: adjust the roadmap deliberately — pull work forward given the extra capacity, add a work-stream for the new constraint — without changing the still-valid diagnosis, guiding policy, or vision; flex the path, hold the direction. And self-check that it's still a real strategy (diagnosis + policy + coherent actions, still refusing things). Why it matters: tests deliberate adjustment versus thrash or rigidity.

Practical exercise

Audit a strategy (yours or your org's) against the anti-patterns catalogue: is it a real strategy (diagnosis + policy + coherent actions) or one of the non-strategies (roadmap, goal-list, diagnosis-free, refuses-nothing, incoherent)? Then conduct a strategy review: is the diagnosis still right, are the actions working (what would the leading indicators show), has the landscape changed, and what would you adjust deliberately — distinguishing a roadmap flex from a direction change.

Acceptance criteria: your audit identifies whether the strategy is real or a recognised non-strategy, naming any anti-pattern present; your review honestly asks whether the diagnosis still holds and the actions are working (not just defending the original), checks whether the landscape has changed, and proposes deliberate adjustments (flexing the roadmap/actions while keeping the vision stable, unless the diagnosis itself has genuinely shifted) rather than either rigidity or thrash.

52.10 A quick-reference for technical strategy

A compact reference distilling the Part into the checks that matter most when you set or assess technical direction.

The strategy checklist

[ ] Do I know which I'm writing — vision, strategy, roadmap, or plan? (Don't conflate.)
[ ] Does my STRATEGY have a real DIAGNOSIS (a cause, not a symptom)?
[ ] Does the GUIDING POLICY refuse things? (A strategy that says yes to everything
    has made no choices.)
[ ] Are the ACTIONS coherent — each reinforcing another? (Where strategies die.)
[ ] Is the VISION measurable and tied to business numbers? (Not a slogan.)
[ ] Is the ROADMAP sequenced by dependency + risk, with an early win, sized to
    EFFECTIVE capacity? Are deferrals explicit?
[ ] Is tech debt managed as a PORTFOLIO — classified, measured in real units,
    funded by interest rate (and cheap debt deliberately carried)?
[ ] Is new tech evaluated on FIT and EXIT COST (not one exciting number), adopted
    in stages?
[ ] Is the strategy COMMUNICATED repeatedly, MEASURED (leading indicators,
    falsifiable signals), and REVIEWED on a cadence?

The enduring principle

The whole Part reduces to one idea: strategy is choice — a diagnosis of the real problem, a policy that commits to an approach and refuses others, and coherent actions that reinforce each other — made measurable, communicated relentlessly, and kept honest through review. Most things called strategy are non-strategies (roadmaps with the reasoning removed, goal-lists that choose nothing), and most real strategies fail not in the thinking but in the sustaining — never measured, never defended, left to go stale. When you set direction, ask: what is the honest diagnosis, what will we refuse, do the actions reinforce each other, how will we know it's working, and how will I keep it alive? And bias toward the boring choice, saying no to technology that doesn't earn its cost, because the simplest thing that meets the requirement wins.

Return to this reference when setting or assessing technical direction; the reasoning behind each line is in the sections above.

Senior Checklist — Part 52

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can tell the difference between a vision, a strategy, a roadmap and a plan, and I never confuse them
  • I can write a strategy kernel with a real diagnosis, a guiding policy that refuses things, and coherent actions
  • My diagnoses name causes, not symptoms, and I am willing to name the awkward ones
  • I write visions that are measurable and tied to business numbers
  • I sequence roadmaps by dependency and risk, with an early win, sized to effective capacity
  • I make deferrals explicit so they stop getting re-asked
  • I manage technical debt as a portfolio: classify, quantify in real units, and fund by interest rate
  • I deliberately carry cheap debt rather than fixing everything
  • I evaluate new technology on fit and exit cost, not on a single exciting number
  • I can say no to technology with a reasoned, falsifiable, recorded decision

Part 52 — Key Takeaways

  • Strategy, vision, roadmap and plan are four different things; conflating them produces documents that do none of their jobs, and most "strategies" are really roadmaps or goal-lists with the reasoning removed.
  • A real strategy has three parts: a diagnosis that names the cause, a guiding policy that chooses an approach and refuses alternatives, and coherent actions that reinforce one another.
  • The diagnosis is the hardest and most valuable part; skip it and your actions treat symptoms, and a strategy that refuses nothing has made no choices.
  • A vision must be measurable and tied to business numbers, or it is a slogan that loses its funding to anything that can show a return.
  • Roadmaps are sequenced by dependency and risk: respect prerequisites, front-load the plan-killers, schedule an early visible win, and size to effective, not nominal, capacity.
  • Make deferrals explicit with reasons, because an unstated no gets re-asked forever and an explicit one reduces thrash.
  • Manage technical debt as a portfolio: classify it, measure its cost in incidents, lead-time and toil hours, and fund paydown by interest rate rather than by guilt.
  • Deliberately carry cheap debt; paying down low-interest debt wastes capacity that high-interest compounding debt needs.
  • Evaluate new technology on weighted criteria dominated by fit and exit cost, run POCs that try to kill the candidate, compute three-year TCO including the forgotten costs, and adopt in stages.
  • At scale, build only what differentiates you, buy or adopt open source for the rest, and treat contract terms — caps, exit clauses, data export — as architecture.
  • Saying no to technology is one of a principal's highest-leverage habits; make every no reasoned, falsifiable and recorded, so it sticks and the boring, correct choice wins.

Part 53 — Architecture Governance, Standards and Paved Roads

Governance is a word engineers flinch at, because most of them have only seen the bad kind: a review board that takes three weeks to approve a config change, a standards document nobody reads, an architect who says no to everything. This Part is about the good kind — governance that makes the right thing the easy thing, so that forty teams build consistent, reliable systems without anyone policing them. Part 48 catalogued the anti-patterns that governance aims to prevent; Part 29 covered CI/CD; Part 8 covered API design. This Part is about scaling those good practices across a whole organisation without strangling it.

The central idea is a shift in mechanism. Heavy governance tries to enforce good architecture through approval — a human gate every change must pass.
