Good governance achieves it through defaults — paved roads, templates, libraries and automated checks that make the correct choice the path of least resistance. The first scales linearly with the number of reviewers and becomes a bottleneck; the second scales infinitely because it requires no human in the loop.

The reader this Part assumes is a staff or principal engineer who has seen standards decay and review boards stall, and wants to know how to get consistency across many teams without becoming the bottleneck or the villain.

53.1 Why governance exists, and why heavy governance fails

Concept

Governance exists to produce consistency and quality across many teams that would otherwise each make their own choices, leading to a system nobody can operate. Without any governance, forty teams produce forty error formats, forty logging conventions, forty ways to paginate, and an operational nightmare. But heavy governance — the kind built on mandatory human approval of every decision — fails for a different reason: it becomes a bottleneck, it breeds resentment, and engineers route around it, which is worse than no governance because now the rules are both ignored and resented.

Why does it exist?

Imagine forty teams, each free to choose how their service reports errors. One returns {"error": "..."}, another {"message": "..."}, another an HTTP 200 with an error inside, another a bare string. Now imagine being the on-call engineer trying to debug an incident that spans six of these services at 3 a.m., each speaking a different error dialect. Or the engineer building a client that must handle all forty formats. The cost of inconsistency is paid continuously, by everyone, forever. Governance exists to prevent that cost.

But heavy governance creates its own cost. Imagine every one of those forty teams having to get an architecture review board's approval before adding an endpoint. The board has five people and sees two hundred requests a month. The queue grows to three weeks. Teams start batching changes to avoid the queue, or making changes without approval and backfilling, or designing around the board's known preferences rather than the actual problem. The board, meant to improve quality, now degrades it — by delaying everything and by teaching engineers to game the process. Heavy governance fails because human approval does not scale and because people resent and route around gates.

Mental model

Imagine two ways to make drivers stop at a dangerous junction. The first is to station a police officer there to check every car — expensive, it only works while the officer is present, it creates a queue, and drivers resent it and speed up the moment the officer looks away. The second is to build a roundabout — a piece of infrastructure that makes stopping-and-yielding the natural, easy thing to do, with no officer required, working the same at 3 a.m. as at noon, for every driver forever. Heavy governance is the police officer. Good governance is the roundabout. The roundabout scales; the officer does not. Build infrastructure that makes the safe behaviour the easy behaviour, and you need no police.

How it works

The failure modes of heavy governance are predictable:

Bottleneck:    approval queue grows faster than reviewers can clear it.
Resentment:    engineers feel distrusted and slowed; morale drops.
Routing around: changes made without approval, or batched to dodge the gate.
Gaming:        designs shaped to please the board, not to solve the problem.
Staleness:     the board can't keep up, so it rubber-stamps or blocks blindly.
Centralisation of judgement: the board becomes a single point of failure
               for decisions it doesn't have the context to make well.

Good governance inverts the mechanism. Instead of a gate that every change passes through, it provides:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Heavy["Heavy governance (fails)"]
        T1["Team"] --> GATE["Approval board"] --> PROD1["Production"]
        GATE -.->|"queue, resentment, routing around"| T1
    end
    subgraph Good["Good governance (scales)"]
        T2["Team"] --> PR["Paved road - template, libs, defaults"]
        PR --> CI["Automated checks in CI"] --> PROD2["Production"]
    end

In the good model, the correct architecture is baked into the template the team starts from, the libraries they use by default, and the automated checks that run on every pull request. There is no human gate for the common case; the human attention is reserved for the genuinely novel, high-stakes decisions (via lightweight mechanisms covered in 53.4). The rules are enforced by making the right thing the easy thing, not by checking every change against a person.

Practical example

An org has a heavy architecture review board. Every new service and every significant change needs its sign-off. The board is three principal engineers; the queue is two to three weeks. Teams hate it. A new principal engineer measures the cost: the board approves 95% of requests essentially unchanged, meaning 95% of the queue time is pure delay adding no value, and the 5% it does change could have been caught by a few automated rules plus office hours for the genuinely novel cases. She replaces the universal gate with a paved road (a service template that bakes in the standards) plus automated CI checks (that enforce the common rules) plus optional office hours (for the novel 5%). Review-board load drops by 95%, delay disappears for the common case, and consistency actually improves, because the template enforces the standards uniformly rather than relying on three humans to remember them.

Artifact example

A governance model one-pager — the artifact that establishes how governance works in the org, replacing "everything needs board approval" with a tiered model.

# How architecture governance works at GreenCart

## Principle
We achieve consistency by making the right thing the easy thing — paved
roads and automated checks — not by gating every change on human approval.
Human attention is reserved for genuinely novel, high-stakes decisions.

## Three tiers (match the mechanism to the stakes)
| Decision type | Mechanism | Human approval? |
|---|---|---|
| Routine (new endpoint, new service of a known shape) | Paved-road template + CI checks | No — automated |
| Standard-affecting (new shared library, API convention change) | RFC (Part 51) + review guild | Async, lightweight |
| Novel / high-stakes (new datastore, cross-cutting pattern) | RFC + architecture office hours | Yes, but advisory not gatekeeping |

## What this means in practice
- Starting a new service? Use the template. No approval needed; the
  standards are built in.
- Every PR runs fitness functions (layering, dependency rules, error
  format). They enforce the rules so humans don't have to.
- Doing something genuinely new? Bring it to office hours. We advise and
  help; we rarely block, because you own your service.

## What we explicitly rejected
A mandatory review board for all changes. It was a 3-week bottleneck that
approved 95% unchanged. We replaced it with the model above.

The one-pager's power is that it is explicit about matching mechanism to stakes, it reserves scarce human judgement for the rare novel case, and it names what it rejected (the universal board) and why (3-week bottleneck, 95% rubber-stamped). It turns governance from a gate into a service.

Real-world scenario

A company's architecture review board is a prestigious, dreaded institution. Getting on its calendar takes weeks; presenting to it is nerve-wracking; its decisions are final and often context-poor because the board members do not operate the systems they rule on. A principal engineer who sits on the board realises it has become exactly the ivory-tower failure mode from Part 44 — architects ruling on systems they have never run. He leads the board to dissolve itself as a universal gate and reconstitute as office hours plus a set of fitness functions. The same expertise is still available — more available, because office hours have no three-week queue — but it is advisory, context-aware, and no longer a bottleneck. Decisions that used to take three weeks of waiting now happen in a thirty-minute conversation, and the ones that are routine happen with no conversation at all because the template and the checks handle them.

Failure scenario

A new VP, alarmed by an architecture inconsistency, institutes a mandatory architecture review board for all changes. For a month it catches a few real issues and everyone agrees it is valuable. Then the queue builds. By month three it is two weeks deep. Teams start batching a quarter's worth of changes into one board submission to minimise trips through the gate, which means the board now reviews enormous, un-reviewable change sets and rubber-stamps them because it cannot absorb them. Other teams simply stop submitting and make changes quietly, so the board's records no longer reflect reality. The inconsistency the VP worried about is now worse, because the board gave an illusion of control while actual decisions moved underground. The gate did not produce consistency; it produced a queue, a workaround culture, and a false sense of safety. Infrastructure — a template and automated checks — would have produced the consistency the gate only pretended to.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Approval queue bottleneck. Human review does not scale; the queue grows without bound and delays everything.
  • Routing around the gate. Teams batch changes or make them quietly, so the governance records diverge from reality.
  • Rubber-stamping under load. An overwhelmed board approves without real review, giving an illusion of control.
  • Context-poor rulings. Boards decide on systems they do not operate, so their decisions carry the wrong assumptions (the Part 44 ivory-tower failure).
  • No governance at all. The opposite failure: forty teams, forty error formats, an operational nightmare.
  • Governance that never sunsets rules. Old standards that no longer make sense stay enforced because nobody owns removing them.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat governance as an infrastructure problem, not an approval problem: the goal is to make the right thing the easy thing, so that consistency emerges from defaults rather than from policing. They are deeply suspicious of universal human gates, because they have watched every one of them become a bottleneck that teaches engineers to route around it. They reserve scarce human judgement for the genuinely novel, high-stakes decisions and automate everything routine, because a human reviewing a routine change is both a waste of an expensive person and a delay for the team.

They also keep governance advisory wherever possible rather than gatekeeping, because the team that owns and operates a service has better context than any central board, and the principal's job is to make the good choice easy and visible, not to substitute their judgement for the owner's. And they are willing to dissolve their own governance institutions when those institutions have become the bottleneck — the board that cannot let go of being a gate is itself the problem.

Common mistakes

  • Equating governance with approval, so every change needs a human gate that cannot scale.
  • Building a review board that rules on systems its members do not operate, producing context-poor decisions.
  • Letting the approval queue become a bottleneck that teaches teams to route around it.
  • Having no governance at all, producing forty incompatible ways to do everything.
  • Never sunsetting old rules, so governance accretes stale constraints nobody can justify.

Interview questions

  1. Why does heavy, approval-based architecture governance tend to fail? Expected answer: human approval does not scale, so the queue becomes a bottleneck; teams resent it and route around it (batching changes, making them quietly), boards rubber-stamp under load and rule on systems they do not operate. The result is worse consistency plus an illusion of control. Follow-up: what would you replace it with.

  2. How do you get consistency across forty teams without a review board for every change? Expected answer: make the right thing the easy thing — paved-road templates that bake in the standards, default libraries, and automated fitness functions in CI that enforce the rules on every PR; reserve lightweight human review (RFC, office hours) for the genuinely novel cases. Why it matters: this is the core of the whole Part.

  3. When is a central architecture decision gate actually appropriate? Expected answer: rarely, and only for genuinely novel, high-stakes, hard-to-reverse decisions (a new datastore, a cross-cutting pattern) — and even then advisory is better than gatekeeping, because the owning team has better context. Routine changes should never hit a human gate. Why it matters: tests judgement about proportionality.

Practical exercise

Audit your org's current architecture governance. For each mechanism (review board, approval step, standards doc, CI check), classify it as a gate (human approval required) or infrastructure (makes the right thing easy automatically). Count how many routine changes require human approval. Then propose a tiered model that moves routine decisions to paved roads and automated checks, and reserves human review for the genuinely novel.

Acceptance criteria: you can name at least one human gate that could be replaced by an automated check or a template, estimate the delay it currently adds, and describe the infrastructure (template section or CI rule) that would enforce the same standard without a human in the loop.

53.2 Paved roads and golden paths

Concept

A paved road (also called a golden path) is the well-supported, opinionated, default way to do a common thing — create a service, add a queue consumer, expose an API — where all the hard decisions have been made for you and all the standard pieces come pre-wired. A team on the paved road gets observability, CI/CD, security defaults, the standard error format and the standard libraries for free, just by starting from the template. The road is paved, so travelling it is smooth; going off-road is allowed but you do the paving yourself. This is the single most powerful governance mechanism, because it achieves consistency through convenience rather than coercion.

Why does it exist?

Imagine every team, starting a new service, having to decide from scratch: which logging library, how to structure config, how to wire up health checks, how to set up the CI pipeline, which error format, how to add tracing. Each team spends a week or two on this undifferentiated setup, each makes slightly different choices, and the result is forty services that are each subtly unique and collectively impossible to operate consistently. Multiply by forty teams and you have wasted months of engineering on solved problems and produced an inconsistent estate.

The paved road exists to make all of that a non-decision. The team runs one command, gets a service with everything wired correctly, and starts on their actual problem the same day. Consistency is a side effect of the convenience, not a burden imposed on top of it.

Mental model

Imagine a city that wants everyone to use public transit. It could ban cars (coercion — resented, routed around). Or it could build transit so good — frequent, clean, cheap, going everywhere you need — that taking it is simply easier than driving. The second city gets high transit use with no bans, because the good option is the easy option. A paved road is that excellent transit system: so convenient that teams choose it freely, and the consistency the org wants emerges from the free choices of teams who found the paved road easier than paving their own.

How it works

A paved road has layers, and the more layers you pave, the more value it delivers:

1. Service template:   `create-service orders` scaffolds a full service with
                       structure, config, health checks, error format, tests.
2. Default libraries:  the blessed logging, HTTP client, resilience, auth
                       libraries, pre-wired and version-managed centrally.
3. CI/CD pipeline:     the standard pipeline (lint, test, build, deploy)
                       generated with the service, no setup.
4. Observability:      metrics, structured logs, tracing, dashboards and the
                       standard alerts, wired by default.
5. Security defaults:  authn/authz middleware, secret management, dependency
                       scanning, all on by default.
6. Runtime/deploy:     the standard way to deploy, scale, and roll back.

The key properties that make a paved road work:

  • Opinionated. It makes choices for you. A paved road with options is not paved; it is a fork in a dirt track.
  • Complete for the common case. A team using it should need zero additional setup for a standard service.
  • Maintained as a product. Someone owns it, improves it, and keeps it current (see Part 55 on platform-as-product). An abandoned paved road becomes a legacy trap.
  • Off-road is allowed. Teams with genuinely different needs can leave the road, but they take on the cost of paving themselves. The road is the default, not a mandate.
flowchart LR
    CMD["create-service orders"] --> SVC["New service"]
    SVC --> S1["Standard structure + error format"]
    SVC --> S2["CI/CD pipeline"]
    SVC --> S3["Observability + alerts"]
    SVC --> S4["Security defaults"]
    SVC --> S5["Default libraries pre-wired"]

Practical example

A platform team builds a create-service CLI. An engineer runs create-service inventory-pricing, answers three prompts (team name, does it need a database, does it need a queue consumer), and gets a NestJS service with: the standard module structure, config loaded from the environment the standard way, a /health and /ready endpoint wired to Terminus, the standard error filter producing the org's error format, structured JSON logging with trace IDs, a CI pipeline that lints, tests and deploys, a dashboard with the standard metrics, and the three standard alerts. The engineer writes their first real endpoint within an hour. Compare to the pre-paved-road world where this setup took a week and every service did it slightly differently. The paved road converted a week of inconsistent setup into an hour of consistent setup, forty times over.

Artifact example

The contents of a paved-road service template, shown as the manifest of what a team gets for free — this is what makes the road worth taking.

# What `create-service` gives you (paved road v3)

## Structure & conventions
- NestJS 10 module layout: controller / service / repository / dto / entity
- Standard error filter -> org error format (see §53.3)
- Config from env via @nestjs/config with a validated schema
- OpenAPI spec generated from controllers (contract-first, §53.6)

## Reliability (on by default)
- @nestjs/terminus /health and /ready
- Resilience library: timeouts, retry-with-backoff, circuit breaker
- Graceful shutdown wired (drains in-flight requests)

## Observability (on by default)
- OpenTelemetry tracing with propagated trace IDs
- Structured JSON logs (level, trace_id, service, msg)
- Prometheus metrics endpoint + a default Grafana dashboard
- Standard alerts: error-rate, p99 latency, saturation

## CI/CD (generated)
- GitHub Actions: lint, typecheck, test, build, deploy
- Dependency + container scanning in the pipeline
- Fitness functions run on every PR (§53.5)

## Security (on by default)
- Auth guard wired; endpoints are authenticated unless explicitly @Public()
- Secrets from the secret manager, never in env files or code
- Sensible CORS, security headers

## You write
- Your endpoints. Your domain logic. That's it.

The manifest is the sales pitch for the road: a team sees that everything tedious and standard is handled, so taking the road is obviously easier than paving their own. The last line — "you write your endpoints, your domain logic, that's it" — is the whole value proposition. Consistency comes for free because the easy path is the consistent path.

Real-world scenario

A company with a mature paved road ships a security fix — a patch to the auth library and a new security header — by releasing a new template version and a library update. Because every service on the paved road uses the central library and template, the fix propagates to the whole estate through a routine dependency bump, and the fitness functions flag any service that has drifted. A company without a paved road faces the same security fix as forty separate tickets, forty teams each implementing it slightly differently, weeks of coordination, and no guarantee of completeness. The paved road turned an estate-wide security fix from a multi-week coordination program into a library release. That leverage — fix once, propagate everywhere — is why paved roads are the highest-value governance investment an org can make.

Failure scenario

A platform team builds a paved road, celebrates its launch, and then moves on to other work. The road is not maintained as a product. Eighteen months later, the template still scaffolds NestJS 8 (two majors behind), the default libraries have known vulnerabilities, the CI pipeline uses a deprecated action, and the observability wiring points at a monitoring system the company migrated away from. New teams who use the template inherit all of this rot on day one and spend their first week removing the paved road's broken defaults — the road now makes things harder, not easier. Teams start avoiding it, paving their own again, and the consistency it once provided fragments. The paved road did not fail because the idea was wrong; it failed because an unmaintained paved road is worse than none, actively spreading rot to every new service. A paved road is a product with an owner and a roadmap, or it is a trap.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Unmaintained road. Falls behind on versions, security and integrations, and actively spreads rot to new services.
  • Not opinionated enough. A template full of choices and TODOs is not a paved road; the team still has to make all the decisions.
  • Incomplete for the common case. The road covers 70% of setup, so every team still does the remaining tedious 30% differently.
  • Mandated, not made attractive. Forcing teams onto a road they find worse than their own produces resentment and gaming; the road must be genuinely easier.
  • No off-road option. Teams with real, different needs are forced onto a road that does not fit, so they fight the template or fork it badly.
  • One road for incompatible needs. Trying to pave one road for web services, data pipelines and ML workloads; each needs its own paved road.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They see the paved road as the highest-leverage governance investment available, because it achieves consistency through convenience — teams choose it freely because it is easier, so there is nothing to enforce. They insist the road be opinionated and complete for the common case, because a road with options or gaps is just a slightly nicer dirt track that still leaves teams making and diverging on decisions. They treat the road as a product with an owner, a roadmap and a maintenance commitment, because they know an abandoned paved road rots into a trap that spreads vulnerabilities to every new service.

They also preserve the off-road option deliberately, because a mandate breeds resentment and gaming, whereas a genuinely-better default earns voluntary adoption — and the small number of teams with real, different needs should be able to leave the road and pay for their own paving rather than fight a template that does not fit. The principal's measure of success is not "everyone is forced onto the road" but "the road is so good that leaving it is a deliberate, rare, justified choice".

Common mistakes

  • Building the road and abandoning it, letting it rot into a trap.
  • Making the road full of options and TODOs instead of opinionated and complete.
  • Mandating the road instead of making it the easiest choice, which breeds gaming.
  • Paving only part of the common case, so teams still diverge on the unpaved remainder.
  • Trying to serve incompatible workloads with one road instead of several purpose-built ones.

Interview questions

  1. What is a paved road and why is it more effective than mandates for achieving consistency? Expected answer: a paved road is the opinionated, complete, well-supported default way to do a common thing (create a service, add a consumer), with all standard pieces pre-wired; it beats mandates because it achieves consistency through convenience — teams choose it freely because it is easier — so there is nothing to enforce or route around. Follow-up: what makes a paved road attractive enough to be chosen.

  2. Why is an unmaintained paved road worse than no paved road? Expected answer: because new teams adopt it on day one and inherit its rot — outdated versions, vulnerable libraries, broken integrations — spending their first week removing broken defaults; the road actively spreads problems to the whole estate. A paved road must be owned and maintained as a product. Why it matters: tests whether they understand platform-as-product, not platform-as-project.

  3. A paved road gives you estate-wide leverage. Give an example. Expected answer: a security fix (patch the central auth library + update the template) propagates to every service on the road through a routine dependency bump, with fitness functions catching drift — turning a forty-ticket coordination program into a library release. Why it matters: tests whether they see the compounding value of shared infrastructure.

Practical exercise

Design the manifest for a paved road for your org's most common service type. List everything a team should get for free when they create a new service: structure, reliability, observability, CI/CD, security. Then honestly assess your current reality: for each item, is it paved (automatic) or does each team do it themselves? Identify the three highest-leverage items to pave first.

Acceptance criteria: your manifest is opinionated (makes specific choices, not "pick a logging library") and complete enough that a team using it would need zero additional setup for a standard service; and you can name three currently-unpaved items whose paving would save the most repeated, divergent effort across teams.

53.3 Standards that scale

Concept

Standards are the shared conventions that let services across an org interoperate and be operated together: a standard API shape, a standard event schema format, a standard error format, standard logging and metrics conventions, standard naming. A standard that scales is one that is enforced by infrastructure (the paved road and automated checks) rather than by documents and goodwill, is minimal (covering only what genuinely benefits from being shared), and is owned (someone maintains and evolves it). A standard that lives only in a wiki page is not a standard; it is a suggestion that decays.

Why does it exist?

Imagine debugging an incident spanning six services where each logs differently — one logs plain text, one logs JSON with a msg field, one with a message field, none include a trace ID, and timestamps are in three different timezones. Correlating the incident across services is nearly impossible; you cannot grep for a request's journey because there is no common field to grep for. Now imagine the same six services all logging structured JSON with a trace_id, level, service and msg, all in UTC. You filter by trace_id and see the entire request's path across all six in one query. The standard is the difference between a debuggable system and an opaque one.

Standards exist to make a fleet of services behave like one coherent system for the purposes that matter: debugging, monitoring, client integration, and operation. Without them, every cross-service activity pays a translation tax forever.

Mental model

Imagine shipping containers. Before the standard shipping container, every cargo was loaded and unloaded by hand in a different shape, and moving goods between ship, train and truck was slow and manual. The standardised container — one size, one set of fittings — made the whole global logistics system interoperable: any crane, any ship, any truck handles any container. The container standard did not constrain what you put inside it (that is still your business); it standardised only the interface so everything could interoperate. Good software standards are the same: they standardise the interface (error format, log shape, API conventions) so the fleet interoperates, while leaving the internals (your domain logic) entirely up to you.

How it works

The standards worth having, and what each enables:

Standard What it fixes What it enables
API conventions (REST shape, status codes, pagination) Every service's API is subtly different Clients and gateways handle all services uniformly
Error format Forty error shapes Uniform error handling, debuggable incidents
Event schema format Events that can't be consumed generically Any consumer can parse any event; schema registry
Logging conventions (structured, trace_id, fields) Un-correlatable logs Grep a trace across the whole fleet
Metrics conventions (naming, labels) Dashboards that don't compose One dashboard template works for every service
Naming (services, topics, resources) Chaos in discovery and ownership You can find and attribute anything

Three principles make standards scale:

  1. Enforce by infrastructure, not documents. The standard error format is produced by the paved road's error filter and checked by a fitness function, not by a wiki page asking nicely. A standard that depends on humans remembering decays.
  2. Keep it minimal. Standardise only the interface that genuinely benefits from being shared. Over-standardising (mandating internal structure, forcing one way to do everything) is the heavy-governance failure in a new costume. Standardise the container, not the cargo.
  3. Own and evolve it. A standard has an owner who maintains it, versions it, and sunsets parts that no longer make sense. Standards that nobody owns rot.

Practical example

An org standardises its error format. The standard: every error response is { "error": { "code": "ORDER_NOT_FOUND", "message": "...", "trace_id": "...", "details": {...} } } with a specific HTTP status. It is enforced not by asking teams to produce it but by a shared NestJS exception filter in the paved road that every service uses by default, which turns thrown exceptions into this shape automatically. A fitness function in CI asserts that the service uses the standard filter. The result: every service's errors look the same, clients handle errors uniformly, and the trace_id in every error links straight to the trace and logs. No team had to read a document and remember to comply; the paved road made compliance the default and the fitness function caught drift. That is a standard that scales.

Artifact example

A standard definition done right — the error format standard, specifying the interface precisely, with its enforcement mechanism named.

# Standard: HTTP error format (v2, owner: platform team)

## Scope
All HTTP APIs. Applies to error responses only. Does NOT constrain success
response shapes (those are each API's business).

## The format
Every error response body:
{
  "error": {
    "code": "SNAKE_CASE_STABLE_CODE",   // stable, documented, machine-readable
    "message": "Human-readable description",  // for developers, not end users
    "trace_id": "abc123...",             // always present, links to trace+logs
    "details": { }                       // optional, structured, error-specific
  }
}
Status codes: 400 validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 unauthorized,
404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 unprocessable, 429 rate limited,
500 internal, 503 unavailable. No error returned with a 2xx status.

## Enforcement (this is what makes it a standard, not a suggestion)
- The paved-road exception filter produces this format automatically.
- Fitness function `error-format.spec` asserts the filter is wired and that
  a sample of error responses match the schema. Runs on every PR.
- The OpenAPI contract check (§53.6) verifies documented error schemas match.

## Evolution
- Breaking changes to this format require an RFC and a migration plan.
- v1 (bare {"message"}) is deprecated; services migrate via the template bump.

The standard is precise (exact shape, exact status codes), scoped (errors only, not success shapes — minimal), and — critically — names its enforcement (the filter plus the fitness function). A standard document without an enforcement mechanism is a wish; this one is enforced by infrastructure, so it scales.

Real-world scenario

A company adopts standard logging conventions enforced through the paved road: structured JSON, mandatory trace_id, standard field names, UTC timestamps. The payoff shows up during a cross-service incident. An order is failing intermittently, touching six services. The on-call engineer takes the trace_id from the error response (which is standardised, so it is always there) and queries the log aggregator for that one ID. Because every service logs with the standard trace_id field, the query returns the complete journey of that request across all six services in chronological order, and the failing step is obvious within two minutes. In the pre-standard world, this same investigation took hours of manually correlating differently-shaped logs across six systems, if it was possible at all. One logging standard, enforced by the paved road, converted a multi-hour correlation nightmare into a two-minute query.

Failure scenario

An architect writes an excellent, comprehensive standards document: API conventions, error formats, logging, the works. It is thorough and correct. It is published on the wiki and announced in an all-hands. And then nothing enforces it. New services are not generated from a template that implements it; no CI check verifies it; compliance depends entirely on each engineer reading the document and choosing to follow it. Within a year, the standard describes a fantasy: new services drift because nobody remembers the wiki page, existing services were never retrofitted, and the gap between the documented standard and the actual estate grows until the document is actively misleading — an engineer who trusts it builds a client expecting an error format that half the services do not produce. The standard failed not because it was wrong but because it was enforced by goodwill and memory, which do not scale. A standard must be baked into infrastructure, or it is just a document slowly diverging from reality.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Standard enforced by documents only. Depends on memory and goodwill; drifts until it describes a fantasy.
  • Over-standardising. Mandating internal structure and one-way-to-do-everything, which is heavy governance in disguise and breeds resentment.
  • Unowned standard. Nobody maintains or evolves it, so it rots and stale parts stay enforced.
  • Standard with no migration path. A new version lands with no way for existing services to adopt it, so the estate splits into old and new forever.
  • Standardising the cargo, not the container. Constraining domain internals instead of just the interoperability interface.
  • No deprecation path. Old standard versions are never sunset, so the fleet carries every version simultaneously.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They judge a standard by its enforcement mechanism, not its prose: a beautifully written standard with no automated enforcement is a wish, and they will not call it a standard until it is baked into the paved road and checked in CI. They keep standards minimal — standardise the interoperability interface (error shape, log fields, API conventions) and nothing more — because over-standardising is the heavy-governance failure wearing new clothes, and it provokes the same resentment and routing-around.

They insist every standard has an owner and an evolution path, because an unowned standard rots and a standard with no migration path splits the estate permanently. And they think about standards in terms of the fleet-wide capabilities they unlock — a logging standard is worth it because it makes the whole fleet debuggable from one query, an error standard because it makes incidents correlatable and clients uniform. The standard is justified by the cross-service capability it enables, not by tidiness for its own sake.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing a standard as a document with no enforcement, so it drifts into fiction.
  • Over-standardising internals instead of just the interoperability interface.
  • Leaving a standard unowned, so it rots and stale parts stay enforced.
  • Shipping a new standard version with no migration path, splitting the estate.
  • Justifying standards by tidiness instead of by the fleet-wide capability they unlock.

Interview questions

  1. What makes a standard actually scale across many teams? Expected answer: it is enforced by infrastructure (paved road + automated checks) rather than by documents and goodwill, it is minimal (only the interoperability interface), and it is owned with an evolution and migration path. A wiki-only standard decays into fiction. Follow-up: give an example of a standard and its enforcement mechanism.

  2. Which things should be standardised across services, and which should not? Expected answer: standardise the interoperability interface — error format, log shape and trace IDs, API conventions, event schema format, metrics naming — because they unlock fleet-wide debugging, monitoring and client uniformity. Do NOT standardise internal structure or domain logic; that is over-standardising (the container, not the cargo). Why it matters: tests the minimalism principle.

  3. A comprehensive standards document was published a year ago. How would you tell if it is real? Expected answer: check whether it is enforced — is it baked into a paved-road template, is there a CI fitness function, were existing services retrofitted? If compliance depends on people reading the wiki, the estate has almost certainly drifted and the document is now misleading. Why it matters: tests whether they distinguish documented standards from enforced ones.

Practical exercise

Pick one standard your org needs or has (error format, logging, API conventions). Write its precise definition, scoped minimally to the interoperability interface. Then — the important part — specify its enforcement: which paved-road component produces it automatically, and which automated check verifies it on every change. If no enforcement exists, that is your finding.

Acceptance criteria: the standard is scoped to the interface only (it does not dictate domain internals); it names a specific infrastructure mechanism that produces compliance by default and a specific automated check that catches drift; and it has a named owner and a migration path for existing services. If any of these is missing, you have identified why the standard does not currently scale.

53.4 Architecture review boards and their lightweight alternatives

Concept

An architecture review board (ARB) is a group of senior engineers who review and approve architectural decisions. They can be genuinely valuable — a place to catch cross-cutting mistakes and share hard-won judgement — or they can become the bottleneck and ivory tower from 53.1. The skill is knowing when a board helps, when it becomes a liability, and what lighter mechanisms — office hours, review guilds, RFC-with-advisors — deliver most of the value without the bottleneck. The modern consensus leans heavily toward the lightweight alternatives, reserving anything board-like for the rare, genuinely cross-cutting decision.

Why does it exist?

Imagine an org with no forum at all for architectural judgement. Every team decides in isolation. The hard-won lesson one team learned about why not to share a database is never transmitted; the next team learns it the same painful way. A genuinely cross-cutting decision — say, how the whole org will do tenant isolation — is made by whoever happens to face it first, with no input from the people it affects. Some mechanism is needed to pool senior judgement and catch cross-cutting mistakes.

But the heavy ARB exists as an answer to that need and then overshoots: it inserts itself as a mandatory gate on everything, becoming the bottleneck from 53.1. The lightweight alternatives exist to meet the real need (pool judgement, catch cross-cutting issues) without the overshoot (gating everything, centralising decisions away from the teams who own them).

Mental model

Imagine a town's building decisions. The heavy ARB is a committee that must approve every change to every house — painting a door, moving a shelf — which is absurd and creates a queue a mile long. The lightweight model is: clear building codes (standards) that most work just follows, an architect you can book a consultation with when you are doing something unusual (office hours), and a guild of experienced builders who review each other's plans and share techniques (review guild). Only a genuinely town-altering project — a new high-rise that affects everyone's light and traffic — goes to a formal hearing. Most work needs no committee at all; the codes and the available expertise suffice.

How it works

The spectrum of mechanisms, from heaviest to lightest:

flowchart LR
    ARB["Mandatory ARB - gate on everything"] --> SEL["Selective ARB - only novel/cross-cutting"]
    SEL --> RFC["RFC + named advisors"]
    RFC --> GUILD["Review guild - peers review peers"]
    GUILD --> OH["Office hours - book a consult when you need it"]
    OH --> AUTO["Fitness functions - no humans for routine"]
  • Mandatory ARB (avoid). Gates everything. The 53.1 bottleneck. Almost never the right default.
  • Selective ARB. Convenes only for genuinely novel, cross-cutting, hard-to-reverse decisions (a new datastore for the org, a tenancy model, a cross-cutting security pattern). Advisory where possible. A handful of times a quarter, not a standing gate.
  • RFC with named advisors. The RFC process (Part 51) plus a norm that certain kinds of RFC must get review from named domain experts (the security lead for anything auth-related, the data lead for schema-wide changes). Async, no meeting required.
  • Review guild. A community of practice where engineers from different teams review each other's designs, share patterns, and build shared judgement. Peer-to-peer, not top-down. Spreads lessons without a gate.
  • Office hours. Senior engineers and architects hold regular open slots. Any team doing something tricky books a consult. Advice flows on demand, with no queue and no gate. This is often the single best mechanism.
  • Fitness functions. For routine decisions, no human at all (see 53.5).

The decision of which to use:

Situation Best mechanism
Routine decision of a known shape Fitness functions + paved road, no humans
Team wants advice on a tricky design Office hours
Change affects a specific domain (security, data) RFC + named advisor
Spreading patterns and judgement across teams Review guild
Genuinely novel, org-wide, hard-to-reverse Selective ARB (advisory)

Practical example

An org replaces its mandatory ARB with a blend. Routine service decisions are handled by the paved road and fitness functions — no humans. A team designing a tricky distributed transaction books an office-hours slot and gets an hour of a principal engineer's time the same week, far faster than the old board's three-week queue. A change to how auth works must, by norm, get an async review from the security lead on its RFC. A monthly review guild meeting is where teams present interesting designs and the org's shared patterns evolve. And twice that quarter, a genuinely org-wide decision — adopting a new primary datastore, defining the tenancy model — convenes a selective, advisory ARB. The heavy board's one job (gate everything) is gone; its valuable job (pool senior judgement) is distributed across mechanisms that have no queue.

Artifact example

An office-hours charter plus a selective-ARB trigger list — the artifacts that make lightweight governance concrete.

# Architecture office hours
When: Tue & Thu, 14:00-15:00. Book a 20-min slot, or drop in.
Who: rotating principal/staff engineers + domain leads as needed.
What it's for: get advice on a design, pressure-test an approach, find out
  if someone's already solved your problem, sanity-check before an RFC.
What it is NOT: an approval gate. We advise; you own your decision. You
  never NEED office hours to ship. It's a service, not a checkpoint.
Prep: bring a one-pager or a diagram. We'll give you more if you give us more.

---

# When a decision goes to the selective ARB (advisory)
Bring it to the ARB ONLY if it is ALL of:
- Cross-cutting: affects many teams or the whole estate, AND
- Novel: not covered by an existing standard or paved road, AND
- Hard to reverse: expensive to unwind once adopted.
Examples that qualify: adopting a new primary datastore org-wide; the
  multi-tenancy isolation model; a new cross-cutting auth pattern.
Examples that do NOT: a new endpoint (paved road), choosing a library for
  your service (your call), a schema change in your own tables (your call).
The ARB advises and helps de-risk. It does not own your decision.

The charter makes office hours explicitly a service, not a gate ("you never NEED office hours to ship"), which is what keeps it from sliding back into a bottleneck. The ARB trigger list uses an AND of three strict conditions, which keeps the board rare — most things fail at least one condition and are therefore handled by lighter mechanisms. Together they pool senior judgement without creating a queue.

Real-world scenario

A review guild at a food-delivery company meets fortnightly. There is no agenda beyond "someone presents a design they are working on, and everyone else probes it". Over a year, the guild becomes the org's immune system for architecture: a team about to make a mistake another team already made gets caught, not by a gate, but by a peer in the guild saying "we tried that, here is what happened". Patterns spread horizontally — one team's elegant idempotency approach becomes the org's default because the guild saw it and liked it. None of this required authority or approval; it required a forum where engineers review each other's work as peers. The guild delivers the ARB's real value (pooled judgement, spread lessons) with none of its cost (no queue, no gate, no ivory tower), because it is peer-to-peer rather than top-down.

Failure scenario

An org keeps its mandatory ARB but tries to make it faster by adding more members and meeting more often. It does not work, because the problem was never throughput; it was the model. More board members means more scheduling complexity and more conflicting opinions, so decisions take longer, not shorter. Meeting more often consumes more senior-engineer time without reducing the queue, because the queue grows with the org's change rate, which no amount of board meetings can match. Worse, the expanded board makes even more context-poor decisions, because now eight people who do not operate the systems are ruling on them instead of three. The org doubled its investment in the wrong mechanism and got a slower, worse version of the same bottleneck. The fix was never a bigger board; it was replacing the gate with infrastructure and distributed, advisory judgement.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Scaling a bottleneck instead of removing it. More board members or more meetings; the gate model cannot keep up with the org's change rate.
  • Office hours that become a gate. If "we should check with office hours" becomes a de facto requirement, the lightweight mechanism has become the heavy one.
  • ARB that rules instead of advising. Even a selective ARB, if it gates rather than advises, centralises decisions away from the owning teams.
  • Guild with no psychological safety. If presenting a design to the guild feels like a trial, people stop presenting, and the forum dies.
  • No forum at all. The opposite failure: lessons never spread, cross-cutting mistakes recur, judgement never pools.
  • Advisors who never get consulted. Named-advisor norms that nobody follows, so domain expertise is routinely bypassed.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They default to the lightest mechanism that meets the need and escalate heaviness only when genuinely required: fitness functions for routine, office hours for advice, named advisors for domain-specific changes, a guild for spreading judgement, and a rare advisory ARB only for the cross-cutting-and-novel-and-irreversible intersection. They are vigilant that advisory mechanisms stay advisory — the moment office hours or the guild becomes a de facto gate, it has reacquired the bottleneck they were avoiding.

They understand that the real value of any board-like forum is pooling judgement and spreading lessons, not gating, and that those goals are better served by peer-to-peer and on-demand mechanisms than by a top-down gate. And they protect the psychological safety of the guild and office hours fiercely, because the moment presenting a design feels like a trial, engineers stop bringing their real, half-formed, improvable designs, and the forum loses the very thing that made it useful.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to fix a slow ARB by making it bigger instead of replacing the gate model.
  • Letting office hours or the guild harden into a de facto gate, recreating the bottleneck.
  • Running an ARB that rules rather than advises, centralising decisions away from owners.
  • Having no forum at all, so lessons never spread and mistakes recur.
  • Killing guild safety by making design presentations feel like trials.

Interview questions

  1. When does an architecture review board help, and when does it become a liability? Expected answer: it helps as a rare, advisory forum for genuinely novel, cross-cutting, hard-to-reverse decisions; it becomes a liability when it gates everything (bottleneck), rules rather than advises (centralises decisions away from owners), or decides on systems its members do not operate (ivory tower). Follow-up: what lighter mechanisms would you use instead for the common cases.

  2. Your ARB is a three-week bottleneck. The proposed fix is to add more members and meet weekly. Why won't that work? Expected answer: the problem is the gate model, not throughput; the queue grows with the org's change rate, which no board can match, and more members means slower, more conflicting, more context-poor decisions. The fix is to remove the gate — paved road + fitness functions for routine, office hours and named advisors for the rest — not to scale the board. Why it matters: tests whether they diagnose mechanism versus capacity.

  3. What makes a review guild effective at spreading architectural judgement? Expected answer: it is peer-to-peer (not top-down), has no approval power (so it is a forum, not a gate), and has psychological safety (presenting a design is not a trial), so engineers bring real, improvable designs and lessons spread horizontally. Why it matters: tests understanding of distributed versus centralised judgement.

Practical exercise

Map your org's current architecture-decision mechanisms onto the spectrum from mandatory ARB to fitness functions. For each decision type your teams make (new service, library choice, schema change, novel pattern), identify which mechanism currently handles it and which should. Then design a selective-ARB trigger list (the strict AND conditions) and an office-hours charter that explicitly positions it as a service, not a gate.

Acceptance criteria: at least one decision type currently going through a heavy mechanism is reassigned to a lighter one; your ARB trigger list requires all three conditions (cross-cutting AND novel AND hard-to-reverse) so the board stays rare; and your office-hours charter explicitly states that teams never need it to ship, keeping it advisory.

53.5 Architecture fitness functions

Concept

An architecture fitness function is an automated test that checks whether the system still has the architectural properties you want: that layers are respected, that dependency rules hold, that latency stays within budget, that bundle sizes do not balloon. It is the mechanism that turns a standard from a document into an enforced rule, because it runs on every change and fails the build when the architecture drifts. If standards and paved roads are how you establish good architecture, fitness functions are how you keep it — they are the automated immune system that catches architectural erosion the moment it happens, not two years later during an incident.

Why does it exist?

Imagine an architecture where the rule is "the controller layer may call the service layer, but the service layer must never import a controller". Everyone agrees. Then, over two years and a thousand pull requests, someone, under deadline pressure, imports a controller into a service "just this once". Nobody notices in review. Then it happens again. Slowly, the clean layering erodes into a tangle, and by the time anyone notices, unwinding it is a major project. The rule was real, everyone believed in it, and it decayed anyway, because nothing enforced it on every change.

Fitness functions exist because architectural rules enforced by human vigilance always decay — reviewers get tired, deadlines press, new people do not know the rule. An automated check never gets tired and runs on every single change, so the rule holds for years. It converts "we try to respect layering" into "the build fails if you violate layering".

Mental model

Imagine a bank vault with a rule: certain doors must never be open at the same time. You could post a guard to watch (human vigilance — tires, gets distracted, leaves at night). Or you could install an interlock that physically makes it impossible to open the second door while the first is open (automated enforcement — never tires, works at 3 a.m., no exceptions). A fitness function is the interlock. The architectural rule is enforced by a mechanism that cannot be forgotten or pressured, so the property holds continuously rather than depending on everyone remembering it on every change forever.

How it works

Fitness functions come in several kinds, enforcing different properties:

- Dependency / layering rules: service layer must not import controllers;
  module A must not depend on module B's internals.
- Module boundary rules:       cross-module imports must go through public APIs.
- Latency budgets:             a critical endpoint's p99 must stay under N ms
  (checked in a perf test in CI, or as an alert in prod).
- Resource budgets:            bundle size, image size, dependency count.
- Convention checks:           every service uses the standard error filter;
  every endpoint is authenticated unless explicitly public.
- Schema / contract checks:    events match the registered schema; the API
  matches the OpenAPI contract (§53.6).

They run where changes happen — in CI, on every pull request — so a violation fails the build and is fixed before it merges, when it is a one-line change, rather than after it has spread.

A dependency-cruiser configuration enforces layering and module rules in a TypeScript/NestJS codebase:

{
  "forbidden": [
    {
      "name": "no-service-to-controller",
      "comment": "Service layer must never import a controller",
      "severity": "error",
      "from": { "path": "\\.service\\.ts$" },
      "to": { "path": "\\.controller\\.ts$" }
    },
    {
      "name": "no-cross-module-internals",
      "comment": "Modules may only import another module's public index",
      "severity": "error",
      "from": { "path": "^src/modules/([^/]+)/" },
      "to": {
        "path": "^src/modules/(?!\\1)([^/]+)/(?!index\\.ts)",
        "pathNot": "^src/modules/[^/]+/index\\.ts$"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "no-orphans",
      "comment": "No unreachable dead modules",
      "severity": "warn",
      "from": { "orphan": true },
      "to": {}
    }
  ]
}

A latency-budget fitness function as a Jest test, run in CI against a built service, keeps a critical path within its budget:

import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from '../src/app.module';
import * as request from 'supertest';

describe('architecture fitness: latency budget', () => {
  let app: INestApplication;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
      imports: [AppModule],
    }).compile();
    app = moduleRef.createApplication();
    await app.init();
  });

  afterAll(async () => { await app.close(); });

  it('GET /products/:id p95 stays under the 50ms budget', async () => {
    const server = app.getHttpServer();
    const samples: number[] = [];
    // warm up, then measure 200 requests against a seeded test DB
    for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) await request(server).get('/products/seed-1');
    for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
      const start = performance.now();
      await request(server).get('/products/seed-1').expect(200);
      samples.push(performance.now() - start);
    }
    samples.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const p95 = samples[Math.floor(samples.length * 0.95)];
    // The budget is the architectural property we refuse to lose
    expect(p95).toBeLessThan(50);
  });
});

If a change introduces an N+1 query or a slow dependency on this path, the test fails in CI and the regression never reaches production. The budget (50 ms) is an architectural commitment enforced automatically.

A convention fitness function asserting every service wires the standard error filter:

import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import { APP_FILTER } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from '../src/app.module';
import { StandardErrorFilter } from '@org/paved-road';

it('architecture fitness: uses the standard error filter', async () => {
  const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
    imports: [AppModule],
  }).compile();
  // The paved-road standard is enforced, not merely hoped for
  const filters = moduleRef.get(APP_FILTER, { strict: false });
  const usesStandard = (Array.isArray(filters) ? filters : [filters])
    .some((f) => f instanceof StandardErrorFilter);
  expect(usesStandard).toBe(true);
});

Practical example

An org that enforces module boundaries with the dependency-cruiser rule above gets a concrete benefit when it later wants to extract a module into its own service (Part 54). Because the boundary rule has been enforced on every PR for a year, the module has no illegal cross-module imports — the fitness function made that impossible. Extraction, which is a nightmare when modules have tangled into each other, is a clean operation: the module already talks to others only through public interfaces, so replacing those interfaces with network calls is mechanical. The fitness function did not just keep the codebase tidy; it preserved the optionality to extract, which is worth far more. Architecture kept clean by automation stays extractable; architecture kept clean by hope does not.

Artifact example

A fitness-function catalogue — the artifact that documents which architectural properties are automatically enforced, so teams know the rules are real and checked.

# Architecture fitness functions (run on every PR)

| Property enforced | Mechanism | Severity | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service layer never imports controllers | dependency-cruiser | error (blocks) | platform |
| Cross-module imports go through public index only | dependency-cruiser | error | platform |
| No orphaned / dead modules | dependency-cruiser | warn | platform |
| GET /products/:id p95 < 50ms | Jest perf test vs seeded DB | error | catalog team |
| Service wires the standard error filter | Jest unit test | error | platform |
| Every endpoint authenticated unless @Public() | custom lint rule | error | security |
| Bundle/image size within budget | CI size check | warn | platform |
| Events match registered schema | schema-registry check | error | data |

## Principles
- Fitness functions enforce architecture so humans don't have to remember.
- "error" blocks merge; "warn" surfaces drift without blocking (for trends).
- Each has an owner who maintains it and handles false positives.
- A new standard isn't "done" until it has a fitness function (§53.3).

The catalogue makes the enforced architecture visible and owned, distinguishes blocking from advisory checks, and ties back to the standards principle: a standard is not real until a fitness function enforces it. It is the proof that the architecture is kept by automation, not hope.

Real-world scenario

A team adds a latency-budget fitness function to its checkout endpoint after an incident where a well-meaning refactor introduced an N+1 query that only showed up under production load, causing a slow checkout during a sale. The fitness function runs 200 requests against a seeded database on every PR and fails if p95 exceeds the budget. Three months later, a different engineer makes a change that re-introduces an N+1 pattern — and the build fails, in CI, before the change merges, with a clear message that the latency budget was exceeded. The engineer finds and fixes the N+1 in twenty minutes, and it never reaches production. The same class of bug that previously caused a customer-facing incident during a sale is now a routine failed check caught in review. The fitness function converted a recurring production incident into a caught-in-CI non-event.

Failure scenario

A team writes a latency fitness function but runs it against an empty, unseeded test database. With no data, every query is instant, so the test always passes regardless of the actual query efficiency — it would pass even for a query that does a full table scan, because there is nothing to scan. For a year the team believes their latency is protected. Then a change ships an O(n) query that is instant on the empty test DB and catastrophic on the production table with ten million rows. The incident happens exactly as if there were no fitness function at all, because the fitness function tested a fiction. A fitness function is only as good as the realism of what it tests; a performance check against unrealistic data is false assurance, which is worse than no check because the team stops watching the thing they believe is guarded. Fitness functions must test against realistic conditions, or they enforce an illusion.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Testing against unrealistic data. A latency check against an empty DB passes for any query; it enforces an illusion.
  • Flaky fitness functions. A perf test with high variance fails randomly, so people add retries or disable it, and the enforcement evaporates.
  • No owner for false positives. When a fitness function blocks a legitimate change wrongly, someone must own fixing it fast, or teams will route around all of them.
  • Fitness functions as warn-only forever. A check that only warns and never blocks is advisory; drift accumulates because nothing is forced.
  • Checking the wrong property. A fitness function that enforces a rule nobody actually cares about adds friction without value.
  • No fitness function for a critical standard. The standard exists on paper but nothing enforces it, so it decays (the 53.3 failure).

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat fitness functions as the enforcement arm of every standard: a standard without a fitness function is a wish, so they consider a standard "done" only when an automated check guards it. They insist fitness functions test realistic conditions — seeded data for latency, real module graphs for dependency rules — because they know a check against a fiction is false assurance that is worse than no check, since it stops people watching the thing they believe is guarded.

They distinguish blocking (error) from advisory (warn) checks deliberately: block the properties you refuse to lose (layering, auth, critical latency), warn on the ones you want to watch as trends (bundle size creep). And they assign every fitness function an owner responsible for keeping it green and handling false positives quickly, because a flaky or wrongly-blocking check teaches teams to disable checks, which destroys the whole enforcement regime. The goal is architecture that stays correct for years without human vigilance — and that only works if the automated checks are realistic, stable, and owned.

Common mistakes

  • Latency/perf checks against empty or unrealistic data, enforcing an illusion.
  • Flaky fitness functions that get retried or disabled, evaporating the enforcement.
  • Leaving every check as warn-only, so drift accumulates with nothing forced.
  • Writing a standard without the fitness function that enforces it, so it decays.
  • No owner for false positives, so a wrongly-blocking check teaches teams to bypass all checks.

Interview questions

  1. What is an architecture fitness function and why is it necessary? Expected answer: an automated test (in CI, on every change) that checks the system still has a desired architectural property — layering, dependency rules, latency budget, conventions. It is necessary because rules enforced by human vigilance always decay under deadline pressure and turnover, while an automated check never tires and runs on every change. Follow-up: give a concrete example and how you'd implement it.

  2. Your latency fitness function always passes, but production latency regressed anyway. What likely went wrong? Expected answer: the check probably runs against unrealistic data (empty or tiny test DB), so inefficient queries are instant in the test and catastrophic in production; the fitness function enforced a fiction. Fix by testing against seeded, realistic data. Why it matters: tests whether they understand that a check is only as good as the realism of what it tests.

  3. How do fitness functions relate to standards and paved roads? Expected answer: the paved road establishes good architecture by default, standards define the rules, and fitness functions enforce them automatically on every change — turning a documented standard into an enforced one. A standard is not real until a fitness function guards it. Why it matters: ties the whole governance model together.

Practical exercise

Write one real fitness function for a system you work on. Options: a dependency-cruiser rule enforcing a layering or module boundary, a Jest latency-budget test against a seeded database for a critical endpoint, or a convention check that a standard (error filter, auth guard) is wired. Add it to CI so it runs on every change.

Acceptance criteria: the fitness function enforces a property you genuinely care about; if it is a performance check, it runs against realistic seeded data (not an empty DB); it is stable (not flaky) so it will not get disabled; and it actually fails when you deliberately introduce a violation, proving it enforces the rule rather than passing vacuously.

53.6 Dependency policy, shared libraries, waivers and measuring compliance

Concept

Four governance topics that come up once you have many services. Dependency and version policy is how you handle the constant churn of upgrades across dozens of services — upgrade cadence, support windows, end-of-life handling. Inner source and shared libraries is how teams share code internally without creating the shared-library trap, where a shared dependency becomes a coupling nobody can change. Exceptions and waivers is the process for when a team legitimately needs to deviate from a standard. And measuring compliance is how you know whether your governance is working without turning into the police.

Why does it exist?

Imagine forty services, each pinning its own versions of Node, NestJS and a dozen libraries, each upgrading on its own whim or never. A critical security vulnerability drops in a widely-used library. You now need to know which of the forty services use the vulnerable version, coordinate forty separate upgrades, and chase the teams that never upgrade anything. Without a version policy, this is an archaeology project under time pressure during a security incident. Without a way to measure compliance, you do not even know which services are affected. The policies exist to make the fleet upgradable and auditable rather than a collection of forty independently-rotting codebases.

The shared-library concern exists because sharing code is the obvious way to avoid duplication, but a shared library that many services depend on becomes a form of coupling: changing it affects everyone, so nobody dares change it, so it ossifies. Inner-source practices exist to get the benefit of sharing without this trap.

Mental model

For dependencies, imagine a fleet of company cars. If every driver services their car whenever they feel like it (or never), the fleet is a mix of well-maintained and dangerously-neglected vehicles, and when a recall hits a specific part, you cannot even tell which cars have it. A fleet policy — service every N months, retire cars past a certain age, keep a registry of what is in each — makes the fleet maintainable and auditable. Version policy is fleet maintenance for software.

For shared libraries, imagine a load-bearing wall shared between many apartments. It is efficient (one wall, many homes) but it is also a coupling: you cannot renovate it without affecting every apartment, so it never gets renovated and slowly becomes a constraint everyone works around. A shared library is a load-bearing wall; share deliberately, and only what truly benefits from being shared.

How it works

Dependency and version policy:

- Upgrade cadence: a defined rhythm (e.g. patch within a week, minor within
  a month, major within a quarter), not "whenever".
- Support window: which versions are supported (e.g. current + previous major
  of Node and NestJS). Older than that, you must upgrade.
- EOL handling: a dependency approaching end-of-life is scheduled for
  replacement BEFORE it reaches EOL, tracked as debt (Part 52.4).
- Automated upgrades: bots (Renovate/Dependabot) open PRs for upgrades; the
  paved road's fitness functions and tests gate them.
- Centralised version management: shared libraries pin blessed versions, so
  a bump propagates through the fleet via the paved road.

Inner source and the shared-library trap. The trap: a shared library grows to serve everyone's needs, accumulates every team's special case, becomes impossible to change without breaking someone, and ossifies. Avoiding it:

  • Share deliberately, not reflexively. Not all duplication is bad. Two slightly different implementations are often cheaper than one shared library coupling two teams. Share only stable, genuinely common things (the error filter, the auth client), not volatile domain logic.
  • Version shared libraries, and support multiple versions. Consumers upgrade on their own schedule within the support window, so a change does not force a synchronised fleet-wide deploy.
  • Clear ownership. A shared library has an owning team responsible for it, a public API, and a deprecation policy. Ownerless shared libraries rot fastest.
  • Inner-source model. Other teams can contribute (open a PR) but the owner reviews and maintains coherence, so the library does not become a dumping ground.

Exceptions and waivers. Standards need an escape hatch, or teams with real different needs will either suffer or route around governance entirely:

flowchart LR
    T["Team needs to deviate from a standard"] --> R["Request a waiver - state why + for how long"]
    R --> O["Standard owner reviews"]
    O -->|"granted"| W["Waiver recorded, time-boxed, revisited"]
    O -->|"denied, with help"| H["Owner helps find a compliant path"]

A good waiver is explicit, time-boxed, recorded, and revisited. "Team X may skip the standard error format until Q3 because they are mid-migration; revisit at Q3" is a healthy waiver. A permanent, undocumented exception is governance decay.

Measuring compliance without policing. You want to know the state of the fleet without making engineers feel watched:

  • Measure at the system level (dashboards of fleet-wide compliance), not the individual level (naming and shaming).
  • Use automated signals: what fraction of services use the current paved-road version, use the standard error filter, are within the support window.
  • Make non-compliance visible to the team itself (a service scorecard the owning team sees), so they fix it because they can see it, not because they are policed.

Practical example

An org uses Renovate to open upgrade PRs across all services, with the paved road's fitness functions and tests gating each one. When a security vulnerability drops, they query their service registry (which records each service's dependency versions) and immediately know which twelve of forty services are affected. Renovate opens the patch PR for all twelve; the fitness functions verify each still passes; most merge automatically within a day. The one service that fails (its tests break on the patch) gets human attention. What would have been a week-long archaeology-and-coordination project is a one-day, mostly-automated fleet upgrade — because the version policy, the automated upgrades, and the registry were in place before the incident.

Artifact example

A service scorecard — the artifact that makes compliance visible to the owning team without policing them.

# Service scorecard: orders-service (auto-generated weekly, seen by the team)

## Paved road & standards
- [x] On paved-road template v3 (current)
- [x] Standard error format (fitness function green)
- [x] Standard logging + trace IDs
- [ ] OpenAPI contract published and matching  <- GAP
- [x] Standard alerts wired

## Dependencies & versions
- [x] Node 22 (supported)
- [ ] NestJS 9  <- support window is 10 + previous; upgrade by Q3
- [x] No known critical vulnerabilities
- [ ] 1 dependency approaching EOL (lib-x, EOL in 5 months) <- schedule

## Reliability
- [x] p99 latency within budget
- [x] Error budget healthy (99.95% this month)
- [ ] 2 alerts fired with no runbook link  <- add runbooks

## Waivers (active)
- Error-format v1 -> v2 migration: WAIVED until Q3 (mid-refactor). Recorded.

## Score: 10/13 green. Trend: improving (was 8/13 last month).

The scorecard is addressed to the owning team, not to management. It shows gaps the team can act on, records their active waiver so the gap is not held against them, and shows a trend so progress is visible. Teams fix the gaps because they can see them and want a green scorecard, not because anyone is policing them. This is how you measure compliance without turning into the police: make the data serve the team, not surveil it.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer introduces service scorecards across the org, auto-generated weekly and visible to each owning team (and aggregated, anonymised, at the fleet level for leadership). He deliberately does not create a leaderboard or name laggards in all-hands, because he knows that policing produces gaming (teams juking the metric) and resentment. Instead, teams see their own gaps and, because engineers generally want their service to be healthy and green, they fix them. Fleet-wide compliance with the paved road rises from 60% to 90% over two quarters, driven almost entirely by teams self-correcting against their own scorecards. The one time a VP suggests a public ranking, the principal pushes back hard, explaining that the moment the metric becomes a stick, it stops measuring reality and starts measuring who is best at gaming it. Compliance measured to help teams rises; compliance measured to police them gets gamed.

Failure scenario

An org has a widely-used shared library for "common order utilities". It started small and useful. Over three years, every team that needed anything order-related added their special case to it, because adding to the shared library felt more correct than duplicating. Now the library is a 20,000-line tangle that every service depends on, encoding six teams' conflicting assumptions. Changing anything in it risks breaking an unknown number of consumers, so nobody dares, so it is frozen. A genuinely needed change — fixing a bug that affects three teams — cannot be made safely, because the blast radius is the entire fleet and there is no owner and no versioning. The shared library, meant to reduce duplication, has become the single most coupled, most feared, least changeable piece of the codebase. Sharing reflexively, with no owner, no versioning, and no discipline about what belongs in it, turned a convenience into the org's worst coupling. Deliberate sharing — only stable common things, versioned, owned — would have avoided the trap.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No version policy. Forty independently-rotting services; a security fix becomes an archaeology project.
  • The shared-library trap. A reflexively-shared library accumulates everyone's special cases, ossifies, and becomes the worst coupling in the system.
  • Ownerless shared libraries. Rot fastest; no one maintains coherence or handles deprecation.
  • No waiver process. Teams with real different needs either suffer or route around governance entirely, which is worse.
  • Permanent undocumented exceptions. Waivers that are never revisited; governance decays into "the rules apply except where they do not, and nobody remembers why".
  • Measuring compliance as policing. Leaderboards and naming produce gaming and resentment; the metric stops measuring reality.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat the dependency fleet as something to keep continuously upgradable and auditable — automated upgrades, a clear support window, a registry — because they know the alternative is discovering during a security incident that they cannot even tell which services are affected. They share code deliberately and sparingly, only stable genuinely-common things, with an owner and versioning, because they have seen the shared-library trap turn convenience into the worst coupling in a codebase, and they would rather tolerate some duplication than create a frozen 20,000-line shared tangle.

They insist on a waiver process with time-boxes and revisits, because they know standards without an escape hatch get routed around, and permanent undocumented exceptions are how governance quietly dies. And they measure compliance to help teams, never to police them — scorecards addressed to owners, trends not rankings — because the moment a compliance metric becomes a stick, it gets gamed and stops telling the truth. The principal wants a fleet that is healthy because teams can see and want to fix their gaps, not one that performs health for an audience.

Common mistakes

  • No version/upgrade policy, so the fleet rots independently and security fixes are archaeology.
  • Sharing code reflexively into ownerless, unversioned libraries that ossify into the worst coupling.
  • No waiver process, so teams route around governance or suffer.
  • Permanent, undocumented exceptions that decay the standards.
  • Measuring compliance as policing, which produces gaming and resentment instead of health.

Interview questions

  1. How do you keep dependencies and versions healthy across forty services?
