Expected answer: a defined upgrade cadence and support window, automated upgrade PRs (Renovate/Dependabot) gated by fitness functions and tests, EOL handling scheduled before end-of-life, and a registry so you can audit which services use which versions during a security incident. Follow-up: how would you respond to a critical vulnerability across the fleet.

  2. What is the shared-library trap and how do you avoid it? Expected answer: a reflexively-shared library accumulates every team's special cases, becomes impossible to change safely, and ossifies into the worst coupling in the system. Avoid it by sharing deliberately (only stable, genuinely common things), versioning shared libraries and supporting multiple versions, giving each a clear owner and public API, and tolerating some duplication rather than over-sharing. Why it matters: tests whether they understand that sharing is coupling.

  3. How do you measure governance compliance without becoming the police? Expected answer: measure at the system level with automated signals, make non-compliance visible to the owning team via a scorecard addressed to them (not a leaderboard), show trends, and let teams self-correct because they want a healthy service — never name-and-shame, because policing produces gaming and resentment and the metric stops measuring reality. Why it matters: tests understanding of incentives and Goodhart's law.

Practical exercise

Design a service scorecard for your org: list the paved-road, standards, dependency and reliability checks it would show, and decide how each is measured automatically. Then write your dependency policy: the upgrade cadence, the support window, and how EOL dependencies get scheduled. Finally, design the waiver process: what a waiver request must contain and how it stays time-boxed.

Acceptance criteria: the scorecard is addressed to the owning team (not a management leaderboard) and shows a trend; the dependency policy specifies a concrete cadence and support window rather than "upgrade regularly"; and the waiver process requires every waiver to be time-boxed and recorded, with a revisit date, so exceptions cannot become permanent and undocumented.

53.7 Worked example: rolling out a standard error format and OpenAPI-first contracts across 25 services

This section brings the whole Part together: introducing two standards — a uniform error format and OpenAPI-first API contracts — across 25 NestJS services, using paved roads, fitness functions, waivers and compliance measurement rather than a mandate from a review board. It is the canonical "governance rollout" problem, and doing it well is a principal-level skill.

The situation

An e-commerce org has 25 NestJS services, each with its own error format and each documenting its API however it likes (some with hand-written docs, some with nothing). Clients and the API gateway have to special-case every service. Incidents are hard to correlate because errors do not carry a consistent trace_id. The principal engineer wants two standards adopted fleet-wide: the error format from 53.3, and OpenAPI-first (the contract is written first and the code is verified against it). The naive approach — mandate it via a review board and chase 25 teams — would take a year and breed resentment. Here is the governance approach.

The rollout, step by step

1. Bake the standard into the paved road (make the right thing the default). The shared paved-road package gets a StandardErrorFilter (produces the standard error format automatically) and OpenAPI generation wired into the service template. Any new service gets both for free, with zero effort. This stops the problem from growing while you fix the existing fleet.

2. Write the fitness functions (make drift impossible going forward). Two fitness functions, added to the shared CI config:

  • error-format.spec: asserts the service wires StandardErrorFilter and that sampled error responses match the schema (the 53.5 convention check).
  • openapi-contract.spec: asserts the service publishes an OpenAPI spec and that the live endpoints match it (contract-first verification).
// openapi-contract fitness function (sketch)
it('every endpoint is described in the OpenAPI contract', async () => {
  const app = await buildTestApp();
  const document = loadPublishedOpenApiSpec();     // the committed contract
  const liveRoutes = extractRoutesFromApp(app);     // what the code exposes
  const documented = extractPathsFromSpec(document);
  // The contract and the code must not drift apart
  expect(liveRoutes.sort()).toEqual(documented.sort());
});

3. Migrate the fleet incrementally, highest-value first (not big-bang). Rank the 25 services by how much they would benefit: the ones in the gateway's hot path and the ones most involved in incidents go first. Each migration is small: swap in the StandardErrorFilter (the paved road makes this a few lines), generate the OpenAPI spec, turn the fitness functions from warn to error. Because the error format is produced by the shared filter, migrating a service is mostly deleting its bespoke error handling and adopting the filter — a day or two of work, not a rewrite.

4. Measure with scorecards (make progress visible, not policed). Each service's scorecard (53.6) shows the two standards as checks. Teams see their own gaps and a fleet-wide dashboard shows the migration trend. Nobody is named or shamed; teams migrate because they can see the gap and want a green scorecard, and because the paved road makes it easy.

5. Grant waivers where legitimate (keep an escape hatch). Two of the 25 services are legacy systems slated for decommissioning in six months. Mandating migration there is waste. They get a recorded, time-boxed waiver ("decommissioning by Q4; no migration required; revisit if timeline slips"). This keeps the governance credible — teams see it is pragmatic, not dogmatic.

6. Use office hours, not a review board (reserve human attention). Teams with tricky cases — a service with an unusual error-handling need, or a public API where the OpenAPI spec affects external partners — book office hours for help. No gate, no queue; advice on demand.

The timeline and outcome

Month 1: Standards in the paved road; new services compliant by default.
         Fitness functions written, run as WARN on existing services.
Month 2: Top 8 services (hot path, incident-prone) migrated. Fitness
         functions flipped to ERROR on those 8.
Month 3-4: Next 15 services migrated opportunistically (teams pull it in
         when touching the service), scorecards driving self-correction.
Month 4: 2 legacy services waived (decommissioning). Fleet compliance ~92%.
         Error correlation across services now trivial via trace_id;
         gateway and clients handle all services uniformly.

Artifact example

The rollout plan as a one-pager — the artifact the principal circulates to align the org.

# Rollout: standard error format + OpenAPI-first (25 services)

## Why (the problem, with evidence)
25 services, 25 error formats. Incidents take hours to correlate (no
consistent trace_id in errors). Clients & gateway special-case every
service. 2 of last quarter's long incidents were prolonged by this.

## How we're doing it (governance, not mandate)
1. Baked into the paved road -> new services compliant free, problem stops growing.
2. Two fitness functions -> drift impossible once a service is migrated.
3. Migrate incrementally, highest-value first -> not a big-bang.
4. Scorecards -> teams self-correct; no policing.
5. Waivers for legacy/decommissioning services -> pragmatic, credible.
6. Office hours for tricky cases -> help on demand, no gate.

## What we are NOT doing
- NOT mandating via a review board (bottleneck, resentment).
- NOT a big-bang cutover (too risky across 25 services).
- NOT forcing migration on services being decommissioned (waste).

## Success measure
Fleet compliance > 90% in 4 months; error correlation across services via
trace_id in one query; gateway handles all services uniformly.

Every mechanism from this Part appears: paved road (make it the default), fitness functions (enforce it), incremental migration (manage risk), scorecards (measure without policing), waivers (escape hatch), office hours (reserve human attention). No mandate, no review-board gate, and it lands in four months with ~92% compliance and rising, because the right thing was made the easy thing and drift was made impossible.

Why this beats the mandate approach

The mandate approach — a review board decrees the standard and chases 25 teams — would take far longer, breed resentment, and leave compliance fragile (services drift back the moment the chasing stops, because nothing enforces it). The governance approach lands faster, with buy-in, and compliance is durable, because the paved road makes new services compliant for free and the fitness functions make drift impossible. The difference is the difference between enforcing architecture with people (does not scale, decays) and enforcing it with infrastructure (scales, holds). That difference is the entire thesis of this Part.

Practical exercise

Pick a standard your org needs across many services (error format, logging, a security header, OpenAPI contracts). Write the full rollout plan using the six mechanisms: bake it into the paved road, write the fitness functions, migrate incrementally highest-value-first, measure with scorecards, grant waivers where legitimate, and use office hours for tricky cases. Include a timeline and a compliance success measure.

Acceptance criteria: the plan makes the standard the default for new services (so the problem stops growing), enforces it with at least one automated fitness function (so drift is impossible), sequences migration by value rather than all-at-once, measures progress via team-facing scorecards rather than policing, and includes a time-boxed waiver path for legitimate exceptions. A reader can see that it will land without a mandate and that compliance will be durable rather than fragile.

53.8 Event schema governance and the schema registry

Concept

Of all the standards an organisation needs, event schemas are among the most important and most often neglected. When services communicate through events (Part 17), every event has a shape, and if those shapes are inconsistent or change incompatibly, consumers break. Event schema governance is the discipline of standardising how events are defined, versioned, and evolved, enforced by a schema registry — a central service that holds the canonical schema for every event type and enforces compatibility rules, so a producer cannot publish an event that breaks existing consumers. It is the governance that keeps an event-driven architecture from decaying into a mess of incompatible, undocumented messages.

Why does it exist?

Imagine twenty services communicating through events, each team defining its event shapes however it likes, with no central definition and no compatibility checking. One team changes an event's field from a string to an object, and every consumer of that event breaks in production, because nothing stopped the incompatible change. Another team's events have no documented schema, so consumers reverse-engineer the shape from examples and break when an edge case appears. Events arrive that no consumer can parse because the producer and consumer disagree on the format. The event-driven architecture, meant to decouple services, has instead coupled them through undocumented, unstable message shapes.

Event schema governance and a registry exist to prevent exactly this: to give every event a canonical, documented schema, and to enforce that schema changes are backward-compatible so a producer cannot break its consumers. They exist because events are contracts between services (Part 32), and contracts without governance drift into incompatibility, turning the loose coupling of events into the tight, fragile coupling of undocumented message shapes.

Mental model

Imagine a postal system where anyone can define their own envelope and address format. Some letters have the address on the front, some on the back, some in a format the sorting machine cannot read; and one day the post office changes the address format, so all existing letters become undeliverable. Chaos. A schema registry is the standard that says: every envelope has this format, the address goes here, and you cannot change the format in a way that makes existing letters undeliverable. The registry is the post office's envelope standard, enforced, so every letter (event) can be delivered and understood by any recipient (consumer), and format changes never break letters already in the system.

How it works

The pieces of event schema governance:

- A schema format: every event has a defined schema (JSON Schema, Avro,
  Protobuf). The schema is the contract — it defines the event's shape.
- A schema registry: a central service holding the canonical schema for each
  event type, versioned. Producers register schemas; consumers fetch them.
- Compatibility enforcement: when a producer tries to register a new version of
  a schema, the registry CHECKS it against compatibility rules and REJECTS
  incompatible changes. This is the key mechanism — it prevents breaking changes.
- Compatibility modes (per Part 32):
  * Backward: new consumers can read old events (add optional fields, don't remove).
  * Forward: old consumers can read new events.
  * Full: both. Usually the target for events with many independent consumers.
- Conventions: naming (order.placed.v1), required metadata (event id, timestamp,
  tenant_id), envelope structure — standardised across all events.

The registry's enforcement is what makes it governance rather than documentation: a producer physically cannot publish an event whose schema change would break existing consumers, because the registry rejects the incompatible schema. This turns "please don't make breaking changes" (a wish) into "you cannot make breaking changes" (an enforced invariant).

flowchart LR
    P["Producer: register schema v2"] --> REG{"Schema registry: compatible with v1?"}
    REG -->|"incompatible"| REJ["REJECTED — breaking change blocked"]
    REG -->|"compatible"| ACC["Accepted — v2 registered"]
    ACC --> PUB["Producer publishes events (validated against schema)"]
    PUB --> C1["Consumer A fetches schema, parses safely"]
    PUB --> C2["Consumer B fetches schema, parses safely"]

Artifact example

An event schema standard and a registry compatibility check — the artifacts that keep an event-driven architecture coherent.

# Event schema standard (owner: platform/data team)

## Every event MUST have
- A registered schema in the schema registry (no schema, no publish).
- A standard envelope: { event_id (uuid), event_type, version, occurred_at,
  tenant_id, payload }.
- A versioned type name: `order.placed.v1`.

## Schema evolution rules (enforced by the registry)
- Compatibility mode: FULL (events have many independent consumers).
- Allowed changes: add OPTIONAL fields, add new event types.
- Forbidden changes: remove a field, change a field's type, rename a field,
  make an optional field required. (A truly breaking change = a new version,
  e.g. order.placed.v2, with both running until all consumers migrate — the
  strangler/parallel approach, Part 54.)

## Enforcement (this makes it governance, not a wish)
- The registry REJECTS an incompatible schema registration at publish time.
- A fitness function (Part 53.5) in CI validates events against their schema.
- A producer cannot publish an unregistered or schema-violating event.

---
# Registry compatibility check (what happens on a schema change)
Producer attempts to register order.placed.v1 with `total` changed string->object:
-> Registry: INCOMPATIBLE (type change on existing field). REJECTED.
-> Producer must either: keep `total` as-is, OR publish order.placed.v2 and run
   both until all consumers migrate. The breaking change CANNOT reach consumers.

The standard's power is that it defines the event contract precisely (envelope, versioning, evolution rules) and — crucially — names the enforcement: the registry rejects incompatible changes at registration time, so a breaking change physically cannot reach consumers. This turns event compatibility from a fragile convention that teams forget into a database-of-schemas-enforced invariant, which is exactly what keeps a twenty-service event-driven architecture from decaying into incompatible-message chaos.

Real-world scenario

An organisation with a schema registry avoids a class of production incidents that plague event-driven architectures without one. A team, under deadline pressure, changes an event's field type in a way that would break three downstream consumers — exactly the kind of change that, without governance, ships and causes a multi-service incident. But the registry rejects the incompatible schema at registration time, with a clear message that the change breaks compatibility, so the producer learns about the problem in CI before it ships, not in a production incident after. The team instead publishes a new event version and runs both until the consumers migrate (Part 54's parallel approach). The registry converted a would-be multi-service breakage into a caught-in-CI non-event. Over time, this is the difference between an event-driven architecture that stays coherent as it grows and one that decays into a minefield of incompatible messages where every schema change is a gamble — the registry is the governance that keeps events as the reliable contracts they are meant to be.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat event schemas as contracts between services (Part 32) that require governance, because they know that events without governance drift into incompatibility, turning the intended loose coupling of an event-driven architecture into the fragile tight coupling of undocumented, unstable message shapes. They insist on a schema registry that enforces compatibility, because they understand the difference between "please don't make breaking changes" (a wish teams forget) and "you cannot register an incompatible schema" (an enforced invariant) — and only the enforced version keeps a growing event-driven architecture coherent.

They standardise the event envelope and versioning conventions so every event is self-describing and every consumer can parse any event, and they handle genuinely breaking changes with versioning and parallel running (Part 54) rather than breaking consumers. They wire the registry into CI with a fitness function (53.5) so schema violations are caught before production. The senior engineer's view is that event schema governance is among the highest-value standards an organisation can enforce, because events are the contracts that hold a distributed architecture together, and a registry is what keeps those contracts from silently breaking — converting a whole class of multi-service incidents into caught-in-CI non-events.

Common mistakes

  • No schema registry, so event shapes drift and incompatible changes break consumers in production.
  • No compatibility enforcement, relying on teams to remember not to make breaking changes.
  • No standard envelope, so events lack consistent metadata (id, timestamp, tenant_id) and cannot be handled generically.
  • Breaking changes shipped as in-place edits instead of new versions run in parallel until consumers migrate.
  • Schemas documented but not enforced, so the documentation drifts from the actual events (the 53.3 failure applied to events).

Interview questions

  1. Why do event-driven architectures need a schema registry? Expected answer: events are contracts between services, and without governance their shapes drift and incompatible changes break consumers in production — turning the intended loose coupling into fragile tight coupling through undocumented, unstable messages. A schema registry holds the canonical versioned schema for each event type and enforces compatibility, rejecting incompatible changes at registration so a producer physically cannot break its consumers. Why it matters: this is critical governance for any event-driven system.

  2. How do you handle a genuinely breaking change to an event schema? Expected answer: you cannot make it in place (the registry rejects it and it would break consumers); instead publish a new version (order.placed.v2) and run both v1 and v2 in parallel until all consumers have migrated to v2, then retire v1 — the strangler/parallel approach (Part 54). The registry enforces that the breaking change goes into a new version, not an edit to the existing one. Why it matters: tests schema evolution under compatibility constraints.

  3. What's the difference between documenting event schemas and governing them, and why does it matter? Expected answer: documentation describes the schemas but relies on teams to comply and drifts from reality; governance via a registry enforces the schemas — a producer cannot publish an unregistered or incompatible event because the registry rejects it and a CI fitness function validates events — so the schemas are an enforced invariant, not a wish. Only enforcement keeps a growing event architecture coherent. Why it matters: tests the enforce-don't-document principle applied to events.

Practical exercise

Design event schema governance for a set of services communicating through events. Define the standard event envelope (required metadata), the versioning convention, and the compatibility mode (and why). Specify how a schema registry would enforce compatibility (rejecting incompatible changes at registration), and how you would handle a genuinely breaking change. Add the CI fitness function that validates events against their schemas.

Acceptance criteria: every event has a registered, versioned schema with a standard envelope (id, timestamp, tenant_id, etc.); the registry enforces a compatibility mode (backward/forward/full, justified) by rejecting incompatible changes at registration, not by asking teams nicely; a genuinely breaking change is handled as a new version run in parallel until consumers migrate (not an in-place edit); and a CI fitness function validates events against their schemas — demonstrating that event compatibility is an enforced invariant, not documentation that drifts.

53.9 Governance anti-patterns and measuring governance health

Concept

A final lens on the Part: the recurring governance anti-patterns that make governance fail, and how to measure whether governance is actually healthy — producing consistency and quality without becoming a bottleneck or being routed around. Governance is itself something to be governed: a principal watches for the anti-patterns that creep in (heavy gates, stale standards, unmaintained paved roads) and measures the health signals (adoption, drift, compliance trends, developer satisfaction with the paved road) to know whether the governance is helping or harming.

Why does it exist?

Imagine governance that everyone assumes is working because it exists — there is a review board, there are standards, there is a paved road. But nobody checks: the review board has quietly become a three-week bottleneck, the standards describe a system that no longer exists, the paved road is two years stale and teams avoid it. The governance looks healthy (all the structures are present) but is actually harmful (bottleneck, fiction, avoided). Without measuring governance health, you cannot tell the difference between governance that works and governance that merely exists, so you keep investing in structures that are actively hurting.

Measuring governance health exists to make the difference visible: adoption (are teams using the paved road voluntarily, or avoiding it), drift (are services complying or diverging), bottleneck signals (is a gate delaying things), and satisfaction (do engineers find the governance helpful or obstructive). The anti-patterns catalogue exists because governance decays in predictable ways, and naming the decay patterns lets a principal catch them before the governance turns from help into harm.

Mental model

Imagine a garden you planted well but never inspect. You assume it is fine because you planted it, but weeds (heavy gates) have crept in, some plants have died (stale standards), and the path you laid (the paved road) is overgrown and nobody walks it. A gardener who never inspects cannot tell a thriving garden from an overgrown one. Measuring governance health is inspecting the garden: checking what is actually growing (adoption, compliance), what has died (stale standards), and what has become a weed (a gate that is now a bottleneck). The anti-patterns are the weeds and dead plants to watch for, and measurement is the inspection that catches them before the garden is lost.

How it works

The governance anti-patterns (drawn from across the Part):

- The universal gate: a review board that gates everything, becoming a
  bottleneck teams route around (53.1).
- The stale standard: a standard documented but not enforced, now fiction that
  misleads (53.3).
- The abandoned paved road: a road built and not maintained, now spreading rot
  to every new service (53.2).
- The illusory fitness function: a check that tests unrealistic conditions
  (empty DB) and enforces an illusion (53.5).
- The ossified shared library: a reflexively-shared, ownerless library that
  became the worst coupling (53.6).
- The permanent waiver: an exception never revisited, decaying the standard (53.6).
- The policing metric: compliance measured as a leaderboard, breeding gaming (53.6).
- Governance by poster: declared standards that nothing enforces (the whole
  anti-thesis of the Part — enforcement by infrastructure, not declaration).

Measuring governance health — the signals that tell you governance is helping, not harming:

- Paved-road adoption: % of new services / deploys using the paved road
  VOLUNTARILY. High = the road is genuinely the easiest path. Low = it's stale
  or not good enough; teams are avoiding it.
- Compliance / drift trend: % of services meeting standards, over time (from
  scorecards, 53.6). Rising = governance working; falling = decaying.
- Bottleneck signals: time-in-queue for any human gate (office hours wait, RFC
  decision latency). Rising = a gate becoming a bottleneck.
- Fitness-function health: are checks green, stable (not flaky), and testing
  realistic conditions. Flaky/disabled checks = enforcement evaporating.
- Developer satisfaction with governance: survey — do engineers find the paved
  road and standards helpful or obstructive? Obstructive = governance is harming.
- Estate-wide leverage realised: can you make a fleet-wide change (security fix,
  version bump) via the paved road quickly? Slow = the leverage isn't there.

The key health principle: healthy governance is adopted voluntarily (because it is the easiest path) and drift is low (because it is enforced), while unhealthy governance is routed around (because it is a bottleneck) or drifted-from (because it is not enforced). Measuring adoption and drift tells you which you have.

flowchart TB
    M["Measure governance health"] --> A["Paved-road adoption (voluntary %)"]
    M --> D["Compliance/drift trend"]
    M --> B["Gate bottleneck signals (queue time)"]
    M --> S["Developer satisfaction with governance"]
    A --> H{"Healthy?"}
    D --> H
    B --> H
    S --> H
    H -->|"adopted + low drift + no bottleneck + satisfied"| GOOD["Healthy: helping"]
    H -->|"routed around / drifting / bottleneck / obstructive"| BAD["Unhealthy: fix the anti-pattern"]

Artifact example

A governance health dashboard — the artifact that makes the difference between governance-that-works and governance-that-merely-exists visible.

# Governance health dashboard (quarterly)

## Paved road
- New-service adoption: 94% use the paved road voluntarily (HEALTHY — it's the
  easiest path). (If this were low, the road would be stale/avoided.)
- Paved-road version currency: template is current (NestJS 10, patched libs).
- Estate leverage: last security fix propagated to 92% of services in 3 days
  via a template+library bump (HEALTHY — the leverage is real).

## Standards compliance (from scorecards, 53.6)
- Error format: 96% of services compliant (up from 80% — trend RISING, healthy).
- Fitness functions: all green, stable, testing realistic data. 2 flaky checks
  fixed this quarter (prevented them being disabled).

## Gates (watching for bottlenecks)
- Office hours wait: same-week (HEALTHY — not a bottleneck).
- RFC decision latency: median 5 days (HEALTHY). Watching — if it rises, act.

## Developer satisfaction with governance (survey)
- "The paved road makes me faster": 4.3/5 (HEALTHY — governance is helping).
- Open feedback: 2 teams want a paved road for data pipelines (a gap — not yet
  paved; prioritise).

## Anti-pattern watch (none active, but monitored)
- No universal gate. No stale standards (all enforced). Paved road maintained.
- 3 active waivers, all time-boxed with revisit dates (none permanent).

The dashboard's power is that it measures whether governance is actually helping — voluntary adoption (the road is the easiest path), rising compliance (enforcement working), low gate latency (no bottleneck), and high developer satisfaction (governance helps, not obstructs) — rather than assuming governance works because the structures exist. It also actively watches for the anti-patterns (no universal gate, no stale standards, no permanent waivers). This turns governance from a set-and-forget assumption into a measured, maintained system, which is how you keep it on the helpful side of the line over time.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat governance as something that must itself be governed — measured and maintained — because they know governance decays in predictable ways (gates become bottlenecks, standards become fiction, paved roads rot) and that the structures existing is not the same as the governance working. They measure the health signals that reveal the difference: voluntary paved-road adoption (healthy governance is chosen because it is the easiest path, not mandated), compliance/drift trends (rising means enforcement works), gate latency (rising means a bottleneck is forming), and developer satisfaction (obstructive means governance is harming).

They watch actively for the anti-patterns — the universal gate, the stale standard, the abandoned paved road, the policing metric, the permanent waiver, governance-by-poster — because they have seen each one turn governance from help into harm, and they catch them via the health signals before they do damage. Above all, they hold the Part's central principle as the test of governance health: governance should make the right thing the easy thing, so healthy governance is adopted voluntarily and drift is low, while governance that is routed around or drifted-from has failed regardless of how impressive its structures look. The senior engineer inspects the governance garden regularly, because governance that is not measured and maintained decays into the very bottleneck and bureaucracy it was meant to replace.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming governance works because the structures exist, without measuring adoption, drift, or bottlenecks.
  • Not measuring voluntary paved-road adoption, so you don't notice teams avoiding a stale road.
  • Not watching gate latency, so a review mechanism becomes a bottleneck unnoticed.
  • Ignoring developer satisfaction with governance, so obstructive governance persists.
  • Letting anti-patterns creep in (universal gates, stale standards, permanent waivers) without a watch for them.

Interview questions

  1. How do you tell whether your governance is actually healthy versus just existing? Expected answer: measure the health signals — voluntary paved-road adoption (healthy governance is chosen because it's the easiest path), compliance/drift trends (rising means enforcement works), gate latency (rising means a bottleneck is forming), and developer satisfaction (obstructive means it's harming) — rather than assuming it works because the structures (board, standards, paved road) exist. Healthy governance is adopted voluntarily with low drift; unhealthy is routed around or drifted-from. Why it matters: tests whether they measure governance or assume it.

  2. What are the recurring ways governance decays, and how do you catch them? Expected answer: the universal gate becoming a bottleneck, standards becoming stale fiction, paved roads rotting, fitness functions testing illusions, shared libraries ossifying, waivers becoming permanent, policing metrics breeding gaming, and governance-by-poster. Catch them by measuring the health signals (adoption, drift, latency, satisfaction) and actively watching for each anti-pattern. Why it matters: governance decays predictably, and a principal must catch it before it harms.

  3. Why is voluntary adoption the best signal of paved-road health? Expected answer: because the whole governance thesis is making the right thing the easy thing — a paved road teams choose freely is genuinely the easiest, best path (healthy), while a road teams avoid or must be mandated onto is stale, not good enough, or obstructive (unhealthy). Voluntary adoption directly measures whether governance is achieving consistency through convenience rather than coercion. Why it matters: ties the health metric to the Part's core principle.

Practical exercise

Build a governance health dashboard for your org. Measure (or estimate) voluntary paved-road adoption, compliance/drift trends, gate latency (any human review queue time), and developer satisfaction with the governance. Then audit for the anti-patterns: is there a universal gate, a stale standard, an unmaintained paved road, a permanent waiver, or a policing metric. Identify whether your governance is on the healthy side (adopted voluntarily, low drift, no bottleneck) or the unhealthy side (routed around, drifting, bottleneck, obstructive).

Acceptance criteria: your dashboard measures whether governance is helping (voluntary adoption, rising compliance, low gate latency, developer satisfaction) rather than assuming it works because structures exist; your anti-pattern audit identifies at least one decay pattern present or at risk; and you can state whether your governance achieves consistency through convenience (healthy — adopted voluntarily) or through coercion/neglect (unhealthy — routed around or drifted-from), with a plan to fix any anti-pattern found.

53.10 A quick-reference for governance that scales

A compact reference distilling the Part into the decisions and checks that matter most when you design or assess governance.

The governance-mechanism decision

Match the mechanism to the stakes — the core move of the whole Part:

Routine decision of a known shape    -> paved road + fitness functions (NO humans)
A new shared library / convention     -> RFC + review guild (async, lightweight)
Genuinely novel, cross-cutting,       -> selective ARB (advisory) OR office hours
  hard-to-reverse                        (reserve scarce human judgement here only)
Need advice on a tricky design        -> office hours (a service, not a gate)
Enforcing a standard on every change  -> a fitness function in CI (not a document)

The "is this governance healthy?" check

[ ] Is the right thing the EASY thing? (Paved road, not mandates.)
[ ] Is the paved road ADOPTED VOLUNTARILY? (Low adoption = stale/avoided.)
[ ] Are standards ENFORCED by infrastructure, not documents? (Else they drift.)
[ ] Are standards MINIMAL? (The interoperability interface, not the internals.)
[ ] Is human review reserved for the genuinely novel? (Not a universal gate.)
[ ] Do fitness functions test REALISTIC conditions and stay stable? (Not illusions.)
[ ] Is the dependency fleet upgradable and auditable? (Automated upgrades + registry.)
[ ] Is shared code deliberate and owned? (Avoid the shared-library trap.)
[ ] Are waivers time-boxed and revisited? (No permanent undocumented exceptions.)
[ ] Is compliance measured to HELP teams (scorecards), not to police them?

The standard-rollout recipe (from 53.7)

To roll out any standard across many services without a mandate:

1. Bake it into the paved road (new services compliant free; problem stops growing).
2. Write the fitness functions (drift impossible once migrated).
3. Migrate incrementally, highest-value first (not big-bang).
4. Measure with team-facing scorecards (self-correction, not policing).
5. Grant time-boxed waivers where legitimate (pragmatic, credible).
6. Use office hours for tricky cases (help on demand, no gate).

The enduring principle

The whole Part reduces to one shift: enforce architecture with infrastructure, not with people. People-enforced governance (approval gates, wiki standards, hoped-for compliance) does not scale and decays; infrastructure-enforced governance (paved roads, fitness functions, registries, scorecards) scales and holds. Everything else — paved roads, standards, fitness functions, the lightweight review alternatives, the compliance measurement — is an application of that one principle. When you design or assess governance, ask: is this enforced by infrastructure that makes the right thing the easy thing, or by people who will become a bottleneck and whose vigilance will decay? The first scales; the second does not.

Return to this reference when designing or assessing governance; the reasoning behind each line is in the sections above.

Where to start if you inherit ungoverned chaos

If you arrive at an organisation with no effective governance — forty services each doing everything differently, no paved road, standards that are wiki fiction — the temptation is to impose a review board and a thick standards document. Resist it; that is the heavy-governance failure (53.1). Instead, start where the leverage is highest and the resistance lowest:

1. Build a paved road for the single most common operation (usually service
   creation or deploy). Make it genuinely the easiest path. This stops the chaos
   from GROWING — new services are consistent by default — while you deal with
   the existing mess. (Highest leverage, voluntary adoption, no mandate.)
2. Pick the ONE standard whose inconsistency hurts most (often the error format
   or logging/trace IDs, because they cripple incident debugging). Bake it into
   the paved road and enforce it with a fitness function. One standard, enforced.
3. Build a service catalog to surface what exists and who owns it — including the
   orphans (Part 55.3) that are your biggest hidden risk.
4. Only then, and only if needed, add lightweight human mechanisms (office hours,
   a guild) for the genuinely novel decisions. Never a universal gate.

The sequence matters: paved road first (stop the bleeding, highest leverage, voluntary), then one enforced standard (prove the model works), then visibility (the catalog), then — minimally — the human mechanisms. This builds governance that teams adopt because it helps them, establishing the infrastructure-not-approval model from the start, rather than imposing a bottleneck they will resent and route around. Governance earned through usefulness holds; governance imposed through authority decays.

Senior Checklist — Part 53

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain why heavy approval-based governance fails and what scales instead
  • I build paved roads that are opinionated, complete for the common case, and maintained as a product
  • I enforce standards through infrastructure and automated checks, not documents and goodwill
  • I reserve human review for genuinely novel, cross-cutting decisions, and use office hours and guilds for the rest
  • I can write a fitness function that enforces a real architectural property against realistic conditions
  • I keep the dependency fleet upgradable and auditable, with automated upgrades and a support window
  • I share code deliberately and avoid the shared-library trap
  • I run a waiver process that is explicit, time-boxed and revisited
  • I measure compliance to help teams, via scorecards, not to police them
  • I can roll out a standard across many services without a mandate, so compliance is durable

Part 53 — Key Takeaways

  • Governance exists to produce consistency across many teams, but heavy, approval-based governance fails because human gates do not scale, become bottlenecks, and get routed around.
  • The core shift is from enforcement-by-approval to enforcement-by-default: make the right thing the easy thing through paved roads, standards and automated checks.
  • A paved road is the single highest-leverage governance investment; it achieves consistency through convenience, and it gives you estate-wide leverage (fix once, propagate everywhere).
  • An unmaintained paved road is worse than none; it spreads rot to every new service, so it must be owned and maintained as a product.
  • Standards scale only when enforced by infrastructure, kept minimal (the interoperability interface, not the internals), and owned with an evolution path; a wiki-only standard decays into fiction.
  • Reserve scarce human judgement for genuinely novel, cross-cutting, hard-to-reverse decisions; use office hours, review guilds and named advisors for everything else, and never scale a bottleneck by enlarging it.
  • Architecture fitness functions are the automated immune system that keeps architecture correct for years; they must test realistic conditions, stay stable, and be owned, or they enforce an illusion.
  • Keep the dependency fleet upgradable and auditable with automated upgrades, a support window, and a registry, so a security fix is a one-day propagation, not an archaeology project.
  • Share code deliberately and sparingly; a reflexively-shared, ownerless, unversioned library becomes the worst coupling in the system (the shared-library trap).
  • Give standards an escape hatch: a waiver process that is explicit, time-boxed and revisited, or teams route around governance entirely.
  • Measure compliance to help teams, with scorecards addressed to owners and trends rather than leaderboards; the moment a compliance metric becomes a stick, it gets gamed and stops measuring reality.

Part 54 — Large-Scale Migrations and Legacy Modernization

Every large engineering organisation is, at any moment, somewhere in the middle of a migration it started two years ago and is not sure how to finish. The database engine it is moving off. The framework it is moving onto. The monolith it is decomposing. The cloud it is migrating to. Migrations are the dominant form of large-scale engineering work above the feature level, and they are where principal engineers earn their keep or destroy their credibility, because migrations are uniquely good at failing slowly, expensively, and in public.

Part 47.6 covered the strangler pattern. Part 31 covered schema migrations. Part 32 covered compatibility. Part 5 covered monolith versus microservices. This Part is about running a migration as a program — the organisational and technical discipline that gets a large migration all the way to done, including turning the old thing off, which is the part almost everyone skips.

The defining fact about large migrations is in this Part's first section: they fail by getting stuck at 80% done forever. Not by blowing up. By slowly stalling, as the easy 80% completes, the team's attention drifts to the next shiny thing, and the hard last 20% — the awkward callers, the legacy edge cases, the final cutover — never gets done. The result is the worst of both worlds: two systems running in parallel permanently, double the operational cost, and none of the benefit of finishing. Avoiding that fate is what this Part is about.

The reader this Part assumes is a senior or staff engineer who has been on a migration that stalled, or is about to lead one, and wants to know how to get it to actually finish.

54.1 Why large migrations fail: the 80% done forever problem

Concept

Large migrations rarely fail by exploding. They fail by stalling — getting to roughly 80% complete and staying there indefinitely. The first 80% is the exciting, high-value, straightforward part: migrate the main services, the common cases, the cooperative teams. The last 20% is the awkward part: the obscure caller nobody owns, the legacy edge case the new system does not handle, the one team too busy to migrate, and the final act of turning the old system off and deleting it. That last 20% is unglamorous, politically hard, and easy to defer, so it gets deferred, and the migration enters a permanent limbo where both systems run forever.

Why does it exist?

Imagine renovating a house while living in it. You enthusiastically do the kitchen and the living room — big, visible, satisfying wins. Then you are left with the awkward spare room full of boxes, the weird plumbing in the basement, and the final step of disposing of all the old furniture. Those are annoying, so you live with them "for now". A year later the old furniture is still in the garage, the spare room is still boxes, and you are paying to store things you meant to throw away. You are 80% renovated forever, carrying the cost of both the new and the old.

Migrations stall for exactly this human reason: the incentives all point at the first 80% (visible progress, early wins, cooperative teams) and all point away from the last 20% (invisible, hard, political, requires chasing people). Without deliberate countermeasures, the rational local behaviour of every individual produces a globally stalled migration. The "80% done forever" problem exists because finishing is nobody's favourite work and everybody's easiest thing to defer.

Mental model

Imagine a tug of war between "start the exciting new migration" and "finish the boring old one". The new migration always wins, because it is fresh, visible, and has executive enthusiasm, while finishing the old one is a grind with no applause. So the org accumulates a graveyard of 80%-done migrations, each carrying the full operational cost of running two systems, none delivering the benefit of being finished. The mental model to hold is that a migration delivers its value only at 100%, because until the old system is off, you pay for both. An 80%-complete migration has most of the cost and almost none of the benefit. Half a migration is not half the value; it is negative value, because you now operate two systems instead of one.

How it works

The stall happens in a predictable sequence:

flowchart TB
    S["Migration starts - high energy, exec support"] --> E["Easy 80% migrates fast - visible wins"]
    E --> D["Attention drifts - team wants the next new thing"]
    D --> H["Hard 20% remains: orphan callers, edge cases, cutover"]
    H --> L["Limbo: both systems run forever, double cost, no benefit"]
    L -.->|"the fix: treat finishing as the goal, not starting"| F["Forced completion"]

The forces that drive the stall:

  1. Declining marginal visibility. The first migrations are the big, obvious ones, so progress looks fast. The last ones are obscure, so progress looks like nothing even when it is hard work.
  2. Rising marginal difficulty. The easy cases were easy because they were well-understood and well-owned. The remaining cases are hard precisely because they were skipped — orphaned, weird, or politically stuck.
  3. Attention economics. Executives and engineers alike are drawn to starting new things over finishing old ones. The migration loses the competition for attention the moment it stops being new.
  4. No completion incentive. Nobody is rewarded for turning off the old system; they are rewarded for shipping the new one. So the new one ships and the old one lingers.
  5. The orphan problem. The last callers of the old system are often owned by nobody, or by a team with no incentive to move, so migrating them requires someone to do unpaid political work.

The cost of limbo is concrete and continuous: two systems to operate, two on-call surfaces, two sets of bugs, data split across both, every new engineer confused about which to use, and the constant risk that the un-migrated 20% contains the one path that causes an incident.

Practical example

A company decides to migrate from a legacy order system to a new one. In six months, 80% of order volume flows through the new system — all the main flows, the big partners, the cooperative internal teams. It looks like a triumph; there is a celebration. Then the migration stalls. The remaining 20% is: a batch import used by three enterprise customers, a reconciliation job owned by a finance team that is slammed, and a handful of internal tools that call the old API directly and whose owners have left. Each is individually small and individually annoying. Two years later, the legacy order system is still running — for 20% of volume — with its own on-call rotation, its own servers, and its own bugs, because finishing those last three things was never anyone's priority. The company pays for two order systems indefinitely. The migration that looked like a triumph at 80% is, at 100%-never, a permanent tax.

Artifact example

A migration status framing that makes the 80% trap visible and measurable — the artifact that reframes "progress" so finishing becomes the goal.

# Order system migration — status framing (the honest version)

## The WRONG metric (what makes us stall)
"80% of order volume is on the new system." -> sounds like success, hides
the trap. Volume migrates fast because the big flows are easy.

## The RIGHT metrics (what actually matters)
- Legacy system still running? YES  -> we have 0% of the BENEFIT. We pay for
  both systems until this is NO.
- Callers still using the legacy API: 7 (down from 40). These 7 are the
  whole job now. Named below with owners.
- Date the legacy system can be DELETED: NOT SCHEDULED  <- the real red flag.

## The remaining 7 callers (the actual work)
| Caller | Owner | Status | Blocker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enterprise batch import | Integrations team | Not started | Needs new bulk API |
| Finance reconciliation | Finance eng | Not started | Team at capacity |
| Legacy admin tool | ORPHANED | Not started | No owner — needs assignment |
| 4 internal scripts | Various | 2 done, 2 orphaned | Find owners or delete |

## Definition of DONE (non-negotiable)
Legacy order system is powered off and its code deleted. Not "95% migrated".
OFF. Until then, this migration has not delivered its value.

The reframing is the whole point: it replaces the flattering "80% of volume" metric with the honest ones — is the legacy system still running (if yes, 0% of benefit), how many callers remain (the real work), and is deletion scheduled (if not, the red flag). It names the remaining callers and their owners, surfacing the orphans. And it defines done as "powered off and deleted", not "mostly migrated". This artifact is how a principal engineer stops a migration from stalling: by measuring the thing that matters (finishing) instead of the thing that flatters (volume).

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer is brought in to "finish" a migration that has been 80% done for eighteen months. She finds exactly the expected pattern: the easy work is long done, the hard 20% is orphaned callers and political blockers, and nobody is measuring completion — they are measuring volume, which has not moved in a year. Her first move is not technical; it is to change the metric. She makes "the legacy system is still running" the headline status, visible to the executive sponsor, and she schedules a deletion date for the legacy system, working backward from it. Suddenly the orphaned callers have a deadline, the political blockers have an escalation path (the deletion date is coming whether they move or not), and the migration that was nobody's priority becomes a dated program with a finish line. The legacy system is deleted four months later. The technical work was never the hard part; the hard part was making finishing the goal, and that was a measurement and incentive change, not an engineering one.

Failure scenario

A team runs a database migration from the old engine to the new one. They migrate 80% of the tables and the main application paths, declare victory in a sprint review, and move on to feature work. The remaining 20% is a set of reporting queries and a nightly batch job that still hit the old database. "We'll migrate those next quarter." Next quarter never comes, because features always win. For two years, the company runs two database engines: the new one for the app, the old one for reporting and the batch job. They pay for both. They patch both. On-call must understand both. Then the old engine reaches end of life and the vendor drops support — and now the never-finished 20% is an emergency, because the unsupported old engine is a security and reliability liability, and the batch job that depends on it is business-critical. The migration that could have been finished calmly in a quarter two years ago must now be finished in a panic under a security deadline, with the original team dispersed and the context lost. The slow stall became a crisis, which is the usual way the 80%-forever problem finally gets resolved — badly.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Measuring volume instead of completion. "80% of traffic migrated" flatters while hiding that the legacy system still runs and delivers 0% of the benefit.
  • No scheduled deletion date for the old system. Without a finish line, the last 20% is never anyone's priority.
  • Orphaned callers. The remaining users of the old system are owned by nobody or by over-capacity teams, so migrating them requires unpaid political work.
  • Celebrating at 80%. The celebration drains the urgency to finish, because it feels done.
  • Attention drifting to the next migration before the current one is actually finished, accumulating a graveyard of 80%-done migrations.
  • The forced-crisis finish. The never-finished 20% becomes an emergency when the old system hits EOL, turning a calm quarter of work into a panic.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat finishing as the entire goal and are deeply skeptical of migration progress reported as volume or percentage of traffic, because those metrics flatter while the benefit — which comes only from turning off the old system — stays at zero. They schedule a deletion date for the old system early and work backward from it, because they know that without a finish line the last 20% loses every competition for attention and the migration stalls forever.

They refuse to celebrate at 80%, because the celebration drains the urgency to do the hard, unglamorous last part. They actively hunt for the orphaned callers early, assigning owners before the migration stalls on them, because they have learned that the last 20% is hard precisely because it is the stuff everyone skipped, and it will not resolve itself. And they hold the line that a migration is not done until the old system is powered off and deleted, because they have seen too many "successful" migrations become permanent two-system taxes. The principal's distinctive contribution to a migration is usually not the technical plan; it is the relentless, unpopular insistence on finishing.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting progress as volume or percent-migrated, which hides that the old system still runs and delivers no benefit.
  • Never scheduling a deletion date for the old system, so the last 20% is never prioritised.
  • Celebrating at 80% and letting the urgency to finish evaporate.
  • Letting attention drift to the next migration before finishing the current one.
  • Ignoring orphaned callers until they become the permanent blocker that stalls everything.

Interview questions

  1. Why do large migrations usually fail, and what does failure actually look like? Expected answer: they fail by stalling at ~80% done forever, not by exploding; the easy, visible 80% completes fast and the hard, unglamorous, political last 20% (orphaned callers, edge cases, final cutover) gets deferred indefinitely, leaving two systems running permanently — full cost, no benefit. Follow-up: what would you do differently to avoid the stall.

  2. How do you measure a migration so it actually gets finished? Expected answer: measure completion, not volume — the headline metric is "is the old system still running" (if yes, 0% of benefit) and "how many callers remain, with owners"; schedule a deletion date for the old system and work backward from it. Define done as "old system powered off and deleted", not "95% migrated". Why it matters: this measurement change is the single most effective anti-stall intervention.

  3. A migration has been 80% done for eighteen months. You're asked to finish it. What's your first move? Expected answer: change the metric and set a deletion date for the old system — making "the legacy system still runs" the visible status and giving the orphaned callers and political blockers a deadline and escalation path. The remaining work is usually political and orphan-chasing, not technical. Why it matters: tests whether they understand the stall is an incentive problem, not an engineering one.

Practical exercise

Find a migration in your organisation (or one you have been part of) that is or was stuck. Write its honest status framing: replace any volume/percentage metric with the real ones (is the old system still running, how many callers remain with named owners, is a deletion date scheduled). Identify the orphaned callers — the ones owned by nobody or by an over-capacity team. Then propose the deletion date and the escalation path that would force the last 20% to completion.

Acceptance criteria: your status framing makes "the old system is still running" the headline (not a flattering volume number), lists the remaining callers with owners and surfaces at least one orphan, and proposes a specific deletion date for the old system with a plan for the orphaned and politically-stuck callers. A reader can see that the remaining work is finite and that finishing is now the measured goal.

54.2 Running a migration as a program

Concept

A large migration is not a project; it is a program — a long-running, multi-team effort that needs its own scoping, milestones, owners, tracking, and communication cadence, run with the same discipline as a product launch. The difference between a migration that finishes and one that stalls is usually not the technical plan; it is whether someone ran it as a program with a visible dashboard, named owners for every piece, and a regular drumbeat of communication that keeps it from fading into the background. A migration without program management is a migration that will stall, because nobody is holding the whole thing and nothing is keeping it visible.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a migration run as a loose collection of tickets in various teams' backlogs, with no overall owner, no dashboard, and no regular status. Each team does its piece when it gets around to it. There is no one person who knows the overall state, no one chasing the stragglers, and no visibility to leadership about whether it is on track. Predictably, it drifts: teams deprioritise their migration tickets for features, nobody notices because there is no dashboard, and leadership assumes it is fine because nobody is reporting problems. Six months later someone asks "how is that migration going?" and the honest answer is "nobody knows".

Program management exists to prevent exactly this. A migration needs a single owner who holds the whole thing, a visible dashboard so drift is noticed immediately, named owners for every component so nothing is orphaned, and a communication cadence that keeps it from fading. These are not bureaucracy; they are the mechanisms that keep a long, boring, multi-team effort alive and moving when every local incentive pulls toward ignoring it.

Mental model

Imagine a large building construction. It has a general contractor who owns the whole thing, a schedule with milestones everyone can see, a named subcontractor responsible for each trade (plumbing, electrical, framing), a site meeting every week to surface blockers, and a visible progress board. Nobody would run a building by throwing tasks into various crews' backlogs and hoping. A migration is a construction project, and it needs the same scaffolding of program management: a general contractor (the program owner), a visible schedule (the dashboard), named responsible parties (component owners), and a regular site meeting (the comms cadence). Remove any of these from a building site and it stalls; remove them from a migration and it stalls the same way.

How it works

The program-management elements of a migration:

1. Scoping. Define precisely what is in and out, and what "done" means (the old system is off). Inventory everything that must migrate — every table, every caller, every job — because the things you do not inventory are exactly the orphans that stall you later. The inventory is the foundation; an incomplete inventory guarantees surprises in the last 20%.

2. Milestones. Break the migration into phases with dates, each with a clear exit criterion. "Phase 1: new system live and taking 1% of traffic. Phase 2: 50% of callers migrated. Phase 3: old system read-only. Phase 4: old system deleted." Milestones make progress legible and make slippage visible early.

3. Owners. Every component to be migrated has a named owner who is accountable for migrating it. The program has a single overall owner — the general contractor — who holds the whole thing and chases the stragglers. Unowned components are orphans waiting to stall you.

4. Tracking dashboard. A single, always-current view of the migration state: what is migrated, what remains, who owns what, and the headline "is the old system still running". The dashboard makes drift immediately visible, which is what keeps the migration from fading quietly.

5. Communication cadence. A regular drumbeat — a weekly or fortnightly update to all stakeholders and leadership — that keeps the migration visible and keeps the pressure on. The moment a migration stops being communicated, it starts being deprioritised.

flowchart TB
    O["Program owner - holds the whole thing"] --> SC["Scope + full inventory"]
    O --> M["Milestones with dates + exit criteria"]
    O --> CO["Named owner per component"]
    O --> DB["Live dashboard - is old system still running?"]
    O --> CC["Comms cadence - weekly update to stakeholders"]
    DB --> V["Drift visible immediately"]
    CC --> P["Migration stays visible, stays prioritised"]

Practical example

A staff engineer runs a migration from a PHP monolith to NestJS services (the full worked example is in 54.7). She runs it as a program. The inventory lists every endpoint, every background job, every database table, and every external caller — 140 items. Each is assigned to an owning team. The dashboard, auto-generated, shows the count migrated versus remaining and the headline "legacy monolith: STILL RUNNING". Milestones have dates: strangler proxy live (month 1), 50% of endpoints migrated (month 8), monolith read-only (month 15), monolith deleted (month 18). Every Friday she posts a one-screen update to the whole org and the executive sponsor: what moved this week, what is blocked, and the countdown to the deletion date. The cadence is relentless and slightly boring, which is the point — the migration never fades into the background, so it never stalls. Eighteen months later the monolith is deleted, on schedule, because it was run as a program, not a backlog.

Artifact example

A migration dashboard and the weekly update it feeds — the two artifacts that keep a program alive and visible.

# Migration dashboard: PHP monolith -> NestJS services (auto-updated)

## HEADLINE
Legacy monolith: STILL RUNNING. Scheduled deletion: 2027-06-30 (T-112 days).
Benefit delivered so far: 0% (we pay for both systems until deletion).

## Progress (completion, not volume)
Endpoints migrated:        118 / 140   (22 remain)
Background jobs migrated:    9 / 12    (3 remain)
Tables with data ownership moved: 31 / 34
Callers off the legacy API: 36 / 43   (7 remain — 2 orphaned, flagged)

## Milestones
[x] M1: Strangler proxy live (done, month 1)
[x] M2: 50% endpoints migrated (done, month 8)
[>] M3: Monolith read-only (target month 15 — ON TRACK)
[ ] M4: Monolith deleted (target month 18)

## Blocked (needs attention THIS WEEK)
- Enterprise batch import: owner Integrations, blocked on new bulk API (ETA 2wk)
- Legacy admin tool: ORPHANED — needs an owner assigned (escalated to director)

---

# Weekly update (every Friday, to all stakeholders + exec sponsor)
Subject: Monolith migration — week 54 — ON TRACK for June 30 deletion

- This week: migrated 6 endpoints (checkout flow complete), moved refunds
  table ownership. 118/140 endpoints done.
- Blocked: legacy admin tool still orphaned; need a director to assign an
  owner by Wednesday or M4 slips. (This is my one ask this week.)
- Next week: batch import, then we hit the read-only milestone.
- Countdown: 112 days to monolith deletion. We pay for both systems until then.

The dashboard leads with the headline that matters (old system still running, benefit 0%, countdown to deletion), measures completion not volume, and flags the orphan and the blocker. The weekly update is short, specific, has exactly one ask, and repeats the countdown — which keeps leadership attention and keeps the migration from fading. Together they are the program-management machinery that turns a stall-prone migration into a dated, visible, finishing program.

Real-world scenario

Two migrations start in the same org in the same quarter, of similar technical difficulty. One is run as a program: single owner, full inventory, dashboard, milestones, weekly updates. The other is run as "tickets in backlogs": each team migrates its piece when it can, no overall owner, no dashboard, no cadence. Eighteen months later, the program-run migration is finished and the old system deleted. The backlog-run migration is 80% done and stalled — nobody can even say exactly how much remains, because there is no inventory and no dashboard, and the last pieces are orphaned. The technical work was comparable; the difference was entirely program management. The visible, owned, communicated migration finished; the invisible, unowned, uncommunicated one stalled. This is the most reliable pattern in large-scale migrations: the one that is run as a program finishes, and the one that is not, does not.

Failure scenario

A migration is run with milestones and a dashboard but no communication cadence — the program owner builds the dashboard and assumes people will look at it. They do not. Without a regular update actively pushed to stakeholders, the migration fades from everyone's attention within weeks. Teams quietly deprioritise their migration tickets for features, and because nobody is pushing the status, nobody notices until the next quarterly review, where it emerges that the migration has not moved in two months. By then, momentum is lost, the context has gone cold, and restarting it costs a re-planning effort. The dashboard existed but was passive; a dashboard nobody is pushed to look at is a dashboard nobody looks at. The communication cadence — the active, relentless, slightly annoying weekly push — is what keeps a migration in people's attention, and without it even a well-instrumented migration drifts into the background and stalls. Visibility is not a passive property of having a dashboard; it is an active practice of communication.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No single program owner. Nobody holds the whole thing; the migration is a collection of tickets that each team deprioritises independently.
  • Incomplete inventory. The things you did not inventory become the orphans that stall you in the last 20%.
  • Passive dashboard, no cadence. A dashboard nobody is pushed to look at fades from attention, and the migration drifts.
  • Milestones with no exit criteria. "Phase 2: migrate more stuff" cannot be declared done or slipped, so slippage is invisible.
  • Unowned components. Orphans that nobody is accountable for migrating, which become the permanent blocker.
  • Comms that are status theatre. Updates full of green lights and no asks or blockers, so leadership cannot help and problems stay hidden until they are crises.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They run a large migration with the discipline of a product launch, because they know the technical plan is rarely the thing that fails — the program management is. They insist on a single accountable owner who holds the whole thing, because a migration owned by everyone is owned by nobody. They build a complete inventory up front, because they have learned that the items left off the inventory are exactly the orphans that stall the last 20%.

They treat the communication cadence as the load-bearing practice, not the dashboard, because a dashboard is passive and attention is the scarce resource — a relentless weekly push with specific asks is what keeps a long, boring migration alive against the constant pull of features. And they make every update honest and useful, leading with blockers and asks rather than green lights, because status theatre hides problems until they are crises, whereas an update that says "I need a director to assign an owner by Wednesday or we slip" actually gets the owner assigned. The principal's program management is what converts a technically-sound migration from one that could finish into one that does.

Common mistakes

  • No single program owner, so the migration is nobody's whole responsibility.
  • An incomplete inventory, which guarantees orphan surprises in the last 20%.
  • Building a dashboard but running no communication cadence, so the migration fades from attention.
  • Milestones without exit criteria, so slippage is invisible.
  • Status updates that are all green lights, hiding problems until they become crises.

Interview questions

  1. Why run a large migration as a program rather than as tickets in teams' backlogs? Expected answer: because migrations stall when they are nobody's whole responsibility and fade from attention; a program gives it a single accountable owner, a complete inventory, dated milestones with exit criteria, a live dashboard, and a communication cadence — the machinery that keeps a long, boring, multi-team effort visible and moving against the constant pull of features. Follow-up: which of these is the most load-bearing and why.

  2. A migration has a dashboard but is drifting anyway. What's likely missing? Expected answer: an active communication cadence — a dashboard is passive, and without a relentless regular update pushed to stakeholders with specific asks, the migration fades from attention and gets deprioritised. Visibility is an active practice, not a property of having a dashboard. Why it matters: tests whether they understand attention as the scarce resource.

  3. What makes a migration status update useful versus theatre? Expected answer: a useful update leads with blockers and has specific asks ("I need an owner assigned by Wednesday or we slip"), measures completion not volume, and repeats the countdown to the old system's deletion; theatre is all green lights, which hides problems until they are crises and gives leadership no way to help. Why it matters: tests communication judgement under long-running pressure.

Practical exercise

Take a migration you are leading or have observed. Produce its program-management artifacts: a scope statement with a definition of done (old system off), a complete inventory of everything that must migrate, a milestone plan with dated exit criteria, an owner assignment for every component (flagging orphans), and a dashboard design that leads with "is the old system still running". Then write one weekly update in the useful (not theatre) style, with exactly one specific ask.

Acceptance criteria: the inventory is complete enough that you would be surprised to discover an un-listed caller later; every component has a named owner or is explicitly flagged as an orphan needing assignment; the milestones have exit criteria you could objectively declare met or slipped; and your weekly update leads with a blocker and a specific, actionable ask rather than a list of green lights.

54.3 Choosing the migration strategy

Concept

There is no single way to do a migration; there is a family of strategies, each with a different risk profile, and choosing the right one for your situation is a principal-level decision. The main strategies are big bang (cut everything over at once), incremental (migrate piece by piece), strangler (route traffic gradually from old to new, covered in Part 47.6), parallel run (run both systems and compare outputs before cutting over), and branch by abstraction (introduce an abstraction layer, then swap the implementation behind it). Each trades off speed, risk, and complexity differently, and picking the wrong one for your blast radius is how migrations turn into incidents.

Why does it exist?

Imagine using a big-bang cutover for a payment system migration — flip everything from the old system to the new one at midnight on a Saturday. If the new system has any bug the testing missed, you have broken payments for the entire company at once, with no gradual signal to warn you and no easy way back. Now imagine using a slow incremental strategy for a trivial, low-risk internal tool migration — you spend months on scaffolding and dual-running for something a weekend big-bang would have handled safely. Each strategy is right for some situations and catastrophic for others.

The family of strategies exists because migrations differ enormously in blast radius and reversibility. A strategy that is prudent for a payment system is overkill for an internal tool, and a strategy that is fine for an internal tool is reckless for payments. Choosing deliberately, based on blast radius and reversibility, is what separates a controlled migration from a gamble.

Mental model

Imagine changing the engine of a vehicle. Big bang is swapping the whole engine in one go while the vehicle is switched off — fast if it works, but if the new engine does not start, you are stranded. Incremental is replacing components one at a time — cylinders, then pistons — keeping the vehicle running throughout, slower but never stranded. Strangler is building the new engine alongside the old and gradually diverting the fuel line from old to new, so you can divert it back instantly. Parallel run is running both engines and comparing their output before trusting the new one. Branch by abstraction is installing a universal mount that either engine can bolt onto, then swapping engines on the mount. The right choice depends on how bad it is to be stranded (blast radius) and how easily you can switch back (reversibility).

How it works

Each strategy, with its risk profile:

Big bang. Cut everything over at once. Fast, simple to reason about, no dual-running complexity. But the blast radius is total and the rollback is hard — if it fails, everything fails at once, and reverting is a second big cutover under incident pressure. Appropriate only for low-risk, well-understood, easily-reversible migrations, or where dual-running is genuinely impossible.

Incremental. Migrate one piece at a time, each piece going fully live before the next. The blast radius of each step is one piece, so failures are contained and the system keeps running throughout. Slower, and requires the old and new to coexist (which has its own complexity), but far safer. The default for most large migrations.

Strangler (Part 47.6). Put a routing layer (a proxy or facade) in front, and gradually route calls from the old implementation to the new one, feature by feature or percentage by percentage, until the old one receives no traffic and can be removed. Reversible at every step (route back instantly), observable (you see the new path under real traffic gradually). The gold standard for migrating a live system with callers you control.

Parallel run. Run both the old and new systems on the same inputs, serve from the old (trusted) system, but compare the new system's output against the old. Only cut over once the outputs match for long enough to trust the new one. The safest strategy for correctness-critical migrations (payments, billing, anything where a wrong answer is catastrophic), because you verify the new system against the old on real production data before trusting it.

Branch by abstraction. Introduce an abstraction layer over the thing being migrated (an interface the rest of the code uses), move all callers onto the abstraction, then swap the implementation behind it from old to new without the callers knowing. Ideal for migrating a library or a component used by many callers within a codebase, because the abstraction decouples the callers from the migration.

flowchart TB
    A["How bad is the blast radius + how reversible?"] -->|"low risk, reversible, dual-run impossible"| BB["Big bang"]
    A -->|"large system, callers you control"| ST["Strangler"]
    A -->|"correctness-critical - payments, billing"| PR["Parallel run"]
    A -->|"a component used by many internal callers"| BA["Branch by abstraction"]
    A -->|"large system, piece by piece"| IN["Incremental"]

The decision matrix:

Strategy Speed Risk / blast radius Reversibility Best for
Big bang Fast Total Hard Low-risk, well-understood, dual-run impossible
Incremental Slow Per-piece Good Most large migrations (default)
Strangler Medium Gradual, controlled Instant (route back) Live systems with controllable callers
Parallel run Slow Low (verify first) Instant (serve old) Correctness-critical migrations
Branch by abstraction Medium Contained by the abstraction Good (swap back) Components with many internal callers

These are not mutually exclusive. A large migration often combines them: strangler for the traffic routing, parallel run for the correctness-critical parts, branch by abstraction for shared components.

Practical example

A company migrating its order system chooses a combination. The overall approach is strangler: a routing layer sends order traffic to old or new per endpoint, reversible at every step. For the refund calculation specifically — where a wrong number means a customer is charged incorrectly — they layer in a parallel run: both systems calculate every refund, the old one's answer is served, and the new one's answer is compared and logged. Only after two weeks of matching refund calculations do they cut refunds over to the new system. For the shared "order formatting" library used by twelve internal callers, they use branch by abstraction: an interface is introduced, all twelve callers move onto it, then the implementation is swapped. Three strategies, each applied where its risk profile fits: strangler for controllable live routing, parallel run for correctness-critical money math, branch by abstraction for the shared component. Using big bang for the refund calculation would have risked charging customers wrong at scale; using parallel run for everything would have been needlessly slow.
