Matching the strategy to the blast radius of each part is the skill.

Artifact example

A migration strategy decision record — the artifact that documents which strategy applies where and why.

# Migration strategy decision: order system -> new platform

## Overall: STRANGLER
A routing facade sends each order endpoint to old or new. Reversible per
endpoint (route back instantly). Lets us migrate and verify under real
traffic, gradually. Rejected big-bang: blast radius is all orders — too total.

## Refund calculation: STRANGLER + PARALLEL RUN
Refund amounts are money; a wrong number charges a customer incorrectly.
So on top of the strangler routing, we PARALLEL RUN: both systems compute
every refund, old is served, new is compared and logged. Cut over only
after 14 days of 100% match. Rejected cutting over on test confidence alone
— test coverage can't match real production refund diversity.

## Shared order-formatting library (12 internal callers): BRANCH BY ABSTRACTION
Introduce an OrderFormatter interface, move all 12 callers onto it, then
swap the implementation old -> new behind it. Callers never change again.
Rejected migrating each caller's inline formatting: 12x the work, 12x the risk.

## Legacy admin tool (1 orphaned caller, low traffic, read-only): BIG BANG
Low risk, read-only, easily reversible. A weekend cutover with a tested
rollback is proportionate. Rejected strangler: scaffolding cost exceeds the
risk it would mitigate.

## Why a mix
Each part's strategy matches its blast radius and reversibility. One
strategy for everything would be either too risky (big bang on refunds) or
too slow (parallel run on the admin tool).

The decision record's value is that it is explicit about matching strategy to blast radius per component, and it names what each choice rejected and why. It shows the principal-level judgement: not dogmatically applying one strategy, but choosing deliberately based on how catastrophic a failure would be and how easily it could be undone.

Real-world scenario

A team migrating a billing system wisely chooses parallel run for the core billing calculation. For six weeks, both the old and new billing engines process every invoice; the old engine's result is sent to customers, and the new engine's result is computed and diffed. In week three, the diffs reveal that the new engine rounds tax differently on multi-currency orders — a bug that every test had missed because the tests did not include the specific multi-currency edge case that real production data contained. Because of the parallel run, this bug is caught in a log, affecting zero customers, rather than in a customer's incorrect invoice. The team fixes the rounding, the diffs go to zero, and after six weeks of perfect matching they cut over with justified confidence. Had they used big bang or cut over on test confidence, that rounding bug would have shipped to every multi-currency customer's invoice, producing a billing incident and a mass of corrections. The parallel run converted a would-be billing incident into a logged diff nobody outside the team ever saw. For correctness-critical migrations, parallel run is worth its slowness precisely because real production data contains edge cases no test suite anticipates.

Failure scenario

A team migrates a payment processing system with a big-bang cutover, confident because their test suite is comprehensive and staging looked perfect. At midnight on a Saturday they flip all payment traffic to the new system. Within minutes, a bug that only manifests under concurrent load — invisible in single-threaded testing — causes a fraction of payments to be recorded twice. Because it is a big bang, all payment traffic is on the new system, so the bug affects everyone immediately, and because there is no parallel run, there is no comparison that would have caught it before cutover. Rolling back means a second emergency cutover under incident pressure, during which more payments are mis-recorded in the chaos. The incident lasts hours, affects thousands of customers, and requires weeks of financial reconciliation to untangle the double-charges. The big-bang strategy, chosen for speed and simplicity, was catastrophically wrong for a correctness-critical system with a total blast radius — a parallel run would have caught the concurrency bug in a diff, affecting no one, and an incremental or strangler approach would have limited the blast radius to a small percentage. The strategy choice, not the bug, is what turned a caught-in-diff issue into a company-wide payment incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Big bang on a correctness-critical or high-blast-radius system. A missed bug fails everything at once, with a hard rollback under incident pressure.
  • Cutting over on test confidence alone for correctness-critical migrations, when real production data contains edge cases no test anticipated.
  • Over-engineering a low-risk migration with parallel run or strangler scaffolding that costs more than the risk it mitigates.
  • Strangler with no actual rollback. A routing layer that cannot route back (because the new path wrote incompatible data) is not reversible, defeating the point.
  • Parallel run that never ends. Both systems running forever because the team never gains the confidence to cut over, or never schedules the cutover.
  • Branch by abstraction where the abstraction leaks. If the abstraction does not fully decouple callers from the implementation, swapping the implementation still breaks callers.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They choose the migration strategy by blast radius and reversibility, not by habit or fashion, and they are comfortable mixing strategies across a single migration because different components have different risk profiles. They reach for parallel run whenever correctness is critical and a wrong answer is catastrophic, because they know that real production data contains edge cases no test suite anticipates, and verifying the new system against the old on real data is the only way to gain justified confidence. They reserve big bang for the genuinely low-risk, reversible cases where the scaffolding of a safer strategy would cost more than the risk it mitigates.

They are skeptical of confidence based on testing and staging for high-stakes migrations, because they have seen too many concurrency bugs, data-diversity edge cases, and load-only failures that staging never surfaced. And they insist that whatever strategy is chosen preserves a real rollback — a strangler that cannot route back, or a cutover with no reverse path, has thrown away the safety the strategy was supposed to provide. The principal's judgement is in matching the strategy's safety to the component's stakes, spending safety where failure is catastrophic and speed where it is cheap.

Common mistakes

  • Big bang on a high-blast-radius or correctness-critical system, risking a total, hard-to-reverse failure.
  • Trusting test confidence over a parallel run for correctness-critical migrations.
  • Over-engineering a low-risk migration with heavy scaffolding.
  • A strangler or cutover with no real rollback, throwing away the safety the strategy promised.
  • A parallel run that never ends, running both systems forever without ever cutting over.

Interview questions

  1. What migration strategies do you know, and how do you choose between them? Expected answer: big bang, incremental, strangler, parallel run, branch by abstraction; choose by blast radius and reversibility — big bang only for low-risk reversible cases, strangler for live systems with controllable callers, parallel run for correctness-critical migrations, branch by abstraction for components with many internal callers, incremental as the general default. Mix them across one migration. Follow-up: which would you use for a billing calculation and why.

  2. Why is a parallel run worth its slowness for a payment or billing migration? Expected answer: because real production data contains edge cases (multi-currency rounding, concurrency, data diversity) that no test suite anticipates; running both systems on real inputs and diffing the outputs catches these bugs in a log affecting zero customers, before cutover, giving justified confidence that testing alone cannot. Why it matters: tests understanding of why real-data verification beats test confidence for critical systems.

  3. A team wants a big-bang cutover for payments because their tests pass. What's your concern? Expected answer: big bang gives a total blast radius with a hard rollback, and test/staging confidence misses load-only and data-diversity bugs; for a correctness-critical system, a missed bug would affect everyone at once with no gradual warning. Recommend strangler for gradual, reversible routing plus a parallel run to verify correctness on real data before cutover. Why it matters: tests risk judgement on a high-stakes migration.

Practical exercise

Take a migration you are planning (or decompose a large one into its components). For each major component, choose a migration strategy and justify it by blast radius and reversibility. Identify at least one component that warrants a parallel run (correctness-critical) and at least one that warrants a lightweight big bang (genuinely low-risk). Write the strategy decision record showing the mix and what each choice rejected.

Acceptance criteria: different components are assigned different strategies based on their risk profiles (not one strategy applied uniformly); the correctness-critical component uses parallel run or an equivalent real-data verification; the low-risk component is not over-engineered; and every choice names the blast radius and reversibility that justify it, plus what it rejected and why.

54.4 Monolith decomposition: seams, the first service, and data ownership

Concept

Breaking a monolith into services is the most common large migration, and the hardest part is not the code — it is the data. Decomposition means finding the seams (the natural boundaries where the monolith can be split), extracting the first service (which is disproportionately hard because you are building all the platform scaffolding for the first time), splitting data ownership (deciding which service owns which tables, the genuinely difficult part), and managing the shared database phase (the transitional period where the new service still reads the monolith's tables, which must be temporary or it becomes a permanent distributed monolith). Part 5 covered monolith versus microservices as a choice; this is about executing the decomposition when you have decided to do it.

Why does it exist?

Imagine trying to extract an "orders" service from a monolith where the orders code reads and writes the users table, the products table, the inventory table, and the payments table directly, and where other parts of the monolith read and write the orders table directly. You cannot simply lift the orders code out, because it is entangled with everyone else's data, and everyone else is entangled with its data. Pull it out naively and you either break a dozen other features or you create a service that still reaches into the monolith's database — which is a distributed monolith, the worst of both worlds (network calls and shared-database coupling).

Decomposition discipline exists because a monolith's modules are usually entangled at the data layer, and untangling that entanglement — deciding who owns what data and severing the direct cross-module database access — is the real work. The code extraction is mechanical once the data ownership is sorted; the data ownership is where decompositions succeed or fail.

Mental model

Imagine separating two trees whose roots have grown together underground. Above ground they look like two separate trees (two modules), and you might think you can just cut between them. But below ground, their roots are intertwined (the shared database), and if you cut carelessly you kill both. Separating them requires carefully tracing which roots belong to which tree and untangling them one at a time, often leaving some shared root structure in place temporarily while the trees establish their own. Monolith decomposition is root-untangling: the visible module boundary is easy, but the data roots underneath are intertwined, and the whole job is tracing and separating them without killing either side.

How it works

1. Find the seams. Seams are the natural boundaries — usually bounded contexts (Part 5) — where coupling is low across the boundary and high within it. Signs of a good seam: the module has a clear domain, few other modules read its tables, and it reads few other modules' tables. Signs of a bad seam (do not cut here): the module shares tables promiscuously with others, or there is a transaction that spans the proposed boundary. Enforcing module boundaries first (Part 53.5's fitness functions) makes the seams visible and clean before you cut.

2. Extract the first service (the hard one). The first extraction is disproportionately expensive, because you are building everything for the first time: the service template, the deployment pipeline, the inter-service communication, the observability, the data-ownership pattern. Budget for this; the first service might take as long as the next five combined. Choose a first service that is valuable but not the riskiest — a context with a clean seam, moderate importance, and a cooperative owning team, so you learn the mechanics on a forgiving case.

3. Split data ownership. This is the crux. Each service must own its data — be the only one that reads and writes its tables directly. Other services access that data only through the owning service's API or events, never by reaching into its database. Splitting ownership means: identify which tables belong to the extracted context, make the new service the sole owner, and replace every other module's direct access to those tables with API calls or events.

4. Manage the shared-database phase. In reality you cannot sever all data access at once. There is a transitional phase where the new service runs but still reads (or even writes) some of the monolith's tables, because untangling every access takes time. This phase is acceptable only as a temporary bridge with a scheduled end. If it becomes permanent, you have a distributed monolith: services that are separately deployed but still coupled through a shared database, which has all the costs of distribution and none of the benefits of true independence.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Phase1["Phase 1: in monolith"]
        M1["Monolith: orders code + orders tables + others' tables"]
    end
    subgraph Phase2["Phase 2: shared DB (TEMPORARY)"]
        OS2["Orders Service"] -->|"owns"| OT2[("orders tables")]
        OS2 -.->|"still reads (bridge)"| MT2[("monolith tables")]
    end
    subgraph Phase3["Phase 3: full ownership (GOAL)"]
        OS3["Orders Service"] -->|"owns"| OT3[("orders tables")]
        OS3 -->|"API / events"| MS3["Monolith / other services"]
    end
    Phase1 --> Phase2 --> Phase3

Practical example

A team extracts an orders service from an e-commerce monolith. They find the seam: the orders context owns the orders, order_items, and order_status_history tables, and its main entanglements are reading the products table (for product details on an order) and the users table (for customer info). They extract the orders service as their first service, building the template, pipeline, and inter-service communication in the process — it takes three months, far longer than later services will. For data ownership: the orders service becomes the sole owner of the three order tables, and the monolith's code that used to read orders directly is changed to call the orders service's API. For the orders service's reads of products and users, they enter a temporary shared-database phase: the orders service reads those tables directly for now, with a scheduled task (two months out) to replace those reads with API calls to a future products service and the users module. The shared-database phase is explicitly temporary and dated, so it does not calcify into a distributed monolith.

Artifact example

A data ownership map and shared-database phase plan — the artifacts that make the hard part (data) explicit and time-bound.

# Orders service extraction: data ownership map

## Tables the orders service will OWN (sole read/write)
- orders
- order_items
- order_status_history
Other code accesses these ONLY via the orders service API/events after cutover.

## Tables the orders service READS but does NOT own
| Table | Owner (now/future) | Access after extraction | Bridge end date |
|---|---|---|---|
| products | monolith -> future products svc | TEMP: direct read (bridge) | Q3 (via products API) |
| users | monolith users module | TEMP: direct read (bridge) | Q3 (via users API) |
| inventory | monolith -> future inventory svc | TEMP: direct read (bridge) | Q4 (via inventory events) |

## Who currently reads the tables we will OWN (must be cut over)
| Current direct reader | New access | Owner | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monolith checkout flow | orders service API | checkout team | migrated |
| Monolith admin panel | orders service API | admin team | migrated |
| Reporting job | orders service read-replica API | data team | IN PROGRESS |
| Legacy export script | ORPHANED — assign or delete | ? | escalated |

## Shared-database phase: RULES
- Every bridge (direct cross-service table read) has an END DATE above.
- No bridge may become permanent. A bridge past its date is escalated as a
  distributed-monolith risk.
- No new bridges after extraction without an RFC and an end date.

The artifacts make the invisible data entanglement visible: what the service owns, what it temporarily bridges (with an end date for each bridge), and who currently reaches into the tables it will own (which must be cut over). The explicit end dates and the "no permanent bridge" rule are what prevent the shared-database phase from becoming a distributed monolith. This is the real work of decomposition, made concrete.

Real-world scenario

A team extracts their first service and, because they treated data ownership rigorously, the extraction is clean: the new service owns its tables, every other reader was cut over to the API, and the two temporary bridges to the monolith's tables have end dates. Six months later, they extract their fifth service, and it takes three weeks instead of three months. The platform scaffolding built during the first extraction — the template, the pipeline, the communication patterns, the data-ownership playbook — all apply directly. The first extraction was expensive because it was pathfinding; the later ones are cheap because the path is paved. This is the normal shape of a well-run decomposition: a slow, expensive, educational first service, then an accelerating series of cheaper extractions, because the hard platform work and the data-ownership discipline established on service one compound across all the rest.

Failure scenario

A team extracts an orders service but skips the hard data-ownership work. The new orders service is deployed separately, which feels like progress, but it still reads and writes the monolith's tables directly — including tables other modules also write — and the monolith still reads and writes the orders tables directly. They have created a distributed monolith: two separately-deployed systems that are coupled through a shared database. Now they have all the costs of distribution (network calls, two deploy pipelines, two on-call surfaces, distributed debugging) and all the costs of the shared database (any schema change to a shared table requires coordinating both systems, transactions that used to be local now span the database in uncontrolled ways, and a change in one system can break the other through the shared tables). This is strictly worse than the monolith they started with, because the monolith at least had everything in one deployable with local transactions. The decomposition, by skipping data ownership, produced negative value: more operational cost, more coupling, and no independence. The shared-database phase, never ended, became the permanent architecture — the exact failure that data-ownership discipline and bridge end-dates exist to prevent.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cutting at a bad seam. Splitting where tables are shared promiscuously or a transaction spans the boundary, producing a service that cannot own its data.
  • Skipping data ownership. Extracting the code but leaving shared-database access, creating a distributed monolith that is worse than the original.
  • The permanent shared-database phase. Bridges with no end date that calcify into permanent coupling.
  • Underestimating the first extraction. Not budgeting for the disproportionate cost of building all the platform scaffolding the first time.
  • Choosing the riskiest service first. Learning the mechanics on the highest-stakes context, so mistakes are expensive.
  • A transaction that spanned the boundary. An operation that must be atomic across the old boundary now spans two services, requiring a saga (Part 47.3) that nobody planned for.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They understand that monolith decomposition is fundamentally a data problem, not a code problem, and they spend their attention on data ownership — who owns which tables, who currently reaches into them, and how to sever that access — because that is where decompositions succeed or fail. They enforce module boundaries first (Part 53) so the seams are clean and visible before cutting, because cutting at a bad seam produces a service that can never own its data. They budget realistically for the disproportionate cost of the first extraction and choose a forgiving first service, because the first one is pathfinding and the platform work it builds compounds across all the rest.

Above all, they treat the shared-database phase as a temporary bridge with a hard end date, and they watch it like a hawk, because they know the single most common decomposition failure is the shared-database phase becoming permanent — producing a distributed monolith that is strictly worse than the monolith they started with. A principal would rather delay an extraction than ship one that leaves permanent shared-database coupling, because a half-decomposed service with shared data is negative value, carrying all the costs of distribution with none of the independence.

Common mistakes

  • Treating decomposition as a code problem and neglecting the data ownership that actually determines success.
  • Extracting the code but keeping shared-database access, creating a distributed monolith.
  • Letting the shared-database phase become permanent by not setting and enforcing bridge end dates.
  • Underestimating the first extraction and under-resourcing the platform scaffolding it must build.
  • Choosing the riskiest service to extract first, making the learning expensive.

Interview questions

  1. What is the hardest part of decomposing a monolith into services, and why? Expected answer: splitting data ownership — the modules are usually entangled at the data layer, and the real work is deciding who owns which tables and severing every other module's direct access to them, replacing it with APIs or events. The code extraction is mechanical once data ownership is sorted; the data is where decompositions fail. Follow-up: what is a distributed monolith and how does skipping data ownership cause it.

  2. What is a distributed monolith and why is it worse than the monolith you started with? Expected answer: services that are separately deployed but still coupled through a shared database; it has all the costs of distribution (network calls, multiple pipelines, distributed debugging) plus all the costs of the shared database (coordinated schema changes, cross-service coupling via shared tables), with none of the independence — strictly worse than a monolith that at least had local transactions and one deployable. Skipping data ownership during extraction causes it. Why it matters: this is the central decomposition failure.

  3. Why is the first service extraction so much more expensive than later ones? Expected answer: the first extraction is pathfinding — you build all the platform scaffolding for the first time (template, pipeline, inter-service communication, observability, the data-ownership playbook), which later extractions reuse. Budget for a slow first service and an accelerating series after it. Follow-up: how would you choose which service to extract first.

Practical exercise

Take a monolith (yours or a hypothetical e-commerce one) and plan the extraction of one service. Find the seam: which context has a clean boundary (owns a coherent set of tables, with limited entanglement). Produce the data ownership map: the tables the service will own, the tables it temporarily reads but does not own (each with a bridge end date), and the current direct readers of the tables it will own (each needing cutover). Flag any transaction that spans the proposed boundary.

Acceptance criteria: the chosen seam has a coherent set of owned tables and limited cross-boundary data sharing; the data ownership map explicitly lists every temporary bridge with an end date and every current reader that must be cut over; and you have identified whether any atomic operation spans the boundary (requiring a saga). A reader can see that the shared-database phase is temporary and bounded, not a path to a distributed monolith.

54.5 Data migrations at scale: dual writes, CDC, backfills, and reconciliation

Concept

Moving the data itself — billions of rows from an old store to a new one, while the system keeps running and the data keeps changing — is the hardest technical part of most migrations. It requires getting the existing data across (a backfill of potentially billions of rows without taking the system down), getting new and changed data across continuously while both systems run (dual writes or change-data-capture), and proving the two stores agree (reconciliation and verification). Get any of these wrong and you silently lose or corrupt data, which in a payment or order system is catastrophic and often invisible until much later.

Why does it exist?

Imagine migrating ten billion order rows from the old database to the new one. You cannot take the system down for the hours or days a naive copy would take — the business runs continuously. And while you are copying, new orders are being placed and existing orders are being updated, so the data is a moving target: by the time your copy finishes, the source has changed. And when you are done, how do you know the new store is correct? If 0.3% of rows silently failed to copy, you will not notice until a customer complains that their order is missing, long after the cutover.

Scaled data migration techniques exist to solve these three problems: copy the existing data without downtime (backfill in batches), keep the stores in sync while both run (dual write or CDC), and verify they agree (reconciliation). Without all three, you have a migration that is fast, live, and silently wrong.

Mental model

Imagine moving the water from one reservoir to another while the first reservoir is still being filled by rivers and drained by cities. You cannot just scoop it across once, because it keeps changing. You need three things: a pump that moves the existing water over gradually (backfill), a pipe that diverts the incoming rivers to also fill the new reservoir while the old one is still in use (dual write / CDC), and gauges on both reservoirs to confirm the levels match before you shut off the old one (reconciliation). Shut off the old reservoir before the levels match, and a city goes thirsty (data loss). The whole discipline is moving a live, changing body of data without losing a drop.

How it works

Backfilling existing data. Copy the historical rows in batches, not all at once, to avoid overwhelming the database or holding long locks:

-- Backfill in bounded batches, by primary key, so each batch is fast and
-- holds no long lock. Run until no rows remain.
INSERT INTO new_store.orders (id, customer_id, total_minor, status, created_at)
SELECT id, customer_id, total_minor, status, created_at
FROM old_store.orders
WHERE id > :last_copied_id        -- keyset pagination, not OFFSET (Part 14)
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5000
ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;      -- idempotent: safe to re-run a batch

Backfill properties that matter at billions of rows: batch by key (keyset pagination, never OFFSET on a huge table), make each batch idempotent (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) so you can re-run safely, throttle to avoid saturating the database, and checkpoint progress so you can resume after a failure. A ten-billion-row backfill at 5,000 rows per batch and a safe rate might run for days; that is fine, because it runs alongside the live system.

Keeping the stores in sync (new/changed data). Two approaches:

  • Dual writes. The application writes to both stores on every change. Simple to understand, but dangerous: if the write to one store succeeds and the other fails (crash, timeout), the stores diverge — the dual-write problem from Part 19.4. Dual writes need the same care as any dual write: ideally an outbox, or at minimum careful error handling and reconciliation to catch divergence.
  • CDC (change data capture). Read the old database's replication log (e.g. PostgreSQL logical replication, or Debezium) and stream every change to the new store. The new store is kept in sync by consuming the change stream. CDC is generally safer than application-level dual writes because it captures every committed change from the source of truth (the log) rather than relying on the application to write twice, so it cannot miss a change that committed.
flowchart LR
    APP["Application"] -->|"writes"| OLD[("Old store")]
    OLD -->|"replication log"| CDC["CDC pipeline - Debezium / logical replication"]
    CDC -->|"stream changes"| NEW[("New store")]
    BF["Backfill job - batched, idempotent, throttled"] -->|"historical rows"| NEW

The combination — backfill for history, CDC for ongoing changes — is the standard pattern: the backfill catches up the past while CDC keeps the present in sync, and when the backfill finishes, the new store is fully caught up and staying caught up.

Reconciliation and verification. Prove the stores agree before cutover. Run a reconciliation job that compares the two stores — by row counts, by checksums over ranges of rows, by sampling and comparing individual records, or by comparing aggregates (sum of all order totals in both stores). Any discrepancy is investigated and fixed before cutover. Reconciliation is not optional for anything important: it is the only way to know your migration did not silently lose or corrupt data.

Practical example

A team migrates five billion order rows to a new store. They run a backfill: batched by id with keyset pagination, 5,000 rows per batch, idempotent on conflict, throttled to keep the source database under 60% CPU, checkpointing the last copied id. It runs for four days. Simultaneously, they set up CDC via PostgreSQL logical replication, streaming every new and changed order from the old store to the new one, so that changes during the four-day backfill are captured. When the backfill finishes and CDC lag is near zero, the new store is fully caught up. Before cutover, they run reconciliation: compare total row counts (match), compare the sum of all order totals (match to the cent), and sample 100,000 random orders and compare every field (match). Only after reconciliation passes do they cut reads over to the new store, keeping CDC running so they can fall back. The backfill moved the past, CDC moved the present, and reconciliation proved correctness — the three pieces that make a billions-of-rows live migration safe.

Artifact example

A reconciliation report and cutover-readiness checklist — the artifacts that gate a data cutover on proof, not hope.

# Order data migration: reconciliation report (pre-cutover gate)

## Backfill
Rows in old store:  5,012,443,901
Rows in new store:  5,012,443,901   -> MATCH
Backfill completed: 2027-05-10. Checkpoints clean, no gaps.

## CDC sync
CDC lag (old -> new): 0.4s  -> within tolerance (< 5s)
Changes applied since backfill start: 48,221,004. Errors: 0.

## Reconciliation checks (ALL must pass to cut over)
| Check | Old store | New store | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total row count | 5,012,443,901 | 5,012,443,901 | PASS |
| Sum of order totals (checksum) | 918,443,221,05 | 918,443,221,05 | PASS |
| Count by status (10 buckets) | — | — | PASS (all match) |
| Random sample 100k, all fields | — | — | PASS (0 diffs) |
| Orders in last 24h (freshness) | 1,204,331 | 1,204,331 | PASS |

## Cutover readiness
[x] Backfill complete, no gaps
[x] CDC lag within tolerance
[x] All reconciliation checks PASS
[x] Rollback plan: keep CDC running, reads can fall back to old store in <5min
[x] Old store NOT deleted until 30 days post-cutover (safety window)

## Decision: CLEARED FOR CUTOVER
Reconciliation proves the stores agree. Cut reads over; keep writing both +
CDC for 30 days as a safety net before deleting the old store.

The report's whole purpose is to replace "we think the data is fine" with "here is proof the stores agree, by five independent checks". The row counts, the checksum over all order totals, the per-status counts, the 100k-field-level sample, and the freshness check together make silent data loss extremely unlikely to slip through. The cutover is gated on this proof, and the old store is kept for 30 days as a safety net. This is how you migrate billions of rows and know you did not lose any.

Real-world scenario

A team migrating order data runs reconciliation before cutover and the row counts match exactly — but the checksum over order totals is off by a tiny amount, a few cents across billions of dollars. Row counts matching but totals not matching is a telltale sign: the right number of rows copied, but some rows copied with wrong values. Investigation reveals that a handful of orders with a rare currency had their totals truncated by a type mismatch between the old and new schema (a precision difference). Because reconciliation caught it — specifically the checksum check, which row counts alone would have missed — the team fixes the type handling, re-syncs the affected rows, re-runs reconciliation until the checksum matches to the cent, and only then cuts over. Had they reconciled on row count alone (a common shortcut), the truncated totals would have shipped silently, corrupting a small number of orders in a way nobody would notice until a customer or an auditor found it months later. The multi-dimensional reconciliation — counts and checksums and field-level sampling — is what caught a corruption that any single check would have missed. For money data, reconciling on count alone is a trap.

Failure scenario

A team migrates data using application-level dual writes with no reconciliation. The application writes every order to both the old and new stores. For months it seems fine. But dual writes have the dual-write problem: occasionally, the write to the new store fails (a timeout, a transient error) after the write to the old store succeeded, and the error handling just logs it and moves on. Each such failure is a single order that exists in the old store but not the new one — a tiny, silent divergence. Over months, these accumulate: 0.3% of orders are missing from the new store. Because there is no reconciliation, nobody knows. At cutover, reads switch to the new store, and suddenly 0.3% of customers cannot see some of their orders — orders that were silently dropped during the dual-write period. The incident is severe (lost order data in production), hard to diagnose (the data was lost months ago, gradually), and expensive to fix (reconstruct the missing orders from the old store, which is still around only by luck). The root causes are two: dual writes without the dual-write protections (outbox or CDC), and no reconciliation to catch the divergence before cutover. Either safeguard alone would have caught it; together they are the standard discipline, and skipping both turned a routine migration into a data-loss incident. (This is the 0.3%-of-refunds incident story referenced in the outline, generalised.)

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Dual writes without protection. A failed write to one store silently diverges the data; without an outbox/CDC and reconciliation, the divergence accumulates unseen.
  • Reconciling on row count alone. Matches the number of rows but misses rows copied with wrong values (truncation, type mismatches) — catastrophic for money data.
  • No reconciliation at all. You cut over with no proof the data is correct, and discover loss or corruption only when a customer does.
  • Backfill with OFFSET on a huge table. OFFSET on billions of rows gets catastrophically slow; use keyset pagination.
  • Non-idempotent backfill. A re-run (after a failure) double-inserts or errors; make batches idempotent (ON CONFLICT).
  • Deleting the old store immediately after cutover. No safety net if a problem surfaces days later; keep the old store for a safety window.
  • CDC that silently falls behind or drops events. Unmonitored CDC lag means the new store drifts from the source without anyone noticing.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat "prove the data is correct" as a non-negotiable gate on any data cutover, and they reconcile on multiple independent dimensions — counts, checksums over values, field-level sampling, freshness — because they know that any single check has blind spots and that silent data loss or corruption is the worst outcome of a migration precisely because it is invisible until much later. For money and order data especially, they would never reconcile on row count alone, because they have seen value-corruption that count checks miss entirely.

They prefer CDC over application-level dual writes when feasible, because CDC captures every committed change from the source of truth (the log) and cannot miss a change that committed, whereas dual writes rely on the application succeeding twice and silently diverge when it does not. When dual writes are unavoidable, they insist on the dual-write protections (outbox) and on reconciliation as the backstop. And they keep the old store alive for a safety window after cutover and keep the sync running, because they know problems can surface days later, and a migration that has deleted its fallback has thrown away its rollback. The principal's defining instinct in a data migration is distrust: assume the data migrated wrong until proven right, and build the proof.

Common mistakes

  • Dual writes with no outbox/CDC and no reconciliation, accumulating silent divergence.
  • Reconciling on row count alone, missing value corruption (truncation, type mismatches).
  • Skipping reconciliation entirely, cutting over with no proof of correctness.
  • Backfilling with OFFSET or non-idempotent batches, which is slow and unsafe to re-run.
  • Deleting the old store immediately after cutover, leaving no fallback when a problem surfaces later.

Interview questions

  1. How do you migrate billions of rows to a new store while the system keeps running, and prove you didn't lose any? Expected answer: backfill the historical rows in idempotent, throttled, keyset-paginated batches; keep new/changed data in sync via CDC (preferred) or carefully-protected dual writes during the backfill; then reconcile on multiple dimensions (row counts, value checksums, field-level sampling, freshness) before cutover, keeping the old store and the sync running as a safety net afterward. Follow-up: why reconcile on more than row count.

  2. Why is reconciling on row count alone dangerous for money data? Expected answer: row count confirms the right number of rows copied but not that they copied with correct values; truncation or type mismatches can corrupt values while the count still matches. For money data you must also check value checksums (e.g. sum of all totals) and field-level samples, or silent corruption ships. Why it matters: tests whether they understand the blind spots of a single reconciliation dimension.

  3. Why is CDC generally safer than application-level dual writes for keeping two stores in sync? Expected answer: CDC captures every committed change from the source of truth (the replication log), so it cannot miss a change that committed; application dual writes rely on the app successfully writing to both stores, and when one write fails (crash, timeout) the stores silently diverge — the dual-write problem. If dual writes are unavoidable, use an outbox and reconcile. Follow-up: what do you monitor on a CDC pipeline.

Practical exercise

Design the data-migration plan for moving a large table (orders, or a table you work with) to a new store while the system runs. Specify: the backfill (batching strategy, idempotency, throttling, checkpointing), the sync method for ongoing changes (CDC or protected dual writes, and why), and the reconciliation checks that must pass before cutover (at least three independent dimensions, including a value checksum if the data includes money). Include the post-cutover safety window.

Acceptance criteria: the backfill uses keyset pagination and idempotent batches (safe to re-run); the sync method is justified (CDC preferred, or dual writes with explicit protection); the reconciliation includes at least three independent checks with a value checksum for any money data (not row count alone); and the plan keeps the old store and the sync running for a safety window after cutover so a late-surfacing problem can fall back.

54.6 Deprecating, platform migrations, and risk management

Concept

Three topics that complete the migration toolkit. Deprecating and turning things off is the discipline of actually removing the old system — using usage telemetry to find the real callers, deprecation notices and brownouts to push them off, and specific tactics for the stubborn last 5%. Platform migrations are the specific flavours of migration where you change a foundational layer: the database engine, the cloud provider, or the framework (Express to NestJS, Sequelize to TypeORM). Risk management is the set of safety mechanisms — rollback points, kill switches, blast-radius control — that let you run a large migration without betting the company on it.

Why does it exist?

Imagine you have migrated 95% of callers off the old API and want to turn it off, but you do not actually know who the remaining 5% are, because you never instrumented it. You cannot turn it off, because it might break something critical that you cannot identify. So it stays on, forever, carrying the full cost of the old system for 5% of usage — the 80%-done-forever problem of 54.1, in its final act. Deprecation telemetry and tactics exist to find and evict those last callers so the old system can actually be deleted.

Platform migrations exist as a category because changing a foundational layer is riskier than changing an application: everything sits on top of it, so a mistake has a huge blast radius, and these migrations tend to be big-bang-tempting (it feels like you have to switch the database all at once) when they should usually be done with the safe, gradual strategies from 54.3. Risk management exists because large migrations, done without safety mechanisms, are a bet-the-company gamble; the mechanisms turn a gamble into a controlled, reversible process.

Mental model

For deprecation, imagine trying to demolish an old building that might still have tenants. You cannot just demolish it; you must first find out who still lives there (telemetry), give them notice to move (deprecation notices), make it progressively less comfortable to stay (brownouts — turning off the heating for an hour at a time), and finally, for the last stubborn tenant, knock on their door personally (chase the last callers). Only when it is empty and you have confirmed it is empty do you demolish. Turning off a system is an eviction process, and skipping the "find out who still lives there" step means you can never safely demolish.

For risk management, imagine a climber who places protection points as they ascend. Each piece of protection means that if they fall, they only fall to the last point, not to the ground. A migration's rollback points, kill switches and blast-radius controls are the climber's protection: they bound how far you fall when something goes wrong, turning a fatal fall into a short, recoverable one.

How it works

Deprecating and turning off:

  1. Usage telemetry. Instrument the old system so you know, precisely, who is still calling it — which callers, how often, which endpoints. You cannot turn off what you cannot see. This should be in place before you start migrating, so you can watch usage decline and identify the stragglers.
  2. Deprecation notices. Announce the deprecation with a date, through every channel the callers use (docs, response headers like Deprecation and Sunset, direct outreach to known teams). Give a realistic timeline.
  3. Brownouts. Deliberately make the old system temporarily unavailable for short, announced windows (e.g. return errors for one hour) as the deprecation date approaches. Brownouts flush out callers who ignored the notices, because their system breaks briefly and they finally investigate — far better than discovering them at the permanent shutdown.
  4. The last 5%. The stubborn remainder: orphaned callers, teams that keep deprioritising, systems whose owners have left. Tactics: escalate to management with the deletion date as leverage, offer to do the migration for them, or (for truly orphaned, low-value callers) simply turn it off and see who screams, with a fast rollback ready. The last 5% is where deletion dates and escalation paths (54.1, 54.2) earn their keep.

Platform migrations. Each has specifics:

  • Database engine change (e.g. MySQL to PostgreSQL): use the data-migration techniques from 54.5 (backfill + CDC + reconciliation). The risk is correctness (SQL dialect differences, type differences, transaction semantics), so parallel run and reconciliation are essential.
  • Cloud migration (e.g. on-prem to AWS, or AWS to GCP): huge blast radius, many interdependent pieces. Do it incrementally, service by service, with the ability to run across both environments during transition.
  • Framework migration (Express to NestJS, Sequelize to TypeORM): ideal for strangler and branch-by-abstraction. For Express to NestJS, run both frameworks side by side (NestJS can mount Express middleware), migrating route by route. For Sequelize to TypeORM, introduce a repository abstraction, then swap the ORM behind it per repository.

Risk management mechanisms:

- Rollback points: at every stage, a defined way to return to the previous
  safe state. If you can't roll back from a step, don't take it until you can.
- Kill switches: a feature flag that instantly reverts to the old path. The
  single most valuable migration safety mechanism (Part 49 flags).
- Blast-radius control: migrate a small percentage / one tenant / one region
  first, so a failure affects a fraction, not everyone.
- Canary + gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%, watching metrics at each step.
- Backward-compatible changes: never make a change the old path can't survive,
  so rollback stays possible (expand-contract, Part 31).
flowchart LR
    S["Migration step"] --> KS{"Kill switch ready?"}
    KS -->|"no"| STOP["Don't proceed - add the kill switch first"]
    KS -->|"yes"| BR["Ramp with blast-radius control: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%"]
    BR --> W["Watch metrics at each step"]
    W -->|"bad"| RB["Flip kill switch - instant rollback"]
    W -->|"good"| NEXT["Next step"]

Practical example

A team turning off a legacy order API has usage telemetry in place from the start, so they can see the caller count fall from 43 to 7 as the migration proceeds. They publish a deprecation notice with a sunset date and add a Sunset header to every legacy response. As the date approaches, 3 callers remain, so they run a brownout: the legacy API returns 503 for one announced hour. Two of the three callers break during the brownout, investigate, and migrate within the week — the brownout flushed them out. The last caller is an orphaned script with no owner; the team escalates with the deletion date, nobody claims it, so they turn it off with a fast rollback ready. Nothing screams. The legacy API is deleted. The telemetry found the callers, the brownout evicted the laggards, and the escalation-plus-turn-it-off handled the orphan — the full deprecation toolkit used to actually finish, which is the part that usually does not happen.

Artifact example

A deprecation and shutdown plan — the artifact that turns "we should turn off the old system" into an executed eviction.

# Legacy order API: deprecation and shutdown plan

## Telemetry (in place since migration start)
Per-caller request counts logged. Current callers: 7 (was 43). Dashboard
shows each caller's last-seen time and daily volume.

## Timeline
- Now: deprecation notice published (docs + Deprecation/Sunset headers +
  direct email to the 5 known caller teams).
- T+4 weeks: brownout #1 — legacy API returns 503 for 1 hour, 14:00 UTC,
  announced. Purpose: flush out callers who ignored the notice.
- T+6 weeks: brownout #2 — 503 for 2 hours. Final warning.
- T+8 weeks: SHUTDOWN. Legacy API returns 410 Gone permanently.
- T+12 weeks: DELETE legacy API code and infrastructure.

## The last callers (named, with plan)
| Caller | Owner | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| Reporting job | data team | Migrating now, ETA T+2wk |
| Partner webhook | integrations | Migrating, ETA T+3wk |
| Orphaned export script | NONE | Escalated. If unclaimed by T+6wk, turn off with rollback ready. |

## Safety
- Kill switch: shutdown is a flag; if something critical breaks at T+8wk,
  flip it back on in <5 min while we investigate.
- Old code kept (not deleted) until T+12wk as the rollback window.

## Definition of done
Legacy API code and infra DELETED at T+12wk. Not "returning 410" — DELETED.

The plan uses telemetry to know the callers, deprecation notices and escalating brownouts to evict them, a named plan for the stubborn last callers including the orphan, and safety mechanisms (kill switch, retained code) so the shutdown itself is reversible. Crucially, "done" is defined as deleted, not merely returning 410 — because a system that returns 410 is still running infrastructure, still costing money, still the 80%-done-forever trap in disguise. This artifact is how the final, usually-skipped act of a migration actually gets executed.

Real-world scenario

A company migrating from AWS to GCP (a cloud migration, huge blast radius) manages the risk by doing it region by region and service by service, never big-bang. They run services across both clouds during the transition, with a traffic-routing layer that can shift load between them and roll back instantly. For the database, they use CDC to keep the GCP database in sync with the AWS one, with reconciliation gating each cutover. When one service's cutover reveals a latency problem (cross-cloud calls to a dependency still in AWS), they roll that one service back in minutes via the routing layer, fix the dependency ordering, and retry — a contained, recoverable setback affecting one service, not a cloud-wide incident. The blast-radius control (one service, one region at a time) and the instant rollback (routing layer) turned what could have been a catastrophic cloud migration into a series of small, reversible steps. The migration takes longer than a big-bang would have, but it never risks the whole company, which is the correct trade for a change with that blast radius.

Failure scenario

A team migrates from Sequelize to TypeORM with no abstraction layer and no kill switch — they rewrite each data-access call directly from Sequelize to TypeORM, service by service, deploying each as they go. Partway through, a subtle difference in how the two ORMs handle transactions (Sequelize's default isolation versus TypeORM's) causes a race condition in the order service under production load, producing occasional duplicate orders. Because there is no kill switch — the Sequelize code was deleted as each call was rewritten — there is no way to instantly revert to the old data-access path; reverting means a code rollback and redeploy, which takes much longer than flipping a flag, extending the incident. And because they did not use a repository abstraction, the fix must be applied call-by-call across every already-migrated service. The migration, done without the branch-by-abstraction safety (which would have let them swap ORMs behind an interface and keep the old implementation as a kill-switch fallback) and without a kill switch, turned an ORM difference into a production incident with a slow rollback. The safety mechanisms — an abstraction to swap behind and a kill switch to revert instantly — are exactly what a framework/ORM migration needs, and skipping them converted a routine technical difference into an extended incident.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No usage telemetry. You cannot find the remaining callers, so you can never safely turn the old system off.
  • Defining "done" as returning 410/deprecated rather than deleted, leaving infrastructure running forever.
  • No brownouts. Laggard callers are discovered at the permanent shutdown instead of during a recoverable one-hour brownout.
  • Big-bang platform migration. Changing the database engine or cloud all at once, with a total blast radius.
  • No kill switch. A problem after cutover requires a slow code rollback instead of an instant flag flip.
  • A step with no rollback point. Taking a migration step you cannot undo (e.g. deleting old data) before you are certain, so a problem is unrecoverable.
  • Deleting the old system before the safety window. No fallback when a problem surfaces days later.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They insist on usage telemetry from the start of a migration, not the end, because they know the final act — turning the old system off — is impossible without knowing who still calls it, and that the last 5% is where migrations go to die. They define "done" as the old system deleted, and they use the full eviction toolkit (notices, escalating brownouts, named plans for stragglers, escalation with the deletion date as leverage) because they have learned that stubborn callers do not migrate on their own and that a brownout flushes out laggards far more safely than a permanent shutdown.

For platform migrations, they resist the big-bang temptation that foundational-layer changes create, and apply the gradual, reversible strategies (strangler, branch-by-abstraction, incremental) with the blast-radius matched to the stakes, because a database or cloud migration has a company-wide blast radius that no amount of testing confidence justifies betting all at once. And they treat kill switches, rollback points and blast-radius control as the non-negotiable safety equipment of any large migration — they will not take a migration step that has no rollback, and they would rather a migration be slow and reversible than fast and a gamble. The principal runs migrations like a climber places protection: every step bounded, every fall recoverable.

Common mistakes

  • No usage telemetry, so the old system can never be safely turned off.
  • Treating "deprecated" or "returns 410" as done instead of deleted.
  • Skipping brownouts, so laggard callers surface at the permanent shutdown.
  • Big-bang platform migrations, betting a company-wide blast radius all at once.
  • No kill switch or rollback point, turning a post-cutover problem into an extended incident.

Interview questions

  1. How do you actually turn off a legacy system, and why do so many never get turned off? Expected answer: use usage telemetry (from the start) to find the real callers, publish deprecation notices with a sunset date, run escalating brownouts to flush out laggards, and handle the stubborn last callers with escalation (using the deletion date as leverage), offering to migrate them, or turning off with a rollback ready. They never get turned off because teams define "done" as migrated-the-easy-part, lack telemetry to find the last callers, and have no deletion date forcing the issue. Follow-up: what is a brownout and why does it help.

  2. What risk-management mechanisms make a large migration safe? Expected answer: rollback points at every stage, a kill switch (feature flag for instant revert — the most valuable one), blast-radius control (migrate a small percentage/one tenant/one region first), canary and gradual ramp with metric-watching at each step, and backward-compatible changes so rollback stays possible. Never take a step you cannot roll back. Why it matters: tests whether they can run a migration without betting the company.

  3. How would you migrate from Sequelize to TypeORM (or Express to NestJS) safely? Expected answer: use branch-by-abstraction — introduce a repository (or routing) abstraction, move callers onto it, then swap the implementation behind it per repository/route, keeping the old implementation as a kill-switch fallback; migrate incrementally with a kill switch, not by deleting the old path as you go. Why it matters: tests knowledge of safe framework/ORM migration specifically.

Practical exercise

Take a legacy system or API in your org that should be turned off. Write its deprecation and shutdown plan: the usage telemetry you need (or have), a timeline with deprecation notice, escalating brownouts, shutdown, and deletion dates, a named plan for the stubborn last callers (including any orphans), and the safety mechanisms (kill switch, retained-code window). Define "done" as deleted. Separately, for a platform migration you face (DB, cloud, or framework), identify the strategy and the risk-management mechanisms you would use.

Acceptance criteria: your deprecation plan relies on telemetry to identify the actual remaining callers, includes at least one brownout before permanent shutdown, has a specific plan for stubborn/orphaned callers, and defines done as the old system deleted (not merely deprecated); your platform-migration note uses a gradual, reversible strategy proportionate to its blast radius, with a kill switch for instant rollback.

54.7 Worked example: PHP monolith on MySQL to NestJS services on PostgreSQL

This section brings the whole Part together in one eighteen-month migration: moving an order system from a PHP monolith on MySQL to NestJS services on PostgreSQL. It exercises every tool in this Part — run as a program, decomposed by data ownership, migrated with the right strategies, data moved with backfill + CDC + reconciliation, and the old system actually turned off. It also contains the incident story the outline asks for: the migration that silently lost 0.3% of refunds, and how reconciliation caught it.

The situation

OrderCo runs its whole order system as a PHP monolith on a single large MySQL database. It is 400,000 lines of PHP, deploys are scary, and the team wants to move to NestJS services on PostgreSQL to enable independent deploys, better tooling, and the type safety the rest of the company has. The migration is expected to take eighteen months. A principal engineer leads it. Here is how it runs, compressed.

Run as a program (54.2)

A single program owner (the principal) holds the whole thing. The inventory lists all 140 endpoints, 12 background jobs, 34 tables, and 43 external/internal callers. A dashboard shows completion (not volume) and the headline "legacy monolith: STILL RUNNING, scheduled deletion month 18". Milestones have dates. A weekly update goes to all stakeholders and the exec sponsor, with the countdown to deletion. This is what keeps the migration from stalling at 80%.

Strategy: strangler + parallel run (54.3)

The overall strategy is strangler: a routing facade (an Nginx/NestJS gateway) sits in front and routes each endpoint to either the PHP monolith or the new NestJS service, reversible per endpoint. For the money-critical parts — refund and payment calculations — a parallel run is layered on: the new service computes the result, the old monolith's result is served, and the two are diffed and logged until they match. For shared logic used by many internal callers, branch-by-abstraction.

Decomposition by data ownership (54.4)

The monolith's 34 tables are assigned to bounded contexts: orders, payments, inventory, notifications. The orders service is extracted first (the hard, pathfinding first service, three months) and becomes the sole owner of the order tables. Temporary shared-database bridges (the orders service reading the products and users tables directly) are created with end dates. Every other reader of the order tables is cut over to the orders service API. The data-ownership map governs this.

Data migration: backfill + CDC + reconciliation (54.5)

Order data moves from MySQL to PostgreSQL: a batched, idempotent, throttled backfill of the historical rows (several days), CDC via Debezium reading the MySQL binlog streaming ongoing changes to PostgreSQL during the backfill, and reconciliation (row counts, value checksums, field-level sampling) gating every cutover. This is where the incident happens.

The incident: 0.3% of refunds silently lost

# Incident retro (blameless): refund data divergence caught by reconciliation

## What happened
During the refunds cutover prep, the reconciliation report showed row counts
matching between MySQL and PostgreSQL, but the VALUE CHECKSUM over refund
amounts was off — PostgreSQL's total was lower than MySQL's by an amount that
worked out to ~0.3% of refunds being wrong or missing.

## Why (root cause)
The refund sync used application-level DUAL WRITES during an early phase of
the migration (before CDC was in place for that table). About 0.3% of the
time, the write to PostgreSQL failed (a transient timeout) after the MySQL
write succeeded, and the error handler just logged and continued. Each
failure was one refund that existed in MySQL but not PostgreSQL — a silent,
gradual divergence (the classic dual-write problem, Part 19.4).

## How it was caught
The value-checksum reconciliation check. Row counts ALONE would have missed
it in some cases, and even where counts differed, it was the checksum that
quantified the money impact and flagged it as critical. This is exactly why
we reconcile on value, not just count (54.5).

## Why it did NOT become a customer incident
Because reconciliation GATES cutover. We had not cut refunds over to
PostgreSQL yet — MySQL was still the served source of truth. The divergence
was caught in a report, affecting ZERO customers.

## Fix
1. Replaced the refund dual-writes with CDC (captures every committed change
   from the binlog; cannot miss a committed write).
2. Backfilled the missing 0.3% of refunds from MySQL into PostgreSQL.
3. Re-ran reconciliation until the value checksum matched to the cent.
4. Only then cut refunds over.

## Lesson
Dual writes silently diverge; reconciliation on VALUE (not just count) is what
stands between a silent data-loss migration and a safe one. Had we cut over on
test confidence or row-count-only reconciliation, 0.3% of refunds would have
shipped wrong to production — a financial incident requiring mass corrections.

This is the migration that "silently lost 0.3% of refunds" — except reconciliation caught it before cutover, so it lost nothing that reached a customer. The difference between a catastrophe and a non-event was a single reconciliation check on value rather than count, run as a gate before cutover. That is the entire lesson of 54.5 made concrete.

Turning the monolith off (54.6)

With all contexts extracted and data migrated, the final act: usage telemetry shows the remaining callers of the PHP monolith declining to 7, then to 2 orphans. Deprecation notices go out. Two brownouts flush out the laggards. The orphaned callers are escalated with the deletion date; one is claimed and migrated, one is turned off with a rollback ready and nobody screams. At month 18, on schedule, the PHP monolith is powered off and its code deleted. The migration is done — not 95% done, not "the monolith returns 410", but deleted. OrderCo now pays for one system, deploys independently per service, and has the type safety and tooling it wanted.

Why this migration succeeded

Trace it against the Part. It was run as a program with a single owner, a complete inventory, a completion-focused dashboard, and a relentless weekly cadence — so it never stalled. It used the right strategy per component — strangler for routing, parallel run for money math — so the blast radius always matched the stakes. It decomposed by data ownership with temporary, dated bridges — so it never became a distributed monolith. It moved data with backfill + CDC + reconciliation — so it never silently lost data, and the one divergence that occurred was caught in a report affecting zero customers. And it actually turned the old system off — telemetry, brownouts, orphan handling, a scheduled deletion date — so it delivered its full value instead of becoming the 80%-done-forever tax. Every one of those was a deliberate choice by the principal, and skipping any one of them is how the many migrations that stall or cause incidents go wrong.

Practical exercise

Plan a real or hypothetical platform migration end to end using every tool in this Part. Produce: the program setup (owner, inventory, completion-focused dashboard, cadence), the strategy choice per major component (justified by blast radius), the data-ownership decomposition plan, the data-migration plan (backfill + sync + multi-dimensional reconciliation), and the deprecation-and-deletion plan (telemetry, brownouts, orphan handling, deletion date). Define done as the old system deleted.

Acceptance criteria: the plan measures completion (old system running: yes/no) not volume; assigns different migration strategies to components by blast radius with parallel run for anything correctness-critical; decomposes by data ownership with time-boxed bridges; reconciles data on value (not just count) as a cutover gate; and ends with a scheduled deletion of the old system, with a plan for the orphaned last callers. A reader can see that this migration is designed to finish and to never silently lose data.

54.8 Migration verification, observability, and the human side

Concept

Two aspects of large migrations that determine success as much as the technical plan. Migration verification and observability is how you continuously prove the migration is working and catch problems early — comparison dashboards, diffing old versus new outputs, metrics that show the migration's health, and the reconciliation that gates each cutover (54.5). The human side is managing the people through a long migration — keeping morale up during the unglamorous grind, maintaining momentum when the migration competes with features, and handling the organisational fatigue that sets in during a multi-year effort. A migration that is technically sound but loses the people (burnout, lost momentum, fatigue) stalls as surely as one with a bad plan.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a migration running without verification — you cut over and hope the new system is correct, discovering problems only when customers complain. Or imagine a migration with no observability — you cannot tell whether it is healthy, how far along it is, or whether the new path is working under real traffic. Verification and observability exist because a migration touches live, important systems, and you must know, continuously and with evidence, that it is working — not hope, not assume, but prove via diffs, metrics, and reconciliation.

The human side exists because large migrations are long, unglamorous grinds that compete with exciting feature work for people's energy and attention over months or years. The engineers doing the migration can burn out on the tedium; the organisation can lose patience and momentum; fatigue sets in as the migration drags. A migration that ignores the human side loses the very people it depends on, and a demoralised team or a fatigued organisation stalls a technically-sound migration. The human side exists because migrations are run by people over a long time, and sustaining those people is as essential as the technical plan.

Mental model

For verification, imagine a parallel flight test of a new aircraft. You do not just build the new plane and put passengers on it; you fly it alongside proven conditions, instrument everything, and compare its behaviour to the expected, catching problems in telemetry before they endanger anyone. Migration verification is the parallel flight test: run the new system, instrument it, compare its outputs to the old (diffing), and prove it is correct via telemetry and reconciliation before you trust it with real traffic.

For the human side, imagine a long expedition — a months-long trek. The route (technical plan) matters, but so does keeping the team's morale up through the tedious middle stretches, maintaining momentum when energy flags, and managing the fatigue of a long journey. An expedition leader who only plans the route and ignores the team's morale finds the team exhausted and demoralised halfway, and the expedition stalls. A long migration is an expedition, and leading the people through it is as essential as the route.

How it works

Verification and observability:

- Diffing old vs new: during parallel run (54.3), compare the two systems'
  outputs on the same inputs. Any diff is investigated. Catches correctness
  bugs (the 0.3% refunds, 54.7) before cutover, affecting zero customers.
- Comparison dashboards: show the diff rate over time. Trending to zero = the
  new system matches = confidence to cut over.
- Migration-health metrics: progress (completion, not volume — 54.1), error
  rates on the new path, latency comparison, CDC lag (54.5), reconciliation status.
- Reconciliation as a cutover GATE (54.5): data cutover requires reconciliation
  (multi-dimensional, value checksums) to pass. Proof, not hope.
- Canary observability: as you ramp (54.6), watch the new path's metrics at each
  step; a regression means roll back (kill switch) before going further.

The principle: you must be able to prove, continuously, that the migration is working — via diffs that trend to zero, metrics that show health, and reconciliation that gates cutover. A migration you cannot observe is a migration you cannot trust.

The human side:

- Morale through the grind: the migration's unglamorous middle is where morale
  sags. Celebrate milestones (completion milestones, 54.2), rotate people through
  the tedious parts, and make the progress visible (the dashboard) so people see
  they're advancing.
- Momentum vs features: the migration constantly competes with feature work. The
  program owner (54.2) defends the migration's resourcing and keeps it visible
  (the cadence) so it isn't quietly deprioritised.
- Organisational fatigue: in a multi-year migration, patience wears thin ("are we
  STILL doing this?"). Combat it by showing progress against completion, delivering
  incremental value where possible, and holding the deletion date (54.1) as the
  visible finish line.
- Avoid the death march: a migration driven by overwork is unsustainable; pace it,
  and protect the team (Part 56.5).
flowchart LR
    V["Verification: diff old vs new, trending to zero"] --> CONF["Confidence to cut over"]
    OBS["Observability: progress, error rates, CDC lag, reconciliation"] --> CONF
    REC["Reconciliation GATES cutover (proof, not hope)"] --> CONF
    H["Human side: morale, momentum, fatigue, no death march"] --> FINISH["Migration finishes"]
    CONF --> FINISH

Artifact example

A migration verification dashboard and a human-side health note — the artifacts that prove the migration works and keep the people with it.

# Migration verification dashboard: order system (parallel run phase)

## Output diffing (old vs new, same inputs)
- Refund calculation: 0 diffs over last 7 days (was 0.3% — fixed, 54.7). READY.
- Order totals: 0 diffs. READY.
- Status transitions: 2 diffs/day — investigating (edge case in cancellations).
  NOT YET ready to cut over status handling.

## Data reconciliation (gates data cutover, 54.5)
- Row counts match. Value checksums match to the cent. 100k sample: 0 field diffs.
- CDC lag: 0.4s. DATA CUTOVER: CLEARED.

## New-path health (canary at 10%)
- Error rate: 0.02% (vs 0.02% old — equivalent). Latency: p99 better. HEALTHY.

## Progress (completion, not volume, 54.1)
- Legacy system: STILL RUNNING. Deletion: T-112 days. Callers remaining: 7.

---
# Human-side health note (for the program owner)
- Team morale: dipping — we're in the unglamorous middle. ACTION: celebrated the
  50% milestone publicly; rotating the two engineers off the tedious backfill
  verification next sprint.
- Momentum: a feature push threatened to pull 1 engineer off. Held the line
  (reframed: the migration enables the features). 
- Org fatigue: "are we still doing this?" surfaced in a review. ACTION: shared the
  deletion countdown and the incidents the migration has already prevented.
- Pace: sustainable, no death march. Watching for burnout on the 2 core engineers.

The dashboard's power is that it proves the migration is working — output diffs trending to zero (per sub-system, so you cut over each only when its diffs are zero), reconciliation gating data cutover, canary health — rather than hoping. And the human-side note treats morale, momentum, fatigue, and pace as first-class risks to actively manage, because a migration that loses its people stalls regardless of how good the verification looks. Together they address the two things beyond the technical plan that determine whether a long migration finishes: continuous proof that it works, and sustained people to carry it.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer running a long migration treats verification and the human side as seriously as the technical plan. On verification: she runs output diffing throughout the parallel-run phase, cutting over each sub-system only when its diff rate reaches zero, and she gates every data cutover on multi-dimensional reconciliation — so she proves correctness rather than hoping, and the one real bug (a refund-calculation edge case) is caught in a diff affecting zero customers. On the human side: she notices morale dipping during the unglamorous middle, so she celebrates the completion milestones publicly and rotates engineers off the most tedious work; when a feature push threatens the migration's resourcing, she defends it by reframing it as what enables the features; and when organisational fatigue surfaces ("are we still doing this?"), she combats it by showing the deletion countdown and the incidents already prevented. The migration finishes on schedule, because it was both continuously proven correct and carried by a team whose morale and momentum she actively sustained. A peer running a comparable migration with a sound technical plan but no verification discipline (cutting over on hope) and no attention to the human side (letting morale and momentum erode) sees it stall — a correctness bug reaches production, and the demoralised, fatigued team loses momentum. The technical plans were comparable; the difference was verification and the human side, which determine whether a long migration actually finishes.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat verification as non-negotiable: they prove the migration is working continuously — via output diffing that must trend to zero before cutover, migration-health metrics, and reconciliation that gates every data cutover — because they know that a migration touches live important systems and must be proven correct, not hoped correct, and that the cost of a correctness bug reaching production (data corruption, a breach of trust) is far higher than the cost of the verification. They observe the migration thoroughly (progress by completion, error rates, CDC lag) because a migration they cannot see is a migration they cannot trust or steer.

They also treat the human side as a first-class risk, because they understand that a long migration is a grind carried by people over months or years, and that a demoralised team, lost momentum, or organisational fatigue will stall a technically-sound migration as surely as a bad plan. So they actively manage morale (celebrate milestones, rotate the tedious work), defend momentum (protect resourcing against feature pulls, keep the cadence), combat fatigue (show progress and the finish line), and avoid the death march (sustainable pace, protect the team). The senior engineer knows that finishing a large migration — the whole challenge of this Part — requires three things together: a sound plan, continuous proof it is working, and sustained people to carry it to completion, and that neglecting either of the latter two is how good plans still fail.

Common mistakes

  • Cutting over on hope instead of proving correctness via diffing and reconciliation.
  • No output diffing during parallel run, so correctness bugs reach production instead of being caught in a diff.
  • No migration observability, so you cannot tell if it is healthy or how far along (by completion).
  • Ignoring team morale through the grind, so the engineers burn out on the tedium and the migration stalls.
  • Not defending the migration's momentum, letting it be quietly deprioritised for features.
  • Running a death march, an unsustainable pace that burns out the team before the finish.

Interview questions

  1. How do you prove a migration is working, rather than hoping? Expected answer: output diffing during parallel run (compare old vs new on the same inputs; cut over each sub-system only when its diff rate reaches zero), migration-health observability (progress by completion, error rates, latency comparison, CDC lag), and reconciliation that gates every data cutover (multi-dimensional, value checksums). A migration you cannot observe or verify is one you cannot trust. Why it matters: verification catches correctness bugs before they reach customers.

  2. Why is the human side as important as the technical plan in a large migration? Expected answer: a long migration is an unglamorous grind carried by people over months or years, competing with exciting feature work; if morale erodes (burnout on tedium), momentum is lost (deprioritised for features), or organisational fatigue sets in ("are we still doing this?"), the migration stalls regardless of how sound the technical plan is. You must actively manage morale, momentum, fatigue, and pace. Why it matters: tests whether they see migrations as human efforts, not just technical ones.

  3. How do you sustain momentum and morale through the unglamorous middle of a multi-year migration? Expected answer: celebrate completion milestones publicly, rotate people off the most tedious work, make progress visible (the completion dashboard), defend the migration's resourcing against feature pulls (reframe it as enabling features), combat organisational fatigue by showing the deletion countdown and the value already delivered (incidents prevented), and keep a sustainable pace (no death march).
