Why it matters: tests the human-leadership side of long migrations.

Practical exercise

For a migration you are planning or running, design its verification and observability: how you will diff old versus new outputs during parallel run, the migration-health metrics you will track, and how reconciliation will gate each cutover. Then write a human-side plan: how you will sustain morale through the grind, defend momentum against feature competition, combat organisational fatigue, and keep a sustainable pace.

Acceptance criteria: your verification proves correctness (output diffing that must trend to zero before cutover, reconciliation gating data cutover) rather than relying on hope; your observability covers progress by completion, new-path health, and sync lag; and your human-side plan actively manages morale (milestone celebration, rotating tedious work), momentum (defending resourcing), fatigue (showing progress and the finish line), and pace (no death march) — demonstrating that you treat finishing a migration as requiring a sound plan, continuous proof, and sustained people together.

54.9 A quick-reference for large migrations

A compact reference distilling the Part into the checks that matter most when you plan or run a large migration.

The migration checklist

[ ] Am I measuring COMPLETION (is the old system still running?), not volume?
[ ] Is there a scheduled DELETION DATE for the old system, worked backward from?
[ ] Is it run as a PROGRAM — single owner, full inventory, dashboard, cadence?
[ ] Is the STRATEGY matched to blast radius per component? (Parallel run for
    correctness-critical; strangler for live systems; big bang only low-risk.)
[ ] For a monolith split: decomposed by DATA OWNERSHIP, with the shared-database
    phase time-boxed? (Else a distributed monolith.)
[ ] For data: backfill (idempotent, keyset) + CDC + RECONCILIATION on VALUE
    (not just row count), gating cutover?
[ ] Is there a KILL SWITCH and rollback point for every step? Blast radius controlled?
[ ] Am I PROVING it works (output diffing, reconciliation), not hoping?
[ ] Is the old system actually being TURNED OFF — telemetry, deprecation,
    brownouts, orphan handling — and DELETED (not just "returns 410")?
[ ] Am I managing the HUMAN side — morale, momentum, fatigue, sustainable pace?

The enduring principle

The whole Part reduces to one hard truth: a migration delivers its value only at 100%, when the old system is off — so finishing, not starting, is the goal. Large migrations fail by stalling at 80% done forever, as the easy work completes and the unglamorous, political last 20% gets deferred. Everything in this Part serves finishing: measure completion not volume, schedule the deletion date, run it as a program, match the strategy to blast radius, decompose by data ownership, prove correctness with reconciliation, control risk with kill switches, actually turn the old system off, and sustain the people through the grind. When you run a migration, hold the deletion of the old system as the definition of done, and relentlessly drive the last 20% that everyone wants to skip — because that is where migrations go to die, and finishing them is where a principal earns their keep.

Return to this reference when planning or running a large migration; the reasoning behind each line is in the sections above.

Senior Checklist — Part 54

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I understand why migrations stall at 80% and I measure completion (old system off), not volume
  • I run a large migration as a program: single owner, full inventory, dashboard, cadence
  • I choose the migration strategy per component by blast radius and reversibility, and mix strategies
  • I use parallel run for correctness-critical migrations rather than trusting test confidence
  • I decompose monoliths by data ownership and never leave a permanent shared-database phase
  • I migrate data with backfill + CDC + multi-dimensional reconciliation, and reconcile on value, not just count
  • I keep a kill switch and rollback point for every migration step
  • I control blast radius with gradual ramps and per-tenant/per-region rollout
  • I use telemetry, deprecation notices and brownouts to actually turn the old system off
  • I define done as the old system deleted, and I schedule its deletion date early

Part 54 — Key Takeaways

  • Large migrations fail by stalling at 80% done forever, not by exploding; the easy 80% completes fast and the hard, political, unglamorous last 20% gets deferred, leaving two systems running permanently — full cost, no benefit.
  • A migration delivers its value only at 100%, when the old system is off; measure completion (is the old system still running) not volume, and schedule the deletion date early to force the last 20%.
  • Run a large migration as a program: a single accountable owner, a complete inventory, dated milestones, a live dashboard, and a relentless communication cadence — the technical plan is rarely what fails.
  • Choose the migration strategy per component by blast radius and reversibility — big bang only for low-risk reversible cases, strangler for live systems, parallel run for correctness-critical ones, branch-by-abstraction for shared components — and mix them in one migration.
  • Monolith decomposition is a data problem, not a code problem; split data ownership so each service owns its tables, and never let the temporary shared-database phase become permanent, or you build a distributed monolith that is worse than the original.
  • Migrate data at scale with a batched idempotent backfill plus CDC for ongoing changes plus reconciliation to prove correctness; reconcile on value (checksums), not just row counts, especially for money.
  • Dual writes silently diverge; prefer CDC, and use reconciliation as the backstop that catches divergence before cutover, affecting zero customers instead of becoming a data-loss incident.
  • Keep a kill switch and a rollback point for every step, control blast radius with gradual ramps and per-tenant/per-region rollout, and never take a step you cannot undo.
  • Actually turn the old system off: instrument usage telemetry from the start to find the real callers, use deprecation notices and escalating brownouts to evict them, and handle orphaned last callers with escalation and a rollback-ready shutdown.
  • Define done as the old system deleted and the code gone, never as "mostly migrated" or "returns 410", because a system still running is still the 80%-done-forever tax in disguise.
  • Resist the big-bang temptation that platform migrations (database engine, cloud, framework) create; their company-wide blast radius demands gradual, reversible strategies, not a confidence-based cutover.

Part 55 — Org Design, Conway's Law and Platform Engineering

Here is a claim that sounds like management fluff until you have seen it happen three times: the shape of your software is determined by the shape of your organisation, whether you intend it or not. The boundaries between your services will end up matching the boundaries between your teams. The APIs between components will be as clean or as messy as the communication between the people who own them. If you want to change your architecture, you often have to change your org, and if you change your org without thinking about architecture, your architecture will change anyway, usually for the worse.

This is Conway's Law, and it is the most important idea a principal engineer holds about org design. It means architecture and organisation are the same problem viewed from two angles, and that designing teams is designing systems. Part 29.8 covered DORA metrics; Part 37.3 covered on-call. This Part is about the org side of architecture: Conway's Law and how to use it deliberately, team topologies, cognitive load as a design constraint, service ownership, platform engineering and the internal developer platform, measuring and improving developer experience, and when a reorg is actually the right architectural change.

The reader this Part assumes is a staff or principal engineer who has noticed that their architecture problems are often really org problems in disguise, and wants to learn to design the org as deliberately as they design the system.

55.1 Conway's Law and the inverse Conway maneuver

Concept

Conway's Law, stated by Melvin Conway in 1967, is: organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. In plain terms: the way your teams are divided and the way they talk to each other will be reflected in the way your software is divided and the way its parts talk to each other. If you have four teams, you will tend to get four major components, with interfaces between them that mirror how those teams communicate. The inverse Conway maneuver is the deliberate use of this law: instead of letting your org accidentally shape your architecture, you design your org to produce the architecture you want.

Why does it exist?

Imagine you want a clean, modular architecture with four well-separated services, but your org is one big undifferentiated team of forty engineers who all work on everything. No matter how hard you try to keep the services separate, they will blur together, because the people have no boundaries between them — anyone can change anything, so everything ends up coupled to everything. The architecture cannot be cleaner than the org, because the people build what their communication structure allows them to build.

Conway's Law exists as an observation because this pattern is nearly universal and nearly inescapable. It exists as a tool (the inverse maneuver) because once you know architecture mirrors org, you can stop fighting the current and start using it: shape the teams to shape the software. Trying to impose an architecture that fights the org structure is swimming upstream; aligning the org to the desired architecture makes the architecture emerge naturally.

Mental model

Imagine water flowing down a hillside. It does not flow where you wish it would; it flows along the contours of the land. If you want the water to reach a particular place, you do not stand there shouting at it — you reshape the land so the water flows where you want. Conway's Law says software flows along the contours of the organisation. The communication paths between teams are the contours, and the software flows along them. The inverse Conway maneuver is reshaping the land (the org) so the software flows into the shape you want. Fighting Conway's Law by imposing an architecture against the org's contours is like trying to make water flow uphill; it is exhausting and it does not hold.

How it works

The mechanism of Conway's Law:

  1. Communication cost shapes design. It is easy to coordinate within a team (you sit together, you talk constantly) and hard across teams (meetings, docs, waiting). So engineers naturally put tightly-coupled things inside one team's boundary (cheap to coordinate) and loosely-coupled things across boundaries (expensive to coordinate). The architecture's coupling mirrors the org's communication cost.
  2. Ownership shapes boundaries. A component owned by one team gets a clean boundary because that team controls it. A component owned by no one, or by everyone, gets no clean boundary because no one defends it. Service boundaries form where ownership boundaries are.
  3. The accidental version. If you do not design the org deliberately, the architecture still mirrors it — just accidentally. An org that grew haphazardly produces software that is shaped haphazardly, because the software followed the accidental org contours.

The inverse Conway maneuver, done deliberately:

flowchart LR
    A["Decide the target architecture - e.g. 4 bounded-context services"] --> B["Design teams to match - one team per bounded context"]
    B --> C["Give each team ownership of its context's code + data + deploys"]
    C --> D["Architecture emerges to match the team boundaries"]
    D --> E["Clean service boundaries, because they mirror team boundaries"]

You decide the architecture you want, you organise teams so that each team owns one piece of that architecture, and then the architecture emerges to match, because the teams build along their own boundaries. The org becomes the mould that shapes the software.

Practical example

A food-delivery company wants to move from a tangled monolith to four clean services: ordering, restaurant management, delivery logistics, and payments. The naive approach is to keep the existing one big team and ask them to build four clean services — which fails, because one undifferentiated team produces one tangled thing regardless of intent (there are no team boundaries for the service boundaries to mirror). The inverse Conway approach: first reorganise into four teams, one per intended service, each owning its context's code, data, and deploys. Now, when the ordering team builds, they build the ordering service, with a clean boundary to the others, because crossing to another team's code is expensive (Conway's communication cost) so they naturally minimise it and define a clear API instead. The four clean services emerge because four clean teams exist. The org change produced the architecture change; trying to produce the architecture without the org change would have failed.

Artifact example

An inverse Conway plan — the artifact that documents the target architecture and the org design that will produce it, side by side.

# Inverse Conway plan: monolith -> 4 bounded-context services

## Target architecture (what we want the software to be)
Four services with clean boundaries, each owning its data:
- Ordering (cart, checkout, order lifecycle)
- Restaurant (menus, availability, restaurant onboarding)
- Delivery (driver assignment, routing, tracking)
- Payments (charges, refunds, payouts)

## Target org (the mould that produces it)
| Team | Owns (code + data + deploys) | Interfaces to |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering team | Ordering service + order tables | Restaurant (menu API), Payments (charge API), Delivery (events) |
| Restaurant team | Restaurant service + restaurant tables | Ordering (menu API) |
| Delivery team | Delivery service + delivery tables | Ordering (order events) |
| Payments team | Payments service + payment tables | Ordering (charge API) |

## The principle
We organise the TEAMS first, to match the architecture we want. The service
boundaries will emerge to mirror the team boundaries (Conway's Law). Trying
to build 4 clean services with 1 undifferentiated team would fail — there'd be
no team boundaries for the service boundaries to form along.

## Team interactions (deliberately designed, not accidental)
Interfaces between teams = interfaces between services. We design them: each
cross-team interaction is a versioned API or an event contract, NOT shared
code or a shared database. Cheap-to-coordinate things stay within a team.

The plan's insight is making the org design and the architecture design the same document, because they are the same decision. It names each team's ownership (which becomes a service boundary) and each team interaction (which becomes an API or event contract). The architecture is produced by the org, deliberately, rather than fought for against an org that would prevent it.

Real-world scenario

A company's architects spend a year trying to refactor a monolith into clean modules, fighting a constant losing battle: every time they establish a clean boundary, engineers from across the one big team erode it, because within one team crossing a boundary is cheap and nobody owns defending it. The architecture refuses to stay clean because the org has no boundaries for it to mirror. A principal engineer finally applies the inverse Conway maneuver: the org is split into teams aligned to the intended module boundaries, each team owning its module. Within two quarters, the boundaries that the architects could not maintain by willpower hold effortlessly — because now crossing a boundary means crossing a team boundary, which is expensive, so engineers naturally respect it. The year of architectural willpower achieved less than one quarter of org alignment, because Conway's Law was working against the architects the whole time and with them the moment the org matched the target. The lesson: an architecture that fights the org loses; align the org and the architecture comes for free.

Failure scenario

A company decides to adopt microservices and splits its monolith into fifteen services — but it does not change the org, which remains a few large, broadly-scoped teams where everyone works across all the services. The result is a distributed monolith produced by Conway's Law: because the teams span all the services, the services are coupled across team-less boundaries, deployed together (since a feature touches many services owned by the same broad team), and changed in lockstep. The company has fifteen services that must be deployed together, which is strictly worse than one monolith — they got the operational cost of microservices (network calls, fifteen deploy targets, distributed debugging) with none of the independence, because the org structure produced coupling across the service boundaries. Conway's Law shaped the architecture to mirror the broad-team org, overriding the intended microservices design. The architecture diagram said fifteen independent services; the org structure said a few broad teams; and Conway's Law ensured the org won. Splitting services without splitting teams is fighting Conway's Law, and Conway's Law always wins.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Fighting Conway's Law. Trying to impose an architecture that does not match the org, which erodes constantly because the org structure keeps reshaping it.
  • Splitting services without splitting teams. Produces a distributed monolith, because broad teams span the service boundaries and couple them.
  • One undifferentiated team expecting clean modularity. No team boundaries means no boundaries for the architecture to mirror; everything blurs together.
  • Accidental org shaping accidental architecture. An org that grew haphazardly produces haphazard software; not using Conway deliberately does not escape it.
  • Reorganising without a target architecture. Changing the org randomly produces a random architecture; the inverse maneuver needs a target architecture to aim the org at.
  • Ignoring the data boundary. Teams that share a database stay coupled regardless of team boundaries; ownership must include data (Part 54.4).

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They hold architecture and org design as the same problem, and they never design one without the other, because they know Conway's Law means the org will shape the architecture whether they plan for it or not. When they want an architecture change, their first question is often "what org change produces this", because they have learned that fighting the org to impose an architecture is a losing battle, while aligning the org makes the architecture emerge for free. They use the inverse Conway maneuver deliberately: decide the target architecture, then design the teams as the mould that produces it.

They are especially alert to the trap of splitting services without splitting teams, because they have seen it produce the distributed monolith — the worst of both worlds — over and over. And they insist that team ownership includes data, not just code, because teams that share a database stay coupled through it regardless of how clean the team boundaries look on paper (the Part 54.4 lesson). The principal's distinctive move is to treat the org chart as an architecture diagram, because Conway's Law guarantees that is what it will become.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to achieve a clean architecture by willpower against an org that fights it, instead of aligning the org.
  • Splitting services without splitting teams, producing a distributed monolith.
  • Expecting one big team to produce cleanly-separated modules, when there are no team boundaries for them to mirror.
  • Reorganising with no target architecture in mind, producing a random architecture.
  • Aligning teams by code but not by data, leaving them coupled through a shared database.

Interview questions

  1. What is Conway's Law and why does it matter for architecture? Expected answer: organisations produce systems that mirror their communication structure — team boundaries become service boundaries, and the coupling between components mirrors the communication cost between teams. It matters because you cannot achieve an architecture cleaner than your org allows; architecture and org are the same problem. Follow-up: what is the inverse Conway maneuver.

  2. A company split its monolith into fifteen services but kept its few broad teams. What happened? Expected answer: a distributed monolith — because the broad teams span all the services, the services are coupled across the (team-less) boundaries and deployed together, giving the operational cost of microservices with none of the independence. Conway's Law shaped the architecture to the broad-team org, overriding the intended design. You must split teams to split services. Why it matters: this is the most common and most expensive Conway failure.

  3. You want to change your architecture. Why might your first move be an org change? Expected answer: because of Conway's Law — the org shapes the architecture, so imposing an architecture against the org is a losing battle while aligning the org makes the architecture emerge naturally (the inverse Conway maneuver). Decide the target architecture, then design teams as the mould that produces it, including data ownership. Why it matters: tests whether they see org and architecture as one problem.

Practical exercise

Look at your current architecture and your current org chart side by side. Map which team owns which component, and identify where the architecture does not match the org — components owned by nobody, components owned by multiple teams, or team boundaries that cut through what should be one component. Then pick an architecture change you want and design the org change (team boundaries and data ownership) that would produce it via the inverse Conway maneuver.

Acceptance criteria: you can point to at least one place where Conway's Law explains a current architecture problem (a coupling that mirrors a team structure, or a blurred boundary that mirrors shared ownership); and your proposed org change assigns each team a clear ownership of code and data for one piece of the target architecture, so that the architecture would emerge to mirror the teams rather than being fought for against them.

55.2 Team topologies: the four team types and interaction modes

Concept

Team Topologies, from the book of the same name by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, gives a vocabulary for designing teams deliberately. It says there are really only four fundamental team types you need — stream-aligned, platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem — and three ways teams should interact — collaboration, X-as-a-service, and facilitating. Most teams should be stream-aligned (owning a flow of work for part of the product), supported by a small number of platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams. Having a shared vocabulary for team types turns org design from vibes into deliberate engineering.

Why does it exist?

Imagine an org that has grown into a zoo of ad-hoc teams: a "backend team", a "frontend team", a "DevOps team", a "database team", a "tools team", a "special projects team", each defined by technology or by historical accident rather than by a clear purpose and interaction model. Nobody is sure who owns what end to end, work constantly crosses team boundaries (a single feature needs the backend team, the frontend team, and the DevOps team to coordinate), and handoffs between technology-layer teams create delay and finger-pointing. The org has teams, but no coherent design.

Team Topologies exists to replace this zoo with four well-defined types, each with a clear purpose and a defined way of interacting, so that work flows within a team wherever possible (fast) rather than across teams (slow). It exists because "we have some teams" is not org design; deliberately choosing team types and interaction modes is.

Mental model

Imagine a well-run hospital. Most of the work is done by ward teams (stream-aligned) — each ward owns a flow of patients end to end, from admission to discharge, and a patient's care happens mostly within one ward. Supporting them are shared services: the pathology lab and the pharmacy (platform teams) that any ward can use as a service without coordinating care; specialist consultants (enabling teams) who come in to help a ward build a new capability and then leave; and highly specialised units like the cardiac surgery team (complicated-subsystem) that owns one deeply complex thing everyone else relies on but nobody else could run. The hospital works because each unit has a clear type and a clear way of interacting — wards do not hand patients back and forth through technology layers; they own the flow and pull in support as a service. Team Topologies is this hospital design applied to software.

How it works

The four team types:

Team type Purpose Example How many
Stream-aligned Owns a flow of work for part of the product, end to end Ordering team, Payments team The large majority of teams
Platform Provides internal services that make stream-aligned teams faster, as a product The paved-road / IDP team (Part 53) A few
Enabling Helps stream-aligned teams adopt a new capability, then leaves A testing or security enablement team Few, small
Complicated-subsystem Owns one deeply complex component others depend on but could not build A pricing-optimisation or ML-ranking team Rare, only where truly justified

The three interaction modes:

  • Collaboration. Two teams work closely together for a limited time on something new, accepting the high coordination cost because the discovery is worth it. Temporary by design — long-term collaboration means the boundary is wrong.
  • X-as-a-service. One team consumes another's output as a service, with minimal coordination (just a clear API or contract). This is the goal for most interactions — it is low-friction and scalable. A stream-aligned team consumes the platform as a service.
  • Facilitating. One team (usually enabling) helps another team learn or adopt something, then the interaction ends. The enabling team facilitates, it does not do the work for the other team.
flowchart TB
    SA1["Stream-aligned: Ordering"] -->|"X-as-a-service"| PLAT["Platform team - paved road, IDP"]
    SA2["Stream-aligned: Payments"] -->|"X-as-a-service"| PLAT
    EN["Enabling: Security enablement"] -.->|"facilitating (temporary)"| SA1
    SA1 -->|"X-as-a-service"| CS["Complicated-subsystem: Pricing engine"]
    SA1 <-->|"collaboration (temporary, new work)"| SA2

The design principle: maximise X-as-a-service interactions (low friction, scalable) and minimise and time-box collaboration (high friction, only for genuine discovery). An org where teams are permanently collaborating across boundaries has drawn its boundaries wrong — the collaboration should either be internalised (one team) or turned into a service interface.

Practical example

A ride-booking company designs its org with Team Topologies. The bulk are stream-aligned teams, each owning a product flow end to end: the rider-app team (booking a ride), the driver-app team (accepting and completing rides), the pricing-display team. A single platform team provides the paved road and internal developer platform (Part 55.5) that all the stream-aligned teams consume as a service — they self-serve service creation, deployment, and observability without coordinating with the platform team. A small enabling team helps stream-aligned teams adopt a new observability standard, pairing with each for a sprint, then moving on. And one complicated-subsystem team owns the surge-pricing optimisation engine — a genuinely complex piece of applied math that the stream-aligned teams consume as a service (they call it for a price) but could not build or maintain themselves. Each team has a clear type, and the interactions are mostly X-as-a-service, so work flows within teams and friction is low. The pricing-display team gets a price from the pricing engine as a service, builds its display within its own boundary, and ships without coordinating with three other teams.

Artifact example

A team topology design for an org — the artifact that assigns every team a type and an interaction mode, replacing the ad-hoc zoo.

# Team topology: ride-booking engineering (18 teams)

## Stream-aligned teams (14 — the majority, own product flows end to end)
- Rider app, Driver app, Pricing display, Trip history, Ratings, Promotions,
  Onboarding, Support tooling, ... (each owns its flow + data + deploys)

## Platform team (1 — provides internal services as a product)
- Developer Platform: paved-road template, CI/CD, observability, deploy
  self-service. Interaction with all stream-aligned teams: X-AS-A-SERVICE.
  Measured on stream-aligned teams' speed, not on tickets closed.

## Enabling teams (2 — help others adopt, then leave)
- Reliability enablement: pairs with a stream team for ~1 sprint to improve
  their SLOs/alerts, then moves on. Interaction: FACILITATING, temporary.
- Security enablement: helps teams adopt secure defaults. FACILITATING.

## Complicated-subsystem team (1 — owns one deeply complex thing)
- Surge-pricing engine: applied optimisation; other teams consume a price
  via API. Justified because it needs specialist skills + is used by many.
  Interaction: X-AS-A-SERVICE.

## Design rules
- Default team type is stream-aligned. We justify every non-stream team.
- Default interaction is X-as-a-service. Collaboration is temporary and
  time-boxed; permanent cross-team collaboration means a boundary is wrong.
- A complicated-subsystem team must clear a high bar (genuine complexity +
  broad reuse); otherwise the work belongs in a stream-aligned team.

The design's power is that it assigns every team a type with a clear purpose and a defined interaction mode, and it states the rules (default to stream-aligned, default to X-as-a-service, time-box collaboration, high bar for complicated-subsystem). This turns the org from an accidental collection of technology-layer teams into a deliberate design where work flows within teams and friction between them is minimised. It is architecture, applied to people.

Real-world scenario

An org restructures from technology-layer teams (backend team, frontend team, DevOps team, QA team) to stream-aligned teams (each owning a product area full-stack, from database to UI to deploy). The change is dramatic. Before, a single feature required coordination across four technology teams, with handoffs and queues at each boundary — the feature waited in the backend team's queue, then the frontend team's queue, then DevOps for deployment, then QA. Lead time was weeks of mostly waiting. After, one stream-aligned team owns the feature end to end — it does the backend, frontend, and deployment itself, pulling the platform in as a service — and ships in days with no cross-team handoffs. The technology-layer org had maximised cross-team handoffs (every feature crossed every layer); the stream-aligned org minimised them (features stay within one team). The lead-time improvement came almost entirely from eliminating the handoff queues between technology layers, which is exactly what stream-aligned teams are designed to do. This is the single most common and most valuable Team Topologies transformation: from technology-layer teams with handoff queues to stream-aligned teams that own a flow.

Failure scenario

An org adopts the Team Topologies vocabulary but misuses it: it declares nearly every team a "platform team" because platform sounds important and senior. Now there are eight "platform teams" and only a few stream-aligned teams, which inverts the intended ratio. The eight platform teams each build internal tools, but there are too few stream-aligned teams actually consuming them, so the platform teams build speculative infrastructure for demand that does not exist, while the overloaded handful of stream-aligned teams drown in product work. Worse, the platform teams, lacking real stream-aligned customers, start collaborating heavily with each other and with the stream teams on everything, so the org is permanent cross-team collaboration — the high-friction mode that was supposed to be rare. The vocabulary was adopted but the principles were not: the default should be stream-aligned (most teams), platform teams should be few and measured on stream-team speed, and interactions should default to X-as-a-service. Misapplying the types — too many platform teams, permanent collaboration — recreates the ad-hoc zoo with fancier labels. The types are only valuable if the ratios and interaction principles are respected, not just the names.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Too many platform or complicated-subsystem teams. Inverts the intended ratio; most teams should be stream-aligned, and the others justified against a high bar.
  • Technology-layer teams disguised with new names. Calling the backend team a "platform team" does not change that features still cross every layer.
  • Permanent collaboration. Teams collaborating long-term across a boundary means the boundary is wrong; collaboration should be temporary and time-boxed.
  • Enabling teams that do the work instead of facilitating. An enabling team that takes over a stream team's work creates dependency instead of capability.
  • Complicated-subsystem teams for things that are not actually complicated. Carving out a specialist team for ordinary work fragments ownership without justification.
  • Platform team measured on tickets, not on stream-team speed. A platform team optimised for closing tickets builds what is easy to ticket, not what makes teams faster.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They default every team to stream-aligned and treat every non-stream team as something to be justified, because they know the value of the model is work flowing within teams, which requires most teams to own a flow end to end. They keep platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams few and purposeful, and they measure a platform team on the speed of the stream-aligned teams it serves, not on its own output, because a platform team exists to make others faster and will build the wrong things if measured on tickets.

They design interactions to default to X-as-a-service and they time-box collaboration ruthlessly, because they read permanent cross-team collaboration as a signal that a boundary is drawn wrong — the collaborating work should be internalised into one team or turned into a clean service interface. And they are wary of the vocabulary being adopted without the principles, because they have seen orgs relabel their technology-layer teams with Team Topologies names and change nothing. The principal uses the four types as a precise design language, respecting the ratios and interaction principles, not as a set of fashionable labels.

Common mistakes

  • Too many platform/complicated-subsystem teams, inverting the ratio and starving stream-aligned teams.
  • Relabelling technology-layer teams without changing that work crosses every layer.
  • Permanent cross-team collaboration, which signals a wrong boundary.
  • Enabling teams doing the work instead of building the other team's capability.
  • Measuring a platform team on its own output rather than on the speed of the teams it serves.

Interview questions

  1. What are the four team types in Team Topologies, and which should be most common? Expected answer: stream-aligned (owns a product flow end to end — should be the large majority), platform (internal services as a product — a few), enabling (helps others adopt a capability then leaves — few), complicated-subsystem (owns one genuinely complex component — rare). Most teams should be stream-aligned so work flows within teams. Follow-up: how do you justify a non-stream-aligned team.

  2. What does permanent collaboration between two teams tell you? Expected answer: that the boundary between them is probably drawn wrong — collaboration is the high-friction mode and should be temporary and time-boxed for genuine discovery; permanent collaboration means the work should either be internalised into one team or turned into a clean X-as-a-service interface. Why it matters: tests whether they can read org friction as a boundary signal.

  3. How should a platform team be measured, and why does it matter? Expected answer: on the speed and success of the stream-aligned teams it serves (lead time, self-service adoption, developer satisfaction), not on its own ticket throughput — because a platform team exists to make others faster and, if measured on tickets, will build what is easy to ticket rather than what actually unblocks teams. Why it matters: tests understanding of platform-as-product.

Practical exercise

Map your org's teams onto the four Team Topologies types. For each team, assign a type and note whether the assignment fits (does the stream-aligned team actually own a flow end to end, or is it a disguised technology-layer team). Count the ratio of stream-aligned to other types. Then map the interactions: which are X-as-a-service, which are collaboration, and flag any permanent collaboration as a possible boundary problem.

Acceptance criteria: most teams are (or should be) stream-aligned owning a flow end to end; each non-stream team is justified against its purpose; you identify at least one disguised technology-layer team or one permanent collaboration that signals a boundary problem; and you can state how your platform team is measured and whether that measurement drives it to make stream teams faster.

55.3 Cognitive load and service ownership

Concept

Two linked ideas that determine whether teams can actually operate what they own. Cognitive load is the total amount of stuff a team has to hold in their heads to do their job — the systems they own, the domains they must understand, the tools they must operate. It is a finite resource, and a team loaded past its limit gets slow, error-prone, and burned out. Cognitive load should be an explicit design constraint for team and service boundaries: a team should own no more than it can comfortably hold. Service ownership is who is accountable for a service in production — the "you build it, you run it" model, ownership catalogs that make ownership explicit, and the problem of orphaned services that nobody owns.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a team that owns twelve services spanning four unrelated domains, built in three different languages, with four different databases. No individual on the team can hold all of it in their head. When an incident hits one of the twelve services, the person on call may never have touched it. Changes are slow because every change requires relearning a corner of the sprawl. The team is not incompetent; they are overloaded past the limit of what a team can cognitively hold, and the symptoms — slowness, incidents, burnout — are the predictable result of ignoring cognitive load as a constraint.

Cognitive load exists as an explicit concept because org designers routinely overload teams without noticing, treating team capacity as if it were only about person-hours when the real limit is often how much the team can understand. Service ownership exists because a service that nobody clearly owns gets no maintenance, no on-call, and no improvement — it rots until it causes an incident, at which point everyone discovers it was orphaned.

Mental model

Imagine a juggler. They can keep a certain number of balls in the air — say five. Give them a sixth and seventh and they do not juggle seven slightly worse; they drop everything, because they are past their cognitive limit and the whole pattern collapses. A team is a juggler, and the services and domains it owns are the balls. Loading a team past its cognitive limit does not make it a bit slower; it collapses the whole team's effectiveness, because attention and understanding are not infinitely divisible. Good org design keeps each team's ball count within what it can juggle, and when a team is dropping balls, the fix is fewer balls (less scope), not telling them to juggle harder.

How it works

Cognitive load as a design constraint. Three kinds of cognitive load (from the Team Topologies framing, originally cognitive-science):

  • Intrinsic: the inherent difficulty of the domain and the skills (understanding distributed systems, the payment domain). Reduce by training and hiring, not by org design.
  • Extraneous: the accidental overhead — clunky deploys, bad tooling, having to understand the infrastructure to ship a feature. Reduce by the platform/paved road (Part 53, 55.5), which removes this load from stream-aligned teams.
  • Germane: the valuable thinking about the actual problem. You want teams spending their cognitive budget here.

The design move: size a team's ownership so that intrinsic load (the domain) fits, remove extraneous load (via the platform), and leave room for germane load (the real work). A team should own a coherent domain of a size it can hold — typically one bounded context, not twelve unrelated services.

Team cognitive budget (finite)
  = intrinsic (the domain — keep it coherent and bounded)
  + extraneous (accidental overhead — REMOVE via platform/paved road)
  + germane (the real problem-solving — PROTECT this)
Overload one team's budget -> slow, error-prone, burned out (drops all balls)

Service ownership models:

  • You build it, you run it. The team that builds a service also operates it in production — owns its on-call, its alerts, its runbooks, its reliability. This aligns incentives: the people who feel the 3 a.m. page are the people who can fix the design that caused it. The default model for stream-aligned teams.
  • Ownership catalog. A single source of truth (a service registry / catalog like Backstage) recording, for every service: who owns it, its on-call, its dependencies, its runbooks, its tier. Makes ownership explicit and findable, so an incident on any service immediately routes to its owner.
  • Orphaned services. Services that no team clearly owns — because the team was disbanded, because it was built by someone who left, because it fell between team boundaries. Orphans get no maintenance and no on-call, and they are time bombs: they rot until they cause an incident that nobody is prepared for. An ownership catalog's main job is to make orphans visible so they can be assigned or retired before they explode.

Practical example

A team is drowning: it owns eight services across three unrelated domains (ordering, a legacy reporting system, and an internal admin tool), inherited through years of reorgs. Incidents are frequent and slow to resolve because on-call engineers face services they barely know. A principal engineer diagnoses it as a cognitive-load problem, not a staffing one, and acts: the legacy reporting system (a distinct domain) is moved to a team that owns reporting, the internal admin tool is deprecated (its value no longer justifies the cognitive load it imposes), and the team is left owning the four ordering services that form one coherent domain. Extraneous load is further reduced by moving the team onto the paved road so they no longer hand-roll deploys and observability. The team's effectiveness recovers not because they work harder but because their ball count dropped to what they can juggle. The fix for an overloaded team is less scope, delivered by moving ownership elsewhere and removing accidental overhead, not by exhortation.

Artifact example

A service ownership catalog entry and a team cognitive-load assessment — the artifacts that make ownership explicit and overload visible.

# Service catalog entry (one per service, in Backstage/registry)
service: orders-api
owner_team: ordering
on_call: ordering-oncall (PagerDuty)
tier: 1 (customer-facing, revenue-critical)
runbook: link
dependencies: payments-api, inventory-api, order.events (Kafka)
dependents: checkout-web, mobile-bff, admin-panel
data_owned: orders, order_items, order_status_history
last_reviewed: 2026-10
status: healthy
# An ORPHAN would show owner_team: NONE -> flagged for assignment/retirement

---

# Team cognitive-load assessment: ordering team
## Owns
- orders-api, order-events-consumer, checkout-bff, refunds-service (4 services,
  ONE coherent domain — ordering). FITS.
## Load breakdown
- Intrinsic: ordering + payments-adjacent domain. Reasonable for the team's skills.
- Extraneous: LOW — on the paved road, deploys/observability self-service.
- Germane: healthy — team spends most of its time on actual ordering problems.
## Verdict: within capacity. Trend: stable.
## Contrast (before the fix 2 quarters ago):
- Owned 8 services across 3 domains (ordering + legacy reporting + admin tool).
  OVERLOADED. Reporting moved out, admin tool deprecated. Now within capacity.

The catalog entry makes ownership, on-call, dependencies, and data ownership explicit and findable — so an incident routes instantly to the owner and an orphan (owner: NONE) is immediately visible. The cognitive-load assessment treats a team's scope as a budget to be managed, breaks load into intrinsic/extraneous/germane, and shows the before/after of fixing an overload by reducing scope. Together they turn ownership and cognitive load from invisible, accidental properties into deliberately-managed design constraints.

Real-world scenario

A company adopts a service catalog (Backstage) and, for the first time, has a complete, queryable record of every service and its owner. The first query they run — "show all services with no owner" — returns a shocking list of forty orphaned services, built over years by people who had left or teams that had been reorganised away. Some of these orphans are tier-1, customer-facing services that had been running with no on-call and no maintenance, surviving only because they happened not to break. The company systematically assigns each orphan to a team or schedules it for retirement. Three months later, one of the previously-orphaned tier-1 services has an incident — but now it has an owner, an on-call rotation, and a runbook, so it is resolved in twenty minutes instead of being a prolonged scramble to figure out who even owns the thing. The catalog's main value was not the tidy records; it was making the forty invisible time bombs visible so they could be defused before they exploded. Orphaned services are the silent risk in every grown organisation, and an ownership catalog is how you find them.

Failure scenario

A reorg redistributes services among teams based purely on person-count balancing — "this team has capacity, give them these three services" — with no consideration of domain coherence or cognitive load. A team that owns ordering is handed three unrelated services (a notifications service, a legacy import tool, and a fraud-detection component) because they "had room". Each is a different domain requiring different knowledge. The team's cognitive load spikes: they now must understand four unrelated domains, their on-call rotation covers systems half of them have never seen, and their velocity on their actual domain (ordering) collapses because their attention is fragmented across four things. Incidents on the handed-over services are slow and scary because nobody on the team really understands them. The reorg optimised for person-hour balance and ignored cognitive load, treating teams as interchangeable capacity rather than as juggler with a finite ball count. The result is a team that is nominally "balanced" but actually overloaded past its cognitive limit, dropping balls across all four domains. Distributing services by headcount instead of by cognitive load and domain coherence is one of the most common and most damaging reorg mistakes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Distributing services by headcount, ignoring cognitive load. A "balanced" team that is actually overloaded across incoherent domains.
  • Overloading a team past its cognitive limit. Does not make it a bit slower; collapses its effectiveness across everything (the juggler dropping all balls).
  • Orphaned services. No owner, no on-call, no maintenance; time bombs that rot until they cause an unprepared incident.
  • Ownership that exists on paper but not in practice. A team "owns" a service they never touch and could not operate; functionally an orphan.
  • Not removing extraneous load. Teams spending cognitive budget on clunky deploys and infrastructure instead of the real problem, because there is no platform.
  • Confusing cognitive load with workload. Adding people to an overloaded team does not help if the problem is too many unrelated domains, not too few hands.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat cognitive load as a first-class, finite design constraint, sizing each team's ownership to a coherent domain it can actually hold rather than distributing services by headcount as if teams were interchangeable capacity. When a team is struggling, they diagnose cognitive overload before assuming a staffing or skill problem, because they know that a team juggling too many unrelated domains collapses across all of them, and the fix is fewer balls (less, more coherent scope) plus removing extraneous load via the platform — not exhortation or more people.

They insist on explicit service ownership with a catalog, because they have learned that orphaned services are the silent time bombs of every grown organisation, and that the only way to defuse them is to make them visible and assign or retire them before they cause an unprepared incident. They hold the "you build it, you run it" model as the default, because aligning the people who feel the page with the people who can fix the design is what produces reliable services. The principal designs teams around what humans can understand and operate, treating cognitive load with the same seriousness they treat latency budgets — as a hard constraint that, when violated, degrades everything.

Common mistakes

  • Distributing services by headcount rather than by domain coherence and cognitive load.
  • Overloading a team and expecting a proportional slowdown instead of a collapse.
  • Leaving services orphaned, so they rot until they cause an unprepared incident.
  • Not removing extraneous load via a platform, so teams waste cognitive budget on accidental overhead.
  • Adding people to fix cognitive overload when the problem is too many unrelated domains, not too few hands.

Interview questions

  1. What is cognitive load and why should it constrain team and service boundaries? Expected answer: the total amount a team must hold in their heads to do their job — domains, systems, tools; it is finite, and a team loaded past its limit collapses (slow, error-prone, burned out) rather than degrading gracefully. So a team should own a coherent, bounded domain it can actually hold, and the platform should remove extraneous load. Follow-up: how would you reduce an overloaded team's cognitive load.

  2. A reorg distributed services to teams by headcount balance. What's the risk? Expected answer: teams get handed unrelated services across incoherent domains, spiking cognitive load; a nominally "balanced" team is actually overloaded, its on-call covers systems nobody understands, and its velocity on its real domain collapses. Distribute by domain coherence and cognitive load, not headcount. Why it matters: this is a common, damaging reorg mistake.

  3. Why are orphaned services dangerous, and how do you handle them? Expected answer: they have no owner, on-call, or maintenance, so they rot and become time bombs that cause unprepared incidents; handle them with an ownership catalog that makes every service's owner explicit and findable, run a "services with no owner" query to surface orphans, and assign or retire each one. Why it matters: tests awareness of the silent risk in grown organisations.

Practical exercise

Assess one team's cognitive load. List everything it owns (services, domains, tools) and classify the load as intrinsic, extraneous, or germane. Judge whether the ownership is a coherent domain the team can hold, or a sprawl across unrelated domains. Then audit your org for orphaned services: is there a catalog, and if you queried for services with no clear owner, how many would you find.

Acceptance criteria: you can state whether the team's scope is a coherent domain within its cognitive capacity or an overloaded sprawl, and if overloaded, what you would move out or deprecate to bring it within capacity (plus what extraneous load the platform could remove); and you can identify whether your org has an ownership catalog and estimate how many orphaned services it would reveal.

55.4 Platform engineering and the internal developer platform

Concept

Platform engineering is the discipline of building an internal platform that makes the stream-aligned teams faster and more self-sufficient — treating that platform as a product, with the stream-aligned teams as its customers. The internal developer platform (IDP) is the concrete thing: the self-service layer (templates, pipelines, environments, observability, the paved road from Part 53) that lets a product team create, deploy, and operate a service without filing tickets or waiting on anyone. The key disciplines are platform-as-a-product (the platform has customers, a roadmap, and is measured on their success, not its own output), self-service (teams help themselves, no tickets), and the thinnest viable platform (build the minimum that unblocks teams, not a gold-plated everything-platform).

Why does it exist?

Imagine every stream-aligned team having to file a ticket to the operations team to get a new service deployed, wait two days, file another ticket to get a database, wait another day, and another to get monitoring. Every team is blocked on a central team's queue for everything, so the central team is a permanent bottleneck and the product teams spend more time waiting and ticketing than building. The org's velocity is capped by the ticket queue, no matter how fast the product teams themselves are.

Platform engineering exists to remove that bottleneck by making the central capabilities self-service: instead of a team that does operations for you (a ticket queue), a platform that lets you do operations yourself (a self-service product). It exists because central teams that do work on request do not scale — their queue grows with the org — while platforms that enable self-service scale infinitely, because they require no human in the loop for the common case. The IDP is how a growing org keeps its product teams unblocked.

Mental model

Imagine the difference between a restaurant kitchen and a grocery store. A kitchen (the ticket-queue ops team) takes your order and cooks it for you — great until there are a hundred customers and one kitchen, at which point everyone waits. A grocery store (the platform) stocks the ingredients and tools so you can cook for yourself, serving a thousand customers at once because it does not cook each meal — it enables each customer to. Platform engineering is building the grocery store: well-stocked, self-service, so every team feeds itself without waiting in the kitchen's queue. And like a good store, it is curated (the thinnest viable platform — it stocks what people actually need, not every possible product) and run as a business that serves its customers, not as a warehouse that dumps inventory.

How it works

Platform-as-a-product. The platform team treats its platform as a product and the stream-aligned teams as its customers:

  • It has a roadmap driven by customer (stream-team) needs, not by what the platform team finds interesting.
  • It is measured on customer success — the speed, reliability, and satisfaction of the stream-aligned teams — not on its own ticket throughput or lines of platform code.
  • It does user research: it talks to the stream teams, finds their biggest friction, and prioritises removing it.
  • Adoption is earned, not mandated: teams use the platform because it is genuinely the easiest path (the paved road principle, Part 53), not because they are forced.

Self-service. The defining property. A stream team should be able to, without filing a ticket or waiting on the platform team: create a new service (the template), deploy it (the pipeline), get an environment, get observability, get secrets. Anything that requires a ticket to the platform team is a bottleneck that self-service is meant to remove.

Thinnest viable platform (TVP). Build the minimum that unblocks teams, and no more:

Thinnest viable platform:
  Start with the single biggest friction teams face (e.g. deploys).
  Pave JUST that, well. Ship it. Learn.
  Then the next biggest friction. Pave that.
  Resist building a gold-plated, speculative, everything-platform.
A platform is justified by the friction it removes, not by its completeness.

The TVP guards against the biggest platform-team failure: building an elaborate platform nobody asked for while the real friction goes unaddressed. The platform should always be the minimum that removes the current biggest pain.

flowchart LR
    ST1["Stream team"] -->|"self-service, no ticket"| IDP["Internal Developer Platform"]
    ST2["Stream team"] -->|"self-service"| IDP
    IDP --> C["create service"]
    IDP --> D["deploy"]
    IDP --> E["environments"]
    IDP --> O["observability"]
    IDP --> S["secrets"]
    PT["Platform team - runs IDP as a product"] -->|"builds, measured on stream-team speed"| IDP

Practical example

A platform team at a 60-engineer company builds an IDP incrementally, thinnest-viable-first. They do user research and find the biggest friction is deployment — teams wait two days for ops to deploy a service. So they build just the self-service deploy pipeline first, nothing else, and ship it: now any team deploys itself in minutes. Teams adopt it immediately because it is obviously better. The next research round finds service creation is the next biggest pain, so they add the self-service create-service template (Part 53.2). Then observability. Each increment is driven by the measured biggest friction, shipped, and adopted because it is genuinely the easiest path. Two years later the IDP is comprehensive, but it got there by removing one real friction at a time, with teams pulling it in voluntarily — not by building a speculative everything-platform up front. The platform is measured on the stream teams' lead time, which has dropped from weeks to days, which is the only number that justifies the platform team's existence.

Artifact example

A platform-as-product charter and a thinnest-viable-platform roadmap — the artifacts that keep a platform team serving its customers rather than building speculatively.

# Platform team charter (platform-as-a-product)

## Who our customers are
The 14 stream-aligned teams. They are not users we support; they are
customers whose success we are measured on.

## How we are measured (NOT on our own output)
- Stream-team lead time for change (platform should drive it DOWN).
- Self-service adoption (% of deploys/service-creations done without a ticket).
- Developer satisfaction (quarterly survey) with the platform.
- Platform reliability (our SLOs — if the platform is down, every team is).
We are NOT measured on tickets closed or platform features shipped.

## How we decide what to build
User research every quarter: we interview stream teams, find their biggest
friction, and build the thinnest thing that removes it. Teams pull our
platform in because it's the easiest path; we do not mandate it.

---

# Thinnest-viable-platform roadmap (friction-driven)
| Quarter | Built | Biggest friction it removed |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Self-service deploy pipeline | 2-day wait for ops to deploy |
| Q2 | create-service template | 1-week service setup |
| Q3 | Self-service observability + dashboards | teams flew blind |
| Q4 | Self-service ephemeral environments | PR testing blocked on shared env |
## Explicitly NOT building (yet)
- A custom internal UI portal (the CLI is enough; no measured demand).
- Multi-cloud abstraction (we're on one cloud; speculative).
- A service mesh (no mesh-shaped friction reported).
Each would be gold-plating ahead of real demand.

The charter's defining feature is that the platform team is measured on its customers' success (stream-team lead time, self-service adoption, satisfaction), not on its own output — which is what keeps it building what teams actually need. The TVP roadmap is explicitly friction-driven, building the thinnest thing that removes the current biggest pain, and it names what it is not building to resist gold-plating. Together they turn a platform team from an inward-facing builder of speculative infrastructure into a customer-serving product team.

Real-world scenario

Two platform teams at different companies take opposite approaches. The first treats the platform as a product: it does user research, builds the thinnest thing that removes each measured friction, and is judged on the stream teams' lead time. Its platform is adopted enthusiastically because every piece of it obviously helps, and the org's velocity climbs. The second treats the platform as an engineering showcase: it builds an elaborate, technically impressive platform based on what the platform engineers find interesting — a sophisticated multi-cloud abstraction, a custom orchestration layer — without talking to the stream teams about their actual friction. Two years and enormous effort later, adoption is low, because the platform solves problems the stream teams do not have while their real friction (slow deploys, no observability) remains unaddressed. The stream teams route around the impressive platform and build their own simple tools. The first platform succeeded because it served its customers; the second failed despite greater technical sophistication because it served itself. The difference was entirely the product mindset — knowing who the customer is and being measured on their success.

Failure scenario

A platform team builds a gold-plated internal developer platform up front: a beautiful web portal, a plugin system, a multi-cloud abstraction, a custom DSL for defining services — a two-year project before anything ships to the stream teams. When it finally lands, it is impressive but it does not fit how the teams actually work, because it was designed in isolation from them. The teams find it over-complex for their needs (they wanted a simple way to deploy, not a DSL), and critically, the two years spent building the gold-plated platform were two years during which the stream teams' actual friction — slow deploys, manual observability setup — went unaddressed, because the platform team was heads-down on the big build instead of removing current pain. The org paid for two years of platform engineering and got a platform teams do not want, while the real bottlenecks persisted the whole time. Had the team built the thinnest viable platform — ship the self-service deploy pipeline in month one, then iterate on real feedback — the stream teams would have been unblocked from the start and the platform would have grown to fit their actual needs. Building a speculative everything-platform before shipping anything is the signature platform-engineering failure, and the thinnest-viable-platform discipline exists specifically to prevent it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Platform built on what the platform team finds interesting, not on measured customer friction, so adoption is low.
  • Gold-plated everything-platform built up front, delaying any value by years while real friction persists.
  • Platform team measured on its own output (tickets, features) instead of stream-team success, so it builds the wrong things.
  • "Self-service" that still requires tickets. A platform that is really a ticket queue with a nicer interface is still a bottleneck.
  • Mandated adoption of a platform teams dislike, producing resentment and routing-around instead of the paved-road dynamic.
  • Platform with no reliability discipline. If the platform is down, every team is down; a platform needs SLOs like any tier-1 service.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They insist the platform be run as a product with the stream-aligned teams as customers, and they fight to have the platform team measured on its customers' success — their lead time, their self-service adoption, their satisfaction — rather than on the platform team's own output, because they know a platform team measured on tickets or features will build what is easy to ticket or impressive to build, not what actually unblocks teams. They hold self-service as the defining goal, treating any remaining ticket-to-the-platform-team as a bottleneck to be removed, because a central team that does work on request does not scale while a platform that enables self-service does.

They are disciplined about the thinnest viable platform, because they have watched too many platform teams disappear for two years building a speculative everything-platform while the real friction festered. They would rather ship the one thing that removes the current biggest pain this quarter and iterate on real feedback than design a comprehensive platform in isolation. And they treat the platform's own reliability as tier-1, because a platform outage is an everyone outage. The principal's measure of a platform team is simple and external: are the stream teams faster and happier because of it, and are they choosing it freely.

Common mistakes

  • Building the platform on the platform team's interests instead of customers' measured friction.
  • Building a gold-plated everything-platform up front instead of the thinnest viable thing, iterated.
  • Measuring the platform team on its own output rather than on stream-team success.
  • "Self-service" that still routes through a ticket queue, which is still a bottleneck.
  • Mandating a platform teams dislike instead of making it the genuinely easiest path.

Interview questions

  1. What does it mean to run a platform as a product, and why does it matter? Expected answer: treat the stream-aligned teams as customers, drive the roadmap from their measured friction (user research), make adoption earned through being the easiest path, and measure the platform team on the customers' success (their lead time, self-service adoption, satisfaction) not on the platform team's own output. It matters because a platform measured on its own output builds the wrong things. Follow-up: what would you measure a platform team on.

  2. What is the thinnest viable platform and what failure does it prevent? Expected answer: build the minimum that removes the current biggest friction, ship it, learn, then address the next biggest friction — rather than building a comprehensive, speculative platform up front. It prevents the signature platform failure: disappearing for two years building a gold-plated platform teams do not want while their real friction goes unaddressed. Why it matters: tests the iterate-on-real-friction discipline.

  3. Why is self-service the defining property of a good internal developer platform? Expected answer: because a central team that does work on request (a ticket queue) is a bottleneck that does not scale — its queue grows with the org — whereas self-service lets teams help themselves with no human in the loop for the common case, so it scales infinitely. Any remaining ticket-to-the-platform-team is a bottleneck to remove. Why it matters: tests understanding of why platforms scale where ops queues do not.

Practical exercise

Assess your org's platform (or the absence of one). Identify the biggest friction stream teams currently face (what do they wait on, what do they file tickets for). Then design the thinnest viable platform increment that would remove that single biggest friction, and specify how the platform team should be measured (a stream-team success metric, not a platform-output metric). Flag any current "self-service" that actually still requires a ticket.

Acceptance criteria: you identify the stream teams' single biggest current friction from their perspective (not the platform team's); your proposed increment is the thinnest thing that removes that friction (not a comprehensive platform); you specify at least one measurement of the platform team based on stream-team success; and you identify whether the common operations (deploy, create service, get observability) are genuinely self-service or still ticket-gated.

55.5 Measuring and improving developer experience

Concept

Developer experience (DevEx or DX) is how it feels, day to day, to build and ship software in your organisation — how long a change takes from idea to production, how long builds take, how often deploys fail, how much toil engineers endure, how satisfied they are. It is measurable, and measuring it well is how a principal engineer knows whether the platform and org design are actually helping. The key measurement frameworks are DORA (four delivery-performance metrics, from Part 29.8), SPACE (a broader, multi-dimensional view), plus concrete signals like lead time, build times, and survey data. The goal is to measure DevEx, find the biggest friction, and systematically remove it.

Why does it exist?

Imagine an org where leadership believes engineering is slow but has no idea why. Is it the architecture? The process? The tooling? Too many meetings? Without measurement, the debate is anecdote versus anecdote, and "fixes" are guesses — maybe they mandate more process (making it worse) or buy a tool nobody needed. Meanwhile the actual friction — say, a forty-minute build that engineers run twenty times a day — goes unidentified and unfixed because nobody measured it.

DevEx measurement exists to replace anecdote with data: to locate the actual friction so you can fix the right thing. DORA exists specifically to measure delivery performance in four well-validated numbers. SPACE exists because delivery performance alone misses important dimensions (satisfaction, collaboration). Surveys exist because some of the most important friction (frustration, cognitive load, unclear ownership) is subjective and only engineers can report it. Together they let you manage DevEx as a measurable property rather than a vibe.

Mental model

Imagine a factory manager who wants to speed up the production line but has no instruments — no stopwatch, no sensors, just a feeling that it is slow. They cannot improve it, because they cannot see where the bottleneck is; they might speed up a station that was never the problem while the real bottleneck (a jam at station 7) stays invisible. Now give them instruments: timers at each station, a counter of defects, a survey of the workers. Suddenly the bottleneck is obvious (station 7), and they fix the right thing. DevEx measurement is the factory's instruments. Without them, improving developer experience is guessing; with them, you can see the bottleneck and fix the station that is actually jammed.

How it works

DORA — four delivery metrics (Part 29.8):

- Deployment frequency:    how often you deploy to production.
- Lead time for change:    from commit to running in production.
- Change failure rate:     % of deploys that cause a failure needing remediation.
- Time to restore service: how long to recover from a failure.

The first two measure speed; the last two measure stability. The DORA research shows elite teams are better at both — speed and stability are not a trade-off; good practices improve both together. DORA is the standard, well-validated starting point for measuring delivery performance.

SPACE — five broader dimensions: DORA measures delivery output, but DevEx is broader. SPACE adds dimensions:

  • Satisfaction and well-being (are engineers happy, not burning out).
  • Performance (outcomes, not just output).
  • Activity (volume of work, used carefully — activity is not value).
  • Communication and collaboration (how well teams work together).
  • Efficiency and flow (can engineers get into flow, or are they constantly interrupted and blocked).

SPACE exists because optimising DORA alone can miss burnout, bad collaboration, and interruption — an org can ship frequently while its engineers are miserable and its collaboration is broken. Measure across dimensions, not just delivery.

Concrete operational signals:

  • Lead time broken into stages (code review wait, CI time, deploy wait) to find where the delay is.
  • Build / CI times — a slow build is a tax paid on every change, many times a day.
  • Time to first meaningful change for new engineers (onboarding effectiveness, Part 57).
  • Toil hours — time spent on manual, repetitive operational work.

Survey data. Periodic developer surveys capture the subjective friction metrics cannot: "what is the most frustrating part of shipping here", "what wastes your time", "rate your satisfaction with the deploy process". Surveys find the friction that is real but not in any dashboard.

flowchart LR
    M["Measure DevEx"] --> D["DORA: speed + stability"]
    M --> SP["SPACE: satisfaction, flow, collaboration"]
    M --> OP["Operational: lead-time stages, build times, toil"]
    M --> SV["Surveys: subjective friction"]
    D --> F["Locate the biggest friction"]
    SP --> F
    OP --> F
    SV --> F
    F --> FIX["Fix the right thing, remeasure"]

Practical example

A principal engineer wants to improve engineering velocity but, instead of guessing, measures. DORA shows deployment frequency is low and lead time is high. Breaking lead time into stages reveals the culprit: code review wait is a day on average, and CI time is forty minutes. A developer survey confirms it: the top frustration is "waiting for CI" and "waiting for review". Now the friction is located precisely. She addresses the two measured bottlenecks: parallelising and caching the CI pipeline to cut build time from forty minutes to eight, and establishing a review-SLA norm plus smaller PRs to cut review wait. Lead time drops dramatically, deployment frequency rises, and the next survey shows satisfaction up. The improvement worked because it was aimed at the measured friction (CI time and review wait), not at a guess. Had she guessed — say, mandated more process or bought a tool — she might have made it worse while the real bottlenecks persisted. Measure, locate, fix the right thing, remeasure.

Artifact example

A DevEx dashboard and the friction-prioritised improvement plan it drives — the artifacts that turn DevEx from a vibe into managed improvement.

# DevEx dashboard (quarterly, per team + org-wide)

## DORA
Deployment frequency: 2/week (target: on-demand, multiple/day)
Lead time for change: 4 days (target: < 1 day)
Change failure rate: 12% (healthy, keep < 15%)
Time to restore: 45 min (healthy)
-> Speed is the problem, not stability.

## Lead-time breakdown (WHERE the 4 days go)
Code review wait:    1.1 days  <- biggest chunk
CI pipeline time:    40 min (run ~15x/day/eng = big cumulative tax) <- #2
Deploy wait:         0.3 days
Actual coding:       the rest
-> Review wait and CI time are the bottlenecks.

## SPACE / survey signals
Satisfaction with deploy process: 3.1/5 (low)
Top-reported frustration: "waiting for CI" (42% of respondents)
#2 frustration: "waiting for review" (31%)
Flow: 38% report being able to focus; frequent interruptions.

---

# DevEx improvement plan (friction-prioritised, from the data)
| Priority | Friction (measured) | Fix | Expected impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CI = 40 min, run constantly | Parallelize + cache CI -> target 8 min | Big cumulative time saved |
| 2 | Review wait = 1.1 days | Review SLA norm + smaller-PR guidance | Lead time down ~1 day |
| 3 | Low flow (interruptions) | Protected focus time, fewer meetings | Flow + satisfaction up |
## Remeasure next quarter. If a fix didn't move its metric, it was the wrong fix.

The dashboard's value is that it does not just show DORA; it breaks lead time into stages to locate where the delay actually is, and it cross-references objective metrics with survey data so the friction is confirmed from two angles. The improvement plan is prioritised by measured friction and commits to remeasuring — so a fix that does not move its metric is recognised as the wrong fix. This is DevEx managed as an engineering problem: measure, locate, fix the right thing, verify.

Real-world scenario

A company's leadership is convinced its engineers are unproductive and considers introducing stricter process and productivity tracking (individual commit counts, lines of code). A principal engineer intervenes with measurement done right. He points out that activity metrics like commit counts measure the wrong thing (and, per SPACE, activity is not value and tracking individuals breeds gaming and fear). Instead he stands up a proper DevEx dashboard: DORA, lead-time breakdown, and a developer survey. The data tells a completely different story than leadership assumed — the engineers are not slow; they are blocked, spending huge fractions of their time waiting on a forty-minute CI pipeline and a slow review process, and on toil the platform should automate. The fix is not more process and surveillance (which would have made it worse); it is removing the measured friction. Six months later, with CI parallelised and the paved road absorbing the toil, delivery performance improves markedly — not because engineers were pushed harder but because they were unblocked. The measurement redirected the org from a harmful "the people are lazy" intervention to a correct "the system has friction" one. Measuring DevEx well does not just improve DevEx; it protects engineers from misdiagnoses that would have made everything worse.

Failure scenario

An org decides to measure developer productivity and picks the easiest-to-count metrics: individual commits per day, lines of code, pull requests closed. It makes these visible per engineer and uses them in performance reviews. The result is a textbook Goodhart's-law catastrophe: engineers optimise the metrics instead of the outcomes. They split one logical change into many small commits to inflate commit count, write verbose code to inflate lines, and open trivial PRs to inflate PR count. The metrics all go up; actual productivity goes down, because the incentives now reward activity over value and discourage the uncounted-but-valuable work (mentoring, deleting code, careful design, helping teammates). Collaboration suffers because helping a colleague does not show up in your numbers. Morale collapses because engineers feel surveilled and reduced to counters. The org measured activity (the thing SPACE warns against) at the individual level (the thing that breeds gaming and fear), and got exactly what it incentivised: inflated metrics and degraded reality.
