The failure was measuring the wrong things, at the wrong granularity, for the wrong purpose — the opposite of measuring system-level friction to help teams. DevEx measurement helps only when it measures outcomes and friction at the team/system level to improve the system, never activity at the individual level to judge people.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Measuring activity instead of outcomes. Commits and lines of code measure busyness, not value, and reward the wrong behaviour.
  • Measuring individuals instead of teams/systems. Breeds gaming, fear, and degraded collaboration (Goodhart's law); DevEx is a system property.
  • DORA alone, ignoring SPACE dimensions. An org can ship frequently while engineers burn out and collaboration breaks; measure satisfaction and flow too.
  • Measuring without breaking lead time into stages. You see that it is slow but not where, so you cannot target the fix.
  • Not remeasuring after a fix. You never learn whether the fix worked, so you keep investing in things that do not move the metric.
  • Using DevEx metrics as a stick. The moment a metric judges people, it gets gamed and stops measuring reality (same as Part 53.6 on compliance).

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat developer experience as a measurable property to be managed, not a vibe to be argued about, and they measure it to locate friction and fix the system, never to judge individuals — because they know that individual activity metrics breed gaming and fear and degrade the very collaboration and uncounted work that makes teams effective. They start from DORA for delivery performance but insist on the broader SPACE dimensions, because they have seen orgs optimise delivery while their engineers burned out, and they know satisfaction and flow are as real as deploy frequency.

They always break lead time into stages, because "we are slow" is not actionable but "review wait is a day and CI is forty minutes" is, and they cross-reference objective metrics with survey data because some of the most important friction is subjective. And they close the loop by remeasuring after every fix, because a fix that does not move its metric was the wrong fix. Above all, they use DevEx measurement to protect engineers from the misdiagnosis that productivity problems are people problems — because the data almost always shows the problem is friction in the system, and the correct response is to remove the friction, not to push the people harder.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring activity (commits, LOC) instead of outcomes and friction.
  • Measuring individuals instead of teams and systems, breeding gaming and fear.
  • Using DORA alone and missing burnout, flow, and collaboration.
  • Not breaking lead time into stages, so the fix cannot be targeted.
  • Not remeasuring, so you never learn whether a fix worked.

Interview questions

  1. How do you measure developer experience, and what do you measure it for? Expected answer: use DORA (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore) for delivery, SPACE dimensions (satisfaction, flow, collaboration) for the broader picture, operational signals (lead-time stages, build times, toil), and surveys for subjective friction — measured at the team/system level to locate and remove friction, never at the individual level to judge people. Follow-up: why break lead time into stages.

  2. Leadership wants to track individual commit counts to boost productivity. What's your response? Expected answer: that measures activity not value, at the individual level, which triggers Goodhart's law — engineers game the metric (split commits, inflate LOC, trivial PRs) while real productivity drops and collaboration and uncounted valuable work suffer. Measure system-level friction and outcomes instead, to fix the system, not to judge people. Why it matters: tests understanding of measurement incentives, a critical principal judgement.

  3. Your DORA shows high lead time. How do you find and fix the cause? Expected answer: break lead time into stages (review wait, CI time, deploy wait) to locate the bottleneck, confirm with survey data, fix the specific measured friction (e.g. parallelise CI, set review SLAs), then remeasure to verify the fix moved the metric. Do not guess at fixes. Why it matters: tests the measure-locate-fix-remeasure loop.

Practical exercise

Measure one aspect of your org's developer experience. Pick lead time for change, break it into stages (review wait, CI time, deploy wait, coding), and find which stage dominates. Cross-reference with a quick survey question ("what is the most frustrating part of shipping here"). Then propose the fix aimed at the measured biggest friction, and state the metric you would remeasure to verify it worked.

Acceptance criteria: you measure at the team/system level, not the individual level; you break the metric into stages to locate the actual bottleneck rather than just noting "it's slow"; your proposed fix targets the measured biggest friction; and you commit to a specific remeasurement that would tell you whether the fix worked.

55.6 When to reorganise, and the architect's role in the org

Concept

Two topics that close the org-design toolkit. The first is knowing when to split a team, merge services, or reorganise — treating a reorg not as a disruptive political event but as a deliberate architectural change, because (per Conway's Law) changing the org changes the software. The second is the architect's own role in the organisation: whether architecture is embedded (architects sit within teams) or central (a separate architecture group), and the player-coach model where a principal engineer both does hands-on technical work and grows others, rather than drifting into a pure-advisory ivory tower.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a team that has grown to twenty-five people owning one sprawling service. Coordination within the team has become a nightmare — too many people, too many sub-areas, constant stepping on each other. Or imagine two tiny services, each owned by the same team, that are always changed together and never independently — the split between them buys nothing but overhead. Or imagine an org where the architecture no longer fits the business, and no amount of refactoring helps because the team boundaries are wrong. In each case, the right fix is an org change — split the overgrown team, merge the pointless services, redraw the boundaries — but orgs resist reorgs because they are disruptive and political, so these needed changes get deferred until the pain is severe.

The "when to reorganise" judgement exists to recognise these situations and treat the reorg as the architectural change it is. The architect's-role question exists because how architects are positioned in the org determines whether they stay connected to reality (embedded, hands-on) or drift into the ivory tower (central, advisory-only) — which Part 44 identified as the principal's main failure mode.

Mental model

For reorgs, imagine a growing tree that needs occasional pruning and training. A branch that has grown too heavy (an overgrown team) needs to be split so it does not break. Two branches that have grown into each other pointlessly (over-split services) might be better as one. And sometimes the whole tree is being trained against the wrong trellis (the org against the wrong architecture) and needs re-staking. Pruning is disruptive in the moment but essential for the tree's long-term health; avoiding it because it is disruptive lets the tree grow misshapen. A reorg is pruning: deliberate, occasionally necessary, painful in the moment, healthy over time — and, crucially, shaping the tree is shaping how it grows (Conway's Law).

For the architect's role, imagine a sports team's player-coach: someone who still plays in the games (stays sharp, earns respect, feels what the players feel) while also coaching (growing the others, setting strategy). Contrast the coach who stopped playing years ago and now only shouts from the sideline — increasingly out of touch with how the game is actually played. The player-coach architect keeps playing (shipping, taking on-call) so their coaching stays grounded.

How it works

When to split a team: a team has grown past the point where it can coordinate well (typically beyond 8-10 people, the two-pizza limit) or owns multiple distinct domains that could each be a team. Split along a domain/bounded-context boundary (Conway's Law: the split will become an architectural boundary, so split where you want a boundary).

When to merge services: two services are always deployed and changed together, never independently — the split between them buys only overhead (network calls, two pipelines) and no independence. Merging them (or back into a module) removes the overhead. This is the "services back to a monolith" direction from Part 49.2, which is entirely reasonable when the split was premature.

When a reorg is the right architectural change: when the architecture you need cannot be achieved against the current org (Conway's Law), the reorg is the architecture work. Redrawing team boundaries to match the target architecture (the inverse Conway maneuver, 55.1) is sometimes the only way to get the architecture you want.

flowchart TB
    A["Org/architecture symptom"] --> B{"What's the signal?"}
    B -->|"team too big / multi-domain, poor coordination"| SPLIT["Split the team along a domain boundary"]
    B -->|"two services always changed together, never independent"| MERGE["Merge the services"]
    B -->|"needed architecture impossible against current org"| REORG["Redraw boundaries (inverse Conway)"]
    B -->|"none of these — architecture fits, teams coordinate"| NONE["Do NOT reorg — reorgs are costly"]

The crucial judgement is also when not to reorg: reorgs are disruptive and costly (relationships reset, context is lost, momentum drops for a quarter), so they should be deliberate architectural decisions, not frequent or political. A reorg every six months is thrash, not design.

The architect's role:

  • Embedded architecture: architects sit within and work alongside the teams. Pro: stays connected to reality, context-rich, trusted. Con: can lose the cross-cutting, org-wide view.
  • Central architecture: a separate architecture group with the org-wide view. Pro: sees cross-cutting concerns. Con: the Part 44 ivory-tower risk — architects ruling on systems they do not operate, disconnected from reality.
  • The player-coach model: the principal engineer both does hands-on technical work (ships the risky part, takes on-call, prototypes the design) and grows others and sets direction. This is the antidote to the ivory tower: by still playing, the architect keeps their judgement grounded and their credibility renewed (the Part 44 lesson that credibility at senior-plus levels is renewed by delivery, not past reputation).

The healthiest arrangement for most orgs is embedded or hybrid architecture with a strong player-coach norm: architects who are part of the teams, still ship, and spend a large fraction of their time growing others and connecting the cross-cutting dots — not a central board that decides from a distance.

Practical example

A principal engineer notices an ordering team has grown to eighteen people owning two distinct domains — ordering and promotions — with constant internal coordination pain. She recognises this as a split signal and reorganises it into two teams: an ordering team and a promotions team, split along the domain boundary. Per Conway's Law, this split will (and should) become an architectural boundary, so she pairs the team split with a service split along the same line. She does not reorganise the four other teams that are coordinating fine — reorgs are costly, and changing what is working is thrash. And throughout, she works as a player-coach: she personally ships the trickiest part of the ordering/promotions service split (the data-ownership separation, Part 54.4), takes on-call for the new promotions service during its first month, and coaches the newly-appointed promotions tech lead through their first cross-team design. Her hands stay dirty, so her architectural judgement stays grounded and her credibility with the teams stays current.

Artifact example

A reorg proposal framed as an architectural change, plus an architect-role definition — the artifacts that make a reorg deliberate and keep the architect out of the ivory tower.

# Reorg proposal: split the ordering team (framed as architecture)

## The signal (why reorg, with evidence)
Ordering team = 18 people, owns ordering AND promotions (two distinct
domains). Internal coordination overhead is high: ~30% of standup is
cross-domain dependency management. The two domains change independently
~80% of the time (data shows). This is a team that should be two.

## The change (org AND architecture together — Conway's Law)
Split into: Ordering team (8) and Promotions team (7, +2 hires). Split the
service along the same boundary: extract a promotions service owning its
own promotions/coupon tables (data ownership per Part 54.4).

## Why this IS the architecture work
We cannot cleanly separate the promotions code from ordering while one team
owns both — the boundary erodes (Conway). Splitting the team is how we get
the service boundary. The reorg is the architecture decision.

## What we are NOT doing
Not touching the other 4 teams — they coordinate fine; reorging them would
be thrash. This is a targeted split, not a reorg-everything.

---

# Architect role definition (player-coach, anti-ivory-tower)
- Embedded: principal/staff engineers sit within teams, not a central board.
- Player: still ship the risky/exemplary parts, still take on-call, still
  prototype designs before proposing them. Credibility is renewed by
  delivery, not past reputation (Part 44).
- Coach: spend a large fraction of time growing engineers, connecting
  cross-cutting concerns, writing direction (Part 51).
- NOT: a central group that rules on systems it doesn't operate. If an
  architect hasn't shipped or taken a page in 6 months, that's a red flag.

The reorg proposal's power is that it frames the split as an architectural decision justified by data (two domains, 80% independent change, coordination overhead) and pairs the team split with the matching service split per Conway's Law — and it explicitly scopes the change narrowly (not reorg-everything) to avoid thrash. The architect-role definition encodes the player-coach model as a defence against the ivory tower, even flagging the warning sign (an architect who has not shipped or taken a page in six months). Both make the usually-political (reorgs, architect positioning) into deliberate, grounded design.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer is offered a central-architecture role: a prestigious position on an architecture board, no team, no on-call, pure advisory. He declines the pure-advisory version and negotiates a player-coach arrangement instead: he will set direction and grow engineers (the coach part) but he will also stay embedded with a team, ship the risky parts of major initiatives, and take on-call (the player part). Colleagues are puzzled — why keep doing hands-on work at that level? Two years later the reason is obvious: his architectural proposals land, because they come from someone who still operates the systems and whose designs reflect current reality, not two-year-old assumptions. Meanwhile, a peer who took a pure central-architecture role has drifted into exactly the Part 44 failure — producing diagrams and strategies that teams politely ignore, because they come from someone disconnected from the code. The player-coach's hands-dirty discipline kept his judgement current and his credibility renewed; the pure architect's distance eroded both. The arrangement that looked less prestigious produced far more influence, because influence at that level flows from grounded credibility, not from a title on a board.

Failure scenario

An org reorganises constantly — a significant reorg every six months, driven by changing management priorities and politics rather than by architectural need. Each reorg resets team relationships, loses institutional context (people no longer own the thing they built), orphans services (as teams dissolve and reform), and drops momentum for a quarter while everyone finds their feet. Because the reorgs are frequent and not architecturally motivated, they do not produce a coherent architecture — per Conway's Law, the architecture is constantly being reshaped to match the churning org, so it never stabilises into anything clean; it is a permanent half-reorganised mess. Engineers become cynical ("why invest in owning this well, I'll own something else in six months"), ownership decays, and the accumulated orphaned services pile up. The org confused reorganising with progress, treating the reorg as a management tool rather than a deliberate, costly architectural decision used sparingly. Frequent, politically-driven reorgs are thrash: they pay the full cost of reorganising (reset relationships, lost context, dropped momentum, orphaned services) repeatedly while delivering none of the benefit, because no org structure survives long enough to shape a coherent architecture. Reorgs should be rare, deliberate, and architecturally motivated — the opposite of a routine management lever.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Reorging too frequently. Each reorg costs reset relationships, lost context, dropped momentum, and orphaned services; frequent reorgs are thrash, not design.
  • Reorging for political reasons, not architectural need, producing a perpetually half-reorganised mess.
  • Splitting a team without splitting the service (or vice versa), creating a mismatch Conway's Law will fight.
  • Not reorging when you should, letting an overgrown team or a wrong boundary cause ongoing pain because reorgs feel too disruptive.
  • The pure-central architect who rules from a distance and drifts into the ivory tower (Part 44).
  • The architect who stops shipping, whose credibility and judgement erode until teams politely ignore them.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat a reorg as a deliberate architectural change, used sparingly, because they understand via Conway's Law that changing the org changes the software — and they pair every team split with the matching service boundary, because a team split without the service split (or vice versa) creates a mismatch the law will fight. They know the signals (an overgrown multi-domain team, pointlessly-split services, an architecture unachievable against the current org) and they act on them, but they are equally disciplined about not reorging what works, because they have seen frequent political reorgs pay the full cost repeatedly while producing only thrash and orphaned services.

On their own role, they choose embedded, player-coach positioning over the pure-central ivory tower, and they guard their hands-dirty discipline fiercely — still shipping the risky parts, still taking on-call, still prototyping before proposing — because they have internalised the Part 44 lesson that credibility at this level is renewed by delivery, not by past reputation, and that an architect disconnected from the code produces designs teams ignore. The principal is a player-coach by conviction: they grow others and set direction, but they keep playing, because playing is what keeps the coaching grounded.

Common mistakes

  • Reorging too often, paying the cost of reorganising repeatedly for no coherent-architecture benefit.
  • Reorging for politics rather than architectural need.
  • Splitting a team without splitting the service, creating a Conway mismatch.
  • Avoiding a needed reorg because it feels disruptive, letting an overgrown team or wrong boundary cause ongoing pain.
  • Becoming a pure-advisory central architect who stops shipping and drifts into the ivory tower.

Interview questions

  1. When should you split a team, merge services, or reorganise — and when should you not? Expected answer: split a team when it has grown past good coordination or owns multiple distinct domains (split along a domain boundary, which becomes an architectural boundary per Conway); merge services that are always changed together and never independently; reorg when the needed architecture is unachievable against the current org (inverse Conway). Do NOT reorg what is working — reorgs are costly (reset relationships, lost context, dropped momentum, orphans), so they must be rare and architecturally motivated. Follow-up: why pair a team split with a service split.

  2. Why is frequent reorganising harmful even if each reorg seems reasonable? Expected answer: each reorg pays the full cost (reset relationships, lost context, dropped momentum, orphaned services), and because no org structure survives long enough to shape a coherent architecture (Conway's Law), frequent reorgs produce a perpetually half-reorganised mess plus cynicism and decayed ownership. Reorgs should be rare, deliberate architectural decisions, not a routine management lever. Why it matters: tests understanding of reorg cost.

  3. What is the player-coach model for architects, and what failure does it prevent? Expected answer: the architect both does hands-on technical work (ships the risky parts, takes on-call, prototypes) and grows others / sets direction, rather than being a pure-advisory central architect. It prevents the ivory-tower failure (Part 44) where an architect disconnected from the code produces designs teams ignore, because credibility at that level is renewed by delivery, not past reputation. Why it matters: tests self-awareness about the principal's main failure mode.

Practical exercise

Look at your org for a reorg signal: an overgrown multi-domain team that should split, two services that should merge, or an architecture unachievable against the current boundaries. Write a reorg proposal framed as an architectural change — the signal with evidence, the paired org-and-architecture change, and an explicit statement of what you are NOT changing (to avoid thrash). Separately, assess the architect role in your org: is it embedded/player-coach or central/advisory, and are the senior-plus engineers still shipping and taking on-call.

Acceptance criteria: your reorg proposal is justified by data (coordination overhead, independent-change frequency, or an unachievable architecture), pairs the team change with the matching service-boundary change per Conway's Law, and explicitly scopes itself narrowly; and your architect-role assessment identifies whether the senior engineers are grounded player-coaches or drifting toward the ivory tower, with the warning sign (not having shipped or taken a page recently) checked.

55.7 Worked example: redesigning team and service boundaries for a food-delivery company at 60 engineers

This section brings the whole Part together: redesigning the team and service boundaries for a food-delivery company that has grown to 60 engineers. It uses Conway's Law and the inverse maneuver, Team Topologies, cognitive load, platform engineering, and DevEx measurement. It also contains the failure story the outline asks for: a microservices split that followed the org chart and created a distributed monolith, and how to fix it.

The situation

QuickBite is a food-delivery company at 60 engineers. It grew fast and its org grew haphazardly: a handful of large, broadly-scoped teams (a "backend team" of 25, a "mobile team", a "web team", an "infra team") and a monolith that someone started splitting into microservices a year ago — a split that has gone wrong. A principal engineer is asked to redesign the org and architecture together.

The failure she finds: a distributed monolith from the org chart

# Diagnosis: the microservices split created a distributed monolith

## What was done
A year ago, the monolith was split into 12 microservices. But the ORG was
not changed — the 25-person "backend team" still owns and works across all
12 services. The split followed the old code structure / org chart, not
bounded contexts.

## The result (Conway's Law in action)
- Because one broad team owns all 12 services, the services are coupled
  across (team-less) boundaries: they share database tables, call each other
  synchronously in deep chains, and must be deployed together.
- A single feature touches 5-6 services (all owned by the one team).
- Deploys are MORE coordinated than before (12 deploy targets, must be
  ordered), with distributed debugging and 12 on-call surfaces.
- This is strictly WORSE than the monolith: all the cost of distribution,
  none of the independence.

## Why it happened
The split was done WITHOUT splitting the team (fighting Conway's Law, 55.1)
and WITHOUT data ownership (shared tables, 54.4). The services mirror the
broad-team org, so they're coupled. This is the canonical distributed-
monolith failure.

This is the failure story: microservices split along the existing org/code structure, with one broad team spanning all the services and shared databases underneath, producing a distributed monolith. The diagnosis traces it directly to the two root causes from this Part and Part 54: fighting Conway's Law (splitting services without splitting teams) and skipping data ownership (shared tables).

The redesign: inverse Conway + Team Topologies

She redesigns the org and architecture together. First, she defines the target architecture as bounded contexts: ordering, restaurant, delivery, payments, and search. Then — the inverse Conway maneuver (55.1) — she designs the teams to produce that architecture:

# QuickBite org + architecture redesign (60 engineers)

## Stream-aligned teams (per bounded context — Team Topologies 55.2)
| Team | Owns (code + DATA + deploys) | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering | ordering service + order tables | 8 |
| Restaurant | restaurant service + restaurant tables | 7 |
| Delivery | delivery service + delivery tables | 8 |
| Payments | payments service + payment tables | 6 |
| Search | search service + its index | 6 |
(Mobile and web folded INTO the stream teams — each stream team is full-stack,
 ending the technology-layer handoff queues, 55.2.)

## Platform team (1 — 55.4)
| Developer Platform | paved road, CI/CD, observability, self-service deploy | 7 |
(Was the "infra team"; re-chartered as platform-as-a-product, measured on
 stream-team lead time.)

## Enabling team (1, small — 55.2)
| Reliability enablement | pairs with stream teams to improve SLOs, then leaves | 3 |

## The fixes this encodes
- Split the 25-person backend team into stream-aligned teams by bounded
  context -> service boundaries now mirror TEAM boundaries (Conway, 55.1).
- Each team owns its DATA (no shared tables) -> ends the distributed monolith
  (54.4). Shared tables are separated during the migration.
- Technology-layer teams (mobile/web/infra) dissolved into stream teams or
  re-chartered as platform -> ends handoff queues (55.2).
- Cognitive load: each team owns ONE coherent context, sized ~6-8 (55.3).

Fixing the distributed monolith under the new org

With the teams now aligned to bounded contexts, fixing the distributed monolith becomes tractable (it was intractable under the broad-team org, because Conway's Law kept re-coupling the services). Each stream team now owns a coherent subset of the 12 services and, crucially, its own data. They separate the shared database tables along ownership lines (Part 54.4 data-ownership work), replace the synchronous cross-service chains with APIs and events along the team boundaries, and consolidate the over-split services within a team where the split bought nothing (merging services that were always changed together, 55.6). The 12 ill-defined services become 5 well-bounded ones that mirror the 5 teams, each independently deployable because each team owns its code and data. Conway's Law, which was producing coupling under the broad-team org, now produces clean boundaries under the bounded-context org.

Platform and DevEx

The old "infra team" is re-chartered as a platform team running the developer platform as a product (55.4), measured on the stream teams' lead time, building the thinnest viable platform friction-first. A DevEx dashboard (55.5) is stood up: DORA plus lead-time breakdown plus a survey. The initial measurement shows the distributed-monolith deploy coordination as the top friction; as the redesign lands and services become independently deployable, deployment frequency rises and lead time falls, confirming the redesign worked (and catching it if it had not).

Why this redesign succeeds

Trace it against the Part. It designs org and architecture together, using the inverse Conway maneuver (55.1) to make the teams the mould that produces the target architecture. It uses Team Topologies (55.2) to make most teams stream-aligned (ending technology-layer handoff queues) with a platform team run as a product and a small enabling team. It respects cognitive load (55.3) by giving each team one coherent, appropriately-sized context. It fixes the distributed monolith by splitting teams and data ownership (the two things the failed split omitted). It re-charters the platform as a product (55.4) measured on stream-team success. And it measures DevEx (55.5) to confirm the redesign actually helped. The failed microservices split went wrong by fighting Conway's Law and skipping data ownership; the redesign succeeds by aligning the org to the architecture and owning the data — which is the entire thesis of this Part. Org design is architecture, and the two must be designed as one.

Practical exercise

Take your own org (or QuickBite as a template) and redesign its team and service boundaries together. Define the target architecture as bounded contexts. Design stream-aligned teams, one per context, each owning code and data, using the inverse Conway maneuver. Add the minimal platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams, justified. Check each team's cognitive load (one coherent context, appropriate size). Identify any existing distributed-monolith symptoms (services split without teams, shared databases) and show how the redesign fixes them.

Acceptance criteria: the org design and architecture are designed as one (teams mirror the target bounded contexts); each stream team owns its data, not just its code; most teams are stream-aligned with handoff-queue technology-layer teams dissolved; each team's cognitive load is a coherent, appropriately-sized context; and if a distributed monolith exists, your redesign addresses both root causes (split teams AND split data ownership), with a DevEx measurement to confirm it worked.

55.8 Executing an org change safely, and distributed-team considerations

Concept

Two aspects of org design beyond the structure itself. Executing an org change safely is the how of a reorg — because a reorg is an architectural change (55.6) but also a deeply human one, and a poorly-executed reorg, even with the right target structure, causes damage (lost people, lost context, dropped momentum). The techniques: communicate the why, preserve ownership and context, sequence the change, and support people through it. Distributed-team considerations is how org design changes when teams are remote or spread across time zones — Conway's Law still operates, but the communication structure (and therefore the architecture it produces) is shaped by distance and asynchrony, which changes how you draw team and service boundaries.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a reorg with the right target structure (correct team boundaries matching the target architecture) but executed badly: announced abruptly with no explanation, ownership reshuffled so people lose the systems they knew, no transition period, key people blindsided. Even though the structure is correct, the execution causes the best people to leave (they feel disrespected and disrupted), institutional context to be lost (people no longer own what they built), and momentum to drop for longer than necessary. The right structure, wrongly executed, still damages the organisation. Safe execution exists because a reorg is a human event as much as an architectural one, and the human damage of poor execution can outweigh the benefit of the better structure.

Distributed-team considerations exist because Conway's Law operates through the communication structure, and distance and asynchrony fundamentally change that structure. A co-located team communicates constantly and cheaply; a team split across time zones communicates slowly and asynchronously. This changes which boundaries work: a service boundary that assumes constant communication fails across a twelve-hour time-zone gap. Org design for distributed teams must account for how distance shapes communication and therefore architecture.

Mental model

For executing a reorg, imagine moving house. The destination (new house) might be better, but how you move matters enormously: pack carefully (preserve context), tell everyone the plan in advance (communicate the why), move in a sequence that keeps life functioning (sequence the change), and support the family through the disruption (support people). A move to a better house, done chaotically — no warning, belongings lost, no transition — is traumatic despite the better destination. A reorg is a move; the destination structure matters, but the execution determines whether people arrive intact.

For distributed teams, imagine building with teams in different cities who can only exchange letters (asynchronous, slow) rather than talking across a table (synchronous, fast). The letter-exchanging teams naturally build with cleaner, more explicit interfaces between their parts (because coordinating across letters is expensive, they minimise it and define clear contracts), while the table-sharing team builds with tighter, more implicit coupling (because coordinating is cheap). Distance changes the communication structure, which (Conway) changes the architecture. Designing for distributed teams means designing boundaries that work with letter-speed communication, not table-speed.

How it works

Executing an org change safely:

- Communicate the WHY: explain the reasoning (the architectural/strategic driver,
  55.6) so people understand it's deliberate, not arbitrary. Unexplained reorgs
  feel like chaos or politics and destroy trust.
- Preserve ownership and context: where possible, keep people with the systems
  they know, or ensure a real handover. Reshuffling people off their systems
  loses institutional context (and risks orphaned services, 55.3).
- Sequence the change: don't reorg everything at once; phase it so the org keeps
  functioning and people adapt gradually.
- Support people through it: 1-1s, address concerns, help people find their place
  in the new structure. A reorg is stressful; support reduces attrition.
- Pair with the architecture change: the team change and the service-boundary
  change go together (Conway, 55.1/55.6), sequenced deliberately.
- Minimise frequency: reorgs are costly (55.6), so execute them well and rarely.

Distributed-team considerations:

- Conway's Law + distance: remote/time-zone-split teams communicate async and
  slowly, so the architecture they produce has cleaner, more explicit interfaces
  (expensive coordination -> minimise it). Design boundaries that suit this.
- Team boundaries along time zones: a team split across a 12-hour gap struggles;
  prefer teams that are co-located OR fully async-capable, and draw service
  boundaries so that tightly-coupled work stays within one time zone/team.
- Async-first communication: distributed orgs rely even more on writing (Part 51)
  — decisions, designs, and context must be written, because the hallway
  conversation isn't available across time zones.
- Minimise cross-time-zone dependencies: a dependency that requires synchronous
  coordination across a 12-hour gap is painfully slow; design so teams can work
  independently (X-as-a-service, 55.2) across distance.
- Cognitive load + distance: distributed teams have higher coordination cost, so
  keeping ownership coherent and self-contained (55.3) matters even more.
flowchart TB
    R["Reorg (right structure, 55.6)"] --> WHY["Communicate the WHY"]
    R --> CTX["Preserve ownership + context"]
    R --> SEQ["Sequence, don't big-bang"]
    R --> SUP["Support people through it"]
    WHY --> SAFE["Safe execution: structure improves WITHOUT losing people/context"]
    CTX --> SAFE
    SEQ --> SAFE
    SUP --> SAFE
    DIST["Distributed teams"] --> ASYNC["Async-first (writing, Part 51)"]
    DIST --> IND["Minimise cross-time-zone sync dependencies (X-as-a-service)"]
    DIST --> BND["Draw boundaries so coupled work stays within a team/time zone"]

Artifact example

A reorg execution plan and distributed-team design notes — the artifacts that make an org change safe and account for distance.

# Reorg execution plan: split ordering team (the WHAT is in 55.6)

## Communicating the why (so it's not felt as arbitrary/political)
- All-hands: explain the driver (ordering + promotions are two domains; coupling
  slows both; splitting enables independent delivery — the architecture reason).
- 1-1s with every affected person BEFORE the announcement (no one blindsided).

## Preserving ownership + context
- Ordering engineers stay with the ordering service (keep their context).
- Promotions: 3 engineers who've worked on promotions move to the new team
  (they carry the context) + 2 hires. No orphaned systems (55.3).

## Sequencing
- Week 1: announce, 1-1s. Weeks 2-4: new team forms, service boundary work
  begins (paired with the team split, Conway). Not a big-bang.

## Supporting people
- Weekly 1-1s through the transition; address concerns; help the new promotions
  tech lead settle. Watch for attrition risk on the 2 most-affected people.

---
# Distributed-team design notes (teams in SF, London, Bangalore)
- Conway + distance: draw service boundaries so tightly-coupled work stays within
  ONE time zone. The payments service (lots of internal coordination) is owned by
  ONE co-located team (London), not split across time zones.
- Cross-team interactions are X-as-a-service (55.2) with clear async contracts,
  so a London team doesn't block waiting for Bangalore synchronously.
- Writing culture (Part 51) is mandatory: decisions and designs written, because
  the hallway conversation isn't available across the 12-hour SF-Bangalore gap.
- Avoid: a service co-owned by SF + Bangalore requiring daily sync coordination —
  that's a 12-hour-latency coupling that will be painfully slow.

The reorg execution plan's power is that it treats the reorg as a human event — communicating the why (so it is not felt as arbitrary), preserving context (keeping people with their systems or ensuring handover), sequencing (not big-bang), and supporting people (reducing attrition) — so the right structure is achieved without the human damage of poor execution. The distributed-team notes apply Conway's Law to distance, drawing boundaries so coupled work stays within a time zone and cross-team interactions are async contracts, because the communication structure (and thus the architecture) is shaped by distance. Both go beyond the org structure to how it is achieved and how it works across distance.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer executes a necessary reorg (splitting an overgrown team) carefully. She communicates the why in an all-hands and in one-on-ones with every affected person before the announcement, so no one is blindsided and everyone understands it is a deliberate architectural decision, not politics. She preserves context by keeping people with the systems they know where possible and ensuring real handovers where not, avoiding orphaned services. She sequences the change over weeks rather than flipping everything at once, and she supports people through the transition with regular one-on-ones. The reorg achieves the better structure and retains the people and the context — nobody leaves, momentum recovers quickly. A peer executes a structurally-identical reorg badly: announced abruptly, people reshuffled off their systems, no transition, no explanation. The structure is the same, but two key engineers leave (feeling disrespected and disrupted), institutional context is lost, and momentum drops for two quarters. The target structures were identical; the execution determined whether the reorg strengthened or damaged the organisation. Separately, when the principal designs a distributed org across three time zones, she draws service boundaries so coupled work stays within a co-located team and cross-team interactions are async contracts, avoiding the 12-hour-latency couplings that would make work painfully slow — because she knows Conway's Law operates through the communication structure, which distance reshapes.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat a reorg as a human event as much as an architectural one, because they know the right target structure, executed badly, still damages the organisation — losing the best people, the institutional context, and the momentum. So they execute reorgs carefully: communicating the why (so it is not felt as arbitrary or political), preserving ownership and context (keeping people with their systems or ensuring real handovers, avoiding orphaned services), sequencing the change (not big-bang), and supporting people through the stressful transition. They pair the team change with the architecture change (Conway, 55.6) and execute reorgs well and rarely, because they are costly.

For distributed teams, they understand that Conway's Law operates through the communication structure and that distance and asynchrony fundamentally reshape it — so they draw service boundaries so that tightly-coupled work (which needs frequent coordination) stays within one co-located team or time zone, make cross-team interactions async X-as-a-service contracts (so no team blocks on synchronous coordination across a 12-hour gap), and lean even harder on a writing culture (Part 51), because the hallway conversation that co-located teams rely on is not available across time zones. The senior engineer knows that org design is both structure and execution, and that it must account for how distance shapes the communication that Conway's Law turns into architecture — designing boundaries that work at letter-speed, not just table-speed.

Common mistakes

  • Executing a reorg abruptly with no explanation, so it feels arbitrary/political and destroys trust.
  • Reshuffling people off their systems without handover, losing institutional context and risking orphans.
  • Big-bang reorgs that disrupt everything at once rather than sequencing the change.
  • Not supporting people through the transition, causing avoidable attrition.
  • Drawing service boundaries that split tightly-coupled work across time zones, creating painfully slow cross-time-zone synchronous couplings.
  • Relying on synchronous coordination in a distributed org instead of async contracts and a writing culture.

Interview questions

  1. A reorg has the right target structure but risks going badly. What makes execution safe? Expected answer: communicate the why (so it's deliberate, not arbitrary/political), preserve ownership and context (keep people with their systems or ensure handover, avoiding orphans), sequence the change (not big-bang), support people through the stressful transition (1-1s, address concerns, reduce attrition), and pair the team change with the architecture change. The right structure executed badly still loses people, context, and momentum. Why it matters: a reorg is a human event as much as an architectural one.

  2. How does org and service-boundary design change for distributed, cross-time-zone teams? Expected answer: Conway's Law operates through the communication structure, which distance and asynchrony reshape — so draw service boundaries so tightly-coupled work (needing frequent coordination) stays within one co-located team/time zone, make cross-team interactions async X-as-a-service contracts (so no team blocks on synchronous coordination across a 12-hour gap), and lean harder on a writing culture because the hallway conversation isn't available across time zones. Why it matters: distance fundamentally changes what boundaries work.

  3. Two identical reorgs, one strengthens the org and one damages it. What's the difference? Expected answer: execution — the one that communicated the why, preserved people's context, sequenced the change, and supported people through it achieved the better structure while retaining people and context; the one executed abruptly (no explanation, reshuffled people off their systems, no transition) achieved the same structure but lost key people, institutional context, and momentum. The target structure was identical; execution determined the outcome. Why it matters: tests whether they understand reorg execution is as important as reorg structure.

Practical exercise

Take the reorg you designed earlier in this Part (or a real one) and write its execution plan: how you will communicate the why, preserve ownership and context, sequence the change, and support people through it. Then, if your org is (or could be) distributed across time zones, write the distributed-team design notes: how you would draw service boundaries so coupled work stays within a team/time zone, make cross-team interactions async, and strengthen the writing culture.

Acceptance criteria: your execution plan communicates the why, preserves context (keeping people with their systems or ensuring handover, avoiding orphans), sequences the change rather than big-bang, and supports people to reduce attrition — so the right structure is achieved without human damage; and your distributed-team notes draw boundaries so tightly-coupled work stays within a co-located team/time zone, use async X-as-a-service contracts across distance, and rely on a writing culture — demonstrating that you treat org design as both structure and safe execution, accounting for how distance shapes the communication Conway's Law turns into architecture.

55.9 A quick-reference for org design

A compact reference distilling the Part into the checks that matter most when you design or assess an organisation.

The org-design checklist

[ ] Is the org designed TOGETHER with the architecture? (Conway: the org chart
    becomes the architecture diagram.)
[ ] Does each team's boundary match a bounded context you want as a service
    boundary? (Inverse Conway: shape teams to produce the architecture.)
[ ] Does each team own its DATA, not just its code? (Else coupling via shared DB.)
[ ] Are most teams STREAM-ALIGNED (own a flow end to end)? (Not technology-layer
    teams with handoff queues.)
[ ] Is each non-stream team (platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem) justified?
[ ] Are interactions mostly X-AS-A-SERVICE? (Collaboration time-boxed; permanent
    collaboration = a wrong boundary.)
[ ] Is each team's COGNITIVE LOAD a coherent domain it can hold? (Not a sprawl.)
[ ] Is ownership EXPLICIT (a catalog)? Any ORPHANED services? (Time bombs.)
[ ] Is the platform run as a PRODUCT, measured on stream-team success? (Thinnest
    viable platform; self-service.)
[ ] Is DevEx measured to help teams (DORA/SPACE/surveys), not to judge individuals?

The warning signs

Signals that the org design is wrong:

- Services split but teams not (distributed monolith — all cost, no independence).
- A team spanning many unrelated domains (cognitive overload — will collapse).
- Permanent cross-team collaboration (a boundary is drawn wrong).
- Features crossing many teams with handoff queues (technology-layer teams).
- Orphaned services with no owner (silent time bombs).
- A platform team measured on its own output, building what nobody adopts.
- Frequent reorgs (thrash — full cost, no coherent-architecture benefit).
- Architects who've stopped shipping (ivory tower; designs teams ignore).

The enduring principle

The whole Part reduces to one idea: org design IS architecture, because Conway's Law guarantees the org chart becomes the architecture diagram. So you design the two together — shaping teams (and their data ownership) to produce the architecture you want, keeping each team's cognitive load coherent, making ownership explicit, running the platform as a product, and measuring developer experience to improve the system. When you face an architecture problem, ask whether it is really an org problem in disguise (it often is), and when you change the org, remember you are changing the software. Design the org as deliberately as you design the system, because they are the same thing viewed from two angles.

Return to this reference when designing or assessing an org; the reasoning behind each line is in the sections above.

The first question to ask about any architecture problem

When you hit a persistent architecture problem — a boundary that won't stay clean, a coupling you can't eliminate, a service that keeps growing tangled — ask first: is this really an org problem in disguise? More often than engineers expect, the answer is yes, and the root cause is a team structure that Conway's Law is turning into the architecture you don't want. The clean boundary won't hold because one undifferentiated team spans it; the coupling persists because the teams that own the two sides communicate constantly, so the cost of coupling is invisible to them; the service grows tangled because no single team owns it. In each case, no amount of architectural willpower fixes it, because the org keeps reshaping the architecture back. The fix is the org change (the inverse Conway maneuver, 55.1) — align the teams to the architecture you want, and the architecture follows. Treating an org-rooted architecture problem as a purely technical one is a common, expensive mistake; a principal's instinct is to check the org chart first.

Senior Checklist — Part 55

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I understand Conway's Law and use the inverse maneuver to design the org that produces the architecture I want
  • I never split services without splitting teams, and I always include data ownership
  • I design teams using the four Team Topologies types, defaulting to stream-aligned and X-as-a-service
  • I treat cognitive load as a finite design constraint and size each team's ownership to a coherent domain
  • I make service ownership explicit with a catalog and hunt down orphaned services
  • I run the platform as a product, measured on stream-team success, and build the thinnest viable platform
  • I measure developer experience (DORA, SPACE, lead-time stages, surveys) to locate and remove friction, never to judge individuals
  • I treat a reorg as a deliberate, sparingly-used architectural change, not a political lever
  • I work as a player-coach, staying hands-on so my judgement and credibility stay grounded
  • I can recognise and fix a distributed monolith caused by splitting services without splitting teams and data

Part 55 — Key Takeaways

  • Conway's Law: organisations produce systems that mirror their communication structure; team boundaries become service boundaries whether you plan it or not, so architecture and org are the same problem.
  • Use the inverse Conway maneuver: decide the target architecture, then design the teams as the mould that produces it, because fighting the org to impose an architecture is a losing battle.
  • Splitting services without splitting teams (and without data ownership) produces a distributed monolith — all the cost of distribution, none of the independence, worse than the monolith you started with.
  • Team Topologies gives four team types (stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem) and three interactions (collaboration, X-as-a-service, facilitating); default to stream-aligned teams and X-as-a-service, and time-box collaboration.
  • Cognitive load is a finite design constraint; a team overloaded past its limit collapses rather than slowing gracefully, so size each team's ownership to a coherent domain and remove extraneous load via the platform.
  • Make service ownership explicit with a catalog and the "you build it, you run it" model; orphaned services are the silent time bombs of every grown organisation, and the catalog's job is to make them visible.
  • Run the platform as a product with the stream-aligned teams as customers, measured on their success, built as the thinnest viable platform that removes real friction, with self-service as the defining property.
  • Measure developer experience with DORA, SPACE dimensions, lead-time stages and surveys — to locate and remove friction at the system level, never to judge individuals, which triggers gaming and fear.
  • Treat a reorg as a deliberate architectural change used sparingly; pair every team split with the matching service boundary, and never reorg what works, because frequent reorgs are thrash that pay the full cost for no coherent-architecture benefit.
  • Position architects as embedded player-coaches who still ship and take on-call, not as a central advisory board, because credibility at this level is renewed by delivery and an architect disconnected from the code produces designs teams ignore.
  • Design the org and the architecture together, always, because Conway's Law guarantees the org chart will become the architecture diagram.

Part 56 — Influence, Communication and the Business Case

A senior engineer's power comes from what they can build. A principal engineer's power comes from what they can convince others to build, change, fund, or stop. This is a harder kind of power, because you rarely have authority over the people whose behaviour needs to change — they do not report to you, and you cannot order them. You have to influence them. And the people you most need to influence — executives, finance, product leaders — do not speak your language and do not care about your elegant architecture; they care about revenue, risk, cost, and time. Learning to influence without authority, and to translate engineering into the language of the business, is the skill that turns a brilliant engineer into an effective principal.

Part 43.6 covered incident communication; Part 44.4 covered writing at staff level and the mechanics of cross-team influence. This Part goes deeper on the whole discipline of influence and communication: influencing without authority, mapping stakeholders, communicating with executives, building a business case with real numbers, making tradeoffs visible, disagreeing well, saying no and negotiating scope, presenting to mixed audiences, and running decision forums. The through-line is that engineering excellence is necessary but not sufficient; the ability to move people and translate value is what makes it count.

The reader this Part assumes is a strong senior or staff engineer who is often right and often ignored, and wants to understand why being right is not enough and what the rest of the skill is.

56.1 Influencing without authority

Concept

Influencing without authority is getting people who do not report to you to change what they do — adopt your standard, prioritise your project, stop doing a thing — through means other than command. The means are credibility (people trust your judgement), trust (people believe you act in good faith), pre-wiring (you build agreement privately before going public), and coalitions (you gather allies so you are not a lone voice). These are learnable mechanics, not charisma. A principal engineer's entire job depends on them, because their scope is always larger than their authority.

Why does it exist?

Imagine being technically right about a cross-team architecture problem — say, that four teams are building four incompatible event schemas and it will cause chaos. You have no authority over those four teams. You write the correct analysis and send it to them. Nothing happens, because being right does not make people act; they have their own priorities, their own pride, and no reason to do what a person with no authority over them says. Your correctness is invisible to the forces that actually move teams.

Influence-without-authority mechanics exist because this is the normal situation for a principal engineer: the problems worth solving span teams you do not control, and the only way to solve them is to move people who do not have to listen to you. The mechanics — credibility, trust, pre-wiring, coalitions — are how you convert being right into people acting, which is the only thing that matters.

Mental model

Imagine two people trying to get a group to take a new route on a hike. The first stands at the front and announces, with perfect map-reading, that the new route is objectively better, and is baffled when nobody follows. The second has, over previous hikes, built a reputation for good calls (credibility), is known to care about the group's comfort not just being right (trust), quietly talked to the two most influential hikers before suggesting it (pre-wiring), and has those two nodding along when she proposes it (coalition). The group takes her route. Both had the same correct map. The difference is that the second understood that people follow trust and social proof, not maps. Influence without authority is being the second hiker: the map matters, but it is maybe a third of it.

How it works

The four mechanics:

Credibility. People extend trust to your judgement in proportion to your track record. Credibility is earned by being right before (especially about hard calls), by shipping (delivery renews credibility, per Part 44), and by admitting when you are wrong (which paradoxically increases credibility, because it shows you are honest). Credibility is capital: you spend it when you ask people to do something, and you earn it by being right and delivering.

Trust. Distinct from credibility. Credibility is "I believe your judgement is good"; trust is "I believe you are acting in good faith, not just for yourself". You build trust by giving credit away (Part 44.4), by advocating for others' interests not just your own, and by being consistent — doing what you said you would. People will go along with someone they trust even when they are not sure the person is right, because they believe the intent is good.

Pre-wiring. Building agreement privately before any public proposal (Part 44.4, Part 51.4). You talk one-on-one to the people who could block or who are most affected, before the idea goes wide. Either they change your mind (saving a public failure) or you incorporate their concerns and they become supporters. Public proposals that were not pre-wired mostly die in the open.

Coalitions. Gathering allies so your proposal has multiple voices, not just yours. A good idea backed by one person is fragile; the same idea backed by a coalition of respected people across teams is hard to ignore. You build coalitions by pre-wiring, by aligning your proposal with others' interests, and by giving them a stake in it.

flowchart LR
    R["Being right (necessary, ~1/3)"] --> ACT["People act"]
    C["Credibility - track record"] --> ACT
    T["Trust - good faith"] --> ACT
    P["Pre-wiring - private agreement first"] --> ACT
    CO["Coalition - multiple voices"] --> ACT
    ACT --> CHANGE["Behaviour changes without authority"]

The key realisation: being right is roughly a third of influence. The other two-thirds is credibility, trust, framing, timing, pre-wiring, and coalitions. Engineers who believe correctness is sufficient are perpetually frustrated; those who learn the mechanics get their correct ideas adopted.

Practical example

A staff engineer sees the four-incompatible-event-schemas problem. The ineffective approach (being right at people): write the correct analysis, send it to all four teams, wait for them to see reason. Nothing happens. The effective approach (the mechanics): first, she establishes credibility by having shipped a related standard that worked. She pre-wires: she talks one-on-one to the lead of each of the four teams, starting with the most influential, framing the problem in terms of their pain (the integration bugs each team is already hitting), not her architectural preference. Two leads immediately agree because she named a pain they feel; she incorporates the third lead's concern into the proposed standard, turning him into a supporter; the fourth, seeing a coalition of three respected leads already aligned, goes along. By the time she proposes the shared event-schema standard publicly, it has four backers and passes easily. The analysis was the same in both approaches; the difference was using credibility, trust, pre-wiring, and coalition-building to convert being right into people acting.

Artifact example

An influence plan for a cross-team initiative — the artifact a principal engineer uses to convert a correct idea into adopted change.

# Influence plan: adopt a shared event-schema standard (4 teams)

## The change I need
4 teams adopt one event-schema standard (schema registry + conventions).
I have NO authority over them. Being right is ~1/3 of this.

## Credibility I'm drawing on
I shipped the error-format standard last year; it worked and teams liked it.
I'll reference that track record.

## Stakeholder map + pre-wiring order (most influential / most affected first)
| Person | Stance | Their pain (frame in THEIR terms) | Pre-wire plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lead A (most respected) | likely ally | integration bugs cost her team a day/week | 1-1 first; make her a co-sponsor |
| Lead B | neutral | schema drift broke his consumer twice | 1-1; show how standard prevents it |
| Lead C | likely skeptic | worried about migration cost | 1-1; incorporate his concern, offer help |
| Lead D | follower | will go with the group | reach last, once A/B/C aligned (coalition) |

## Framing (THEIR language, not mine)
NOT "we should have architectural consistency." INSTEAD "each of you is
losing time to integration bugs and schema drift; a shared standard + registry
makes those bugs impossible and I'll do the migration work with you."

## Coalition
Target: Leads A, B, C aligned privately BEFORE any public proposal. Then
propose publicly with 3 co-sponsors. D follows. Nobody is ambushed.

## What I give away
Credit to Lead A as co-sponsor. Offer to do the migration work for the
skeptical team. Trust is built by serving their interests, not just mine.

The plan's power is that it treats influence as a deliberate, planned activity: it names the credibility being drawn on, maps stakeholders by stance and their pain, sequences the pre-wiring most-influential-first, frames everything in the stakeholders' language rather than architectural ideals, and builds a coalition before going public. This is what converts a correct idea into adopted change — being right is assumed; the plan is about the other two-thirds.

Real-world scenario

A principal engineer is known for getting cross-team initiatives adopted at a far higher rate than his equally-talented peers. Colleagues assume he is more persuasive or more senior. The real difference is that he treats influence as a craft with a process, while they treat being right as sufficient. Before any cross-team proposal, he spends a week pre-wiring — one-on-one conversations with every person who could block or who is affected, always framing the proposal in terms of their pain, always starting with the most influential. By the time he proposes anything publicly, it already has a coalition of backers and every major objection has been privately resolved. His peers, in contrast, bring correct proposals cold to large meetings, where they get ambushed, picked apart, and die. Same correctness, same seniority; the difference is that he does the invisible two-thirds of influence (credibility, pre-wiring, coalitions) and they rely on the visible one-third (being right). Over years, this compounds: he is seen as the person who gets things done across teams, which itself builds credibility, which makes the next initiative easier. Influence is a flywheel, and he turns it deliberately.

Failure scenario

A brilliant engineer, correct about nearly everything, is consistently ignored and increasingly bitter. He has strong, well-reasoned opinions and delivers them forcefully, usually for the first time in a large meeting, in engineering language, to an audience that includes people who do not operate the systems. He treats disagreement as a failure of the other person to understand the obvious, so he argues harder, which makes people defensive, which makes them dig in. He never pre-wires, because he believes a correct argument should not need private lobbying. He takes all the credit for his ideas, so nobody feels a stake in them. He fights equally hard about formatting and about data-loss risks, so people have learned to discount everything he says. The result is a person who is right about the technical substance and has almost zero influence, watching less-correct but more-skilled colleagues shape the direction he wishes he could. His failure is believing the entire one-third (being right) is the whole thing, and neglecting the two-thirds (credibility management, trust, framing, timing, pre-wiring, coalitions) that actually move people. Being right is necessary and nowhere near sufficient, and an engineer who refuses to learn the rest caps their impact permanently, no matter how good their judgement.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Believing being right is sufficient. Correctness is ~1/3 of influence; relying on it alone produces a frustrated, ignored expert.
  • No pre-wiring. Bringing proposals cold to public forums, where they get ambushed and die.
  • Framing in your language, not theirs. Arguing architectural ideals to people who care about their own pain, revenue, or risk.
  • Taking all the credit. Nobody feels a stake in your ideas, and trust (the good-faith kind) never builds.
  • Fighting every point equally. If you argue as hard about trivia as about real risks, people discount everything you say.
  • Spending credibility recklessly. Pushing hard on too many things, or being wrong after being loud, depletes the capital you need for the important asks.

How a Principal Engineer thinks about this

They treat influence as a craft with learnable mechanics, not as charisma or seniority, and they internalise that being right is only about a third of it — the rest is credibility, trust, framing, timing, pre-wiring, and coalitions. They manage their credibility as capital: they spend it carefully on the asks that matter, they renew it by shipping and by being right about hard calls, and they protect it by not being loud about things they are unsure of. They build trust (the good-faith kind) deliberately by giving credit away and advocating for others' interests, because they know people go along with someone they trust even when unsure they are right.

They pre-wire as a reflex, never bringing a consequential proposal cold to a public forum, because they have watched too many correct ideas die in ambushes. They frame everything in the audience's language — the stakeholders' pain, the business's numbers — not in architectural ideals, because people act on their own concerns, not yours. And they are disciplined about which battles to fight, because they know that fighting trivia as hard as substance teaches people to discount them. The principal's distinctive skill is not being more right than others; it is doing the invisible two-thirds that turns being right into people acting.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on being right and neglecting the two-thirds of influence that actually moves people.
  • Never pre-wiring, so proposals are ambushed in public forums.
  • Framing in engineering ideals instead of the audience's pain and interests.
  • Hogging credit, so nobody has a stake in your ideas and trust never builds.
  • Fighting every point with equal force, teaching people to discount you.

Interview questions

  1. You're technically right about a cross-team problem but you're being ignored. What's going on and what do you do? Expected answer: being right is only ~1/3 of influence; you likely lack pre-wiring, coalition, and framing in the stakeholders' terms. Build credibility (track record), pre-wire the key people one-on-one framing it in their pain, incorporate objections to turn skeptics into supporters, and go public only with a coalition behind you. Why it matters: this is the core principal skill — converting correctness into action.

  2. What is the difference between credibility and trust, and why do both matter for influence? Expected answer: credibility is "your judgement is good" (earned by track record, shipping, admitting errors); trust is "you act in good faith" (earned by giving credit away, advocating others' interests, consistency). Both matter because people act on credibility (they believe you are right) and trust (they believe your intent is good), and trust carries you even when they are unsure you are right. Follow-up: how would you build trust with a team that is wary of you.

  3. Why do experienced influencers pre-wire instead of bringing proposals straight to a meeting? Expected answer: a cold proposal in a public forum invites ambush — affected people feel surprised and defend their territory with every objection, and the idea dies; pre-wiring resolves major objections privately (where nobody loses face), turns skeptics into supporters, and builds a coalition so the public proposal is a ratification, not a battle. Why it matters: tests the single most practical influence mechanic.

Practical exercise

Take a cross-team change you want to make but have no authority to mandate. Write the influence plan: the credibility you are drawing on, a stakeholder map (each person's stance and their pain in their terms), the pre-wiring order (most influential/affected first), the framing in the stakeholders' language rather than architectural ideals, and the coalition you will build before going public. Note what you will give away (credit, help) to build trust.

Acceptance criteria: your plan assumes being right is necessary but insufficient and focuses on the other two-thirds; it maps stakeholders by stance and frames the change in each one's actual pain or interest (not your architectural preference); it sequences pre-wiring to build a coalition before any public proposal; and it identifies concrete things you will give away (credit, migration help) to build the good-faith trust that carries influence.

56.2 Stakeholder mapping and communicating with executives

Concept

Two skills that determine whether your influence reaches the people who matter. Stakeholder mapping is working out, for any initiative, who decides, who is affected, and who can block — so you spend your influence effort on the right people rather than broadcasting equally to everyone. Communicating with executives is a distinct discipline: leading with the bottom line, keeping it to one page, and translating technical risk into business risk — because executives are time-poor, non-technical about details, and make decisions in terms of revenue, cost, risk, and time, not in terms of Kafka partitions.

Why does it exist?

Imagine spending your influence effort evenly across twenty people when, in reality, one person decides, two can block, and the other seventeen are merely affected. You exhaust yourself and the initiative stalls because you under-invested in the decider and the blockers while over-investing in people who were never going to determine the outcome. Stakeholder mapping exists to direct your finite influence effort where it actually changes the result.

Now imagine explaining to a CFO, in a dense technical memo full of latency percentiles and database internals, why a reliability investment matters. The CFO cannot act on it — it is in a language they do not speak, at a length they will not read, framed in terms (p99 latency) they do not value. Executive communication exists because the people who control funding and priority are reached only through a specific style: bottom line first, one page, business terms. An engineer who cannot translate into that style is locked out of the decisions that matter most.

Mental model

For stakeholder mapping, imagine a battlefield commander deciding where to commit limited forces. They do not spread troops evenly across the whole map; they identify the decisive points — the hill that controls the valley, the bridge the enemy must cross — and concentrate force there. Stakeholder mapping is identifying the decisive people (the decider, the blockers) and concentrating your influence there, rather than spreading it thin across everyone.

For executive communication, imagine a news article. It does not build to a conclusion like an essay; it puts the most important thing in the headline and the first sentence (the "inverted pyramid"), because readers may stop at any point and the editor may cut from the bottom. Executive communication is the inverted pyramid: the bottom line (the ask and the why) goes first, because the executive may read only the first few lines, and everything after is supporting detail for those who want it.

How it works

Stakeholder mapping. For any initiative, classify the people involved:

- Decider(s):    who actually makes the call. Often one person. Invest heavily.
- Blockers:      who can stop it (by authority, by owning a resource, by
                 influence). Pre-wire these especially — a blocker who
                 feels ambushed will block.
- Affected:      who is impacted by the change. Keep informed; address their
                 concerns, but they do not decide.
- Influencers:   who the decider listens to. Winning them wins the decider
                 indirectly. Often more reachable than the decider.

A common map is a grid of influence (high/low) by stance (for/against):

flowchart TB
    subgraph HighInfluence["High influence"]
        A["Supporter - make them a champion / co-sponsor"]
        B["Opponent/blocker - pre-wire, address concerns, convert or neutralise"]
    end
    subgraph LowInfluence["Low influence"]
        C["Supporter - keep as backup voice"]
        D["Opponent - monitor, don't over-invest"]
    end

You invest most in the high-influence quadrants: turn high-influence supporters into champions, and pre-wire high-influence opponents to convert or neutralise them. You do not waste effort on low-influence opponents.

Communicating with executives — three rules:

  1. Bottom line up front (BLUF). Start with the conclusion and the ask: "We need to invest two quarters in payment reliability to stop losing an estimated $45k per outage hour; we've had three such outages this quarter." The executive gets the whole point in the first two sentences. Detail follows for those who want it.

  2. One page. Executives are time-poor. A one-page update that is read beats a ten-page memo that is skimmed. If it must be longer, the one-page summary stands alone at the top.

  3. Translate technical risk into business risk. This is the crucial skill. Executives do not value "p99 latency is 820ms" or "we have a dual-write consistency risk"; they value what it means in their terms: revenue at risk, cost, customer churn, regulatory/legal exposure, competitive position, delivery speed. Every technical point must be translated:

Technical statement          ->  Business translation (what the exec hears)
"Our p99 checkout is 820ms"  ->  "Slow checkout costs us ~2% of conversions,
                                 ~$X/month in lost orders."
"We have a dual-write risk"  ->  "There's a risk of silently losing order
                                 data, which would mean refunds, support
                                 cost, and trust damage."
"The DB is at 70% CPU"       ->  "We're one traffic spike from a checkout
                                 outage during peak season — ~$45k/hour."
"Tech debt in the order mod" ->  "Every order feature now takes 3x longer,
                                 slowing our roadmap by ~a quarter/year."

Practical example

A principal engineer wants funding for a reliability program after three payment outages. Stakeholder mapping: the decider is the VP of Engineering (who controls headcount) with sign-off from the CFO (who controls budget); the blockers are the product VP (who would lose feature capacity to the reliability work) and the finance partner; the influencer is the VP of Engineering's trusted staff engineer. She pre-wires the product VP first (the most likely blocker), framing the reliability work not as "stop features" but as "protect the revenue features generate" — converting a blocker into a neutral party. She wins the influencer. Then she presents to the decider with a one-page, BLUF, business-translated case: "Three payment outages this quarter cost an estimated $X in lost orders and support; a two-quarter reliability program costs Y and reduces that risk by Z; ROI positive in N months." The VP and CFO, seeing the business case in their language with the blocker already neutralised, approve. The mapping directed her effort to the decider and blocker; the executive communication made the case in terms they could act on. (Full business case in 56.3.)

Artifact example

A one-page executive update — the artifact that reaches the people who control funding and priority.

# Payment reliability: funding request (1 page, for VP Eng + CFO)

## BOTTOM LINE (read this if nothing else)
We've had 3 payment outages this quarter, costing an estimated $340k in lost
orders and support. A 2-quarter reliability program (2 engineers) would cut
this risk by ~80%. Cost: ~$180k. It pays for itself after the next ~1.5
outages we prevent. ASK: approve 2 engineers for 2 quarters.

## The business risk (in your terms)
- Each payment-outage hour costs ~$45k in lost orders + churn + support.
- We've had 3 outages (7 hours total) this quarter. Trend is worsening as
  traffic grows into peak season.
- Root cause is structural (shared payments DB + retry storms), so it will
  recur and worsen without investment — this is not bad luck.

## What the program does (one line each)
1. Give payments its own database -> removes the single point of failure.
2. Ship a resilience library (timeouts, backoff, circuit breaker) -> ends
   the retry storms that turn one slow dependency into a full outage.
3. Add the two alerts that would have caught all 3 outages early.

## The numbers
| | Cost | Benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Do nothing | $0 now | ~$680k+ expected outage cost next 2 quarters (worsening) |
| The program | ~$180k (2 eng, 2 qtrs) | ~80% risk reduction; ~$540k expected loss avoided |
-> ROI positive after ~1.5 prevented outages.

## What we're NOT asking for
Not a rewrite. Not new technology. Not pausing the roadmap — 2 engineers,
targeted. The other teams keep shipping features.

The update's power is entirely in its form: BLUF (the whole case in the first paragraph), one page, and every technical point translated to business terms (outages in dollars, the fix in risk reduction, the decision as an ROI table).
