And they plan data residency into the architecture early — usually via regional deployments and tenant-to-region routing (silo or regional-pool, 58.1) — because residency is extremely hard to retrofit into a global shared pool. The senior engineer understands that enterprise features are where the architecture meets the sales motion: they are the technical prerequisites that unlock the largest deals, so building them well and proactively is a strategic investment, not a reactive scramble.

Common mistakes

  • Not building enterprise features when pursuing enterprise deals, so deals die in security review.
  • A single global SSO config instead of per-tenant IdP configuration.
  • SCIM that doesn't deprovision immediately, leaving departed employees with access.
  • Customer-readable audit logs that leak across tenants (not tenant-scoped), which is itself a breach.
  • Treating data residency as an afterthought, then finding it near-impossible to retrofit into a global pool.

Interview questions

  1. What enterprise B2B features gate enterprise SaaS deals, and why? Expected answer: SSO (SAML/OIDC, so the enterprise controls authentication via its own IdP), SCIM (automated provisioning/deprovisioning, so offboarding is immediate), customer-readable audit logs (so the customer's security team can audit their tenant), IP allowlists (restrict access to the corporate network), and data residency (data in the required region). They gate deals because enterprise security reviews treat them as non-negotiable requirements — a single unmet one kills the deal. Why it matters: these are the technical prerequisites for enterprise revenue.

  2. Why must SSO be per-tenant and SCIM deprovisioning immediate? Expected answer: each enterprise tenant uses its own identity provider, so a single global SSO config cannot serve them — SSO must be configurable per tenant. SCIM deprovisioning must revoke access immediately because a departed employee retaining access is a serious security gap that the enterprise's offboarding process depends on closing automatically. Why it matters: tests understanding of the enterprise security model.

  3. Why is data residency hard to retrofit, and how do you architect for it? Expected answer: residency requires a tenant's data to live (and often be processed) in a specific region, which is incompatible with a single global shared pool; retrofitting it means re-architecting to regional deployments and tenant-to-region routing, often via silo or regional-pool models. So you architect for it early — regional deployments, tenant-region mapping, routing — rather than trying to add it to a global pool later. Why it matters: tests whether they plan residency into the architecture proactively.

Practical exercise

Design the enterprise feature set for a SaaS moving upmarket. Specify how you would implement per-tenant SSO (SAML/OIDC with per-tenant IdP config), SCIM provisioning/deprovisioning (with immediate access revocation), a customer-readable audit log (tenant-scoped via RLS, comprehensive), IP allowlists (per-tenant config), and data residency (regional deployments and tenant-to-region routing). Identify which of these are the largest engineering investments and must be started earliest.

Acceptance criteria: SSO is per-tenant (each enterprise configures its own IdP); SCIM deprovisioning revokes access immediately; the audit log is strictly tenant-scoped (RLS) and readable by the customer; IP allowlists are per-tenant; data residency is architected via regional deployments and routing (not retrofitted into a global pool); and you identify SSO, SCIM, and residency as substantial investments to build proactively rather than reactively in a sales cycle.

58.7 Compliance-driven architecture, integration patterns, and tenant lifecycle

Concept

Three topics that complete the enterprise SaaS picture. Compliance-driven architecture is how regulations shape your system design: GDPR (right to erasure, data export/portability), PCI DSS (reducing the scope of systems that touch card data), SOC 2 (controls and auditability), and HIPAA (protected health information) each impose concrete architectural requirements. Enterprise integration patterns are how customers integrate your SaaS with their systems: webhooks (you notify them of events), connectors, batch import/export, and idempotent bulk APIs. Tenant lifecycle is the full arc of a tenant: onboarding, migrating between tiers/models, and offboarding including data deletion. Each turns an external requirement (regulation, integration need, lifecycle event) into concrete architecture.

Why does it exist?

Imagine ignoring compliance until an enterprise or regulator demands it. A GDPR erasure request arrives (a user exercising their right to be forgotten) and you discover your architecture cannot actually delete all of a person's data — it is scattered across tables, caches, logs, backups, and a data warehouse, with no mechanism to find and remove it all. Or a PCI audit finds that card data flows through dozens of your services, putting all of them in PCI scope (hugely expensive to audit). Or an enterprise wants to integrate your SaaS with their system and you have no webhooks or bulk API, so integration is impossible. Or a tenant churns and you have no clean way to delete their data, leaving it lingering (a liability and a compliance violation).

These architectural concerns exist because external requirements — regulations, integration needs, lifecycle events — must be designed into the system, not bolted on. GDPR erasure must be an architectural capability (knowing where all of a person's data is and being able to delete it). PCI scope reduction must be a design decision (isolating card handling so most systems never touch it). Integration must be a built capability (webhooks, bulk APIs). Tenant deletion must be a designed process. Retrofitting any of these is painful or impossible, so they shape the architecture from the start.

Mental model

Imagine building a house that must meet building codes (compliance), connect to utilities (integration), and allow residents to move in and out cleanly (lifecycle). You do not build the house and then try to add fire exits, plumbing connections, and a way to move furniture out — you design the house around these requirements from the start, because retrofitting a fire exit into a finished house is far harder than building it in. Compliance, integration, and lifecycle are the building codes, utility connections, and move-in/move-out design of a SaaS: external requirements that must shape the architecture from the beginning, because they are extremely hard to retrofit into a finished system.

How it works

Compliance-driven architecture:

GDPR:
  - Right to erasure: you must be able to find and delete ALL of a person's
    data on request — across tables, caches, search indexes, backups, warehouse.
    Architect: a data map (what personal data lives where) + a deletion pipeline.
  - Data export/portability: provide a person's data in a portable format.
  - Consent + purpose: track lawful basis for processing.
PCI DSS (card data):
  - Scope reduction: minimise systems that touch card data. Use a payment
    provider (tokenisation) so YOUR systems store a token, never the card.
    This takes most of your systems OUT of PCI scope — the key design move.
SOC 2:
  - Controls + auditability: access controls, change management, monitoring,
    audit logs (58.6). Architect for evidence — the audit trail IS the control.
HIPAA (health data / PHI):
  - Access controls, encryption, audit logging, BAAs with subprocessors.
    Isolate PHI, log all access, encrypt at rest and in transit.

The recurring pattern: isolation and minimisation. Isolate the regulated data (card data, PHI, personal data) so that most of your system is out of scope, and minimise what you store. PCI scope reduction via tokenisation is the exemplar: by never storing card data (letting a provider tokenise it), you take almost all your systems out of PCI scope, turning a crushing audit burden into a small one.

Enterprise integration patterns:

  • Webhooks: you notify the customer's system of events (order created, status changed) by POSTing to their endpoint — with retries, signatures (so they trust it is you), and idempotency (so a retried webhook is safe).
  • Connectors: pre-built integrations with common systems the customer uses.
  • Batch import/export: bulk data in/out, for migration and reporting.
  • Idempotent bulk APIs: APIs for creating/updating many records at once, with idempotency keys so a retried bulk operation does not duplicate — critical because bulk operations are big and retries are common.

Tenant lifecycle:

  • Onboarding: provisioning a new tenant (create their data space, apply their plan, set up SSO if enterprise), fast and automated.
  • Migrating between tiers/models: upgrading a tenant from pool to silo (58.1), or changing plans — a data migration (Part 54 techniques).
  • Offboarding and data deletion: when a tenant leaves, delete their data cleanly (across all stores), per contract and compliance (GDPR), with a grace period and confirmation. Lingering data of a departed tenant is a liability and a compliance violation.
flowchart LR
    ON["Onboard: provision tenant, plan, SSO"] --> ACTIVE["Active tenant"]
    ACTIVE --> MIG["Migrate: plan change, pool->silo"]
    MIG --> ACTIVE
    ACTIVE --> OFF["Offboard: delete ALL data across stores (grace period)"]
    ACTIVE -.->|"GDPR erasure (per-person)"| DEL["Deletion pipeline across all data stores"]

NestJS example

An idempotent bulk API and an outbound webhook with retries and signing:

// Idempotent bulk create: a retried bulk operation must not duplicate.
import { Controller, Post, Body, Headers, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('bulk/products')
export class BulkProductController {
  constructor(private readonly svc: ProductBulkService) {}

  @Post()
  async bulkCreate(
    @Body() items: CreateProductDto[],
    @Headers('idempotency-key') key: string,   // caller-supplied; required
  ) {
    if (!key) throw new ConflictException('Idempotency-Key required for bulk ops');
    // If this key was seen, return the stored result (don't re-execute) — so a
    // client retry of a 5,000-item import doesn't create 10,000 products.
    return this.svc.bulkCreateIdempotent(key, items);  // tenant-scoped (RLS)
  }
}
// Outbound webhook: notify the customer's system, signed + retried + idempotent.
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { createHmac } from 'crypto';

@Injectable()
export class WebhookDispatcher {
  async dispatch(tenantId: string, event: object, url: string, secret: string) {
    const body = JSON.stringify(event);
    // Sign so the customer can verify it's genuinely from us.
    const signature = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(body).digest('hex');
    // Deliver via a durable queue with retries + backoff (not inline), and an
    // event id so the customer can dedupe a retried delivery (idempotency).
    await this.enqueueDelivery({ url, body, signature, eventId: /* uuid */ '', tenantId });
  }
  private async enqueueDelivery(_: any) { /* BullMQ with retry/backoff */ }
}

PostgreSQL example

A data map for GDPR erasure and a deletion approach, plus PCI scope reduction via tokenisation:

-- PCI scope reduction: store a TOKEN from the payment provider, NEVER the card.
-- This keeps the card data out of your database -> out of PCI scope.
CREATE TABLE payment_methods (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id   UUID NOT NULL,
  customer_id UUID NOT NULL,
  provider_token TEXT NOT NULL,     -- e.g. Stripe token; NOT a card number
  last4       TEXT                  -- safe to store for display
);
-- No PAN, no CVV, no expiry stored. The provider holds the card; we hold a token.

-- GDPR erasure: you need to know every place a person's data lives.
-- A deletion pipeline (app-orchestrated) must cover ALL of these:
--   app tables (orders, users, audit where it contains personal data),
--   caches (Redis), search indexes, the data warehouse, and backups (per policy).
-- Example of the app-table deletions (run in a transaction, tenant-scoped):
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1);
DELETE FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1;
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = $1;
-- Then: purge from Redis, remove from the search index, propagate deletion to
-- the warehouse (Part 63), and handle backups per your documented policy.

Production scenario

A SaaS handling payments reduced its PCI scope by using a payment provider's tokenisation: card data is entered directly into the provider's hosted field (never touching the SaaS servers), and the SaaS stores only a token. As a result, the vast majority of the SaaS's systems are out of PCI scope — the PCI audit covers only the small, isolated payment-token-handling path, turning what could have been a crushing, expensive, whole-system audit into a manageable one. Separately, when a GDPR erasure request arrives, the SaaS's deletion pipeline — built from a data map of where personal data lives — removes the person's data from the app database, Redis cache, search index, and propagates the deletion to the warehouse, completing a defensible erasure. And when a tenant offboards, an automated deletion process removes all their data across every store after a grace period, leaving no lingering liability. Each of these is compliance designed into the architecture: PCI scope reduction via tokenisation, GDPR erasure via a data map and deletion pipeline, tenant offboarding via a deletion process. The architecture satisfies the regulations because it was built to, not bolted on after an audit failure.

Failure scenario

A SaaS stores card data directly in its own database (PANs, encrypted) across its order and payment services, reasoning it is simpler than integrating a provider's tokenisation. When it pursues enterprise deals requiring PCI compliance, the audit scope is catastrophic: because card data flows through and is stored across many services, all of those services are in PCI scope, meaning every one must meet the full PCI DSS requirements (access controls, encryption, logging, segmentation, regular audits) — an enormous, ongoing, expensive burden. The audit is costly, the remediation (securing dozens of in-scope systems) is huge, and the ongoing compliance overhead drags on every release to those services. Compare the tokenisation approach, which would have kept card data out of the SaaS entirely, leaving only a tiny isolated path in scope. The root cause is storing regulated data (card numbers) throughout the system instead of isolating and minimising it — the opposite of PCI scope reduction. The SaaS pays, in audit cost and ongoing overhead, for having designed card handling into the heart of the system rather than isolating it to a minimal, tokenised path. The lesson: for regulated data (card data, PHI, personal data), the architectural goal is isolation and minimisation — keep the regulated data out of (or minimally within) your systems, so most of the system is out of compliance scope. Designing regulated data throughout the system turns compliance from a small bounded cost into a crushing system-wide one.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Storing card data throughout the system instead of tokenising, putting everything in PCI scope — a crushing, expensive audit burden.
  • No data map for GDPR erasure. You cannot find all of a person's data, so you cannot defensibly delete it (across caches, indexes, warehouse, backups).
  • Deletion that misses stores. Deleting from the app database but leaving data in Redis, the search index, or the warehouse — an incomplete erasure that violates GDPR.
  • Bulk APIs without idempotency. A retried bulk import duplicates thousands of records.
  • Webhooks without signing/retries/idempotency. The customer can't verify they're from you, deliveries are lost on transient failures, or retries cause duplicate processing.
  • Tenant offboarding that leaves data lingering. A departed tenant's data remaining is a liability and a compliance violation; offboarding must delete across all stores.
  • Compliance bolted on after an audit failure, when it should have shaped the architecture from the start.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They design compliance into the architecture from the start, treating regulations as architectural requirements rather than paperwork, because they know retrofitting compliance after an audit failure is painful or impossible. Their recurring strategy for regulated data (card data, PHI, personal data) is isolation and minimisation: keep the regulated data out of (or minimally within) their systems so most of the system is out of scope — the PCI tokenisation move being the exemplar, turning a system-wide audit burden into a tiny isolated one. For GDPR, they maintain a data map of where personal data lives and build a deletion pipeline that covers all stores (database, caches, indexes, warehouse, backups), because an erasure that misses a store is not a defensible erasure.

They build enterprise integration as real capabilities — webhooks that are signed, retried, and idempotent; bulk APIs that are idempotent (so a retried big import does not duplicate) — because they know customers integrate at scale and retries are inevitable. And they treat tenant lifecycle as a designed process, especially offboarding, ensuring a departed tenant's data is deleted across every store, because lingering data is both a liability and a compliance violation. The senior engineer understands that compliance, integration, and lifecycle are external requirements that must shape the architecture early, and that the unifying principle for regulated data — isolate and minimise — is what keeps compliance a bounded cost rather than a crushing system-wide one.

Common mistakes

  • Storing regulated data (card data, PHI) throughout the system instead of isolating and minimising it, exploding compliance scope.
  • No data map or deletion pipeline for GDPR erasure, so you cannot defensibly delete all of a person's data.
  • Incomplete deletion that misses caches, indexes, the warehouse, or backups.
  • Bulk APIs and webhooks without idempotency, causing duplicates on inevitable retries.
  • Tenant offboarding that leaves data lingering, a liability and compliance violation.

Interview questions

  1. How does PCI DSS scope reduction work, and why is it the key design move for card data? Expected answer: use a payment provider's tokenisation so card data is entered directly into the provider (never touching your servers) and you store only a token — which keeps card data out of your systems and takes almost all of them out of PCI scope, turning a crushing system-wide audit into a tiny isolated one. The principle is isolate and minimise regulated data. Why it matters: this is the exemplar of compliance-driven architecture.

  2. What does GDPR's right to erasure require architecturally? Expected answer: the ability to find and delete all of a person's data on request — which requires a data map (what personal data lives where: app tables, caches, search indexes, warehouse, backups) and a deletion pipeline that removes it from every store. An erasure that misses a store (e.g. leaves data in the warehouse or search index) is not a defensible erasure. Why it matters: tests whether they design erasure as an architectural capability.

  3. How do you design enterprise integration (webhooks, bulk APIs) to be robust? Expected answer: webhooks should be signed (so the customer can verify they're from you), delivered via a durable queue with retries and backoff (so transient failures don't lose events), and carry an event id for idempotency (so a retried delivery is deduped); bulk APIs should require idempotency keys so a retried large import doesn't duplicate thousands of records. Retries are inevitable at integration scale, so idempotency is essential. Why it matters: tests understanding of integration robustness.

Practical exercise

Design the compliance, integration, and lifecycle architecture for a multi-tenant SaaS. For compliance: describe your PCI scope-reduction approach (tokenisation), your GDPR data map and deletion pipeline (covering all stores), and the SOC 2 controls (audit logging). For integration: design a signed, retried, idempotent webhook delivery and an idempotent bulk API. For lifecycle: design tenant offboarding with complete data deletion across all stores after a grace period.

Acceptance criteria: your card-data handling isolates and minimises (tokenisation keeps card data out of your systems and out of PCI scope); your GDPR erasure is backed by a data map and a deletion pipeline covering all stores (not just the app database); your webhooks are signed, retried, and idempotent, and your bulk API is idempotent; and your tenant offboarding deletes all tenant data across every store after a grace period, leaving no lingering liability — demonstrating that compliance, integration, and lifecycle are designed into the architecture, not bolted on.

58.8 Worked example: turning a single-tenant inventory product into a multi-tenant SaaS

This section brings the whole Part together: converting a single-tenant inventory management product into a multi-tenant SaaS. It is the canonical "make it multi-tenant" problem, and it exercises every concept in this Part — the tenancy model, RLS isolation, tenant context, noisy-neighbour control, entitlements, enterprise features, compliance, and lifecycle.

The starting point

InventoryCo built a NestJS/PostgreSQL inventory product for a single company: products, stock levels, suppliers, orders. It works well for one organisation. Now they want to sell it as a SaaS to many companies. The naive approach — deploy a separate copy per customer — does not scale (it is the all-silo trap, 58.1). They need true multi-tenancy. Here is the conversion, step by step.

Step 1: Choose the tenancy model (58.1)

They expect many small-to-medium businesses plus some larger enterprises. So they choose a mixed model: pool (shared schema with tenant_id) for the many SMB tenants (dense, cheap), with the ability to silo (dedicated database) an enterprise tenant who needs isolation or residency. The bulk of the work is making the pool model safe.

Step 2: Add tenant_id and row-level security (58.2)

Every tenant-scoped table gets a tenant_id column, a tenant-first index, and row-level security:

ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN tenant_id UUID NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX products_tenant_idx ON products (tenant_id, sku);
ALTER TABLE products ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE products FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON products
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant')::uuid);
-- Repeat for stock_levels, suppliers, orders, every tenant-scoped table.
-- A migration check (fitness function, Part 53.5) enforces RLS on every new table.

RLS makes isolation a database-enforced invariant — even a query that forgets the tenant filter returns only the right tenant's rows. This is the single most important safety mechanism of the conversion.

Step 3: Add the tenant context (58.3)

A tenancy guard resolves the tenant from the authenticated user (validated), stores it in AsyncLocalStorage, and an interceptor sets the RLS session variable per request:

// Per request: guard validates tenant -> AsyncLocalStorage -> RLS session var.
// Every service reads getTenantId() automatically; no manual threading.
// Background jobs carry tenantId in their payload and re-establish the context.

Now feature code does not have to think about tenancy — the context plus RLS handle it, so isolation holds across every code path without each one getting it right.

Step 4: Noisy-neighbour control (58.4)

Per-tenant rate limits (Redis, keyed by tenant), per-tenant fair queuing for the stock-reconciliation background jobs, and statement timeouts on the database — so one tenant's heavy batch import cannot degrade other tenants.

Step 5: Plans, entitlements, billing (58.5)

A plan-to-entitlements mapping (free: basic inventory; pro: + advanced reporting and API; enterprise: + SSO and audit export), checked through a centralised entitlement guard. Per-tenant config for branding and settings. Billing hooks via verified webhooks, graceful payment-status enforcement, and usage metering.

Step 6: Enterprise features for the enterprise tier (58.6)

Per-tenant SSO (SAML/OIDC), SCIM provisioning/deprovisioning, a tenant-scoped customer-readable audit log, IP allowlists, and — for enterprise tenants needing it — data residency via a regional silo. These unlock the enterprise deals.

Step 7: Compliance and lifecycle (58.7)

PCI scope reduction via payment-provider tokenisation (card data never touches InventoryCo's systems). A GDPR data map and deletion pipeline covering all stores. Tenant onboarding automated (provision tenant, apply plan). Tenant offboarding deletes all tenant data across every store after a grace period.

The architecture, assembled

flowchart TB
    REQ["Request"] --> AUTH["Auth (JWT / per-tenant SSO)"]
    AUTH --> TG["Tenancy guard: resolve + validate tenant -> context"]
    TG --> RL["Per-tenant rate limit"]
    RL --> ENT["Entitlement guard (plan-based)"]
    ENT --> IPL["IP allowlist (enterprise)"]
    IPL --> RLSI["Interceptor sets RLS session var"]
    RLSI --> H["Handler: queries RLS-scoped to tenant"]
    H --> PG[("Pooled PostgreSQL: RLS per table")]
    H -.->|"enterprise tenant"| SILO[("Silo DB, regional for residency")]
    H --> AUDIT["Tenant-scoped audit log"]

Why this conversion works

Trace it against the Part. The tenancy model is a deliberate mix — pool for density, silo for demanding tenants (58.1). Isolation is enforced by the database via RLS, not by fragile application discipline (58.2). The tenant context makes correct tenancy the transparent default across all code paths (58.3). Noisy-neighbour control preserves fairness so one tenant cannot harm another (58.4). Plans and entitlements make the product monetizable and differentiated (58.5). Enterprise features unlock enterprise revenue (58.6). Compliance is designed in — PCI scope reduced via tokenisation, GDPR erasure via a data map and deletion pipeline (58.7). And the tenant lifecycle, including clean offboarding deletion, is a designed process (58.7). Each piece addresses a specific requirement of a real multi-tenant SaaS, and the whole hangs together around the first requirement: tenant isolation, enforced in depth (application context + database RLS), because a single isolation failure is a breach that can end the business. The naive "copy per customer" approach would have failed on economics; a pool-without-RLS approach would have risked a breach; this layered architecture delivers density, safety, monetisation, enterprise-readiness, and compliance together — which is what a real multi-tenant SaaS requires.

Practical exercise

Take a single-tenant application (yours, or InventoryCo) and design its conversion to a multi-tenant SaaS using every concept in this Part. Choose the tenancy model (likely a mix); add tenant_id and RLS to every tenant-scoped table; design the tenant context (guard, AsyncLocalStorage, RLS session variable, background-job handling); add noisy-neighbour controls; design plans/entitlements/billing; specify the enterprise features for the enterprise tier; and design compliance (PCI scope reduction, GDPR deletion pipeline) and tenant lifecycle (onboarding, offboarding deletion).

Acceptance criteria: the tenancy model is justified by the tenant mix (pool for density, silo for demanding tenants); every tenant-scoped table has RLS enforcing isolation at the database (fail-closed), not just application filtering; the tenant context makes tenancy transparent to feature code and handles async boundaries; noisy-neighbour controls are per-tenant; entitlements are centralised and plan-derived; enterprise features (per-tenant SSO, SCIM, tenant-scoped audit log, residency) are specified for the enterprise tier; and compliance (PCI tokenisation, GDPR deletion across all stores) and tenant offboarding (complete deletion) are designed in. The whole design centres on tenant isolation enforced in depth, because a single isolation failure is a breach.

58.9 A quick-reference for multi-tenant SaaS architecture

A compact reference distilling the Part into the decisions and checks that matter most when you design or review a multi-tenant SaaS — anchored on the first requirement, tenant isolation.

The tenancy-model decision

Many small, cost-sensitive tenants     -> POOL (shared schema + tenant_id + RLS)
Few large tenants needing isolation    -> SILO (database-per-tenant, maybe regional)
Dozens-hundreds, moderate isolation    -> BRIDGE (schema-per-tenant)
A real mix (SMBs + enterprise)         -> MIXED (pool for the many, silo for the few)

The isolation checklist (the first requirement — get this right)

[ ] Is isolation enforced at the DATABASE (RLS), not just application filtering?
[ ] Does RLS FAIL CLOSED (no tenant context -> no rows, never all rows)?
[ ] Is RLS FORCED (owner doesn't bypass) with WITH CHECK (no cross-tenant writes)?
[ ] Is the session variable set on the SAME connection the queries run on?
[ ] Is the tenant resolved + VALIDATED once (guard), in AsyncLocalStorage, not
    threaded manually (which fails at async boundaries)?
[ ] Do background jobs carry the tenant explicitly and re-establish the context?
[ ] Does every NEW tenant-scoped table get RLS (enforced by a migration check)?

The rest of the multi-tenant checklist

[ ] Noisy neighbours: PER-TENANT (not global) rate limits, quotas, fair queuing?
[ ] Entitlements CENTRALISED and plan-derived (not scattered plan-name checks)?
[ ] Billing hooks safe (verified webhooks, graceful payment enforcement, reliable
    metering)?
[ ] Enterprise features built PROACTIVELY (per-tenant SSO, SCIM, tenant-scoped
    audit logs, IP allowlists) if selling to enterprise?
[ ] Data residency architected via regional deployments (not retrofitted)?
[ ] Compliance designed in: PCI scope reduced via tokenisation; GDPR erasure via
    a data map + deletion pipeline covering ALL stores?
[ ] Integration robust: signed/retried/idempotent webhooks; idempotent bulk APIs?
[ ] Tenant offboarding deletes ALL tenant data across every store?

The enduring principle

The whole Part reduces to one non-negotiable: tenant isolation is the first requirement, and a single isolation failure is a breach, not a bug. So isolation is enforced in depth — the application resolves and validates the tenant (context) and the database enforces it regardless (RLS, fail-closed) — because relying on application discipline alone is a bet that eventually loses. Everything else — the tenancy model, noisy-neighbour fairness, entitlements, enterprise features, compliance, lifecycle — is built on and around that isolation foundation. When you design or review a multi-tenant system, start with the question that matters most: can tenant A ever, under any failure, see tenant B's data — and is the architecture built so the answer is no even when the application code is wrong? Get that right, and the rest is engineering; get it wrong, and nothing else matters.

Return to this reference when designing or reviewing a multi-tenant SaaS; the reasoning behind each line is in the sections above.

Senior Checklist — Part 58

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can choose a multi-tenancy model (silo/pool/bridge, or a mix) based on tenant mix and isolation needs
  • I enforce tenant isolation at the database with row-level security, failing closed, not just in application code
  • I implement a tenant context (guard + AsyncLocalStorage + RLS session variable) that handles async boundaries
  • I prevent noisy neighbours with per-tenant rate limits, quotas, and fair queuing
  • I centralise feature entitlements derived from plans, and handle billing hooks safely
  • I can build the enterprise features (per-tenant SSO, SCIM, tenant-scoped audit logs, IP allowlists) that gate enterprise deals
  • I architect data residency via regional deployments rather than retrofitting it into a global pool
  • I design compliance in: PCI scope reduction via tokenisation, GDPR erasure via a data map and deletion pipeline
  • I build enterprise integration (signed/retried/idempotent webhooks, idempotent bulk APIs)
  • I design the full tenant lifecycle, including clean offboarding with complete data deletion

Part 58 — Key Takeaways

  • The first requirement of a multi-tenant SaaS is tenant isolation; a single isolation failure is not a normal bug but a breach that can end customer relationships and trigger legal consequences.
  • Choose the tenancy model (silo, pool, bridge) by tenant mix and isolation needs; a mature SaaS usually runs a mix — pool for the dense many small tenants, silo for the few demanding enterprise ones — because all-silo is unviable at scale and all-pool cannot satisfy strict isolation.
  • In a pooled model, enforce isolation at the database with PostgreSQL row-level security, so even a query that forgets the tenant filter returns only the right tenant's rows; relying on application discipline alone is a bet that eventually loses.
  • Design isolation to fail closed: no tenant context means no access, never all access.
  • Implement a tenant context (guard + AsyncLocalStorage + RLS session variable) so tenancy is transparent to feature code, and handle async boundaries (background jobs) explicitly, since context does not auto-propagate.
  • Prevent noisy neighbours with per-tenant (not global) rate limits, quotas, and fair queuing, because in shared infrastructure one tenant's behaviour is a threat to all the others.
  • Centralise feature entitlements derived from plans rather than scattering plan-name checks, so a plan change is a single data change; handle billing hooks safely (verified webhooks, graceful payment enforcement, reliable metering).
  • Enterprise features — per-tenant SSO (SAML/OIDC), SCIM provisioning, tenant-scoped customer-readable audit logs, IP allowlists, data residency — gate enterprise revenue and must be built proactively, as they are substantial projects, not sales-cycle add-ons.
  • Design compliance into the architecture: the principle for regulated data (card data, PHI, personal data) is isolate and minimise — PCI scope reduction via tokenisation, GDPR erasure via a data map and a deletion pipeline covering all stores.
  • Build enterprise integration as real capabilities: signed, retried, idempotent webhooks and idempotent bulk APIs, because customers integrate at scale and retries are inevitable.
  • Design the full tenant lifecycle, especially offboarding with complete data deletion across every store, because a departed tenant's lingering data is a liability and a compliance violation.
